TITLE: Invitation to Participate – Virtual Capacity Building Workshop on Infodemic Management | 5th -6th July, 2022

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The COVID-19 pandemic has produced one of the unprecedented relationships between public health issues and media reportage. Accordingly, a key highlight which was underscored within this unexpected pandemic period is the infodemics churned out in the various media cycles. Infodemics is defined by the World Health Organization as an influx of information, some true, some not, that makes it difficult for people to identify trustworthy sources and dependable guidance when they need it, and which comprises outbreak response and information on a disease, its spread, and prevention. At the early stage of the COVID-19 pandemic, the information widely disseminated both online and offline were mostly devoid of proof because of the novelty of the virus, and it has been a gargantuan task to correct and demystify public information based on perception, beliefs and other non-scientific evidence about the virus.

As Science Journalists, interpreting the science and facts behind pandemics and infectious diseases for the public offers several challenges owing to difficulty in assessing high-quality and reliable information, collaborating with the credible sources (scientists and researchers) to

communicate and share their discoveries, as well as the emergence of digital platforms and social media platforms that allow anybody to publish information without any proof. To keep everyone safe and aid in the fight against pandemics, we must first combat infodemics.

This two-day virtual workshop, organized by The COVID-19 Diary programme, will focus on how science journalists, health journalists, communicators, higher education communities, and policymakers can engage with scientists and researchers to combat infodemics and infectious diseases, as well as create and implement strategies and solutions to this problem.

ABOUT THE COVID-19 DIARY

The COVID-19 Diary aims to build on the existing Association of African Universities Television (AAU TV) initiative to promote science engagement in Africa by strengthening collaborations between science journalists, health journalists, communicators, higher education communities, researchers, policymakers, and the general public. Its ultimate goal is to create credible and effective scientific communication narratives and media products on emerging infectious diseases like COVID-19.

AIM – To promote capacity building among African science journalists in the management of infodemics and pandemics.

OBJECTIVES

• Identify the roles of scientists, researchers, and science journalists in the fight against pandemics.

• Develop methods for evaluating and assessing trustworthy and high-quality information on digital platforms.

• Examine strategies for combating and managing with infodemics, as well as pandemic challenges.

• Develop strategies in promoting health literacy in the public and engaging them during pandemics.

EXPECTED OUTCOME

Participants should be able to do the following after the workshop:

• Distinguish between scientifically credible information and fake information on digital platforms.

• Discover the best methods for locating the top information sources, experts, specialists, and professionals.

• Adequately interpret scientific concept, facts, and numbers in context for public understanding.

• Apply the knowledge acquired from this workshop to assist in disseminating factual information on health-related issues without difficulty.

• Build networks among themselves as researchers, scientists, science journalists, communicators, health journalists, policymakers, etc.

TOPICS

• Role of science journalists, scientists, and researchers in fighting infodemics.

• Skills and tools needed to verify online content.

• Guidance in writing and reporting the science of pandemics and infectious diseases.

• Strategies in using new media to fight infodemics.

• How to engage the community and gain their interest in factual news.

TARGET AUDIENCE

This workshop is open to everyone, especially:

• Science Journalists

• Health Journalists

• Scientists

• Researchers

• Communicators

• Policy Makers

• News & Media Organizations

• Health Experts

• Higher Education Communities,

Interested participants are to register via: https://bit.ly/39q9CSA

CONTACT

For more information on the workshop please write to:

AAU TV via e-mail (aautv@aau.org) and copy Isabella Tetteh Ahinakwa (itahinakwa@aau.org)

TITLE: Press Release -AAU-PACCI Inaugurates African Education Trust Fund Organising Committee

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Available in English, French, Arabic and Portuguese

The Association of African Universities (AAU), the Pan-African Chamber of Commerce and Industry (PACCI) and the African Private Sector (APSS) have inaugurated a committee to establish an African Education Trust Fund (AETF). The Committee comprises eminent African scholars, business executives, some representatives of African institutions, an Indian former Vice-Chancellor of an East African university, and two senior advisors.

The Association of African Universities (AAU), Africa’s apex higher education body with a membership of over 400 universities across the continent, and the Pan African Chamber of Commerce and Industry (PACCI) representing the collective interest of Chambers of Commerce and Industry and the business community in Africa, signed a Strategic Partnership Agreement in March 2021 to promote deeper discourse on improving academia-private sector relationships on the continent. The ultimate goal of the Agreement is to expand cooperation towards the integration of Africa through education, trade and investment under the Regional Economic Communities (RECs) and the Africa Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).

In this Partnership Agreement, the Parties agreed to launch a special African Education Trust Fund (AETF) to raise funds to develop and strengthen a resilient African education system that produces the right skills set required to transform the continent into an economic powerhouse through human capacity development, academic scholarships, development of responsive curricula in all disciplines and infrastructural development in African higher education and technical and vocational education and training (TVET) systems.

The AETF is one of several tenets in the AAU-PACCI Agreement that is being lifted by the African Private Sector Summit (APSS) for actualization. One other is the Bill of Rights for an enabling business environment in Africa which is currently being drafted and is funded by United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA).

In a brief but memorable virtual meeting held on 3rd February 2022 and coordinated by the APSS, which has been mandated by the two Parties to coordinate programmes in the Agreement, an Organizing Committee of Fifteen (15) experts in African higher education was inaugurated by the Deputy Chair of the APSS, Mr. Ben Acheampong. The Committee is chaired by Dr. Ekwow Spio-Garbrah, a Ghanaian diplomat and former Minister of Education, and also former Minister of Trade and Industry. The other 14 members of the Committee are:

Dr. Raju Chandrasekar (Chancellor Emeritus, Uganda/ India)

Mr. Kebour Ghenna (Executive Director, PACCI)

Prof. Theresia Nkuo-Akenji (Vice President, AAU)

Prof Jonathan Mba (Former Director of Research & Academic Planning, AAU)

Prof. Dr. Margret King (President/CEO, Global Institute of Planning and Sustainable Development, USA)

Prof. Dr. Sam Ndoga (APSS)

Prof. Goski Alabi (President of Laweh Open University, Ghana)

Jeannine Uwimana- Nicol (Snr Researcher, Faculty of Medicine & Health Sciences, Stellenbosch Univ, S/Africa & Univ. of Rwanda)

Prof. Brahim Elbhiri (Professor of IT & Director of SMARTILAB, a lab of research development and innovation)

Mr. John Binnie Kauya (Group MD, Global Business Network, Botswana)

Mr. Ousman Touray (Student Ambassador, University of The Gambia)

Mr. Adedayo Dayo-Dunmoye (Principal Partner, ThinQfam Consulting Services)

Mr.Jones Williams – Public Policy and Development Professional

African Business Council (TBA)

The Committee also has two Advisory Members, namely:

Abu Bako (President of RHEMA, Nigeria)

Dr. Francis Mangeni

.

Mr. J. Wendell Addy, the Chair of APSS, applauded the AAU and PACCI for committing to implement the MOU, and acknowledged the important roles other sister organizations such as the African Business Council (ABC) have to play to actualize the goals of the MoU. He posited that addressing the skills set needs of the continent is an indispensable enabler, particularly in the conversion of its raw materials for the success of the RECs and AfCFTA.

In his brief remarks, the Executive Director of PACCI, Mr. Kebour Ghenna noted that industry and academia working in tandem becomes a powerful engine for innovation and economic growth for which reason PACCI commits wholly to this initiative and gives full support. Both the Vice President of the AAU, Prof. Theresia Nkuo-Akenji, and the Secretary-General of the Association, Prof. Olusola Oyewole, also assured the Committee of the AAU’s full support in recognition of the synergies in university-industry linkages.

In his acceptance speech after the inauguration, the Chair, Dr. Ekwow Spio-Garbrah, promised professionalism and efficiency in their work and to embrace the expertise of other experts as well as work with other agencies with similar initiatives, such as the African Development Bank, which has also set out to run an education trust fund to build capacity in African higher education institutions.

For further information contact the AAU PR Office at – aodarko@aau.org

The deadline for submission is August 25, 2022, with decisions to be announced in October.

Criteria:

PhD degree received less than 8 years ago; in limited cases, doctoral candidates in the final stages of dissertation completion may be considered.

Current research or teaching affiliation with a higher education institution, association, or research organization.

Commitment to participate in 8-10 remote, online workshops and/or public webinars with co-recipients, SAR staff, network members, and guests (with proper security accommodations).

Ability to lawfully receive stipend funds and complete program requirements in the

country of current location, assuming responsibility for tax or reporting requirements, if any.

Candidates in or from the Global South and from minority or otherwise marginalized communities are strongly encouraged to apply.

A 500-1000 word abstract* summarizing the formal research component of your

TITLE: Donor Profile: Dr. John A. Serri, PhD ’80

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Physics alum has a vision for eye exam app

Sandi Miller | Department of Physics
March 28, 2018

Dr. John A. Serri, PhD ’80

With the invention of two inexpensive optical devices and a free smartphone app that provides a DIY eye exam, John Serri thinks he may be one of the oldest startup entrepreneurs in Silicon Valley. But as he told MIT students and others at a talk in April 2017, when you have what it takes to get an MIT PhD in atomic physics, you can do just about anything.

He recently gave a talk to students, his former PhD advisor, Professor David Pritchard, Physics Department Head Peter Fisher, and others interested in hearing about his transition from receiving an MIT PhD in atomic physics to a successful career as a corporate tech leader. Serri, who received his PhD from MIT in 1980, guided audience members in using a small plastic cylinder that, when attached to their smartphones, produce refraction correction numbers used for ordering corrective eyeglasses.

Serri has a long history as a technical leader at major corporations including AT&T, Bell Laboratories, Lockheed Martin, Loral, Globalstar, and Trimble Navigation along with stints working with the US government. Serri used his background in math and physics to work on such projects as modeling of gas molecules interacting with crystal surfaces, how to determine the best routes to send data through rapidly changing networks, and producing efficient algorithms for data analysis. His interest in large systems led to the development of secure global networks, low-earth–orbit sat-phone networks, sensor distribution networks, and real estate analytic/big-data enterprise applications.

Seeing the Impossible

About EyeQue and Dr. Serri

Dr. John A. Serri, co-founder/COO of EyeQue with CEO Tibor Láczay, of Zenni Optical.

Education: PhD MIT ’80, with Prof. David Pritchard. SUNY Albany BS, mathematics and physics 1975

Fun fact: Serri is a keyboardist who has released several CDs; they are available on Amazon, iTunes, and other music websites.

Other career highlights: technical leader at AT&T, Bell Laboratories, Lockheed Martin, Loral, Globalstar, and Trimble Navigation. 20+ year corporate experience, migrating from tech to management. 10+ in education and consulting roles.

Company: EyeQue, Newark, CA

Employees: 15

Career opportunities: mechanical engineers, optical engineers and software engineers, product managers, marketing, and sales. Interested? Contact John at john.serri@eyeque.com

Funding: $6 million, private investors

Patents/Licenses: 6 patents for hardware design and software processing related to the miniscope; Exclusive worldwide license agreement with MIT for eye refraction using Inverse Shack Hartmann technique. Patent for binocular device/Insight?

Registered with FDA: Class 1 Medical Device

Awards: EyeQue Personal Vision Tracker: Best of Innovation in the Fitness, Sports and Biotech category for the international consumer electronics show CES2017. Finalist for the Prism Awards for Photonics Innovations by the SPIE international society for optics and photonics.

Website: www.eyeque.com

In 2015, he and his friend, Tibor Láczay, CEO of Zenni Optical, the discount online eyewear company, were at one of their wives’ biotech-oriented networking parties. The two of them speculated: What if a low-cost refractive device coupled with a smartphone app could give them the results of a prescription that in turn could be used to order eyeglasses?

Serri had been thinking of retirement, but then he took a quick detour. “We said, ‘How hard could it be to build a little piece of plastic? Let’s do it!’ We then formed a little company called EyeQue to answer the question,” recalled Serri.

While he doesn’t have a background in optometry, Serri said that his rigorous physics training gave him the experience needed to solve any sort of problem, including optometry ones.

The first thing EyeQue did was to obtain the licensing rights to a bit of MIT technology, and they then set up a small office in the San Francisco Bay area to develop the Personal Vision Tracker.

Part of the solution is dependent on a licensing agreement with MIT’s patented smartphone eye refraction test using the inverse of the Shack–Hartmann method. This interactive, portable, and inexpensive solution for estimating refractive errors in the human eye was designed in 2010 by Vitor Pamplona, Ankit Mohan, Manuel Oliveira, and Ramesh Raskar, as part of the MIT Media Lab’s Camera Culture Group. While Shack–Hartmann sensors measure localized slope of the wave front error using spot displacement in a sensor plane, the MIT technology has the user shifting the spots until they are aligned.

One of the challenges was figuring out how to make the technology work on a variety of phones, because screen pixel properties differ by phone model. The optical miniscope attaches to the screen of a smartphone (IOS or Android). The voice on the app, an optometrist friend of Serri’s, guides the user through a series of self-administered tests. Vision measurements are transmitted to the EyeQue Cloud, where algorithms create “EyeGlass Numbers,” the spherical, cylindrical and axis parameters used to order prescription eyeglasses. The data is securely stored online; over time, users can track vision changes or compare results to prescriptions they have received from their eye doctor.

At first, their idea met resistance. “People told me it’s impossible to do this; we were told we needed over $5 million to develop a product,” he says. “It actually took less than $1.5 million.” They decided against securing venture capital, choosing instead to self-fund the company. This allowed the team to focus entirely on product development and marketing.

The product, which is a monoscope form, is easy to use and noninvasive. Serri estimates under good test conditions that the device covers more than 99% of the population’s refractive error range, from extreme hyperopia to extreme myopia. It also accurately measures low to severe astigmatism.

After testing on family and friends, they produced their first round of commercial units in October 2016.

To market the product, they created the website in October 2017 and then did press outreach, press releases, blog postings, and social media; they also launched a Kickstarter campaign. They exhibited at CES 2017 in January and participated in a media event exclusive to CES award winners, which gave the product immediate broad exposure.

Serri said that everything happened so quickly. Serri admits that there was an element of luck in their initial success. At first sales through the Kickstarter campaign were very slow: “We thought we were heading for disaster,” he recalled. And then, the campaign suddenly took off and they soon had sold 5,500 devices and raised over $130,000, exceeding their original funding goal by 540 percent.

They also “lucked out” by using the first manufacturer they met at a conference. “We had a really good feeling about them and went ahead with selecting them as our manufacturer,” Serri says. “I normally wouldn’t recommend a single-source approach, but sometimes with limited time and budget that is the best way to proceed. Overall we didn’t make any big mistakes.”

So far, over 16,000 EyeQue miniscopes have been shipped to customers in 81 countries, and they anticipate selling millions of units via the EyeQue online store, online and brick & mortar retail outlets, and overseas sales.

For the initial product, they didn’t want to get weighed down with too many features. “We just kept it as simple as possible. It’s better to get something out sooner and find out how people use and perceive the device before putting in too much effort to make it perfect.”

This gave the company time and energy to then create its second wish-list item: a binocular device designed to test visual acuity (clarity of distance vision). This EyeQue Insight also uses a smartphone attachment, in the form of a binocular instrument. After completing another successful Kickstarter campaign, the company recently began fulfilling a backlog of pre-orders for these devices. “The development of the binocular device was a strategic investment toward a plethora of future products in that the platform is scalable to support a variety of future vision tests such as providing contacts lens refractive correction numbers and testing for presbyopia,” says Serri.

EyeQue is a game-changer

Serri says his technology “has a great positive but disruptive potential.”

Why is this such a major development? The basic paradigm of getting an eye test once a year will be replaced by taking an eye test anytime, any place, at a low cost, says Serri. This would allow consumers to track their vision changes over shorter time intervals and increase communication about vision changes with their eye care providers. For families with school-aged children, for example, whose eyes develop rapidly, the ability to use a device like the Insight to identify vision changes between doctor’s visits can make an enormous difference in that child’s performance and social engagement, Serri says.

There are also users who want to measure their vision more frequently than their eye insurance-allowed annual eye exam. For those with diabetes, vision can change frequently and dramatically. Having a personal device to track your vision could be invaluable, Serri says. “Our community of users is just beginning to explore the possibilities,” he says.

Furthermore, many don’t live near an eye doctor, and commercial-level auto refractors are $10,000. “Eye care doesn’t exist in many areas of the world,” adds Serri. “A little device like this can make a big difference.”

Serri is quick to point out that the device won’t put eye doctors out of business. It doesn’t diagnose eye problems such as macular degeneration or glaucoma. yeQue urges their customers to visit a doctor annually for a full eye health exam, and warns them to use this product for informational and recreational purposes only.

“What we provide is not an Rx-type prescription, as that can only be provided by a licensed eye care practitioner, but rather good estimates that are often accurate to within 0.25 diopters if the test is done correctly,” he said. However, even though it is not intended for creating Rx prescriptions, EyeQue has registered the device to the FDA as a Class 1 medical device.

Serri has received a lot of positive feedback on this technology. Said one testimonial: “I ordered glasses using your EyeGlass Numbers and I see perfectly with them.”

At the end of the talk, Serri shared a few startup lessons, and many students asked questions about startup do’s and don’ts. Here were his suggestions:

Use the best tools you can buy; for example, don’t scrimp by using buggy freeware.
Hire the best people you can, and pay them well.
Develop a productive positive company culture; hire people who are not only smart but also nice!
Have a clear vision and manageable goals, and communicate those goals clearly to all involved.
Initially work in stealth mode if possible; focus on the product, not on publicity.
Avoid feature-creep; consumers and engineers will want to add a little bit here and there to your product, often creating lots of unneeded complexity.
Don’t heed the advice of experts as immutable truths; in the end listen to your “gut instincts.”
Vigorously plan for and solve the issues you know about so you can survive the unanticipated issues you never thought about.
Work in a corporate environment for a few years before you strike out on your own.

MIT Reunion

Serri’s visit to campus was also a mini reunion with Professor David Pritchard, with whom he worked with to do his doctoral research on state-to-state molecular collisions. “David (Pritchard) was tough on me,” Serri says. “The research challenges he presented were an incredible training, yet humbling experience. I think he eventually saw my potential after a rough start as I stayed on as a post doc, then as a visiting scientist. I always felt I was a lucky person to get into MIT and to have David Pritchard as my thesis advisor.”

One of Serri’s goals with the talk was to also advise students about how they could turn their physics degree into a commercial career. But he also encouraged everyone to take their time with settling into retirement. “I’m not ready to sit in a rocking chair,” he said. “I still have too much energy!”

Consumers are able to purchase the EyeQue Personal Vision Tracker and the EyeQue Insight directly from the EyeQue website at www.eyeque.com, and download the free myEyeQue applications through the iTunes and Google Play stores.

TITLE: Chapter 3: Past, present, and future of the South Asian monsoon

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Ummenhofer, C.C., Geen, R., Denniston, R.F., and Rao, M.P. (2024). Chapter 3: Past, present, and future of the South Asian monsoon. In: The Indian Ocean and its role in the global climate system, Eds. Ummenhofer, C.C. and Hood, R.R., Elsevier, doi:10.1016/B978-0-12-822698-8.00013-5.

Key climatic features of the South Asian monsoon region, including summertime (June-August) rainfall (colored in mm/yr) and winds (vectors in m/s), northernmost location of the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), and position of the Westerlies; locations of paleoclimate proxy records (speleothems and tree rings) mentioned in Ummenhofer et al. (2024) are indicated as well. Image from Ummenhofer et al (2024).

As a key component of the global climate system, the South Asian monsoon represents the largest of the Earth’s monsoon systems and a lifeline for the region’s nearly 2 billion people, who receive most of their annual precipitation during boreal summer. Traditionally characterized as continent‐scale “sea breezes,” where the land heats faster than the ocean during summer, causing rising air over the continent and moist oceanic air to be drawn in, recent theoretical advances view the monsoon as a regional manifestation of the seasonal variation of the global tropical atmospheric overturning and migration of the associated convergence zones. The South Asian monsoon varies intraseasonally with active and break spells, in response to interannual climate modes (e.g., El Niño-Southern Oscillation), as well as on multidecadal and longer timescales. Hydroclimatically-sensitive proxy records (e.g., speleothems, tree-rings) provide a centennial to millennial context for South Asian monsoon variability and its extensive societal impacts. While an anthropogenically-driven weakening of the South Asian summer monsoon in the 20th century is seen, climate model projections suggest a strengthening during the 21st century. Despite progress in operational forecasts, successful predictions of the South Asian monsoon across a range of spatial and temporal scales still represent considerable challenges.

TITLE: DSA Cambridge Fellowship 2027 Applications Open: A 12-Month Leadership Programme for the Algorithmic Age

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the DSA Cambridge Fellowship 2027, an intensive 12-month hybrid leadership development programme designed for professionals working at the intersection of public policy, governance, artificial intelligence, data and digital transformation.

Organised by The Digital Statecraft Academy, the programme aims to prepare established and emerging leaders to navigate the policy, institutional and ethical challenges created by artificial intelligence, algorithmic decision-making, digital public infrastructure and data-driven government.

The programme combines structured online learning, individual expert consultations, peer collaboration, applied project development and a mandatory residential training week in Cambridge, United Kingdom. Fellows will complete approximately 120 hours of structured engagement over four programme quarters while continuing in their existing professional positions.

Applications for the Class of 2027 must be submitted by 14 September 2026.

Prospective applicants should understand that this is not advertised as a fully funded programme. Selected Fellows must pay a substantial participation fee and cover their own travel, visa, additional accommodation and certain project-related expenses.

The application closing time and applicable time zone have not been stated. Candidates should therefore submit well before the deadline rather than assuming the form will remain open until midnight in their local time.

About the DSA Cambridge Fellowship Programme

The DSA Cambridge Fellowship is a selective leadership programme developed for public leaders, policy professionals, researchers and practitioners seeking to govern technology and data responsibly.

According to the official programme overview, the Fellowship brings together an interdisciplinary international cohort drawn from government, public institutions, academia, international organisations and relevant industries.

The programme responds to the growing need for leaders who can understand both the opportunities and the risks associated with:

Artificial intelligence in public decision-making

Algorithmic systems used by governments and institutions

Digital public infrastructure

Data-driven policymaking

GovTech and public-sector innovation

Ethical and accountable digital transformation

Institutional resilience in the algorithmic age

Responsible technology adoption

Evidence-informed policy design

Human oversight of automated systems

The Fellowship is delivered by The Digital Statecraft Academy and supported by a network that includes the Centre for Science and Policy at the University of Cambridge, Cambridge University Press, Microsoft, The GovLab at New York University, Data for Policy CIC and the Centre for Digital Public Infrastructure.

An important clarification is that the completion certificate is issued by The Digital Statecraft Academy. The official FAQ explains that partner institutions, including the Centre for Science and Policy, may appear as programme delivery partners, but DSA remains the awarding institution. Applicants should not describe the programme as a degree or qualification awarded by the University of Cambridge.

Main Areas of Study

The programme concentrates on four interconnected fields of digital statecraft.

1. Digital Public Infrastructure

Fellows will examine the foundational digital systems governments and public institutions use to deliver essential services at scale. This may include identity systems, payments infrastructure, data exchanges, registries and interoperable public platforms.

The programme considers how such systems can be designed and governed in the public interest while addressing privacy, inclusion, security, interoperability and institutional accountability.

2. Algorithmic Governance

This area focuses on the use of algorithms and artificial intelligence in public administration and institutional decision-making.

Fellows will explore how AI-enabled processes can improve government operations while maintaining appropriate human oversight, ethical safeguards, transparency and democratic accountability.

3. GovTech

The GovTech component addresses the use of digital tools and innovative public-private collaboration to modernise public-sector operations.

Participants will consider how governments can adopt technology responsibly, evaluate vendors, manage institutional change, develop implementation capacity and turn digital strategies into workable public services.

4. Data for Policy

The programme will help Fellows understand how data, analytical methods and emerging AI capabilities can be used to produce meaningful policy insights.

The emphasis is not simply on possessing technical data skills. It is also on knowing how evidence should be interpreted, communicated and incorporated into policy decisions.

Who Should Consider Applying?

The programme is primarily intended for senior, established or emerging leaders who are already shaping, or have the potential to shape, institutional policy, strategy, research or innovation.

Potential applicants may be working in:

Government departments and public authorities

Public-sector institutions

Intergovernmental and multilateral organisations

Universities and research institutions

Technology and data-related organisations

Relevant private-sector industries

Civil society and third-sector organisations

Public policy, law and governance

Artificial intelligence and data science

Information systems and digital transformation

Social sciences and humanities connected with digital governance

The official eligibility guidance indicates that strong candidates should demonstrate:

Meaningful professional or academic experience in data science, artificial intelligence, public policy, governance or a related field

An established or emerging leadership position

Potential to create institutional or regional impact

Influence or authority to advance data-driven transformation

A vision for change extending beyond their immediate job responsibilities

Commitment to public value and responsible technology

Readiness to engage with interdisciplinary challenges

Capacity to participate throughout the 12-month programme

Ability to attend the mandatory Cambridge residency

Strong professional and academic English

Direct technical experience in artificial intelligence is not an absolute requirement. The programme explicitly describes itself as multidisciplinary and advises applicants not to be discouraged if they do not have direct AI or digital innovation experience. However, candidates must still demonstrate a convincing connection between their work, leadership interests and the wider field of digital statecraft.

No specific university degree, minimum academic qualification, age limit or number of years of experience is stated in the published eligibility conditions.

Programme Structure

The Fellowship involves approximately 120 hours of structured engagement spread over four quarters. Its design is intended to be manageable for working professionals while still providing a substantial development experience.

Quarter 1: Foundations and Network Building

The first quarter introduces Fellows to the programme, their cohort and the broader DSA and Cambridge-connected ecosystem.

Activities are expected to include:

Comprehensive programme onboarding

Introduction to the foundations of digital statecraft

Expert-led workshops

Initial sessions on AI governance and regulatory frameworks

Exposure to GovTech and digital public infrastructure initiatives

Strategic introductions to experts relevant to each Fellow’s interests

Peer introductions and cohort-building activities

One-to-one meetings with selected researchers and practitioners

Early development of the Fellow’s proposed project

Fellows may identify experts, researchers or institutions they would like to meet. However, the organisers do not guarantee that every requested connection will be arranged.

Introductions are facilitated on a rolling basis. Fellows are expected to complete meetings with experts already introduced before further introductions are arranged.

Quarter 2: Intensive Cambridge Residency

The second quarter includes the compulsory in-person residency in Cambridge from 18 to 24 April 2027.

The residency is organised around three principal training strands:

Systems Thinking for AI-Enabled Governance

Fellows will study strategic frameworks for managing digital transformation within complex institutions and governance environments.

Technology Comprehension and Capacity Building

This strand develops practical understanding across digital public infrastructure, Data for Policy, algorithmic governance and GovTech.

From Vision to Implementation

Fellows will examine how to convert strategic ideas into practical, measurable and deliverable institutional outcomes.

The residency may include workshops, panels, keynote sessions, collaborative exercises and direct engagement with academics, policy professionals and practitioners.

Attendance is mandatory. Remote participation will not be provided as an alternative, and missed residency sessions will not be repeated or made available as recordings for later completion.

Quarter 3: Individual Project Development

During the third quarter, Fellows will focus on developing their individual or collaborative applied projects.

Support may include:

Guidance from academic and professional experts

Peer feedback and review

Collaborative working groups

Publication advice

Project milestone reviews

Methodological guidance

Connections with relevant institutions or practitioners

Help refining the scope and feasibility of the proposed output

Project progress may be monitored through check-ins, reflective documentation and expert feedback. If a project encounters difficulties, its scope, timeline or methodology may be adjusted in consultation with DSA and relevant advisers.

Quarter 4: Project Delivery and Assessment

The fourth quarter focuses on finalising and delivering the Fellow’s principal output.

Possible outputs include:

Policy papers

Policy briefs

Academic publications

Policy workshops

Applied research

Digital or governance prototypes

Implementation frameworks

Institutional strategies

Regional transformation projects

Other outputs addressing a substantive governance or policy challenge

Fellows are also expected to complete a reflective summary documenting their learning and development.

The final quarter includes programme evaluation, cohort assessment and transition into the DSA alumni network. Projects may continue after the Fellowship, and participants are encouraged to maintain the professional relationships developed during the programme.

Further details are available on the official programme structure page.

Learning Outcomes and Benefits

By completing the programme, Fellows are expected to strengthen their capabilities in several areas.

Strategic Leadership for the AI Era

Participants will explore frameworks for governing AI and data in the public interest. The programme aims to develop the strategic vision and change-management capacity required to lead digital transformation while protecting democratic values and institutional accountability.

Technical Fluency

Fellows will build working knowledge across:

Digital public infrastructure

Data for Policy

Algorithmic government and governance

GovTech

AI-enabled institutional systems

Evidence-based technology decisions

The programme is designed to develop leadership-level technical understanding rather than turn every participant into a software engineer or data scientist.

Implementation and Project Management

Fellows will learn how to convert strategic ideas into practical initiatives through:

Project planning

Stakeholder engagement

Institutional coordination

Policy design

Pilot development

Crisis decision-making

Monitoring progress

Scaling successful innovations

Global Professional Network

Participants will join an international community of professionals working in data, AI, policy and governance. Fellows may gain access to relevant academics, practitioners and institutional networks.

However, preferred expert matches and institutional introductions are not guaranteed.

Certificate and Professional Visibility

Fellows who satisfactorily complete the programme may receive a DSA Cambridge Fellowship Certificate of Completion and join the DSA alumni network.

The programme also identifies possible publication and international conference presentation pathways. These are opportunities rather than guaranteed outcomes.

Participation in the Data for Policy conference or publication in the Data & Policy journal is optional. Conference registration, travel and related expenses are not included in the Fellowship fee.

Applied Project

Every Fellow is expected to develop a practical output relevant to their professional or regional context. The goal is to leave the programme with more than theoretical knowledge by producing an initiative, framework, publication or prototype capable of supporting real-world institutional change.

The official learning outcomes provide additional information about the capabilities participants are expected to develop.

Participation Fee and Financial Obligations

£11,700 plus VAT at 20%.

If VAT is charged at the stated 20% rate, the VAT-inclusive amount would be £14,040.

Applicants should confirm the final invoiced amount and applicable VAT treatment directly with DSA before making any financial commitment.

Tuition and online learning modules

Ongoing academic and professional support

Cambridge residency programme activities

International or domestic travel to Cambridge

Data for Policy conference fees

Other external activities not included in the programme

Personal resources

Employer or institutional sponsorship

External sponsorship

Another confirmed funding source

Institutional nomination or sponsorship may strengthen an application, but applications must still be submitted by individuals. Group or team applications are not accepted.

Payment Deadline and Conditions

Selected Fellows must complete payment and enrolment by 7 December 2026.

According to the official terms and conditions, failure to complete payment or enrolment by that date will result in the offer being withdrawn. The terms further state that late or incomplete payment may affect future applications to the Digital Statecraft Academy.

Applicants should independently verify all bank information through the official DSA website or by contacting the programme office before transferring funds.

Refund and Withdrawal Policy

The participation fee becomes non-refundable once enrolment is confirmed.

Refunds and deferrals will not ordinarily be provided when a Fellow is unable to attend because of:

Visa refusal or delay

Travel restrictions

Personal scheduling conflicts

Professional commitments

Other attendance-related circumstances

Applicants are encouraged to obtain appropriate insurance to reduce potential losses associated with travel, visas or unforeseen disruptions.

The organisers also disclaim responsibility for delays, changes or disruptions arising from circumstances outside their control, including force majeure events.

Cambridge Residency Arrangements

The Cambridge residency is scheduled for 18–24 April 2027.

The programme provides:

Six nights of accommodation

Breakfast

Lunch

Tea and coffee services

Scheduled training and programme activities

Fellows are responsible for arranging and financing their own transportation to and from Cambridge.

Those wishing to extend their stay may ask DSA to check whether additional accommodation is available at the residency venue. Any extra nights and associated expenses remain the Fellow’s responsibility.

Accompanying partners or guests must be disclosed to the programme team in advance. Availability is not guaranteed, and Fellows must cover all guest-related costs. Guests under 18 are not permitted, and guests cannot participate in Fellowship sessions or programme content.

Visa Requirements

Participants who require permission to enter the United Kingdom must obtain the appropriate visa themselves.

DSA can provide an official invitation or visa-support letter upon request, but the Fellow remains responsible for:

Determining the correct visa category

Preparing the application

Paying visa fees

Providing supporting evidence

Attending any required appointment

Managing the application timeline

Bearing the consequences of delay or refusal

Because the programme fee is non-refundable after confirmed enrolment, international applicants should evaluate the visa risk carefully and begin preparations early.

Application Requirements

Candidates must submit the following materials through the official application form.

1. Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must upload a CV of no more than two pages.

The CV must include contact information for three referees capable of commenting on the applicant’s suitability for the Fellowship.

Applicants should ensure the CV highlights:

Current position and responsibilities

Leadership experience

Policy or governance contributions

Work involving AI, data, public-sector innovation or digital transformation

Institutional or regional influence

Major projects and measurable results

Research, publications or relevant professional achievements

Contact details for three appropriate referees

The application form accepts one CV file with a maximum size of 10 MB.

2. Fellowship Questions

Applicants must propose three to five Fellowship Questions reflecting their professional interests.

These questions will help the organisers understand the applicant’s learning priorities and arrange tailored networking or expert meetings during the programme.

Effective questions should:

Address a specific policy, governance or institutional challenge

Be directly connected to the applicant’s current work

Be suitable for discussion with academics or practitioners

Demonstrate intellectual curiosity

Connect technology with public value

Be broad enough to benefit from interdisciplinary expertise

Help identify appropriate experts and institutions

3. One-Page Project Proposal

Applicants must submit a one-page proposal explaining the initial idea for the principal output they intend to develop and deliver in the fourth quarter.

The proposal should clearly identify:

The policy or governance problem

Why the problem is important

The institutional or regional context

The intended output

Key stakeholders

Expected results

The applicant’s role

How the Fellowship would strengthen the project

How the output could be implemented or used

The proposed output could be a policy paper, institutional framework, implementation plan, research publication, policy workshop, prototype or similar applied product.

The form accepts one proposal file in PDF or document format with a maximum size of 10 MB.

4. Introductory Video

Candidates must upload a short introductory video of no more than three minutes.

The video should:

Introduce the applicant

Explain their professional background

Describe their current role

State why they want to join the programme

Explain what they hope to gain

Identify what they intend to achieve by the end of the Fellowship

The form permits one video file with a maximum size of 10 MB. Applicants should compress and test the video before attempting to upload it.

5. Confirmation of Travel Availability

Applicants must confirm that they can travel to Cambridge for the mandatory residential component.

Candidates should not confirm availability unless they have realistically considered:

Professional leave

Family responsibilities

Passport validity

Visa requirements

Travel costs

Travel time

Health and accessibility requirements

6. Funding Information

Applicants must explain whether they will be:

Self-funded

Supported by their institution

Externally sponsored

Funded through another confirmed arrangement

Candidates should provide a clear and credible funding explanation rather than leaving the financial position uncertain.

7. Institutional Support Letters

Applicants may upload institutional support letters where applicable.

A useful letter should confirm:

The applicant’s position

Organisational approval for participation

Permission to attend online and in-person activities

Support for the proposed project

Any financial sponsorship being provided

The organisation’s interest in applying the Fellowship’s outcomes

The form allows up to five support documents, with a maximum size of 10 MB for each file.

8. Form Consents

The application form asks whether candidates wish to:

Allow their email address to be shared with other cohort members if selected

Applicants can choose yes or no. They should read the privacy and communication terms carefully before giving consent.

Because the form requires file uploads, applicants should expect to sign in with a Google account. The form explains that the name, email address and profile information associated with the account may be recorded when files are uploaded and the form is submitted.

English-Language Requirement

The entire programme is conducted in English.

Fellows must be able to:

Participate actively in professional discussions

Understand assigned readings

Communicate with experts and peers

Produce written assignments

Present project ideas

Prepare outputs to a high professional standard

No additional language-support service is provided.

The published materials do not specify an IELTS, TOEFL or other formal English test. Nevertheless, applicants must possess sufficient practical English proficiency to participate fully.

Selection Process

The Fellowship is highly selective and admits only a small cohort.

Applications are assessed primarily on:

Individual merit

Professional or academic experience

Leadership record and potential

Relevance of the applicant’s work

Quality of the project proposal

Strength of the applicant’s motivation

Potential institutional or regional impact

Ability to contribute to peer learning

Commitment to public value

Diversity of disciplines, sectors, skills and geographic backgrounds

Candidates may be contacted for clarification or additional information. Applicants should therefore monitor their email and add office@digitalstatecraft.academy to their safe-senders list.

An exact selection-notification date has not been published. The FAQ states that successful applicants will be notified by email several weeks before the programme begins and will receive an official acceptance letter with next-step instructions.

Unsuccessful candidates may reapply for a future cohort with a more developed proposal.

Attendance and Certificate Requirements

Fellows are expected to participate actively in:

Online learning modules

Small-group sessions

Workshops

Expert meetings

Peer discussions

The Cambridge residency

Project-development activities

Programme assessments

Online sessions may be scheduled according to the availability of most cohort members. Because the cohort is international, participants may occasionally need to attend outside normal working hours.

Significant absences may affect eligibility for the completion certificate. Fellows should notify the programme coordinators as early as possible about scheduling conflicts.

Although the terms indicate that video or audio recording may occur during some programme activities, recordings will not be offered as a substitute for attending the mandatory Cambridge residency.

Networking and Expert Engagement

Fellows will have opportunities to interact with professionals and experts from DSA, Data for Policy, the University of Cambridge ecosystem, the Centre for Science and Policy and other relevant partner networks.

Networking may include:

One-to-one expert consultations

Cohort workshops

Peer introductions

Thematic discussions

Research-policy meetings

Collaborative project work

Alumni activities

Selected events and knowledge-sharing initiatives

After an external expert introduction has been made, the Fellow may be expected to arrange the meeting directly according to mutual availability.

The organisers facilitate connections but do not guarantee access to every requested individual or institution. The depth of each professional relationship will depend partly on the Fellow’s own initiative.

Intellectual Property, Ethics and Confidentiality

Policy drafts, prototypes, research ideas and other materials produced by Fellows remain the property of the respective Fellows unless another arrangement is agreed in writing.

Participants must respect:

The intellectual property of peers and mentors

Confidential information shared during meetings

Institutional restrictions

Professional boundaries

Applicable research ethics

Data-protection requirements

Projects involving human participants, sensitive data or regulated research may require approval from the Fellow’s institution or relevant national authority. Obtaining such approval is the Fellow’s responsibility.

The programme generally applies confidentiality principles to expert discussions. Larger group sessions may operate under the Chatham House Rule, allowing information to be used without disclosing the identity or affiliation of the speaker.

Privacy, Communications and Publicity

Personal data is processed in accordance with the UK Data Protection Act 2018, UK GDPR and the Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations.

The programme may use Fellows’ names, professional biographies and photographs for:

Cohort announcements

Programme communications

Professional introductions

DSA network visibility

Partner communications

Contact details may also be shared within relevant programme groups to facilitate networking.

Video and audio recording may take place during programme activities. Fellows who do not wish to appear should notify the programme team in advance.

The cohort is normally announced after selected Fellows have confirmed participation. Applicants should not publicly present themselves as Fellows before enrolment is confirmed and the cohort is officially announced by DSA.

Professional Conduct

Participants must maintain appropriate professional standards throughout online sessions, the Cambridge residency and communications with peers, mentors and partner organisations.

Inappropriate, disruptive or unprofessional behaviour may lead to removal from the programme.

The organisers reserve the right to make reasonable changes to the schedule, content or delivery format when necessary. Fellows will be informed in advance of significant amendments.

How to Apply for the DSA Cambridge Fellowship 2027

Applicants should follow these steps:

Review the official programme overview.

Read the application requirements.

Read the complete terms and conditions.

Review the official Fellowship FAQ.

Confirm that you can meet the fee, travel, visa and attendance obligations.

Prepare a two-page CV with three referees.

Develop three to five meaningful Fellowship Questions.

Prepare the one-page project proposal.

Record and compress the three-minute introductory video.

Obtain institutional support letters where applicable.

Explain your funding arrangements clearly.

Submit the official online application form by 14 September 2026.

Candidates should retain copies of every submitted document and take a screenshot or save any submission confirmation they receive.

Important Dates

Application deadline: 14 September 2026

Registration and payment deadline for selected Fellows: 7 December 2026

Cambridge residency: 18–24 April 2027

Exact programme commencement date: Not expressly stated in the reviewed information

Selection notification date: Not expressly stated; successful candidates will be contacted by email

Contact Information

Questions about eligibility, payment, sponsorship, accessibility, visas or programme arrangements should be directed to:

Email: office@digitalstatecraft.academy

Official website: The Digital Statecraft Academy

Applicants should rely on official DSA communications when verifying payment instructions, selection results or changes to programme dates.

Conclusion

The DSA Cambridge Fellowship 2027 offers an extensive professional development pathway for leaders seeking to understand and shape the future of artificial intelligence, public-sector data, digital infrastructure and technology-enabled governance.

Its combination of online learning, expert engagement, a mandatory Cambridge residency and an applied project may be particularly valuable for professionals capable of translating new knowledge into institutional or regional reforms.

However, candidates must evaluate the financial and logistical obligations before applying. The programme carries a published fee of £11,700 plus VAT, while travel, visas, additional accommodation and project implementation costs remain the Fellow’s responsibility. The fee is also non-refundable after enrolment is confirmed.

Applicants who can demonstrate meaningful leadership, a credible applied project, strong English communication, institutional influence and a clear funding plan should prepare their documents carefully and submit the official application no later than 14 September 2026.

TITLE: Youth Connect: Youth Champions for Environment and Peace 2026 | Apply by 20 September

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Youth Connect: Youth Champions for Environment and Peace 2026 programme is inviting young people living in Cyprus to join an intercommunal youth initiative focused on environmental peacebuilding, sustainability, dialogue, and joint environmental action.

Organised through the regional Youth Connect programme, in collaboration with UNFICYP, the programme will bring together young people from different communities in Cyprus for an immersive workshop at the Ledra Palace Hotel in Nicosia.

Participants will develop the knowledge, confidence, and practical skills needed to work together on environmental challenges and develop action plans that can contribute to a more peaceful, sustainable, cohesive, and resilient Cyprus.

The programme will take place on 3, 4, 10 and 11 October 2026, with environmental actions expected to be implemented by February 2027.

Participation is free.

About the Youth Champions for Environment and Peace Programme

The Youth Champions for Environment and Peace programme focuses on the connection between environmental challenges and peacebuilding.

Climate change, environmental degradation, resource pressures, insecurity, and inequality can affect communities in different ways. The programme seeks to empower young people to work across community divisions and develop practical responses to shared environmental concerns.

Through workshops, group activities, discussions, mentoring, and action planning, participants will have the opportunity to learn from environmental and peace activists while collaborating with other young people from across Cyprus.

The programme is designed to strengthen:

Environmental awareness

Peacebuilding skills

Social cohesion

Intercommunal trust

Inclusive leadership

Critical thinking

Confidence

Adaptability

Environmental cooperation

Sustainable development

Participants will also become part of a wider network of Youth Champions for Environment and Peace, connecting them with local and international organisations, activists, and other young people working on related issues.

What the Programme Will Involve

The programme consists of an immersive in-person workshop followed by the development and implementation of environmental actions.

1. Immersive Workshop

The workshop will take place on:

3, 4, 10 and 11 October 2026

at the:

Ledra Palace Hotel, Nicosia

The sessions will focus on joint learning and collaboration between participants from different communities.

The workshop will include:

Interactive learning sessions

Group work

Discussions with environmental activists

Discussions with peacebuilding activists

Team-building activities

Development of environmental action ideas

Opportunities to build relationships with other participants

During the group work, participants will form teams and work together to develop environmental actions with support from the programme team.

Participation on all four workshop days is mandatory.

Environmental Action Projects

Following the workshop, participants will be expected to finalise their environmental action plans and submit a simple proposal for funding.

Each team will receive a small grant to implement its action, with support from a mentor and experts.

The environmental actions must be implemented by:

February 2027

The actions should reach people across the divide and may take place throughout Cyprus.

This component gives participants an opportunity to move beyond discussions and turn their ideas into practical environmental initiatives.

Who Can Apply?

The programme is specifically seeking dynamic and passionate young people who are living in Cyprus and are interested in contributing to a peaceful and sustainable future.

Applicants must:

Be 18–30 years old.

Be from any community and be living in Cyprus.

Have an interest in the environment and peacebuilding.

Be interested in becoming active in environmental and peacebuilding issues.

Have an interest in contributing to a peaceful and sustainable future in Cyprus.

Be committed and motivated to participate actively throughout the entire workshop.

Be willing to work as part of a team to develop and implement an environmental action.

Have a very good knowledge of English.

Be willing to develop interpersonal relationships with participants from all communities living in Cyprus.

Be interested in working together with others toward a common cause.

Previous Experience Is Not Required

Applicants do not need previous experience in environmental peacebuilding or environmental activism.

The programme is designed to provide participants with the knowledge, tools, and support required to develop their own environmental actions.

However, applicants should demonstrate genuine interest in environmental issues, peacebuilding, cooperation, and creating a sustainable future for Cyprus.

Previous Youth Champions Participants

The call is specifically open to people who did not benefit from previous UN Youth Champions programmes.

Applicants who have previously participated in a UN Youth Champions programme should therefore carefully consider this requirement before applying.

Gender and Community Representation

The organisers aim to promote gender diversity and equal representation among young people from all communities in Cyprus.

This reflects the programme’s broader objective of encouraging dialogue, cooperation, trust-building, and joint action among young people from different communities.

Accommodation

Accommodation in Nicosia may be available on 3 and 10 October, depending on demand.

However, accommodation availability is limited and subject to confirmation.

Applicants should therefore not assume that accommodation will automatically be provided and should consider this when planning their participation.

Important Access Requirement

All programme activities will take place at the Ledra Palace Hotel, which is located in the UN buffer zone in Nicosia.

Participation is therefore dependent on the applicant’s ability to enter the UN buffer zone in Nicosia.

The organisers note that the respective sides have authority over entry from the crossing points, rather than the UN.

Applicants should ensure that they have the required documentation to enter the buffer zone before applying.

Certificate of Participation

Participants who attend all four days of the workshop and actively contribute to the environmental actions will receive a certificate of participation.

Benefits of Participating

The Youth Champions for Environment and Peace programme provides participants with an opportunity to gain practical experience while contributing to environmental and peacebuilding efforts in Cyprus.

Participants can:

Develop Environmental Peacebuilding Skills

Learn how environmental challenges can be addressed through cooperation, dialogue, and peacebuilding.

Work Across Communities

Build relationships and collaborate with young people from different communities in Cyprus.

Develop an Environmental Action

Work in a team to design an environmental initiative addressing a common concern.

Receive Mentorship

Receive support from mentors and experts while developing and implementing an environmental action.

Access Small-Grant Support

Teams will receive a small grant to support implementation of their environmental action following the workshop.

Strengthen Leadership Skills

Develop confidence, adaptability, critical thinking, interpersonal skills, and inclusive leadership abilities.

Expand Your Network

Connect with local and international organisations, activists, experts, trainers, and members of the Youth Champions network.

Programme Schedule

Activity
Date

Workshop Day 1
3 October 2026

Workshop Day 2
4 October 2026

Workshop Day 3
10 October 2026

Workshop Day 4
11 October 2026

Environmental Actions
By February 2027

Location: Ledra Palace Hotel, Nicosia, Cyprus

Application Deadline

The deadline to apply is:

Sunday, 20 September 2026 at 23:00 EEST

Applicants should submit their applications before the stated deadline.

The organisers aim to notify successful applicants by 23 September 2026. Selected participants will then receive a detailed programme for the workshop.

How to Apply

Eligible applicants should complete the official online application form before the deadline.

Application Form: Apply for Youth Connect: Youth Champions for Environment and Peace

Participation in the programme is free.

For further information or enquiries, applicants can contact:

UNFICYP: unficyp-youthchampions@un.org

Application Tips

Before submitting your application, applicants should:

Confirm your age and location: Make sure you are aged 18–30 and currently living in Cyprus.

Check the workshop dates: Participation on 3, 4, 10 and 11 October is mandatory.

Demonstrate genuine motivation: Explain your interest in environmental issues, peacebuilding, and a sustainable future for Cyprus.

Highlight relevant interests: Previous environmental activism is not required, but applicants should demonstrate an interest in environmental and peacebuilding issues.

Show your willingness to collaborate: The programme specifically involves working with participants from different communities.

Check your access requirements: Make sure you have the documentation needed to enter the UN buffer zone in Nicosia.

Apply before the deadline: Submit your application by 20 September 2026 at 23:00 EEST.

Conclusion

The Youth Connect: Youth Champions for Environment and Peace 2026 programme offers young people living in Cyprus an opportunity to combine environmental action with peacebuilding and intercommunal cooperation.

Through an immersive four-day workshop, participants will learn from experts and activists, develop relationships across communities, form teams, and create environmental action plans. Selected teams will then receive small grants and mentorship to implement their initiatives by February 2027.

The programme is open to young people aged 18–30 from all communities living in Cyprus, and previous experience in environmental peacebuilding is not required.

Interested applicants should ensure they can commit to all four workshop days and meet the programme’s access requirements before applying.

Application deadline: 20 September 2026 at 23:00 EEST.
