TITLE: Mission

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Institut des Hautes Etudes Scientifiques (IHES) was created in 1958 at the instigation of Léon Motchane. A businessman with a love of mathematics, his ambition was to create a research center that would become the European counterpart of the famous Institute for Advanced Study (IAS) in Princeton, United States.

Since its creation, the Institute has developed in line with the vision of its founder. It has become a reference point for the international scientific community and achieved undeniable success in mathematics and theoretical physics. The atmosphere of free discussion among scientists, whatever their specialty or background, has also become one of the characteristics that make it so attractive.

IHES as an institution has had the legal status of a foundation in the public interest since 1981.

“Art. 1: The aim of the Foundation known as ‘Institut des Hautes Etudes Scientifiques’ is to enable and encourage theoretical scientific research in the following fields: Mathematics, Theoretical Physics, Methodology of Human Sciences and any other related theoretical discipline”

“Art. 2: The Foundation’s activity consists mainly in providing the Institute’s professors and researchers, both permanent and invited, with the resources required to undertake disinterested research: a center comprising offices, meeting rooms, a library, a conference center and a housing residence for visiting researchers.”

(Extract from the IHES statutes, 1958)

TITLE: Media Masterclass for Higher Education Institutions

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
A Four-Day Media Masterclass for Higher Education Institutions (9-12 September 2025)

Theme: Harnessing Media for Education: Mastering Digital Tools for African Universities

This concept note outlines a comprehensive workshop that will empower participants to effectively harness digital media for educational and other useful purposes. By providing practical skills, theoretical knowledge, and opportunities for hands-on experience, this workshop will contribute to the advancement of media literacy and digital communication in African higher education and beyond.

Executive Summary

In today’s world, where information is constantly shared in countless forms, digital media has become increasingly relevant. Digital media serves as a method of transforming raw data into meaningful communication for people, using formats such as video, audio, text, and images.

This four-day Media Masterclass for Higher Education Institutions aims to equip participants from across the African Universities with the necessary skills to effectively utilize digital media for effective communication. Through theoretical sessions, practical exercises, and group activities, participants will gain a deep understanding of media literacy, digital storytelling, and content creation. This initiative is in response to the focal point “D” of the Association of African Universities’ (AAU) 2024 – 2030 Strategic Plan; i.e., Higher Education Capacity Building and Empowerment. The inaugural Media Masterclass will be delivered in English and follow up sessions will be delivered in French and Portuguese

Introduction

The AAU is a membership-based network of 450 plus universities covering the 5 regions of Africa and its mission is to enhance the quality and relevance of higher education in Africa and strengthen its contribution to Africa’s development. Since 1967, the AAU has been the leading advocate for higher education in Africa, demonstrating the capacity to provide support for its member institutions in meeting their national, continental, and global needs.

As part of creating value for its members the AAU regularly runs various capacity building programs for the benefit of various thematic groups within the member universities. These capacity building programs offer discounted fees to staff from the member universities to demonstrate value for their loyal membership to the AAU. The AAU also hosts various forums for exchanges, discussions, engagements, collaborations, and advocacy towards fulfilling its mission and to improve the functions of its member universities.

The AAU TV, a unit of the AAU, serves as a platform to promote African scholarly works and highlight the relevance of higher education in Africa. It emphasizes the role of education as a cornerstone for socio-economic development and delivers development-focused content aimed at demonstrating the contributions of higher education institutions to socio-economic development.

The AAU TV’s mission is to be the voice of academia in Africa, leveraging academic innovations for public benefit and advancing Africa’s development. The vision of the AAU TV is to continually generate innovative and high-quality content that underscores the significance of higher education in societal development, increases the visibility of AAU member universities, fosters partnerships, and ensures the sustainability of operations through financial resource generation.

Justification

The rapid evolution of digital technology has significantly impacted various sectors, including education. Across Africa, institutions—be they educational, governmental, or corporate—are increasingly recognizing the value of integrating media into their operations. A review of higher education institutions such as the Accra Institute of Technology (AIT), Accra Technical University (ATU), Academic City University, and the Open University of Nigeria highlights a growing trend: the establishment of audio-visual studios to enhance teaching and learning experiences. However, many of these studios face a common challenge—a shortage of skilled professionals capable of fully leveraging their potential. Similarly, the AAU Secretariat’s experience in supporting seven African Higher Education Centers of Excellence for Development Impact (ACE Impact) under the Centers of Competence in Digital Education (C-Code) project underscores the need for ongoing capacity-building efforts to ensure technical teams can effectively manage and optimize digital education studios.

Objectives

The AAU TV’s 4-Day Media Masterclass for Higher Education Institutions aims to provide participants with the skills and expertise needed to harness the power of digital media to improve outcomes across various higher education domains. The objectives of the masterclass are:

To cultivate media literacy among higher education participants.

To equip participants with practical, hands-on experiences in digital media production.

To foster critical thinking skills related to media consumption and creation.

To promote the ethical and responsible use of media in educational contexts.

Expected Outcomes

A deeper understanding of digital tools media usage and its implications for education.

Ability to create high-quality digital media content for educational purposes.

Critical thinking skills for evaluating and analyzing media enhanced.

Ability to contribute to the development of a strong digital presence for their universities.

Methodology

Lectures and presentations

Hands-on exercises

Group activities and discussions

Case studies and examples

Target Participants

Media personnel employed by universities – working in e-learning departments, supporting university television/media units, or working in public relations/communications/social media offices

University and college students enrolled in media-related programs

University communication officers and anyone interested in producing media content

Workshop Outline

Day 1: Media Literacy and the Role of Digital Media in Education

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Name: Leyna J. Shackleton
Title: Pappalardo Fellow in Physics: 2024-2027
Email: hshackle@mit.edu
Phone: TBA

77 Massachusetts Avenue, 6C-339
Cambridge, MA 02139

Related Links:
Pappalardo Fellowships in Physics

Area of Physics

Condensed Matter Theory

Research Interests

Leyna’s research goals are to characterize and predict novel quantum phenomena that can emerge in materials when strong interactions between electrons yield phases of matter with high amounts of quantum entanglement. This entanglement can result in remarkable features, such as fractionalization – where exotic particle-like excitations emerge which cannot be simply constructed from individual electrons – or phases of matter which lack a description in terms of sharply defined quasiparticles. As a graduate student, Leyna studied universal properties of phase transitions between quantum phases of matter, developed new computational methods for analyzing many-body systems, and worked to derive experimental signatures for detecting strongly-interacting phases. Going forward, she is excited to continue pursuing these research directions while exploring the plethora of emerging experimental platforms for realizing macroscopic quantum phenomena.

Biographical Sketch

Leyna grew up in Sault Sainte Marie, Michigan. She attended MIT as an undergraduate, where she graduated with a BS in philosophy and physics in 2018. For her PhD thesis, she took the Red Line up to Harvard and worked with Subir Sachdev on understanding exotic properties of strongly-interacting systems of electrons. In an unusual twist of fate, she will be taking the Red Line back to MIT to spend the next several years as a Pappalardo Fellow.

In her free time, Leyna enjoys fire spinning (a hobby introduced to her as an undergraduate at MIT), building electronic synthesizers, and attending the many concerts that Boston has to offer.

TITLE: UPenn and Microsoft Research India Research Fellows 2026: Pre-Doctoral AI Research Opportunities in Health, Education and Media

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The University of Pennsylvania (UPenn), through its Institute for the Advanced Study of India (UPIASI), in collaboration with Microsoft Research India, is inviting applications for two Research Fellow positions for recent graduates who intend to pursue a Ph.D. The fellows will work on research and development projects focused on using artificial intelligence to improve outcomes in health, education, communication, and media in India.

The two positions are designed to bring together academic research, artificial intelligence, field experimentation, technology development, and real-world deployment. Successful candidates will become full members of the research team, contributing to the development of AI systems, field studies, evaluations, data analysis, research papers, and other research outputs.

The positions are particularly suited to graduates interested in AI research, development economics, public policy, education technology, public health, computer science, data science, human-computer interaction, natural language processing, applied statistics, and technology for social impact.

Both positions are appointed through the University of Pennsylvania Institute for the Advanced Study of India and hosted at Microsoft Research in Bengaluru, India, with regular travel to field sites in Rajasthan, Delhi, and other locations in India.

Overview of the UPenn and Microsoft Research Fellowship

The new research program at the University of Pennsylvania’s Center for the Advanced Study of India is built around a field-first approach to artificial intelligence research.

Rather than developing AI systems exclusively in controlled laboratory environments, the research team aims to understand how these technologies work when they are introduced into real communities, institutions, classrooms, healthcare environments, and media ecosystems.

The program emphasizes three important stages:

Co-designing AI tools with local partners

Deploying the tools under real-world conditions

Evaluating the tools against the alternatives that people currently use

This approach is intended to produce AI systems that are not only technically effective but also culturally appropriate, practical, sustainable, and useful in the environments where they are deployed.

The fellows will therefore have an opportunity to work at the intersection of academic research and practical AI deployment.

Two Research Fellow Positions Are Available

The recruitment is for two complementary pre-doctoral Research Fellow positions.

1. Research Fellow – Field Research and Evaluation

The first position focuses primarily on the research, fieldwork, study design, evaluation, and data analysis side of the program.

The successful fellow will be responsible for helping design and manage studies that evaluate AI systems in real-world environments.

Key responsibilities and areas of work include:

Designing research studies

Developing evaluation strategies

Supporting Institutional Review Board (IRB) processes and partner approvals

Coordinating field teams

Working with survey firms and research partners

Managing data collection

Monitoring data quality

Conducting statistical analysis

Contributing to research papers

Evaluating AI tools against existing alternatives and practices

Supporting research implementation in field locations

Helping determine whether AI interventions produce meaningful improvements

This position would be particularly relevant to graduates with backgrounds in economics, public policy, development studies, statistics, or related disciplines.

Candidates with hands-on experience managing randomized controlled trials or comparable field studies are especially relevant to this role.

Experience at organizations or research institutions such as J-PAL, IPA, or equivalent research-management environments would be considered valuable.

2. Research Fellow – Tool Development and Deployment

The second position focuses on the development, implementation, deployment, and evaluation of AI-powered tools.

This role is intended for candidates with strong technical backgrounds who are interested in understanding how technology performs outside controlled laboratory environments.

The successful candidate may work on areas including:

Artificial intelligence

Machine learning

Natural language processing

Human-computer interaction

Data science

Applied statistics

Software and tool development

AI deployment

Data analysis

Technology for public health

Education technology

AI applications in media

The role also requires an interest in fieldwork because the systems being developed will ultimately be tested and used in real-world environments.

Candidates with a bachelor’s or master’s degree in Computer Science, Engineering, Data Science, or a related field are particularly encouraged to consider this position.

Research Areas Covered by the Fellowship

The fellows will contribute to several major research programs. These projects address practical problems in health, education, communication, and media.

Samvaad: AI Practice for Frontline Health Workers

One of the research programs is called Samvaad, which focuses on using AI to support India’s frontline health workers.

India has approximately one million Accredited Social Health Activists, commonly known as ASHAs. These workers perform important health-related and community-facing responsibilities.

Their work includes counseling families on issues such as:

Contraception

Vaccination

Antenatal care

Family health

Other health-related decisions

However, health communication can be challenging because health workers sometimes have to address resistance or disagreement arising from household power dynamics and other social factors.

The research team is working with Khushi Baby to develop voice-based role-play tools that can help ASHAs practice difficult conversations.

The objective is to explore whether AI-powered practice environments can strengthen communication skills and improve the effectiveness of frontline health workers.

A fellow working on this program could therefore be involved in AI development, field deployment, research design, behavioral evaluation, data analysis, or a combination of these activities.

Clinical Communication Training with AIIMS New Delhi

Another research stream focuses on clinical communication training in partnership with AIIMS New Delhi.

Healthcare professionals frequently have to communicate difficult information to patients and caregivers. These conversations can involve complex medical, emotional, and interpersonal challenges.

The research team is developing and evaluating an AI-based communication training tool intended to help clinicians improve their communication and counseling abilities.

This work builds on previous research published at CSCW 2025.

For researchers interested in healthcare technology, human-computer interaction, AI-assisted training, public health, or communication, this research stream provides an opportunity to investigate how AI can support professional development in healthcare settings.

Bolo: AI Speaking Partners for Low-Income Classrooms

The Bolo research program focuses on spoken English and educational opportunity.

Spoken English can play an important role in economic mobility in India. However, students who could potentially benefit most from additional language practice often have fewer opportunities to practice speaking.

The research team previously field-tested an early version of a voice-based practice chatbot across four low-fee schools in Delhi.

That work was published at CHI 2026.

The next stage of the project will involve delivering a mobile-first version of the tool for sustained classroom use.

Researchers will evaluate outcomes including:

English fluency

Student confidence

Willingness to communicate

Opportunities for speaking practice

How students interact with AI-based speaking partners

The effectiveness of AI-supported language learning compared with existing approaches

This research stream could be particularly interesting to applicants interested in education technology, AI, natural language processing, HCI, learning sciences, or social-impact technology.

Kahani: AI, Entertainment Media and Social Norms

The Kahani research stream explores how entertainment media can influence social norms.

The project builds on an analysis of more than 250,000 films and television series across more than 20 countries.

The research examines how gender norms and other prosocial themes are communicated through:

Films

Television

Digital media

Entertainment content

Other forms of popular media

The program also seeks to develop tools that can help:

Researchers

Policymakers

Creative industries

Other stakeholders

better understand and strengthen the positive social impact of entertainment media.

Applicants interested in AI, computational social science, media studies, gender and social norms research, data analysis, public policy, or digital media may find this research stream particularly relevant.

A Field-First Approach to Artificial Intelligence Research

A major distinguishing feature of these positions is the emphasis on taking AI beyond the laboratory.

The research team is interested in questions such as:

Does an AI tool actually work when deployed in real communities?

How do users interact with AI systems under real-world conditions?

How does an AI intervention compare with existing alternatives?

Are AI tools culturally appropriate?

Can communities and institutions realistically sustain these technologies?

What happens when technology is introduced into schools, healthcare environments, or media ecosystems?

Can AI interventions produce measurable improvements in people’s lives?

The research program therefore combines technology development with rigorous evaluation.

This means fellows may not simply be building AI systems or conducting statistical analysis in isolation. They may be involved in understanding the entire lifecycle of an intervention, from design and development to deployment and evaluation.

TITLE: AAU Hosts the World Conference on Education and Restitution themed – Afrofuturism and Africa’s Development

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Association of African Universities (AAU), the Pan African Heritage World Museum (PAHWM) and UNESCO, under the auspices of the Government of Ghana and the African Union Commission, organized a special Diaspora Conference titled: World Conference on Education and Restitution from August 30th to September 1st, 2022. The overarching theme for this hybrid conference, hosted at the AAU’s Secretariat in Accra, Ghana and online was – Afrofuturism and Africa’s Development. The three subthemes supporting the overall theme and underpinning the discussions at the conference were as follows — Addressing the prerequisites for the implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area; Rethinking Education: Towards Achieving the African Renaissance; and Reclaiming and Reconceptualizing African Arts, Culture, and Heritage.

The conference brought together scholars, artists, political and economic decision-makers, traditional leaders, civil society activists, professionals, and practitioners from across the continent and from the African diaspora to share the results of their research, collaborative work, and practices that address the above-mentioned issues. The overall aim of the event was to provide the platform for key discussions by stakeholders towards reclaiming and recontextualizing African education, technology, politics, languages, histories, arts, culture, music, and spirituality and to heighten the need for a conscious effort of unification in these endeavors for Africa’s rapid development.

At the opening ceremony, the Secretary General of the Association of African Universities (AAU), Prof. Olusola Oyewole, underscored the need for Africans to own our heritage and the relevance of events such as the Diaspora Conference in promoting the African culture. While stating that the AAU welcomes collaborations in this focus area, Prof. Oyewole further called on stakeholders to promote this agenda in the various higher education institutions, especially in this era of Afrofuturism and Pan-Africanism.

Key issues raised from the discussions and engagements included the need to transform the curricula of African higher education institutions to respond to the challenges faced by the continent, as well as the need to teach the history of Africa, as lessons from history are critical in mapping the way forward for the development and decolonization of Africa.

Dr. Kayode Aderinsola of the Durban University of Technology, South Africa/University of Ibadan, Nigeria, mentioned in his submission, that the design of the African curricula lacks indigenous knowledge, cultural values, and black consciousness. He called for a quick review of the curricula currently being followed by higher education institution across the continent, while stressing the need for a clear indication of what content should be decolonized in the African curricula.

Dr. Meghoo and Dr. Kayode recommended the need for a paradigm shift (not necessarily a reinvention), which should be in the form of a reconceptualizing and repositioning of the curricula of African higher education institutions to help solve the current and future problems of Africa. According to him, this should aim at promoting solidarity among Africans and training the youth to address African problems, with home grown solutions.

According to the representative to the African Union endorsed Diaspora African Forum, Dr. Desta Meghoo, Pan Africanism, and Afrofuturism are two powerful tools capable of transforming the African educational system, preserving African heritage, and reclaiming African heritage. Dr. Meghooo indicated that rebooting our indigenous traditional knowledge ignites intellect and values, and thus Africans must remember our dismembered identity. Adding to this, the Quality Assurance Expert of the Association of African Universities, Dr. Violet Makuku, postulated that, for the African continent to solve its problems and promote peace, it is necessary for us to take responsibility for these issues, and thus the time to act is now.

A documentary by Emerita Prof. Sheila Walker, Professor of Anthropology and Documentary Filmmaker/Executive Director of Afrodiaspora, Inc., titled Familiar Faces/Unexpected Places, suggests African technology, spirituality, and culture have been transformed to form and make sense of modern-day civilization in the Global African Diaspora. As such, to restore African dignity and culture, Dr. Laniser Kitchiner proposes “a just compensation” to aggrieved countries and recommends that restitution should adopt an object-centered approach and be geared towards addressing intangible cultural knowledge to understand indigenous African knowledge. All of which can be done through educational campaigns to drive the robust knowledge of African heritage.

The three-day conference concluded with the Chair of the conference planning committee, Prof. Pashington Obeng, commending the stakeholders for their insightful suggestions and contributions. He highlighted the need to follow up on the development of home-grown solutions for Africans to solve our own problems in our quest to achieve the Africa we want.

Other collaborators were PANAFEST, the Ghana National House of Chiefs, the Ghana Cultural Forum, the Diaspora African Forum, the African Private Sector Summit (APSS), the Global Institute of Planning and Sustainable Development (GIPSD), and the All-African Students Union (AASU).

TITLE: 2026-2027 Fulbright Distinguished Awards in Teaching Program for International Teachers

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Fulbright Distinguished Awards in Teaching Program for International Teachers (Fulbright DAI) is sponsored by the Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs, U.S. Department of State. It is part of the overall Fulbright Program, named in honor of Senator J. William Fulbright, which promotes mutual understanding among people of the United States and other countries. The program will bring approximately 22 international teachers to the U.S. for a semester. For international teachers, the program is open to teachers from Botswana, Brazil, Finland, Greece, India, Indonesia, Israel, Mexico, Morocco, New Zealand, Philippines, Senegal, Singapore, Taiwan, and United Kingdom. Two teachers from India will participate in the program.

Fulbright DAI Program is a semester-long non-degree, non-credit, professional development program at a U.S. university. Selected international participants will be placed at a U.S. host university School of Education from August 2027 to December 2027. The program will provide participants with a unique opportunity to develop greater expertise in their subject areas, enhance their teaching skills, increase their knowledge about the United States, and complete an individual or group project. Participants will audit courses in the host university’s school or department of education and thus will be part of the university community. The program will include opportunities to observe and co-teach with U.S. teachers in a U.S. school near the host university, to actively engage participants in the U.S. classroom environment. Cultural enrichment, mentoring, and support will be provided throughout the program.

After returning home, teachers who successfully complete the program will be eligible to compete for small grants awards for essential teaching materials, to offer follow-on training for other teachers, collaborative projects between participating American schools, and other activities that build on the exchange experience. Grant competitions are contingent on federal funding and may not be offered every year.

Eligibility Requirements

The applicant should:

be a citizen of India and reside in India at the time of application.

live and teach in the states of Chandigarh, Delhi, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Punjab, Rajasthan, Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Goa, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu.

hold at least a bachelor’s degree. A teacher training degree is preferred.

be a full-time teacher teaching any subject at any level (primary, middle, secondary, or senior secondary).

primary and secondary level library media specialists, guidance counselors, curriculum specialists, special education coordinators, and administrators who spend at least fifty percent of their time teaching or working directly with students may also apply to the program.

Teacher trainers working with elementary, or secondary pre-service or in-service teachers are eligible to apply.

have completed at least five years of full-time teaching experience by the application deadline.

demonstrate English language skills adequate to audit university courses and to teach, lead seminars, and give presentations in U.S. schools.

demonstrate a commitment to continue teaching or working in their field for at least five years after completion of the program.

If you have taken any standard test of English language proficiency such as the iBT TOEFL, please attach a photocopy of the score report to your application. If you have not taken TOEFL and are selected as a nominee, you will be required to take the iBT TOEFL in June 2026. USIEF will provide fee vouchers towards the TOEFL exam. The nominee should possess an internet based TOEFL score of 61.

Fulbright DAI is a program for practicing teachers and other educators working in elementary or secondary schools. Ministry of Education officials, full-time principals or educational administrators, university faculty, private English Language tutors, part-time teachers are not eligible. The Fulbright DAI Program is not designed for PhD research.

Provisions of the Fellowship

J-1 visa support;

A pre-departure orientation in India;

Round-trip airfare to and within the U.S.;

Academic program fees;

Housing and meals;

Accident and sickness medical insurance coverage (does not cover pre-existing conditions);

Transportation to the local school (if necessary);

A daily allowance for incidentals during the university academic program;

A professional development allowance;

A baggage allowance to offset the cost of travel;

A technology allowance; and

The opportunity to apply for alumni small grants for alumni in good standing (contingent on federal funding).

Dependents cannot accompany the program participants.

Selection Process

Fellows will be selected through a merit-based open competition. After the application deadline, a screening committee will review all eligible applications. Short-listed candidates will be interviewed by a committee which will select nominees whose names will be forwarded to Washington, D.C. for further consideration. All nominations from the participating countries will be reviewed by independent panels of educational experts in Washington, D.C. The panel will then recommend selected applications for further consideration and approval by the J. William Fulbright Foreign Scholarship Board (FFSB). All candidates will be notified of their status in December 2026.

Selection Criteria (not in order of importance)

Demonstrated commitment to elementary or secondary education;

Demonstrated leadership potential;

Professional and educational experience and achievements;

Potential for developing long-term linkages between U.S. and Indian educational institutions and schools;

Preparedness (including maturity, flexibility, and ability to function independently) for an intensive U.S.-based training program with very limited free time for personal travel or sightseeing;

Willingness and capacity to work and live collaboratively with international peers to foster a positive learning community for professional development;

Articulated ideas for applying program experience to improving primary or secondary education in home country upon return;

Ability to express ideas clearly and effectively;

English language skills adequate to manage coursework, develop lesson plans, and team-teach in U.S. schools.

Preference will also be given to applicants who have had few or no opportunities to travel to the U.S., and who have not previously received a Fulbright grant. Preference will be given to qualified candidates who have not previously had a Fulbright and to those who have not had substantial recent experience in the United States. Applicants with previous professional experience in the United States should demonstrate in their applications, how they have implemented in their teaching practice what they learned during this experience. Please note that this program is not intended for alumni of the International Leaders in Education Program.

A candidate who has resided in the United States for five or more consecutive years in the six-year period preceding the date of application is ineligible for a grant. A candidate who has lived in the United States for nine months or more during a calendar year is deemed to have resided abroad for that year; and

If a person received an advanced degree from the United States, preference will be given to those who completed their degree at least 8 years ago.

Application Process

You must submit an application online. Click https://fulbright.irex.org/ to access the online application.

Early May 2026

Interviews of short-listed candidates:
End May 2026

Notification of finalists:
December 2026

Pre-departure orientation in India

TITLE: Call for Expressions of Interest:  Participation in a Computational & Artificial Intelligence Engagement Planning Workshop

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The IEEE Computational Intelligence Society (CIS) and the Association of African Universities (AAU) aim to develop a program for stakeholders in Africa to increase their engagement in computational and artificial intelligence (AI).

This program is motivated by the limited participation of African academics in computational and artificial intelligence – in comparison to the rest of the world. This is evidenced, for example, by the comparatively low numbers of papers submitted and/or published at premier AI conferences and journals by African authors. In addition, to date, there has been limited ‘bottom-up’ activity to establish support and engagement mechanisms such as via IEEE CIS membership and academic community engagement such as via CIS Chapters across most of Africa.

As its overall outcome, the program targets an increase in CI/AI engagement, evidenced including through increased activity such as submission/publication of papers, CIS memberships, and Chapters from the African continent, including from academic, industry, and government stakeholders.

This Call for Expression of Interest

The AAU and the IEEE CIS are calling for academics based in Ghana, Liberia, Sierra Leone, and The Gambia that are keen to be involved in the computational and artificial intelligence program of activities, to respond to this call. The academics that are being targeted include:

Lecturers, researchers and professors whose speciality is broadly in computer science, engineering, STEM and related areas.

Recent PhD graduates / post-docs and PhD students whose speciality is broadly in computer science, engineering, STEM and related areas.

Successful applicants will be engaged in an initial, virtual planning workshop with the following objectives:

Discuss and establish local priorities in the field of computational and artificial intelligence.

Discuss existing barriers and identify primary needs/ requirements/ activities which would be of benefit to support improved engagement with computational and artificial intelligence (CI/AI).

Discuss existing engagement programs run by IEEE CIS, including:

IEEE CIS International Mentoring Program

IEEE CIS Paper Development Workshop

Jointly co-design a plan for a range of engagement activities to be organised at future events.

Targeted Outcomes of this planning workshop

A list of identified local stakeholders who are interested in attending and/or contributing to future engagement activities, including through hosting such events.

A plan for future joint CIS-AAU CI/AI engagement activities for both established and new stakeholders in Africa, complete with associated timeframe, planned activities, and location(s).

How to submit the Expression of Interest

Interested academics are requested to submit their interests by completing the online form via this link: https://forms.office.com/r/15EnwAfDP5

Deadlines and Notification of Acceptance

The deadline for submission of the expressions of interest is close of business on Friday, 6th April 2024. We aim to send notification of acceptance to the planning workshop within three weeks of the above submission deadline.

TITLE: Jean King Whelan, Ph.D.

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Organic Geochemist, WHOI Oceanographer Emeritus

At WHOI, “I was amongst the best people in the world doing oceanography.”

Jean King Whelan, a WHOI organic geochemist, began her life in Reno, Nevada. One of her first mentors was her grandfather, Stanley Palmer, who was the Dean of Engineering at the University of Nevada. Whelan attributed her interest in science to the practical skills she learned from him.

Whelan was a disciplined and conscientious student, and musically inclined. She was one of only two girls in her high school trigonometry class. With the encouragement of her high school chemistry teacher, Whelan applied for the California State Scholarship, and it provided enough financial support that she could attend the University of California Davis.

At Davis, Whelan was one of the only women in her discipline. She was mentored by her organic chemistry professor and worked in his laboratory. Next, she completed a doctorate in organic chemistry at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and did postdoctoral work at Brandeis University. She taught chemistry at Fairleigh Dickinson University for eight years. Her colleagues’ work at Fairleigh’s marine laboratory in St. Croix sparked her interest in how organic chemistry could be used in ocean studies and she pursued a sabbatical at WHOI. While at WHOI, she worked in John Farrington’s lab and went to sea. During this sabbatical, she fell in love with oceanography.

Whelan on the D/V Glomar Challenger, 1977, reading data from gas chromatograph. (U.C. San Diego Library Digital Collections)
“No matter who’s around you, you learn stuff from them.”

Whelan returned to WHOI in the early 1970s as a guest investigator. In 1975 she was one of the first women to join the technical staff in the Department of Marine Chemistry and Geochemistry. She entered the field of organic chemistry at a time when instrumentation was advancing rapidly, especially at WHOI.

Whelan worked with WHOI senior scientist John Hunt, a founder of the organic geochemistry field. She ran his lab and conducted her own research which focused on gases, primarily methane and light hydrocarbons in ocean sediments and water. Her work developing a technique to measure heavy hydrocarbons in gases was so successful that she was asked to bring her system to the drilling vessel Glomar Challenger so that it could be used at sea. In 1983, Whelan became WHOI’s first woman senior research specialist.

Whelan and John Farrington with her pyrolysis apparatus in the lab in 1970. (Photo by Shelley Dawicki, Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution)
Hunt heard about an instrument that French scientists used to study oil generation and he wanted one for his lab. Whelan designed and built one, based on what he described. It heated sediment until hydrocarbons were generated, which could be separated and measured with a gas chromatograph. After building it, Whelan and Hunt learned that the French instrument was just a rumor. Her instrument was the first of its kind.

Onboard the D/V Glomar Challenger, 1983. (U.C. San Diego Library Digial Collections)
At WHOI, Whelan focused on pyrolysis analysis and methane and light hydrocarbons in ocean sediments and waters. She also focused on oil and gas migration processes. Whelan was a leader in the discovery and study of gas reservoirs beneath the sea floor and worked with WHOI engineers to develop instruments to monitor them continuously. Later in her career, Whelan spent time educating the public and funding agencies about the ramifications of a seeping gas system for the earth and atmosphere.

Whelan Aboard the D/V Glomar Challenger, 1977. (U.C. San Diego Library Digial Collections)
Whelan received millions of dollars in grants during her time at WHOI. She was known for her positive attitude, infectious enthusiasm, and was a mentor to many young scientists.

Whelan was an early advocate for inclusion at WHOI and was committed to leadership and mentorship within the scientific and technical staff. She founded the Robert Whelan Award in memory of her husband. This honor is open to all full-time members of the department, with an emphasis on groups that are commonly neglected by other institutional grants. In 1992, she was the first woman to chair the Organic Geochemistry Gordon Research Conference and, in 1998, she won WHOI’s Linda Morse-Porteus Award.

In 1992, Jean Whelan was the first woman to chair the Organic Geochemistry Gordon Research Conference. (Courtesy Ben Van Mooy, Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution)

TITLE: Morgan Stanley 2027 Investment Management Sophomore Summer Analyst Program in New York: Private Credit & Equity Internship

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Are you an undergraduate student interested in investment management, private credit, private equity, financial analysis, valuation, and private-market investing? Morgan Stanley is offering a 10-week 2027 Investment Management Sophomore Summer Analyst Program – Private Credit & Equity in New York, United States.

The program is designed for undergraduate students who want to gain practical exposure to the investment management industry and develop skills that are relevant to careers in private markets and investment analysis.

Participants will join Morgan Stanley Investment Management’s Tactical Value team, where they will work alongside investment professionals on research, financial analysis, investment opportunities, portfolio monitoring, and other activities connected to the investment decision-making process.

The application deadline is September 25, 2026, at 11:55 PM Eastern Time (ET), while applicants must complete their HireVue digital questionnaire by September 27, 2026, at 11:55 PM ET.

About Morgan Stanley Investment Management

Morgan Stanley Investment Management (MSIM), together with its investment advisory affiliates, operates as part of Morgan Stanley’s global investment management platform. According to the opportunity description, MSIM has more than 1,300 investment professionals worldwide and $2 trillion in assets under management or supervision as of June 30, 2026.

Morgan Stanley describes its investment management business as focused on providing long-term investment performance, client service, and investment management solutions to a diverse range of clients, including governments, institutions, corporations, and individual investors.

Morgan Stanley also maintains a dedicated careers platform for students, graduates, and experienced professionals, with opportunities across investment banking, investment management, wealth management, technology, and other areas.

Opportunity Overview

The 2027 Investment Management Sophomore Summer Analyst Program – Private Credit & Equity is a 10-week summer internship beginning in June 2027.

The program combines formal training with practical experience inside a specific Investment Management team.

The structure includes:

One week of training

Nine weeks working within the assigned Investment Management team

During the program, Summer Analysts are expected to gain exposure to the professional environment of Morgan Stanley and perform work that is similar in nature to the responsibilities of a full-time Analyst.

The program is designed as a learning and development opportunity. Morgan Stanley specifically notes that participation in this role does not necessarily correlate with full-time opportunities within the firm.

Program Location

Location: New York, United States

The position is based within Morgan Stanley’s Investment Management business in New York.

Morgan Stanley maintains a global presence and states that its employees work across 41 countries, with opportunities available to students and graduates in different regions.

Team: Tactical Value

Successful participants will join the Tactical Value team.

The Tactical Value team focuses on identifying and evaluating opportunistic investment opportunities across private markets.

This provides Summer Analysts with an opportunity to learn about how investment professionals examine potential investments, conduct research, assess companies and industries, evaluate financial information, and contribute to the investment process.

Summer Analysts will work with senior members of the Fund to conduct due diligence on potential investment opportunities.

Due diligence involves gathering and analyzing information about a prospective investment so that investment professionals can better understand its financial position, business model, industry, risks, opportunities, and overall investment characteristics.

Participants can therefore gain insight into portfolio management and ongoing investment analysis.

Broader market trends

TITLE: AAU Successfully Holds a Workshop on Best Practices in the Management of Higher and Tertiary Education Funded Projects

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
From February 2nd – 17th 2021, the Association of African Universities hosted a virtual workshop to equip participants with the requisite knowledge to enable them better manage Higher and Tertiary Education Projects, which are funded by development partners.

Having the skill to excellently manage such projects is critical in ensuring that Higher Education Institutions build a good track record for themselves, and therefore enhance their chances of getting more grants and funding to scale up their current projects or to implement new projects for the benefit of their institutions. This is a key reason why more institutions are encouraged to get involved or participate in the next workshops that the AAU will organise on this topic.

The February 2021 edition of this workshop recorded participants attending from Ghana, Egypt, Nigeria, Kenya, Uganda and Lesotho. The sessions were facilitated by Dr Violet Makuku, the AAU Quality Assurance Specialist, and co-facilitated by Mr. Osondu Joshua Onwuzuruigbo, an experienced expert on this topic, who has managed several development funded projects himself. Miss Pamela Boamah of the AAU Workshops Unit also supported the overall coordination and organization of the workshop.

In the first session of the above-named workshop, Mr. ONWUZURUIGBO listed key aspects to be considered by any project Implementing team. These included, but were not limited to; Basic Project Documentation, Planning and Control, Implementation Drivers, Personality Catalyst and Project Closure. “One must have a good understanding of three important documents namely, i) the Initial Project Document (which include the Grant Request Proposal and Grant Negotiation), ii) Project Appraisal Report (the document that receives the final approval of the apex authority of the donor) and iii) the Grant Agreement (the legal document without which one can do nothing)” he added.

Mr Onwuzuruigbo also thoroughly took participants through some concepts such as the Grant Agreement, the Purpose of a Grant, Objectives, Implementation, Disbursement, Grant Amount, Recipient’s Representative, Closing Date for Last Imbursement, Commitment to Project, Resolution of Disputes, Anti-Corruption and UN Sanctions.

He further elaborated on certain threats to personality issues and these included – Time Management, Communication Skills, Record Keeping and Integrity. “They all have to be treated and handled carefully,” he said. He advised that Record Keeping and discarding of information should be done properly with some high level of integrity. “Do the right thing at the right time to help people achieve certain set goals,” he added. Summing up his presentation, he said that grants and development partner funding should not be regarded as free money to be spent anyhow but should be handled with utmost care in a fashion which ensures every cent can be accounted for.

Dr. Violet Makuku, the Workshops Coordinator, co-facilitator of the workshop and a Quality Assurance Specialist explained that since AAU is a non-profit organization whose motive is to promote African Higher and Tertiary Education to the highest level, fees charged for the workshops are meant to help maintenance and expansion of platforms, paying facilitators and making sure that good Internet services are available. This helps to offer better services to participants.

Professor Ehile Etienne climaxed the event by urging participants to continue taking part in the AAU organized workshops and events so that they become more equipped with knowledge and skills to help move their institutions forward. He also encouraged participants to make use of the knowledge and skills acquired during the workshops and share it with others for the benefit of themselves, their institutions and ultimately African Higher Education in general.

TITLE: Wilson Center Research Fellowship 2027-2028 ($10,000 stipend)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 30, 2026

Applications are open for the Wilson Center Research Fellowship 2027-2028. The Wilson Center invites scholars, practitioners, journalists, and public intellectuals to take part in its flagship Research Fellowship Program. Fellows conduct research and write in their areas of interest, while interacting with policymakers in Washington and other fellows. The Center accepts policy-relevant, nonpartisan fellowship proposals that address key foreign policy challenges confronting the United States and the world.

Fellows will work remotely during their tenure with the Wilson Center. The program will include a trip to Washington D.C. at the start and end of the fellowship, as paid for by the Wilson Center. The fellowship will commence on June 1, 2027, and end on May 30, 2028.

Stipend

The Center offers a stipend of $10,000 per month for a twelve-month fellowship.

Applicants from academia must have a PhD and have published a book or monograph beyond the PhD dissertation, or a substantial body of research articles (typically five or more) in reputable peer-reviewed journals.

Applicants must be proficient in English, as the Center is designed to encourage the exchange of ideas among its fellows and provide educational opportunities to Congress.

Applicants must be able to attend a fellowship kick-off meeting in June 2027 and a fellowship conclusion meeting in May 2028, both held at the Wilson Center in Washington D.C.

If resident in the United States, applicants must be U.S. citizens or legal permanent residents, as the Wilson Center is not able to sponsor J-1 visas. TITLE: 2027 NASA Hubble Fellowship Program (NHFP): Postdoctoral Fellowship in Astrophysics for International Scientists

Administered by the Space Telescope Science Institute (STScI) on behalf of the NASA Astrophysics Division, the program supports researchers working in astronomy, physics, and related disciplines. Successful applicants will join one of three fellowship tracks — Einstein, Hubble, or Sagan Fellow — depending on their area of research.

The fellowship provides an opportunity for early-career scientists to pursue independent theoretical, observational, and/or instrumental research at a U.S. host institution of their choice, subject to the program’s host-institution rules.

Applications for the 2027 fellowship cycle opened on September 8, 2026, with applications due on October 28, 2026.

The NASA Hubble Fellowship Program is a postdoctoral research fellowship program administered for NASA by the Space Telescope Science Institute (STScI).

The program is designed to support postdoctoral scientists conducting independent research that contributes to NASA’s astrophysics mission.

Research supported through the program can be:

Theoretical

Observational

Instrumental

Or a combination of these approaches

The program gives early-career scientists an opportunity to develop an independent research program while working at a U.S. host institution.

Depending on the research area, successful fellows will be designated as:

NASA Einstein Fellows

NASA Hubble Fellows

NASA Sagan Fellows

These fellowship designations correspond to different areas of astrophysical research within the broader NHFP program.

Astronomy

Physics

Or a related discipline

The program is therefore specifically designed for researchers at the postdoctoral stage who have recently completed, or are about to complete, their doctoral training.

Research Areas

NHFP fellows are expected to conduct independent research that contributes to NASA Astrophysics.

The program allows research to be theoretical, observational, instrumental, or a combination of these approaches.

This broad research structure means that applicants working across different areas of astrophysics may be able to develop fellowship proposals aligned with their specific scientific interests and expertise.

The fellowship designation awarded to a successful applicant — Einstein, Hubble, or Sagan — will depend on the applicant’s research area.

Fellowship Duration

The NASA Hubble Fellowship can last for up to three years.

The fellowship is structured as:

First annual renewal

Second annual renewal

Satisfactory performance

Availability of NASA funding

Therefore, although the program offers the possibility of a three-year fellowship, continuation beyond the initial appointment is not described as unconditional.

U.S. Host Institution

However, the program places limits on the number of new fellows that can be hosted by an individual institution.

This collaborative structure connects the fellowship with several major institutions involved in astrophysical research.

The central purpose of the NHFP is to support postdoctoral scientists conducting independent research.

Research may involve theoretical investigations, observations, instrumentation, or combinations of these approaches.

The independent nature of the fellowship is particularly important because it allows postdoctoral researchers to develop their own research programs and contribute to the broader scientific objectives of NASA Astrophysics.

TITLE: Citi Foundation Global Innovation Challenge 2026: Apply for US$500,000 to Prepare Youth for an AI-Driven Future

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Citi Foundation Global Innovation Challenge 2026 is inviting eligible nonprofit organizations to submit proposals for innovative programmes that prepare low-income young people for employment in an increasingly artificial intelligence (AI)-driven economy.

Through its fourth Global Innovation Challenge, the Citi Foundation is committing US$25 million in total funding to support approximately 50 community organizations, with each selected organization expected to receive a restricted grant of US$500,000.

The initiative focuses on helping young people develop relevant AI, digital, and human-centred skills, improve access to technology, connect with employment opportunities, and strengthen existing youth employability programmes. It is designed to support organizations developing practical, scalable, and innovative solutions that promote economic mobility for low-income youth.

The Letter of Inquiry (LOI) deadline is October 6, 2026, at 12:00 p.m. New York Time (Eastern Time).

Opportunity Overview

Opportunity: Fourth Global Innovation Challenge: Preparing Youth for AI

Funder: Citi Foundation

Funding Type: Restricted grant

Total Funding: US$25 million

Expected Number of Grantees: Up to 50 organizations

Expected Grant Amount: US$500,000 per selected organization

Grant Duration: 24 months

Expected Grant Start: No earlier than June 1, 2027

Primary Beneficiaries: Low-income youth, primarily ages 15 to 24

Eligible Applicants: Registered nonprofit organizations

Geographic Scope: Select countries and communities where Citi has a presence

First-Stage Application: Letter of Inquiry

LOI Deadline: October 6, 2026, at 12:00 p.m. Eastern Time

Expected LOI Decision Notification: By the end of November 2026

Expected Final Funding Decisions: No later than the end of May 2027

The application and announcement timelines are subject to change. Applicants should consult the official Citi Foundation Request for Proposals documentation for the latest information before submitting.

About the Citi Foundation Global Innovation Challenge

The Citi Foundation’s Global Innovation Challenge is a philanthropic funding initiative that supports community organizations developing innovative responses to major social and economic challenges affecting low-income communities.

The 2026 edition focuses on preparing youth for the changing world of work. As AI and digital technologies increasingly influence recruitment, job roles, workplace productivity, and business operations, young people need access to both technical and human-centred capabilities.

The Foundation recognizes that low-income youth may face significant barriers to participating in the AI-enabled economy. These barriers can include:

Limited access to reliable internet connectivity.

Inadequate access to computers, smartphones, and digital tools.

Gaps between existing education or training and emerging labour-market needs.

Limited exposure to AI technologies.

Lack of employment networks and career guidance.

Insufficient opportunities to gain practical experience.

Unequal access to training in digital and human-centred skills.

The challenge therefore seeks to support nonprofit organizations that can develop or expand solutions addressing these barriers and helping young people become more prepared for employment.

The Foundation’s announcement states that the challenge will support programmes that combine AI and digital capabilities with skills such as critical thinking, creativity, adaptability, resilience, and problem-solving. These complementary skills are important because young people will need more than technical knowledge to use AI responsibly and effectively in the workplace.

Why Preparing Youth for AI Matters

Artificial intelligence is transforming industries, job functions, recruitment practices, and the skills employers seek. While AI creates new opportunities, it can also deepen existing inequalities if young people from low-income communities lack access to the tools and training required to participate.

The challenge is based on the understanding that youth employability in the AI-driven economy requires a combination of:

Technical AI literacy

Digital access

Practical workplace readiness

Human-centred skills

Career and employment support

Responsible and ethical use of technology

The Foundation’s Request for Proposals highlights the importance of helping youth understand, guide, interpret, and apply AI tools rather than simply teaching technical concepts in isolation.

The programme is particularly relevant for organizations working with young people who are underserved by traditional education, training, technology, and employment systems.

Focus Areas of the Global Innovation Challenge

The Citi Foundation identifies three major focus areas for potential proposals. Organizations may develop projects within one or more of these areas, provided their solutions align with the overall goal of preparing low-income youth for employment.

1. Cultivating AI and Human-Centric Skills for Youth Employment

The first focus area supports programmes that help low-income youth develop AI-related and human-centred skills relevant to the workplace.

Potential activities may include training in:

AI fundamentals.

AI literacy.

Ethical considerations in the use of AI.

Prompt engineering.

Digital content creation.

AI-enabled workplace tools.

Digital productivity.

Problem-solving.

Critical thinking.

Advanced reasoning.

Creativity.

Adaptability.

Resilience.

Communication and collaboration.

The Foundation is interested in approaches that connect technical AI skills with broader employability capabilities. For example, a programme might teach young people how to use AI tools for research, content creation, data analysis, job applications, or business operations while also helping them develop judgment, creativity, communication, and problem-solving skills.

Strong proposals should demonstrate how the training will lead to practical employment outcomes, such as improved job readiness, access to work opportunities, stronger career pathways, or better alignment with employer needs.

2. Expanding Digital Access

The second focus area supports solutions that improve young people’s access to digital resources and opportunities.

Digital access may involve more than providing internet connectivity. It can also include access to devices, software, safe learning environments, relevant digital tools, and platforms that enable young people to participate in the digital economy.

Potential examples include:

Community technology hubs.

Shared computer or device facilities.

Digital learning centres.

Open-source AI tools.

Low-connectivity digital platforms.

Offline learning resources.

Digital literacy programmes.

Connectivity solutions.

Technology access linked to employment services.

Platforms that connect youth to jobs, internships, apprenticeships, or career opportunities.

This focus area is especially relevant for communities where young people may have limited or unreliable internet access. According to the supplied RFP, approximately 2.2 billion young people globally lack internet access at home, creating barriers to economic participation and mobility.

Proposals should explain how digital access will be connected to meaningful learning, employment, or economic outcomes rather than treating technology distribution as an isolated activity.

3. Building Support for NGO Capacity and Networks

The third focus area supports efforts to strengthen nonprofit organizations’ existing youth employability programmes by integrating AI-enabled tools, training, and resources.

It also encourages organizations to build or expand partnerships and networks across sectors, including:

Education institutions.

Nonprofit organizations.

Technology companies.

Employers.

Government agencies.

Training providers.

Youth-serving organizations.

Community groups.

Research institutions.

Workforce development organizations.

Potential activities may include:

Integrating AI tools into existing youth employment programmes.

Training nonprofit staff to use emerging technologies.

Developing shared curricula or resources.

Building cross-sector partnerships.

Establishing employer networks.

Sharing best practices.

Creating learning communities.

Strengthening monitoring and evaluation systems.

Improving organizational capacity to adapt to changing workforce needs.

The Foundation is interested in solutions that promote continuous learning and adaptation because AI-related skills and labour-market requirements are evolving rapidly.

Funding Amount and Grant Structure

The Citi Foundation plans to award up to 50 restricted grants of US$500,000 each, representing a total commitment of US$25 million.

The grants are expected to be distributed over a 24-month period. The anticipated disbursement structure is:

US$250,000 in Year 1, expected in 2027

US$250,000 in Year 2, expected in 2028

The grant period is expected to begin no earlier than June 1, 2027.

Because the grants are restricted, funding must be used for the specific programme and eligible expenses described in the successful application. Organizations should develop realistic budgets that clearly connect proposed costs to programme activities, outcomes, and implementation plans.

Additional Support Beyond the Grant

In addition to financial support, the Citi Foundation intends to explore ways to support selected grantees through:

Citi employee volunteerism.

A learning community.

Knowledge exchange.

Shared lessons and best practices.

Networking opportunities.

Capacity-building activities.

Opportunities to learn from other grantee organizations.

This additional support may help selected organizations strengthen implementation, improve their approaches, and develop relationships with other organizations working on youth employability and AI readiness.

However, applicants should understand that these additional forms of support are described as potential opportunities and should not be treated as guaranteed benefits beyond the grant award.

Eligible Organizations

The opportunity is intended for registered nonprofit organizations that meet the Foundation’s eligibility requirements.

To be eligible, an organization must generally meet the following conditions:

1. Focus on Low-Income Communities

The organization must demonstrate that its mission or strategic priorities specifically focus on serving low-income individuals or communities.

Applicants should be able to explain:

Which low-income populations they serve.

The barriers faced by their target beneficiaries.

How their proposed programme addresses those barriers.

Why their organization is well-positioned to deliver the proposed solution.

2. Operate or Deliver Impact in an Eligible Geography

The proposed programme must impact at least one of the Foundation’s target geographies.

An organization does not necessarily need to be headquartered in one of the listed countries or regions. However, the programme for which funding is requested must benefit communities within the Foundation’s eligible geographic scope.

3. Be Registered as a Nonprofit Entity

Organizations must be registered as nonprofit entities under applicable local law.

For example, U.S.-based applicants must generally be tax-exempt public charities under Section 501(c)(3) of the U.S. Internal Revenue Code.

Organizations that require fiscal sponsorship are not eligible for this specific funding opportunity.

4. Have the Required Financial Documentation

Organizations invited to the full application stage must be able to provide externally audited financial statements covering at least part of calendar year 2024 or a subsequent year by the anticipated application deadline in early December 2026.

The audited financial documents must include:

An auditor’s signed letter.

Complete financial statements.

Auditor’s notes.

Organizations that cannot meet this requirement should carefully review the eligibility rules before submitting an LOI.

Can Organizations Based Outside the United States Apply?

CAF America will ultimately make the final approval decision for grants to organizations based outside the United States and will have oversight responsibility during the grant term.

Application Process

The Citi Foundation Global Innovation Challenge will use a competitive, two-stage application process.

Round 1: Letter of Inquiry

Interested organizations must first submit a Letter of Inquiry (LOI) through the Foundation’s grant portal.

The LOI is intended to help the Foundation assess whether the organization and proposed programme align with the goals of the Global Innovation Challenge.

The Foundation will review submissions based on factors including:

Strategic alignment.

Feasibility.

Potential for impact.

Organizational eligibility.

Relevance to low-income youth.

Innovation and practicality of the proposed solution.

Alignment with the AI and workforce-readiness focus.

Round 2: Full Grant Application

The Foundation aims to notify organizations by the end of November 2026 whether they will be invited to submit a full grant application.

Organizations invited to Round 2 will receive additional instructions regarding:

The full application process.

Required documents.

Detailed programme information.

Budget requirements.

Monitoring and evaluation expectations.

Submission deadlines.

Grant terms and conditions.

An invitation to submit a full application does not guarantee funding. It is only an invitation to continue in the competitive process.

Final funding decisions are anticipated to be communicated to recipient organizations no later than the end of May 2027.

How to Prepare the Letter of Inquiry

The LOI is the first opportunity for an organization to communicate its programme concept to the Foundation. Applicants should use it to present a clear, compelling, and evidence-informed explanation of the proposed solution.

A strong LOI should clearly address the following areas:

1. Define the Problem

Explain the specific barriers low-income youth face in the target community or geography.

For example, the problem may involve:

Limited access to digital devices.

Low AI literacy.

Lack of employment-focused training.

Skills mismatches.

Limited access to employers.

Inadequate career guidance.

Poor connectivity.

Lack of opportunities to practise digital skills.

The problem statement should be specific rather than relying only on broad statements about AI or youth unemployment.

2. Describe the Proposed Solution

Explain what the organization intends to implement, improve, pilot, or scale.

The proposal should clarify:

What the programme will do.

Who it will serve.

Where it will operate.

How it will work.

Why the approach is innovative.

How it differs from existing programmes.

What makes it practical and scalable.

3. Explain the AI and Human-Centric Skills Connection

The programme should demonstrate how it will prepare young people for employment in an AI-influenced economy.

Applicants should explain whether the programme will provide:

AI fundamentals.

Prompt engineering.

Digital content creation.

AI-enabled tools.

Digital literacy.

Critical thinking.

Creativity.

Problem-solving.

Communication.

Adaptability.

Resilience.

Ethical and responsible technology use.

4. Identify Expected Outcomes

Applicants should explain how they will measure progress and impact.

Potential outcomes may include:

Number of youth trained.

Number of youth gaining digital or AI skills.

Number of participants completing training.

Number of participants accessing employment opportunities.

Number of youth placed in jobs, internships, or apprenticeships.

Improvements in digital literacy.

Improvements in job-readiness skills.

Increased access to devices or connectivity.

Employer partnerships established.

Increased income or economic mobility.

Improved organizational capacity.

5. Demonstrate Organizational Readiness

The Foundation will want to understand whether the organization has the experience, staff, partnerships, systems, and resources needed to deliver the proposed programme.

Applicants should be prepared to demonstrate:

Relevant programme experience.

Knowledge of the target community.

Qualified staff.

Implementation capacity.

Financial management systems.

Monitoring and evaluation capacity.

Partnerships and stakeholder relationships.

Experience serving low-income populations.

Eligible Expenses

Funding will be restricted to the programme and expenses defined in the application.

Potential eligible expenses may include:

Staff salaries.

Technology.

Programme materials.

Training activities.

Events.

Research.

Communications.

Marketing.

Monitoring and evaluation.

Convenings.

Overhead.

Other programme-related costs approved under the grant terms.

Applicants should ensure that every budget item is clearly connected to programme implementation and intended outcomes.

Regranting and Partnerships

Organizations may include regranting in their proposed programme budget if there is a clear programme rationale and implementation plan.

Regranting refers to redistributing part of the Foundation’s funds to another organization, including local affiliates. Vendor payments for goods or services are not considered regrants.

Organizations may also work with partners. However, a single lead organization must submit the LOI on behalf of the partnership.

If a partnership advances to the full application stage and is selected for funding:

The lead organization will receive the grant.

The lead organization will be responsible for the full grant award.

The lead organization will be responsible for programme deliverables.

The lead organization must ensure that partners comply with the Foundation’s grant terms.

Organizations should agree in advance on roles, responsibilities, governance, financial arrangements, and accountability.

Important Restrictions

Applicants should be aware of several restrictions associated with the grant.

No Fiscal Sponsorship

Organizations that require a fiscal sponsor are not eligible to apply for this specific opportunity.

No Political or Lobbying Activities

Grant funds cannot be used directly or indirectly for political or lobbying purposes. This includes activities such as:

Participating in or intervening in political campaigns.

Supporting or opposing political candidates.

Voter registration activities.

Get-out-the-vote activities.

Independent expenditures supporting or opposing political parties or candidates.

Attempting to influence legislation or legislative bodies.

One LOI per Organization

Eligible nonprofit organizations may submit only one LOI.

Separate organizations should not submit multiple LOIs for the same programme. Local affiliates that are separate legal entities and independently meet the eligibility requirements may apply directly, but the same programme should not be submitted more than once by different entities.

English-Language Submission

LOIs must be submitted in English. Organizations invited to the full application stage must also submit their applications in English, subject to any specific exceptions stated in the application form.

No Individual Applications

Individuals and sole proprietorships are not eligible applicants. The funding is intended for qualifying nonprofit organizations.

Organizations That Will Not Be Considered

The RFP identifies several types of organizations and programmes that will not be considered, including:

Private foundations, whether operating or nonoperating.

Organizations that unlawfully discriminate on protected grounds.

Lobbying organizations.

Political causes and campaigns.

Political candidates.

Memorials.

Gift-matching initiatives.

Organizations requiring fiscal sponsorship.

Organizations that do not meet the stated eligibility requirements.

Individuals.

Sole proprietorships.

Applicants should review the complete official terms and eligibility requirements before investing significant time in preparing their submission.

Financial Reporting and Grant Accountability

Selected grantees will be required to submit:

Interim reports during the grant period.

A final report through the Foundation’s online grant portal.

These reports are expected to demonstrate programme progress, use of funds, implementation achievements, challenges, lessons learned, and outcomes.

Organizations should therefore have appropriate systems for:

Financial tracking.

Programme monitoring.

Beneficiary data management.

Outcome measurement.

Documentation.

Reporting.

Compliance with grant conditions.

Practical Tips for Applicants

Organizations considering this funding opportunity can strengthen their preparation by following these recommendations:

Confirm eligibility early. Verify nonprofit registration, target geography, low-income community focus, and financial documentation requirements.

Choose a specific problem. Avoid presenting a broad proposal about AI. Clearly identify the employment or digital-access challenge affecting the target youth population.

Connect AI skills to employment. Explain how training will help participants obtain jobs, internships, apprenticeships, entrepreneurial opportunities, or other meaningful economic pathways.

Combine technical and human-centred skills. Include capabilities such as critical thinking, creativity, adaptability, communication, problem-solving, and ethical judgment.

Demonstrate community relevance. Use evidence, local data, beneficiary insights, employer feedback, or programme experience to show that the proposed solution responds to a real need.

Build practical partnerships. Consider partnerships with employers, educational institutions, technology providers, workforce agencies, and youth-serving organizations.

Prepare a realistic budget. Ensure that proposed expenses are eligible, justified, and connected to measurable programme activities.

Plan for scale and sustainability. Explain how the programme could be expanded, replicated, integrated into existing systems, or sustained after the grant period.

Prepare audited financial statements early. Organizations invited to Round 2 will need the required externally audited financial documentation.

Draft the LOI offline first. The Foundation advises applicants to download the editable PDF version of the LOI, prepare responses offline, and then transfer the answers into the online form.

Save a copy of the submission. Once submitted, applicants may not be able to access the content entered into the online form. Save the completed PDF or a copy of the final submission for organizational records.

Submit before the deadline. Do not wait until the final minutes, particularly if multiple people must review or approve the LOI.

Learn More and Apply HERE

Conclusion

The Citi Foundation Global Innovation Challenge 2026: Preparing Youth for AI represents a major funding opportunity for nonprofit organizations working to improve youth employability, digital inclusion, and economic mobility.

With US$25 million in total funding and expected grants of US$500,000 per selected organization, the challenge seeks innovative solutions that help low-income youth develop AI and digital capabilities while strengthening essential human-centred skills. It also supports efforts to expand digital access and improve the capacity of nonprofit organizations and cross-sector networks.

Eligible organizations should ensure that their proposed programmes serve low-income communities, impact at least one target geography, and demonstrate a clear connection between AI readiness and employment outcomes. Applicants must first submit a Letter of Inquiry by October 6, 2026, at 12:00 p.m. Eastern Time.

Organizations interested in applying should begin by reviewing the official RFP, confirming their eligibility, developing a focused programme concept, preparing a realistic budget, and gathering the necessary organizational and financial information. A strong application should demonstrate not only innovation, but also feasibility, measurable impact, community relevance, and the capacity to help young people participate meaningfully in the future of work.
