TITLE: A. Neil Pappalardo EE ’64 (1943–2026)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Pappalardo Fellowships Program Founder

The mission of the MIT Pappalardo Fellowships in Physics is to sustain a distinguished postdoctoral program that identifies, recruits and supports the most talented and promising young physicists at an early stage in their careers. This initiative was made possible by the encouragement and generosity of Mr. A. Neil Pappalardo (EE ’64) , an MIT alumnus with a long history of generosity to both the Institute and the Department of Physics.

A. Neil Pappalardo (1943–2026), received his SB in 1964 from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, majoring in physics and electrical engineering. Thereafter, he crossed the Charles River to work at the Massachusetts General Hospital, where he pursued his interest in clinical computing; his specialty was computer programming languages.

Jane and Neil Pappalardo (EE ’64)
By the end of 1968 he was back in East Cambridge, founding Medical Information Technology (Meditech), one of the earliest software companies. As Founder and Chairman, he guided Meditech to become a leading supplier of information system software for hospitals in the U.S. and other English‑speaking countries worldwide.

While leading the company, Neil continued to evolve Meditech’s programming language but also spent much of his time in product development. His efforts were focused on developing an innovative clinical management system that guided clinicians through a high‑quality yet low‑cost treatment process. It also empowered the patient to be an active participant in the process.

Neil was a Life Member Emeritus of the MIT Corporation. Previously he was a long‑term member of the MIT Executive, Audit and Salary Committees, and continued serving on four Visiting Committees, including Physics. For the Physics department, he helped fund the construction of a world‑class optical telescope observatory on a Chilean mountaintop, provided the funds to initiate and sustain a program for Physics postdoctoral scholars (the Pappalardo Fellowships in Physics), and helped fund the renovation of a new building for the Department (the Green Center for Physics). Neil also funded multiple initiatives for the Mechanical Engineering department and provided support for MIT’s academic media production outreach.

Neil received honorary degrees from Suffolk University and the Korean Advanced Institute of Science and Technology [KAIST]. The International Astronomical Union named an asteroid in his honor and in 2008. Neil received the Order of Science and Technology Medal from the Prime Minister of the Republic of Korea. In 2010, the Pappalardo Medical Center was dedicated in his honor at KAIST.

Jane Pappalardo is an alumna of Boston University’s School of Music, where she majored in classical piano performance. She is an active supporter of multiple Boston‑area cultural institutions, including MIT’s Council for the Arts, the Museum of Fine Arts, the Rose Kennedy Greenway Conservancy (as a Board Member), and as a Trustee of the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, the Peabody Essex Museum, and the Museum of Science.

Neil Pappalardo passed away on January 27, 2026. He is survived by his wife, Jane, their four children, and 13 grandchildren.

TITLE: Donor Profile: Howard & Colleen Messing

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Howard (’73) and Colleen Messing
Patrons of Physics Fellows

by Elizabeth Chadis, Director of Development // MIT Physics Annual 2007

Howard (’73) and Colleen Messing at the Patrons of Physics Fellows reception.

Fascinated by astronomy throughout his childhood, Howard spent weekends as a teenager at the American Museum of Natural History Planetarium, where he became President of their Junior Astronomy Club. He had his own 3” refractor and free access to the Rutherford Observatory at Columbia University when he heard that the downtown NYU campus had an underutilized IBM computer and a Director who liked working with high school kids. Howard remembers, “I thought it would be great to use the computer on astronomy projects. Before I knew it, the second great intellectual passion of my life, computer science, was born.”

Howard Messing entered MIT in 1969 at age 16. He wanted to concentrate in both physics and computer science and although he did take the full physics sequence, computer science narrowly edged out physics and he graduated with a degree in Course 6. He then began a Ph.D. program in computer science but ended up back in Boston to get a job and save money before returning to graduate school. Howard went for an interview at a hospital software company called MEDITECH. “Neil Pappalardo, then president, conducted a Socratic-style interview with me, leading me through some basics of programming language theory. I was fascinated, for now I could do what I loved and get paid for it!” Thirty-three years later, Howard is President and Chief Operating Officer of MEDITECH, and while much of his responsibility revolves around the non-technical side of the business, he keeps his hand in programming and still loves it.

Unlike departments in Engineering, the Physics Department has far less ability to secure funds from outside sources and industry. We saw that if we contributed, our gift really could make a difference, especially in the lives of these young and energetic graduate students.
Howard Messing (’73)

Howard recognized what a central role MIT had played not only in his own life but in the science and technology life of the world, so he and his wife Colleen had always made modest contributions to MIT. They were, however, somewhat put-off by the large size of MIT’s endowment and the amount of money it collects annually. “We weren’t sure,” commented the Messings, “how our contribution could make a real difference.”

Then about six years ago, the Messing’s attended a Physics Department event held in honor of Neil Pappalardo. “We became hooked! There was, and is, so much passion and enthusiasm. It’s inspiring to see people being able to accomplish their dreams.” Colleen continues, “With so much negativity in the world, the pursuit of this kind of knowledge for its own sake strikes me as grounding for all, connecting us to the world we live in.”

When the Department asked Howard and Colleen to join the newly-formed Patrons of Physics Fellows, their answer was an immediate and enthusiastic “Yes!” They point out that, “Unlike departments in Engineering, the Physics Department has far less ability to secure funds from outside sources and industry. We saw that if we contributed, our gift really could make a difference, especially in the lives of these young and energetic graduate students.”

Howard and Colleen look forward to attending department-sponsored talks and chatting with faculty, postdocs, and students. “Even if we can only understand part of what is being said, it still gives us some insight and makes us feel in some small way a part of the ‘voyage of discovery.’”

TITLE: Erasmus for Young Entrepreneurs 2026: Apply for a Funded 1–6 Month International Business Exchange

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Aspiring entrepreneurs and newly established business owners can now apply for the Erasmus for Young Entrepreneurs programme, a European business exchange initiative that enables participants to learn directly from experienced entrepreneurs in another participating country.

Unlike a traditional classroom course, employment position or student mobility programme, Erasmus for Young Entrepreneurs connects two individual entrepreneurs for a practical period of business collaboration. A new or aspiring entrepreneur spends between one and six months working alongside an experienced host entrepreneur, gaining first-hand knowledge of business development, management, finance, marketing, customer relations and international expansion.

The programme is financed by the European Commission and implemented with the assistance of approved local contact points, including chambers of commerce, start-up centres, incubators and other business-support organisations. Application and participation are free of charge. According to the official programme website, the exchange is partly financed through financial assistance provided to eligible new entrepreneurs.

Erasmus for Young Entrepreneurs 2026 at a Glance

Programme name: Erasmus for Young Entrepreneurs

Programme funder: European Commission

Programme management: European Innovation Council and SMEs Executive Agency

Exchange duration: One to six months

Exchange format: Entrepreneur-to-entrepreneur business collaboration

Location: Another participating country

Financial support: Monthly country-based financial assistance for eligible new entrepreneurs

Host entrepreneur funding: No European funding is provided to hosts

Application fee: None

Participation fee: None

Application deadline: No deadline; applications are accepted throughout the year

Business sectors: All sectors may be considered

Minimum age: Participants must be over 18

Official application portal: Apply through the Erasmus for Young Entrepreneurs IT platform

What Is Erasmus for Young Entrepreneurs?

Erasmus for Young Entrepreneurs is an international business mobility programme created to support people who are planning to establish a business or have recently started one.

The programme helps aspiring and early-stage entrepreneurs develop the practical skills required to establish and manage a sustainable small or medium-sized enterprise. Instead of receiving only theoretical instruction, participants work directly with an experienced entrepreneur in another country.

During the exchange, the new entrepreneur observes how an established business operates while contributing their own knowledge, skills, ideas and understanding of their home market. The collaboration is intended to create benefits for both parties.

The new entrepreneur may gain practical business experience, improve a business plan, understand a foreign market and develop international contacts. The host entrepreneur may receive new ideas, specialised knowledge, access to another market and opportunities for future international cooperation.

The exchange can also lead to longer-term commercial relationships, including:

Joint ventures

Contractor and supplier relationships

Cross-border partnerships

Market-entry cooperation

Product development

Business referrals

Subcontracting arrangements

Continued professional collaboration

However, any future relationship must remain separate from the purpose and approval of the original exchange. The programme will not approve arrangements where a pre-existing commercial or personal relationship makes programme support unnecessary.

Who Can Participate as a New Entrepreneur?

Applicants may participate as new entrepreneurs if they fall within one of the following situations:

They are firmly planning to establish their own business and have developed a viable business plan; or

They have already established a business but have less than three years of total entrepreneurial experience.

The business may operate in any sector. There is no restriction requiring applicants to work in technology, manufacturing or another particular industry.

New entrepreneurs must also:

Be over 18 years of age

Be permanently resident in an eligible EU Member State or participating Single Market Programme country

Have a concrete business idea or project supported by a proper business plan

Be motivated to learn from an experienced entrepreneur in another participating country

Be prepared to contribute useful skills, knowledge and competencies to the host business

Be willing to participate actively throughout the agreed exchange

Have sufficient language ability to communicate and collaborate with the proposed host

Be prepared to supplement the programme’s financial assistance if it does not cover every expense

Personally submit the application through the official programme platform

Participate in the programme as a new entrepreneur only once

The programme’s official eligibility requirements are available on the new entrepreneur profile page.

Who Can Participate as a Host Entrepreneur?

Experienced business owners can apply to host an aspiring or newly established entrepreneur.

A host entrepreneur must:

Be permanently resident in a participating country

Have a company registered in that participating country

Be the owner-manager of a micro, small or medium-sized enterprise; or

Be directly involved in entrepreneurship at the board level of an SME rather than serving only as an employee

Have more than three years of experience operating a business as an entrepreneur

Be willing to share business knowledge and experience

Be prepared to mentor the visiting new entrepreneur

Provide a genuine learning and entrepreneurial collaboration

Sign the programme’s Commitment to Quality

Complete an online feedback questionnaire after the exchange

The host must ensure that the visiting entrepreneur receives meaningful business exposure. The programme must not be used to obtain unpaid labour, recruit an intern or fill an ordinary employee position. Full host requirements are explained on the official host entrepreneur profile page.

What Qualifies as a Small or Medium-Sized Enterprise?

Host businesses are generally expected to comply with the European Union definition of a micro, small or medium-sized enterprise.

The main thresholds are:

Micro-enterprise: Fewer than 10 employees and annual turnover or balance-sheet total not exceeding €2 million

Small enterprise: Fewer than 50 employees and annual turnover or balance-sheet total not exceeding €10 million

Medium-sized enterprise: Fewer than 250 employees and annual turnover not exceeding €50 million or a balance-sheet total not exceeding €43 million

The legal form of the business is not necessarily decisive. Independent professionals, self-employed individuals, eligible cooperatives, foundations, associations and certain non-profit organisations may potentially participate if they conduct an economic activity and satisfy the programme’s SME and entrepreneurial requirements.

Participating Countries

Residency requirements differ for new entrepreneurs and host entrepreneurs.

New entrepreneurs must be permanently resident in an EU Member State or a participating Single Market Programme third country.

Eligible EU Member States include:

Austria

Belgium

Bulgaria

Croatia

Cyprus

Czechia

Denmark

Estonia

Finland

France

Germany

Greece

Hungary

Ireland

Italy

Latvia

Lithuania

Luxembourg

Malta

Netherlands

Poland

Portugal

Romania

Slovakia

Slovenia

Spain

Sweden

Participating Single Market Programme third countries currently listed by the programme include:

Albania

Bosnia and Herzegovina

Iceland

Kosovo

Liechtenstein

Moldova

Montenegro

North Macedonia

Norway

Serbia

Türkiye

Ukraine

Host entrepreneurs may also be based in the following participating non-Single Market Programme destinations:

Canada

Singapore

United Kingdom

United States

Entrepreneurs from EU outermost regions and eligible Overseas Countries and Territories may also participate under the programme’s applicable rules.

Applicants should consult the current official list of participating countries before applying because programme participation and destination availability may change.

How Permanent Residence Is Determined

Eligibility is based primarily on permanent residence rather than nationality.

For an applicant with a registered company, permanent residence is generally treated as the country where that company is registered. Where a company operates through establishments in more than one participating country, the entrepreneur should select the country where they are personally based.

If the applicant does not have a registered company, permanent residence is normally the country where the applicant has spent at least 183 days during the previous 12 months.

An applicant currently living in a non-participating country will normally be considered ineligible, even if that person may satisfy other elements of the residence definition. The detailed residence rules are available in the programme’s permanent residence guidance.

Duration and Structure of the Exchange

An approved Erasmus for Young Entrepreneurs exchange can last from one to six months.

The exchange may take place as one continuous stay or may be divided into shorter weekly periods. Where the exchange is divided into separate periods, all approved periods must generally be completed within an overall timeframe of no more than 12 months.

The final duration is agreed between the new entrepreneur and the host entrepreneur and must be approved by their respective local contact points. Acceptance of an initial application does not automatically guarantee a particular host, destination, duration or amount of funding.

The exchange must take place in another participating country. A new entrepreneur cannot complete the exchange in their own country of residence.

What Can Participants Do During the Exchange?

The precise activities are agreed between the new and host entrepreneurs and documented in their activity plan.

Activities may include:

Working alongside and shadowing the experienced host entrepreneur

Studying the host company’s daily management systems

Conducting market research

Identifying new commercial opportunities

Exploring international or cross-border markets

Supporting entrepreneurship-development projects

Participating in innovation and research-related activities

Improving the new entrepreneur’s business plan

Learning about business finance and financial management

Studying customer relationship systems

Understanding pricing and sales strategies

Reviewing branding and marketing practices

Exploring supply chains, operations and business partnerships

Developing new products, services or international business concepts

Learning about the regulatory and cultural environment of another participating country

The exchange should have clear learning objectives for the new entrepreneur and identifiable business value for the host.

Benefits for New Entrepreneurs

New entrepreneurs can gain practical knowledge that may be difficult to obtain through academic study alone.

Potential benefits include:

Up to six months of practical learning with an experienced business owner

Improved understanding of how to establish and manage an SME

Exposure to marketing, sales, accounting, customer relations and business finance

An opportunity to test and strengthen a business plan

Greater confidence in making entrepreneurial decisions

Development of management, technical and sector-specific skills

Better understanding of international and European markets

Experience of different organisational and business cultures

Improved foreign-language and communication skills

Access to a network of international entrepreneurs

Opportunities to identify future business partners

Potential development of cross-border commercial cooperation

Greater awareness of foreign customers, competitors and regulatory conditions

Financial assistance toward eligible travel and living costs

More information is available on the programme’s benefits for new entrepreneurs page.

Benefits for Host Entrepreneurs

Host entrepreneurs do not receive European financial assistance for hosting. However, the programme can provide significant commercial and professional value.

Benefits may include:

Working with a motivated entrepreneur who brings new ideas and perspectives

Accessing skills or specialised knowledge that may not already exist in the host company

Receiving fresh observations about the company’s products, services or processes

Learning about the new entrepreneur’s home market

Identifying opportunities for international expansion

Developing cross-border contacts

Finding potential future business partners

Strengthening the company’s international network

Improving communication and foreign-language skills

Acting as a mentor and contributing to entrepreneurship development

Increasing the company’s international visibility

Exploring future joint ventures, supply relationships or other cooperation

The programme emphasises mutual value: the host provides experience and guidance, while the new entrepreneur contributes ideas, knowledge and practical support. Further details are available on the benefits for host entrepreneurs page.

Financial Support for New Entrepreneurs

Eligible new entrepreneurs may receive financial assistance toward the cost of travelling to and living in the host country.

The assistance:

Is paid by the new entrepreneur’s selected local contact point

Is governed by a financial agreement between the entrepreneur and the local contact point

Is normally calculated according to a monthly lump sum

Depends on the country where the exchange takes place

Covers only the approved period spent abroad collaborating with the host

Is intended to contribute toward travel, accommodation and subsistence expenses

May be paid in several instalments under the signed agreement

May not cover every cost of the exchange

May need to be supplemented with the participant’s own resources

Host entrepreneurs do not receive European funding under the programme.

The official financial-assistance table currently linked by the programme applies to exchanges beginning on or after 1 June 2024. The listed monthly amounts for currently participating destinations are:

Monthly amount
Country or category

€600

Applicants should treat these figures as contribution rates rather than a promise that all actual costs will be fully covered. The final amount, payment schedule and financial conditions will be established in the agreement with the relevant intermediary organisation. Applicants should verify the latest official monthly financial-assistance table before making travel or accommodation commitments.

Application Documents for New Entrepreneurs

New entrepreneurs should prepare the following before starting their online application:

Curriculum Vitae

The CV should provide a clear and current summary of the applicant’s:

Education

Professional experience

Entrepreneurial experience

Technical competencies

Management capabilities

Business and sector knowledge

The Europass CV format is preferred but is not compulsory. English is strongly encouraged because it can make the applicant’s profile easier for intermediary organisations and potential hosts to understand.

Motivation Statement

The motivation section should explain:

Why the applicant wants to join the programme

What business knowledge they hope to acquire

Why an international exchange is relevant to their business

What skills they can contribute to the host company

How the exchange will strengthen their planned or recently established business

What practical results they expect to achieve

How they will apply the experience after returning home

A generic motivation statement is unlikely to be competitive. It should demonstrate commitment, initiative, seriousness, creativity and clearly defined learning needs.

Full Business Plan

A full business plan is compulsory for new entrepreneurs. A brief idea alone is not sufficient.

The business plan should include at least:

A clear description of the proposed product or service

The problem or customer need addressed

A definition of the target market

Market-size and demand considerations

Competitor analysis

Marketing and sales strategy

Operational requirements

Estimated expenses and revenue for the following two years

Break-even analysis

The applicant’s implementation strategy

The programme does not prescribe a single business-plan template. However, the selected local contact point will assess whether the document is sufficiently complete, viable and professionally prepared.

The full business plan is treated as a confidential document and is generally accessible only to the applicant, the selected intermediary organisation, the programme Support Office and the European Commission.

Business Plan Summary

Applicants must also submit a shorter summary of their business plan. The registration guide indicates a maximum length of 2,000 characters.

Unlike the full confidential business plan, the summary may be visible to accepted entrepreneurs and intermediary organisations in the programme’s online catalogue. Applicants should therefore avoid including trade secrets or other sensitive information.

Language Information

Applicants must be able to communicate effectively with their proposed host. The programme does not provide language training.

There is no universal language examination requirement, but applicants should be comfortable speaking, understanding, reading and writing in the language used during the exchange. The registration guide refers to approximately B2-level ability as a useful benchmark. English is strongly encouraged because it is widely understood across the programme.

Geographical and Sector Preferences

Applicants are asked to identify:

Their principal business sector

Additional sectors relevant to the planned exchange

Their preferred host country

Alternative destination countries

Their proposed exchange duration

The periods during which they are available

Flexibility regarding destinations and dates can increase the likelihood of finding a suitable host.

The complete preparation requirements are explained in the official registration guide for new entrepreneurs.

How to Apply for Erasmus for Young Entrepreneurs

The application and matching process generally involves the following stages:

Step 1: Check Your Eligibility

Determine whether you qualify as a new entrepreneur or an experienced host entrepreneur. Confirm your permanent-residence status and ensure that your country is currently participating.

Step 2: Identify a Local Contact Point

Select an approved intermediary organisation that operates in your country or region of residence. The organisation will guide you through assessment, matching, preparation and implementation.

Applicants living in an eligible country without an active local contact point may be able to select an intermediary organisation in another participating European country.

Step 3: Prepare the Required Documents

New entrepreneurs should prepare their CV, motivation statement, complete business plan and business-plan summary.

Host entrepreneurs should prepare a detailed professional and company profile, explain their motivation for hosting and identify the skills or experience they can offer.

Step 4: Submit the Online Application Personally

Applications must be submitted through the official programme platform. Participants must not allow an external organisation or third party to submit an application on their behalf.

The official Apply Now page also provides access to explanatory material, registration guides and a preview of the online form.

Step 5: Application Assessment

The selected intermediary organisation reviews the application for eligibility, completeness and quality.

The new entrepreneur registration guide indicates that an initial check should normally be conducted within two weeks of receiving the application. The application may be:

Accepted

Placed on hold pending additional information

Returned to the applicant

Refused

If information is missing, the applicant may be asked to provide it within a specified period. Acceptance gives the participant access to the programme’s online catalogue but does not by itself guarantee an exchange.

Step 6: Find a Suitable Entrepreneur

Accepted participants can pursue a match in two ways:

Suggest an eligible entrepreneur with whom they are already in contact, subject to the programme’s restrictions; or

Search the online catalogue with support from the local contact point.

The proposed host should be relevant to the new entrepreneur’s business objectives and capable of providing genuine entrepreneurial learning.

Step 7: Agree on the Exchange Plan

The two entrepreneurs must agree on:

Exchange dates

Duration

Learning objectives

Proposed activities

Expected contributions from each participant

Anticipated business outcomes

These details must be submitted to the local contact points for assessment and approval.

Step 8: Sign the Required Agreements

All parties digitally sign a Commitment to Quality setting out the objectives and activity plan.

The new entrepreneur also signs a financial agreement with the intermediary organisation. This agreement specifies the funding, responsibilities, payment arrangements, timetable and relevant legal conditions.

Step 9: Complete the Exchange

The new entrepreneur travels to the host country and participates in the agreed activities. Financial assistance is provided according to the signed agreement.

Step 10: Submit Feedback

After the exchange, both entrepreneurs must complete the required feedback questionnaires. The new entrepreneur should explain the activities completed, knowledge acquired and effect of the exchange on their business development.

The complete official process is available on the How to Participate page.

Activities and Relationships That Are Not Permitted

Erasmus for Young Entrepreneurs is not an internship, employment scheme or source of unpaid labour.

Proposed exchanges may be rejected where:

The host intends to use the new entrepreneur as an ordinary employee or intern

The parties already have a professional relationship that makes programme support unnecessary

The host is already, or plans to become, a co-owner or investor in the new entrepreneur’s business

The new entrepreneur intends to establish a branch of the host’s business

The parties are close relatives, spouses or partners

A significant personal relationship creates a conflict of interest

The new entrepreneur has already worked at the host’s business through another programme

The exchange provides no clear additional value to both businesses

The application is submitted by a third party

Financial assistance is used for a purpose unrelated to the approved exchange

One host entrepreneur cannot host more than one new entrepreneur at the same time. Where co-founders from the same company participate as hosts, their exchanges must take place at different times.

Application Deadline

There is no fixed deadline to register for Erasmus for Young Entrepreneurs.

The programme accepts online applications throughout the year, according to its official deadline guidance.

Applicants should nevertheless apply early. The assessment, matching, approval and contracting stages can require considerable time, and the availability and budgets of intermediary organisations may affect when an exchange can begin.

Application Cost

Application and participation are completely free of charge.

No intermediary organisation, consultant or external party should charge an applicant an application or participation fee. Applicants must use the official platform and submit their information personally.

Technical Requirements for Applying

The online application system is designed to work with the latest versions of:

Microsoft Edge

Google Chrome

Mozilla Firefox

Applicants should use a reliable email address that they expect to retain, because the registered email address, first name and last name may not be changeable after registration.

Official Application and Contact Information

Official information page: Erasmus for Young Entrepreneurs – Apply Now

Online application portal: Start an Erasmus for Young Entrepreneurs application

Local contact points: Find an intermediary organisation

Support Office email: support@erasmus-entrepreneurs.eu

Support Office telephone: +32 2 282 08 73

Practical Tips for a Strong Application

Prepare a complete business plan with realistic financial assumptions.

Clearly explain what you need to learn from an experienced entrepreneur.

Describe the specific skills and knowledge you can contribute to the host.

Link every proposed exchange objective to the development of your own business.

Use a professional and updated CV, preferably in English.

Avoid vague statements about wanting international exposure.

Select host countries and business sectors that genuinely match your plans.

Remain flexible about dates and alternative destinations.

Prepare a personal budget because the financial assistance may not cover every expense.

Do not disclose commercially sensitive information in the public business-plan summary.

Apply only through the official programme portal.

Never pay an application or participation fee.

Do not describe the proposed exchange as an internship or employment placement.

Conclusion

Erasmus for Young Entrepreneurs offers aspiring founders and newly established business owners an opportunity to gain practical international business experience while learning directly from an experienced entrepreneur.

Through a structured exchange lasting between one and six months, new entrepreneurs can strengthen their business plans, develop management skills, explore international markets and establish valuable professional relationships. Experienced host entrepreneurs can benefit from fresh ideas, specialised knowledge and access to potential markets and partners abroad.

The programme is free to join, accepts applications throughout the year and provides eligible new entrepreneurs with country-based financial assistance toward travel and living expenses. Applicants should carefully confirm their residency eligibility, prepare a serious business plan and submit a clear application demonstrating both what they expect to learn and what they can contribute.

TITLE: LawAI Seasonal Fellowships: Research Opportunities in AI, Law and Policy for Law Students, Professionals and Academics

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The LawAI Seasonal Fellowships provide an opportunity for law students, legal professionals, researchers, academics, and other qualified specialists to engage with some of the most important emerging questions at the intersection of artificial intelligence, law, regulation, and public policy.

As artificial intelligence continues to develop rapidly, governments, regulators, courts, researchers, technology organizations, and policymakers are increasingly confronted with complex questions about how advanced AI systems should be governed. LawAI’s Seasonal Fellowships are designed to bring researchers and practitioners into this evolving field, allowing fellows to contribute to research while interacting with people working on frontier AI policy.

The fellowship opportunities are particularly relevant to individuals interested in AI governance, technology regulation, public policy, legal research, emerging technologies, and the development of legal frameworks for increasingly capable AI systems.

LawAI encourages prospective applicants to review its workstreams and research directions before applying so that they can understand the organization’s areas of interest and identify how their own research experience, legal background, and professional interests could contribute.

What Are the LawAI Seasonal Fellowships?

LawAI’s Seasonal Fellowships are structured research opportunities for individuals who want to work at the leading edge of AI, law, and policy.

The program currently includes three principal fellowship tracks:

Winter Research Fellowship (EU Law)

Summer Fellowship (US)

Summer Research Fellowship (Legal Frontiers)

Each track has a somewhat different geographic and substantive focus. While the US and EU Law tracks place particular emphasis on legal experience in their respective jurisdictions, the Legal Frontiers fellowship provides a broader interdisciplinary pathway for researchers whose work can contribute to the development of law and public policy surrounding advanced AI.

Applicants may apply to multiple tracks where they meet the relevant qualifications. However, a separate application must be submitted for each fellowship track.

1. Winter Research Fellowship in EU Law

The Winter Research Fellowship focuses on legal and policy questions connected to the European Union.

This fellowship is particularly relevant to candidates who have studied or worked with EU law and who are interested in applying their legal research capabilities to questions arising from artificial intelligence and emerging technology regulation.

LawAI strongly encourages fellows in this track to participate in person in Cambridge, United Kingdom. According to LawAI, a significant part of the value of the fellowship comes from developing professional connections with other fellows and interacting directly with LawAI staff and individuals working on frontier AI policy who visit the Cambridge office.

The organization recognizes, however, that circumstances differ between applicants. Remote participation may therefore be considered on a case-by-case basis where a candidate has compelling reasons, such as family commitments.

Convening Week

The Winter Research Fellowship includes an in-person Convening Week in Cambridge, UK, scheduled for:

February 8–12

Applicants considering this track should therefore be prepared to meet any relevant travel, immigration, and participation requirements associated with attending the Convening Week.

Fellowship Subsidy

Fellows participating in the Winter Research Fellowship receive:

£1,000 per week fellowship subsidy.

A one-off £7,000 relocation and housing payment for fellows who relocate to Cambridge.

Candidates with exceptional experience or qualifications may be eligible for higher subsidies.

2. Summer Fellowship in the United States

The Summer Fellowship is focused on US law and policy and is designed for candidates with relevant legal study or professional experience in the United States.

The fellowship is particularly suitable for individuals interested in the relationship between artificial intelligence and US legal and policy frameworks.

LawAI strongly encourages fellows to participate in person in Washington, DC. The organization notes that being embedded within the team and the wider Washington policy community can provide significant opportunities for professional interaction, research collaboration, and engagement with the broader AI policy environment.

Remote arrangements may nevertheless be considered on a case-by-case basis for candidates with compelling reasons to participate remotely.

Convening Week

The Summer Fellowship includes an in-person Convening Week in Washington, DC, scheduled for:

June 21–25

Candidates should take this requirement into account when determining whether the fellowship’s participation arrangements are compatible with their circumstances.

Fellowship Subsidy

The Summer Fellowship provides:

$2,000 per week subsidy.

A $10,000 relocation and housing stipend for fellows who relocate to Washington, DC.

The relocation and housing stipend is treated as taxable income. LawAI states that recipients are not required to submit reimbursement claims or receipts for this stipend.

As with the other tracks, candidates with exceptional experience or qualifications may be eligible for higher subsidies.

3. Summer Research Fellowship in Legal Frontiers

The Summer Research Fellowship in Legal Frontiers provides a broader research pathway for candidates interested in the future of law and public policy in the context of advanced AI.

Unlike the US and EU Law tracks, this fellowship does not require applicants to have a primary background in law. LawAI specifically welcomes applicants from other disciplines where their research can contribute meaningfully to questions involving advanced AI governance.

Potentially relevant backgrounds include:

Computer science

Public policy

Economics

History

Psychology

Physics

Law

Other disciplines relevant to the development of law and public policy

Applicants without specialized knowledge of US, EU, or UK law may still be considered, although LawAI indicates that candidates without expertise in one of these jurisdictions are generally considered only in exceptional circumstances.

Remote-First Structure

The Legal Frontiers fellowship is designed as a remote-first opportunity.

Fellows may have opportunities for in-person participation at LawAI’s Cambridge office in the United Kingdom or with the organization’s US Law & Policy team in Washington, DC.

Previous Summer Research Fellows have found value in being embedded within the organization and participating in the wider research and policy communities.

Convening Week

The Legal Frontiers fellowship’s Convening Week is hosted in Washington, DC:

June 21–25

Applicants should therefore consider the in-person Convening Week requirement when assessing their ability to participate.

Fellowship Subsidy

The Legal Frontiers fellowship provides a weekly subsidy based on the fellow’s location. LawAI gives the following examples:

$1,800 per week for Summer Research Fellows based in the United States.

£1,000 per week for fellows based in the European Union and United Kingdom.

Additional stipends may potentially be available when location-specific conditions are met.

Candidates with exceptional qualifications or experience may also be eligible for higher subsidies.

Who Can Apply for LawAI Seasonal Fellowships?

LawAI’s Seasonal Fellowships are intended for applicants with meaningful legal, policy, research, or academic experience relevant to the fellowship track they select.

The organization explicitly states that it welcomes applications from professionals, meaning the opportunities are not restricted exclusively to current students.

Potential applicants include:

Law students

Practicing lawyers

Legal researchers

Law and policy researchers

Academics

Public policy researchers

Researchers from relevant interdisciplinary fields

Professionals with experience relevant to AI law and policy

The precise requirements depend on the fellowship track.

Requirements for the US and EU Law Tracks

For the US and EU Law tracks, LawAI generally expects applicants to have formal legal training or experience.

This is important because these fellowships require candidates to understand the legal principles applicable to AI regulation within the relevant jurisdiction.

Applicants should therefore have some form of formal legal education, professional legal experience, or another substantive background that demonstrates their understanding of the applicable legal system.

For the US track, relevant experience with US law is expected.

For the EU Law track, relevant experience with EU law is expected.

LawAI also encourages applications from people who previously studied or practiced US or EU law but are currently living and working in another country.

Requirements for the Legal Frontiers Track

The Legal Frontiers fellowship has a broader eligibility approach.

Applicants do not necessarily need to have law as their primary academic or professional discipline. Instead, candidates should be able to clearly demonstrate how their research could positively contribute to the development of law and public policy relating to advanced artificial intelligence.

This makes the fellowship potentially relevant to researchers working across multiple disciplines.

For example, a computer scientist might explore technical developments that have implications for AI governance. An economist might investigate regulatory incentives or the economic effects of AI policy. A historian might contribute research into institutional development and technology governance, while a psychologist could examine human behavior and policy implications associated with increasingly capable AI systems.

Candidates who intend to conduct technical research during the fellowship are responsible for identifying and securing an appropriately qualified technical supervisor.

Is Previous AI Experience Required?

Previous specialized experience with AI-related legal questions is not required.

Applicants should nevertheless have an interest in artificial intelligence, law, and policy and should be prepared to apply their research skills and existing knowledge to questions in the field.

This means applicants do not necessarily need to have already established a career specializing in AI law.

Instead, candidates can demonstrate their suitability through:

Strong research capabilities

Relevant legal or policy knowledge

Academic or professional experience

Interest in AI governance

Ability to investigate complex emerging questions

Ability to connect their existing expertise with AI-related legal and policy issues

The absence of a requirement for previous AI-specific experience potentially makes these fellowships accessible to qualified researchers who are transitioning into the field.

English Language Requirement

Applicants are required to have full professional fluency in English, both spoken and written.

This requirement reflects the collaborative nature of the fellowships. Fellows are expected to actively participate in:

Research discussions

Professional collaborations

Presentations

Meetings

Academic and policy conversations

Other activities requiring effective written and spoken communication

Applicants should therefore be comfortable communicating complex legal, policy, or research ideas in English.

Are Practicing Professionals Eligible?

Yes.

LawAI explicitly welcomes professionals, including practicing lawyers, law and policy researchers, and academics.

Relevant professional experience is highly valued, making these fellowships potentially suitable for candidates who are already working in legal practice, research, academia, regulation, public policy, or related areas.

The opportunities can therefore be relevant to both emerging researchers and established professionals seeking to deepen their involvement in AI law and policy.

Are the LawAI Seasonal Fellowships Paid?

Yes. LawAI provides weekly subsidies to fellows, with the exact amount depending on the fellowship track and the fellow’s location.

The stated financial support includes:

Winter Research Fellowship (EU Law)

£1,000 per week

One-off £7,000 relocation and housing payment for fellows relocating to Cambridge

Summer Fellowship (US)

Remote and In-Person Participation

The Seasonal Fellowships do not all follow the same participation model.

A common feature across the program is the requirement for an in-person Convening Week.

Outside of that period, participation varies according to the fellowship.

Winter Research Fellowship

The Winter Research Fellowship strongly encourages in-person participation in Cambridge. Remote participation may be considered in exceptional circumstances.

The Convening Week takes place in Cambridge from February 8–12.

Summer Fellowship

The US Summer Fellowship strongly encourages in-person participation in Washington, DC. Remote participation may be considered on a case-by-case basis for candidates with compelling reasons.

The Convening Week takes place in Washington, DC, from June 21–25.

Legal Frontiers Fellowship

The Legal Frontiers fellowship is remote-first.

Nevertheless, fellows may have opportunities to participate in person from Cambridge or Washington, DC, and the Convening Week is hosted in Washington, DC, from June 21–25.

Applicants should therefore distinguish between a fellowship being remote-first or allowing remote arrangements and the separate requirement to participate in an in-person Convening Week.

Visa and Immigration Requirements

Successful applicants are responsible for having any visa or immigration authorization required to participate in the fellowship in the relevant country.

LawAI states that, after making an offer, it will make every reasonable effort to support relevant visa applications where appropriate.

However, visa eligibility is ultimately determined by the relevant immigration authorities.

Applicants who would need to travel internationally for a fellowship should therefore investigate applicable immigration requirements early in the application process.

Can Applicants Apply for More Than One Fellowship Track?

Yes.

Applicants may apply for multiple Seasonal Fellowship tracks, including:

US

EU Law

Legal Frontiers

However, applicants must meet the relevant qualifications for each track they select.

A separate application must also be submitted for each fellowship.

Candidates considering multiple tracks should therefore ensure that each application is appropriately tailored to the specific jurisdiction, research focus, and requirements of that fellowship rather than submitting identical materials without modification.

What Makes the Seasonal Fellowships Relevant to AI Governance?

The rapid development of artificial intelligence is creating new questions for legal systems and policymakers.

Issues surrounding advanced AI can involve regulation, liability, governance, public policy, institutional design, technological development, economic impacts, and the relationship between emerging technologies and existing legal frameworks.

LawAI’s Seasonal Fellowships provide a structured environment for researchers to investigate these types of questions while engaging with other people working in the field.

The opportunity is therefore not simply about studying AI as a technology. It is about examining how law and public policy may respond to increasingly capable AI systems.

For applicants with backgrounds in law, public policy, economics, computer science, history, psychology, physics, or related disciplines, this interdisciplinary environment can provide a setting in which existing research expertise can be applied to emerging questions surrounding advanced AI.

How Applicants Can Prepare

Prospective applicants should begin by understanding the research areas relevant to LawAI and the particular fellowship track they intend to apply for.

Useful preparation steps include:

Review LawAI’s research directions.

Applicants should familiarize themselves with the organization’s workstreams and research priorities.

Identify the most suitable fellowship track.

Candidates should consider whether their background aligns most closely with US law, EU law, or the broader Legal Frontiers research agenda.

Connect previous experience to AI law and policy.

Even though previous AI-specific experience is not mandatory, applicants should be able to explain why their existing knowledge and research abilities are relevant to AI-related questions.

Demonstrate strong research ability.

Applications should clearly communicate the candidate’s ability to investigate complex questions, analyze evidence, and develop meaningful research.

Consider the geographic requirements.

Candidates should review the in-person Convening Week dates and determine whether they can meet the relevant participation requirements.

Review visa requirements if international travel is necessary.

Applicants who may need immigration authorization should consider the relevant requirements well in advance.

Prepare for professional collaboration in English.

Since full professional English fluency is required, candidates should be prepared to participate confidently in discussions, collaborations, and presentations.

Can Applicants Receive Individualized Feedback?

LawAI states that it cannot provide personalized feedback to applicants.

The organization carefully reviews applications but receives a high volume of submissions, making individualized feedback impractical.

Applicants should therefore aim to submit complete, carefully prepared applications that clearly demonstrate their qualifications, research interests, and suitability for the particular fellowship track.

How to Stay Updated About Future LawAI Fellowships

Applicants who are interested in future fellowship opportunities can stay connected with LawAI through its communication channels.

LawAI encourages prospective applicants to follow its updates through its newsletter, LinkedIn, and X.

These channels can provide information about upcoming fellowship opportunities, events, research activities, and other ways to engage with the organization.

Long-Term Opportunities at LawAI

The Seasonal Fellowships are not the only opportunities available through LawAI.

The organization also offers longer-term roles through its open positions.

Seasonal Fellowships can provide an avenue for individuals to become involved with LawAI’s work and may serve as a stepping stone toward future full-time opportunities, although participation in a fellowship does not guarantee employment.

Candidates interested in building a longer-term career in AI law and policy should therefore also monitor LawAI’s open positions in addition to its seasonal fellowship announcements.

Important Considerations Before Applying

Before submitting an application, prospective candidates should carefully consider several factors.

First, applicants should select a track that corresponds with their academic, professional, and research background. The US and EU Law tracks require a stronger jurisdiction-specific legal foundation, while the Legal Frontiers track accommodates a broader range of disciplines.

Second, applicants should be prepared for the English-language requirements and the collaborative nature of the program.

Third, candidates should consider whether they can participate in the required in-person Convening Week.

Fourth, international applicants should investigate visa and immigration requirements if their selected fellowship involves participation in another country.

Finally, candidates should carefully review the full description for their selected fellowship before applying because specific details can differ between the US, EU Law, and Legal Frontiers tracks.

For

Deadline

No application deadline is stated in the information provided for the Seasonal Fellowships page.

Applicants should therefore check the individual fellowship descriptions and LawAI’s official opportunity updates for the current application period and any applicable deadline before submitting an application.

Visit HERE to learn more about the LawAI Seasonal Fellowships.

Conclusion

The LawAI Seasonal Fellowships provide research opportunities for individuals interested in the rapidly developing intersection of artificial intelligence, law, regulation, and public policy. With separate pathways focused on EU law, US law, and broader legal frontiers, the program accommodates applicants with different professional, academic, and disciplinary backgrounds.

The Winter Research Fellowship offers a European-focused opportunity with an emphasis on participation in Cambridge, while the Summer Fellowship in the United States focuses on US law and policy and encourages fellows to engage with the Washington, DC policy environment. The Summer Research Fellowship in Legal Frontiers provides a broader, remote-first pathway for researchers whose work can contribute to the development of law and public policy surrounding advanced AI.

Law students, lawyers, legal researchers, academics, policymakers, and researchers from relevant interdisciplinary fields may find the fellowships particularly relevant to their professional and research interests. Importantly, applicants do not need previous specialized experience in AI law, provided they have appropriate research or legal knowledge and a genuine interest in applying their expertise to AI-related questions.

With weekly financial subsidies, potential relocation and housing support, opportunities for professional collaboration, and exposure to researchers and practitioners working on frontier AI policy, the Seasonal Fellowships offer a structured way for qualified candidates to deepen their engagement with one of the most rapidly evolving areas of contemporary law and policy.

Prospective applicants should carefully review the specific requirements of each fellowship track, assess their jurisdictional or interdisciplinary background, prepare a strong research-focused application, and monitor LawAI’s official channels for current application deadlines and future fellowship announcements.

Energy systems around the world are undergoing enormous change. The focus on climate change and sustainability is driving a massive transformation in the energy industry. The historic fleet of coal and natural gas generation is rapidly being replaced by renewable generation and as the penetration of renewables increases, the need for energy storage has followed. Wind and solar power, hydrogen plus new usage patterns and market mechanisms are potential game-changers. Leaders in oil and gas are transforming how they operate to anticipate innovative forms of upstream energy, government regulation, energy transition, and digital disruption. Disclosing climate-related risks, regulations, emissions targets, carbon pricing, investment and financial pressures, and demand destruction require a competitive approach to asset operations. This course will explore the latest thought leadership on oil and gas in terms of the challenges and opportunities facing the industry. Specifically, participants will understand the complexity and interactions in the energy system and be capable of developing a vision for the future of the energy transition.

TITLE: Assistant Scientist Xiaoting Yang

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Photo provided by Xiaoting Yang

Assistant Scientist Xiaoting Yang comes to WHOI from Scripps Institution of Oceanography (SIO), where she was a postdoc associate. Xiaoting received her PhD from the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Harvard University, and her BSc from the School of Physics, Peking University. Xiaoting’s research focuses on large-scale ocean circulation, especially the deep-ocean component. Her current research studies global-scale meridional overturning circulation (MOC) as an important player in the climate system, with significant transports of heat, salt, oxygen, carbon, and nutrients. She aims to understand the different paths of the MOC and their dynamics, in both Eulerian and Lagrangian perspectives.

In her free time, Xiaoting enjoys both indoors and outdoors activities, such as hiking in the mountains and forests, crocheting and baking.

TITLE: Committee on Radio Astronomy Frequencies (CRAF) admitted to CISPR seeking to advance standards for satellite radio-noise

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
News

The Committee on Radio Astronomy Frequencies has been admitted as an I-member of the International Special Committee on Radio Interference. This is a further big step towards the recognition of unintended electromagnetic radiation from satellites as a serious problem for radio astronomy. This membership will lay the groundwork for future mitigation measures to safeguard astronomical research from the negative impacts of large satellite constellations.

In recent years, the number of satellites launched into orbit has greatly increased. “While these systems provide essential services, including global connectivity, navigation, and Earth observation, they were also found to generate unintended electromagnetic radiation (UEMR), radiation not linked to their intended communications,” says Committee on Radio Astronomy Frequencies (CRAF) Chair Benjamin Winkel (MPIfR). Unlike traditional transmission signals, UEMR arises from the satellites’ internal electronics and can leak across wide frequency ranges. Studies conducted with radio telescopes around the world have confirmed the presence of such signals, including signals within frequency bands that are internationally protected for radio astronomy.

The CRAF, an expert committee of the European Science Foundation (ESF), represents the interests of radio astronomy observatories and research institutes across Europe and South Africa in preserving the operating conditions for radio astronomy and other basic sciences.

“Starting with an experiment at the European Low Frequency Array (LOFAR) by members of CRAF and the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO), radio observatories around the world have by now confirmed the presence of such radiation” according to Federico Di Vruno (SKAO), who led the initial observing campaign. “UEMR also occurs within frequency bands that are internationally protected for radio astronomy operations as defined in a United Nations treaty through the International Telecommunication Union (ITU-R)”, Gyula Józsa (MPIfR) adds, coordinator of CRAF’s satellite group and co-author on the original paper.

“Radio astronomy is vulnerable to interference, as it relies on the detection of extremely faint signals originating from distant stars, galaxies, and the early Universe”, former CRAF Chair Michael Linqvist (OSO) explains. Even weak leakage from large numbers of satellites can significantly degrade the scientific environment. Without technical and regulatory safeguards, radio telescopes risk losing their ability to conduct research.

“The International Special Committee on Radio Interference (CISPR), part of the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC), sets global standards to limit electromagnetic interference. With its new role in CISPR, CRAF will advocate for the protection of radio astronomy and try to ensure that the impact of interference on radio telescopes is considered in future standardisation.”, CRAF member Emma van der Wateren (ASTRON) adds, who represents CRAF at CISPR and led the efforts to become a member.

“CRAF’s admission to CISPR creates the opportunity for the committee to work with administrations, industry stakeholders, and technical experts on proposals for an international electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) standard for satellites in orbit”, van der Wateren continues. If taken forward, such a standard would aim to ensure that satellites comply with limits on unintended radiation, much like terrestrial electronic devices must adhere to EMC rules to protect nearby equipment. “This would represent the first coordinated global step towards developing an EMC standard for satellites, with the goal of mitigating UEMR and safeguarding radio astronomy”, so van der Wateren.

In addition to the efforts with CISPR, Linqvist and van der Wateren are engaging with the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) through their respective national standardisation bodies, Swedish Institute for Standards (SIS) in Sweden and Netherlands Norm (NEN) in the Netherlands. These discussions explore the possibility of initiating work on an EMC standard for satellites in operation at ISO, complementing efforts within CISPR.
