TITLE: MPI Young Scholars Program 2027: Paid Research and Communications Internships for Emerging Migration Leaders

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Migration Policy Institute (MPI) is inviting applications for its prestigious Demetrios G. Papademetriou Young Scholars Program 2027, offering aspiring researchers, policy professionals, communicators, and migration specialists an opportunity to gain practical experience in one of the world’s leading independent think tanks focused on migration and human mobility.

The program provides paid internship opportunities for individuals interested in migration policy, refugee and asylum issues, immigrant integration, international development, public policy, communications, and related fields. Interns have the opportunity to contribute directly to meaningful research, policy analysis, communications initiatives, events, and public engagement activities while working alongside experienced professionals.

One of the notable features of the MPI internship program is its international accessibility. Internships are available both remotely and in person, and individuals residing outside the United States may also be eligible to participate under the program’s applicable work and residency requirements.

For the Spring 2027 internship cycle, interested applicants must submit their applications by October 15, 2026.

About the Migration Policy Institute

The Migration Policy Institute is an independent, nonpartisan, and nonprofit think tank dedicated to improving migration and mobility policies around the world. MPI conducts research and analysis on major migration-related issues and provides policymakers, practitioners, researchers, and the public with evidence-based insights into immigration systems and global mobility.

The Institute works across a broad range of issues, including:

Immigration policy and systems

Refugee protection and asylum

Border management and migration enforcement

Immigrant integration

Education and workforce development

International migration

Labor migration

Migration and development

Refugee and forced displacement

Social cohesion

Language access

Returns and reintegration

Through its research, publications, events, and policy engagement, MPI contributes to discussions and decision-making on some of the most important migration challenges facing societies worldwide.

About the Demetrios G. Papademetriou Young Scholars Program

The internship program is named in honor of Demetrios G. Papademetriou, the founding president of the Migration Policy Institute.

The Young Scholars Program was established to pursue two important objectives:

To benefit from the perspectives, skills, and contributions of talented interns supporting MPI’s work.

To help train and prepare the next generation of migration researchers, policy experts, and communications professionals.

The program reflects MPI’s commitment to mentorship and professional development by providing emerging professionals with meaningful exposure to migration research, policy discussions, communications, and public engagement.

The internship program was officially named the Demetrios G. Papademetriou Young Scholars Program in 2021. Papademetriou led MPI from its establishment in 2001 until 2014 and continued serving as President Emeritus and Distinguished Transatlantic Fellow until his death.

Throughout his career, he demonstrated a strong commitment to mentoring and supporting emerging migration thinkers and policy professionals. The Young Scholars Program continues this legacy by creating opportunities for young and early-career professionals to develop their expertise and build careers in migration-related fields.

MPI Internship Program Areas

Research interns can work across several specialized program areas at the Migration Policy Institute. These areas provide opportunities to explore different dimensions of migration policy and develop expertise in specific fields.

1. U.S. Immigration

Interns working in the U.S. Immigration program may contribute to research and policy analysis relating to major immigration issues in the United States.

Areas of focus may include:

Asylum systems

Refugee pathways

Border management

Immigration enforcement

Legal immigration

Temporary and permanent migration pathways

Unauthorized immigration

Employment outcomes of highly educated immigrants

Immigration and demographic trends

Economic trends related to migration

Policy reform proposals

This program is particularly relevant for applicants interested in immigration law, public policy, political science, economics, sociology, and migration studies.

2. International Migration

The International Migration program focuses on comparative migration policies and global mobility challenges.

Research may address areas such as:

Refugee resettlement

Asylum systems

Immigrant integration

Labor market integration

Social cohesion

Labor migration

Borders and mobility

Migration and development

Returns and reintegration

Interns may gain exposure to comparative policy analysis and international migration systems while examining how governments and institutions respond to migration challenges across different regions.

3. U.S. Immigrant Integration

The U.S. Immigrant Integration program focuses on policies and systems that influence how immigrants integrate into communities, education systems, and labor markets.

Research areas may include:

Early childhood education and care

Dual Language Learners

English Learners

K-12 immigrant education

Adult education

Workforce development

Professional training

State and local immigration policies

Integration services

Language access policies

This program may be particularly suitable for individuals interested in education policy, social policy, workforce development, immigrant integration, and community development.

4. Latin America and Caribbean Initiative

The Latin America and Caribbean Initiative examines migration dynamics and policy responses across Latin America and the Caribbean.

Key areas of work include:

Mixed migration flows

Migration from northern Central America

Venezuelan migration

Migration management systems

Host-country responses

Regional development policies

Immigrant integration

Challenges and opportunities affecting migrants and host communities

The initiative pays particular attention to countries such as:

Mexico

Costa Rica

Colombia

Venezuela

Countries in northern Central America

Applicants interested in this program should note that written proficiency and oral fluency in Spanish are required.

5. Refugee and Forced Displacement Initiative

The Refugee and Forced Displacement Initiative focuses on research and policy approaches affecting refugees and forcibly displaced populations.

The initiative examines issues including:

Refugee agency

Lived experiences of displaced populations

Refugee livelihoods

Economic self-reliance

Host-country integration

Global refugee responses

The role of faith in responding to forced displacement

This program offers an opportunity for emerging researchers and policy professionals to engage with some of the world’s most pressing humanitarian and displacement challenges.

What Do MPI Research Interns Do?

Research interns play an active role in supporting the Institute’s research and policy work. Rather than simply observing organizational activities, interns may contribute to projects and research initiatives across their assigned program areas.

Typical responsibilities include:

Conducting independent quantitative research

Conducting qualitative research

Supporting policy analysis

Contributing to broader MPI research projects

Preparing literature reviews and summaries

Drafting research papers and other written materials

Summarizing congressional hearings and relevant events

Monitoring public and private policy discussions

Supporting MPI events and convenings

Performing selected administrative duties

The experience can be particularly valuable for individuals who want to strengthen their research methodology, policy analysis, academic writing, and professional communication skills.

MPI Communications Internship

In addition to research opportunities, MPI offers a dedicated Communications Internship for individuals interested in strategic communications, digital media, public engagement, journalism, and content development.

The communications internship provides participants with exposure to the Institute’s broad range of research activities while supporting the dissemination of research and policy information to diverse audiences.

Communications interns may be involved in:

Media monitoring and tracking

Developing social media campaigns

Creating visual communication assets

Supporting event organization

Assisting with event execution

Promoting the Migration Information Source magazine

Producing short-form written content

Supporting multimedia editing activities

This internship can be especially beneficial for students and early-career professionals interested in combining communications expertise with public policy, international affairs, migration, or social impact.

MPI Internship Duration and Schedule

The MPI internship program lasts for approximately four months and operates through three main cycles each year.

While there may be flexibility in specific internship start and end dates, the standard internship cycles are:

Spring Internship Cycle

January to April

Application deadline: October 15

Summer Internship Cycle

May to August

Application deadline: February 15

Fall Internship Cycle

September to December

Application deadline: June 15

For applicants targeting the Spring 2027 cycle, the application deadline is:

October 15, 2026

Applicants are encouraged to prepare and submit their materials early to avoid last-minute challenges.

Paid Internship Stipend

One of the major benefits of the MPI Young Scholars Program is that selected interns receive financial support during their internship.

Full-time interns receive a stipend of:

$1,472 every two weeks

Part-time interns receive a prorated stipend based on their work schedule.

This financial support helps make the internship more accessible to emerging professionals who want to gain meaningful experience in migration research, policy, and communications.

Students may also be able to arrange academic credit for their internship, depending on the policies and requirements of their colleges or universities.

However, applicants should note that MPI does not cover relocation expenses.

Remote and In-Person Internship Opportunities

The MPI internship program offers flexibility in how participants complete their internships.

Depending on the role and program area, internships may be available:

Remotely

In person

On a full-time basis

On a part-time basis

Full-time interns are particularly sought for:

U.S. Immigrant Integration

Communications

The availability of remote opportunities makes the program especially attractive to qualified candidates who may not be able to relocate to the United States.

MPI also states that internships are available to individuals residing outside the United States, subject to the applicable requirements.

Who Can Apply for the MPI Young Scholars Program?

The Migration Policy Institute welcomes applications from individuals at different stages of their academic and professional journeys.

Applicants should generally meet the following requirements.

Academic and Professional Background

For all internship positions, applicants should be at least a junior in college.

Eligible candidates include:

Undergraduate students

College juniors and seniors

Recent college graduates

Graduate students

Early-career professionals

MPI also considers applicants without college experience if they can demonstrate substantial relevant professional experience.

Communication Skills

Applicants must demonstrate strong:

Oral communication skills

Written communication skills

Because many internship responsibilities involve research, writing, analysis, and communications, the ability to communicate ideas clearly and effectively is essential.

Relevant Experience and Skills

Relevant academic, professional, or research experience may strengthen an application.

Helpful skills include:

Policy research

Academic research

Quantitative analysis

Qualitative analysis

Professional writing

Policy analysis

Migration studies

Communications

Social media

Multimedia editing

Event support

Technical and Software Skills

Proficiency in key software programs, including Microsoft Office and other relevant digital tools, can be advantageous.

Strong quantitative skills may also be helpful for research-focused positions.

Foreign Language Skills

Foreign language proficiency can be an additional advantage depending on the internship area.

However, applicants interested in the Latin America and Caribbean Initiative should note that:

Written proficiency and oral fluency in Spanish are required.

Diversity and Inclusion

MPI is committed to creating an inclusive working environment that reflects diverse experiences, backgrounds, and perspectives.

The Institute aims to recruit and support interns from a broad range of communities and backgrounds in the countries and regions where it works.

The organization particularly encourages applications from:

Minority applicants

Individuals from immigrant backgrounds

Individuals from refugee backgrounds

MPI emphasizes equity and access and seeks to ensure that interns and staff can work in an inclusive professional environment.

Can International Applicants Apply?

Yes. MPI states that applicants do not need to be U.S. citizens to apply.

However, work authorization requirements apply depending on where the selected intern will perform their work.

Applicants who will work within the United States must generally have authorization to work in the country before beginning the internship.

MPI does not provide visa sponsorship or supporting documentation for several visa categories, including:

H-1B visas

J-1 visas

H-3 visas

F-1 visas

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Australian Embassy Direct Aid Program (DAP) 2026–27 is now open for applications, providing an opportunity for individuals, community groups and non-governmental organisations to seek support for small development projects in Lebanon and Syria.

Administered by the Australian Embassy, the Direct Aid Program is designed as a flexible small-grants mechanism that focuses on relieving humanitarian hardship and advancing developmental objectives. Projects supported through the program must be consistent with Australia’s international relations and public diplomacy objectives.

For organisations and community actors working to address humanitarian challenges, strengthen communities and contribute to development outcomes in Lebanon and Syria, the program can provide an avenue to seek financial support for practical, locally relevant initiatives.

What Is the Australian Embassy Direct Aid Program?

The Direct Aid Program (DAP) is a small-grants program operated by the Australian Embassy. Unlike programs that are designed primarily around individual educational or professional development, DAP focuses on supporting development projects and initiatives intended to address humanitarian hardship and developmental needs.

According to the Australian Embassy, the program is flexible and considers proposals for small development projects from eligible applicants involved in development activities on a not-for-profit basis.

The program therefore provides an opportunity for eligible applicants to present practical projects that have the potential to contribute to communities in Lebanon and Syria.

Applicants should ensure that their proposed initiatives fit within the program’s objectives and funding requirements before beginning the application process. The Embassy specifically advises prospective applicants to review the DAP guidelines before submitting an application.

Key Objectives of the Direct Aid Program

The Australian Embassy identifies two central areas of focus for DAP:

Relieving humanitarian hardship

Advancing developmental objectives

Projects should also be consistent with Australia’s international relations and public diplomacy objectives.

This means that prospective applicants should think carefully about the humanitarian or development problem their project is addressing and demonstrate how the proposed intervention can make a meaningful contribution.

A strong proposal should therefore clearly communicate:

The problem or need being addressed.

The community or beneficiaries who will benefit.

The proposed activities.

How the activities respond to the identified need.

The expected development or humanitarian outcomes.

Why the proposed intervention is appropriate for the local context.

How the project aligns with the objectives of the Direct Aid Program.

Individuals

Lebanon and Syria have experienced significant humanitarian and socioeconomic challenges, creating substantial needs for humanitarian assistance, protection, livelihoods and other forms of development support.

The Australian Embassy’s information highlights the scale of these challenges. It states that Lebanon has experienced an unprecedented financial and economic crisis and that millions of people living in the country require humanitarian assistance. The Embassy also notes the effects of poverty among Lebanese communities, displaced Syrian households and Palestine refugee populations.

Syria, meanwhile, has faced more than a decade of conflict, resulting in extensive humanitarian needs and large-scale displacement. The Embassy’s background information describes millions of people in Syria as requiring humanitarian assistance and notes the significant number of internally displaced people and Syrian refugees in neighbouring countries, including Lebanon.

Against this backdrop, small community-based development projects can play an important role in responding to specific needs at the local level.

TITLE: Donor Profile: Thomas Frank

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Tom Frank ’77 PhD ’85
Thomas Frank ’77, PhD ’85

by Erin McGrath // MIT Physics Annual 2010

Tom Frank knew from a young age that he was destined for MIT and in high school a passionate teacher inspired his love of physics. Since arriving on campus, Tom devoted his life to research and discovery in the field of physics.

MIT at once felt like home and exceeded his expectations. “There was so much available in terms of research, talks, colloquia and brilliant teachers,” said Tom. Francis Low became a scientific hero of mine who was within arm’s reach.” Tom spent the next twelve years at the Institute working towards his undergraduate degree, which he received in ’77, and then his PhD in ’85. Tom spent the majority of his graduate years building analysis software and experimental instruments, and was invited to spend two years at the prestigious physics research facility Fermilab in Batavia, IL. Tom was privileged to have Dick Yamamoto as his thesis advisor and mentor.

I’m a huge believer in the Institute — these young people are the future of our society and it’s a privilege to get to know these bright minds. By supporting them, I’m doing my little part, but the faculty and students are pulling the weight.

Thomas Frank (’77, PhD ’85)

In addition to the rewarding experiences at MIT and Fermilab, Tom was inspired to support the Physics Department through fellowships by then-Department Head Marc Kastner, who made financial support for physics students a top priority of the Department. Tom said that as a graduate student he was supported by government grants and has made it a priority to provide other physics students with the opportunity to follow their passion. Thanks to Tom, and other members of the Patrons of Physics Fellows, more first-year students can focus on crystallizing their interests and choosing a path, rather than working as a teaching or research assistant.

Tom has supported a total of seven students in the Physics Department with first-year fellowships. He enjoys learning about each student’s area of research and is inspired by their passion and energy. “I’m a huge believer in the Institute—these young people are the future of our society and it’s a privilege to get to know these bright minds,” said Tom. “By supporting them, I’m doing my little part, but the faculty and students are pulling the weight.”

Tom is currently Executive Vice President and Chief Information Officer of Interactive Brokers LLC, a trading company in Greenwich, CT, where he has helped to grow the company for over 25 years. Tom feels at home in Boston and spends most weekends here and is often on campus attending physics lectures and events. He is a member of the Physics Visiting Committee.

Ben Jones, First-Year Graduate Student and Frank Fellow

Ben Jones, Frank Fellow
Ben Jones, a first-year graduate student from the UK, is working with Prof. Janet Conrad in the field of neutrino physics. He completed his undergraduate degree in Natural Sciences (with a specialization in Physics) at the University of Cambridge, and then worked for a year on the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN in Geneva.

“My research was based on work I had done with the University of Bristol the previous summer, seeking evidence of split supersymmetry by looking for the decays of long-lived, stopped, heavy superparticles in the CMS detector. I submitted my graduate school applications reasonably early during my time at CERN, to institutions which seemed to me to be having a significant impact upon the experiment. The MIT group appeared to be a very prominent force.”

“I was accepted to several prestigious particle physics groups, but as decision time approached I had begun to suspect that perhaps despite all the glamour and publicity, the LHC may not be the experiment for me. I wanted the freedom to explore ideas and be a driving force within my collaboration. So when I had to choose my graduate school, I was in a somewhat difficult situation. Many universities had offered me positions where I would be tied into the LHC groups, and where I wasn’t really sure I wanted to be. However, thanks to the Frank Fellowship, at MIT I have had the opportunity to find a field that is a good fit.”

“Thanks to the support of the Fellowship I have had the chance to take theoretical courses on quantum chromodynamics and quantum field theory and explore the possibility of research in various fields. Now I work on the MicroBooNE experiment, where I have responsibilities in developing the optical systems for the experiment and writing the detector software. I am also about to start work on a phenomenology paper about the spin structure of the nucleon.”

“Having been at MIT for six months, I am beginning to find my feet in my research group. I am very excited about progressing as a scientist on the MicroBooNE experiment, which is a novel type of neutrino detector based on looking for tracks left by neutrinos interacting with a volume of liquid argon. MicroBooNE will run at Fermilab and may shed light on several unanswered questions about neutrinos and their interactions. Neutrinos are some of the least understood known fundamental particles in the universe, primarily because they interact so weakly with the rest of the particles of nature. However, the physics of neutrinos is thought to have played a key role in the process of leptogenesis, which is the mechanism by which the very early universe crystallized into the matter we see around us, rather than simply a maelstrom of matter and antimatter destined to explosively recombine and eventually end up as a sea of featureless, dispersed energy.”

“Neutrinos may also play key roles in the supernovae explosions which populated the universe with the heavy elements. They may have applications in the nonproliferation of nuclear weapons. And, as recently confirmed by the Borexino experiment, they may shed light on the mechanics of nuclear reactions in the mantle of the Earth. As our ability to detect and measure these elusive particles increases, there will doubtless be a plethora of other new physics opportunities. I am extremely pleased to have found my way into this exciting and developing field.”

“I’d like to thank Tom Frank for his fantastic generosity in supporting MIT, physics research, the field of neutrino physics and my education with this Fellowship. I am extremely grateful!”

TITLE: Scotland Pakistan Scholarships for Young Women and Girls 2026: Fully Funded Bachelor’s and Master’s Study in Pakistan

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the Scotland Pakistan Scholarships for Young Women and Girls 2026, an important higher education funding opportunity designed to support Pakistani women pursuing undergraduate and postgraduate education at Higher Education Commission (HEC)-recognised universities across Pakistan.

Funded by the Scottish Government and administered in Pakistan by the British Council, the scholarship programme aims to make quality higher education more accessible to women and girls, particularly those who may face financial, geographical, social or accessibility-related barriers to continuing their education.

The programme provides financial assistance towards tuition fees and other education-related expenses for eligible women studying selected priority subjects at universities in Pakistan. Depending on their level of study, successful applicants may receive support for a four-year bachelor’s degree or a master’s/MPhil programme lasting up to two years.

Women with disabilities, women from rural communities and women belonging to minority groups are particularly encouraged to apply.

Importantly, the application deadline has been extended to 15 September 2026, giving eligible candidates additional time to prepare and submit their applications.

About the Scotland Pakistan Scholarships for Young Women and Girls 2026

The Scotland Pakistan Scholarships for Young Women and Girls programme is an initiative funded by the Scottish Government to increase access to higher education for Pakistani women.

Higher education can provide women with greater opportunities for professional development, economic participation, leadership and contribution to their communities. However, the financial costs associated with university education can prevent talented students from pursuing or completing their studies.

The Scotland Pakistan Scholarships seek to address some of these barriers by providing financial support to eligible female students pursuing degrees in selected fields considered important for Pakistan’s social, economic and sustainable development.

The programme is administered by the British Council in Pakistan, which coordinates with successful scholars and their respective universities. Coordination may take place directly with scholarship recipients and universities or through nominated university focal persons.

What Levels of Study Are Supported?

The Scotland Pakistan Scholarships for Young Women and Girls 2026 support eligible students at both undergraduate and postgraduate levels.

Applicants may be pursuing one of the following:

1. Four-Year Bachelor’s Degree

Female students pursuing a four-year bachelor’s degree at an HEC-recognised university in Pakistan may apply, provided their programme falls within one of the scholarship’s eligible subject areas.

This provides an important opportunity for young Pakistani women beginning or pursuing undergraduate higher education in fields connected to education, sustainability, agriculture, health, science, technology and climate.

2. Master’s or MPhil Degree

The programme also supports eligible women pursuing a master’s or MPhil degree of up to two years at an HEC-recognised university in Pakistan.

Applicants must be pursuing their postgraduate qualification within one of the programme’s designated subject areas and must meet all other eligibility requirements.

Financial Benefits of the Scotland Pakistan Scholarships 2026

Successful applicants can receive substantial financial support to help reduce the costs associated with pursuing higher education.

The Scotland Pakistan Scholarships for Young Women and Girls Scheme provides award holders with support that may include:

Tuition Fees

The scholarship covers tuition fees for courses in eligible subject areas.

Tuition costs can represent one of the largest financial barriers to university education. By providing support towards eligible tuition fees, the scholarship allows selected students to concentrate more fully on their studies and academic development.

University Hostel Costs

The scholarship provides support for university hostel costs where applicable.

This is particularly valuable for students who need to relocate from their home communities to attend university and require accommodation on or around their university campus.

Travel Between Home and University

Students staying in on-campus university hostels can receive support for travel between their home and university twice per year.

For students studying away from their families, particularly those coming from rural or geographically distant communities, this provision can help reduce the additional costs associated with university attendance.

Research Support for Master’s Students

Master’s-level scholarship recipients may also receive funding for research work to access quality laboratories, equipment and tools required for their chosen course of study.

This research support is specifically identified for master’s students and can be particularly valuable for candidates pursuing programmes requiring laboratory work, specialist equipment, practical research or technical resources.

Eligible Subject Areas

The Scotland Pakistan Scholarships for Young Women and Girls 2026 are not available for every university discipline.

Applicants must be studying within one of the programme’s specified priority subject areas.

The scholarship covers eligible four-year bachelor’s degrees and up to two-year master’s degrees in the following areas:

Education

Students pursuing eligible programmes related to education can apply for scholarship support.

Education plays an important role in developing skilled communities, improving learning outcomes and strengthening future generations of educators and education professionals.

Sustainable Energy

Eligible programmes related to sustainable energy are covered by the scholarship.

As countries work towards more sustainable and resilient energy systems, expertise in renewable and sustainable energy is increasingly important for addressing environmental, economic and development challenges.

Food Security and Agriculture

Women pursuing eligible programmes related to food security and agriculture can also apply.

This area is particularly relevant to sustainable food production, agricultural development, rural livelihoods, food systems and long-term food security.

Health Sciences

The programme supports eligible students pursuing health sciences.

Supporting women in health-related education can contribute to strengthening healthcare capacity, research and services while creating additional professional opportunities for women in the sector.

STEM

Eligible programmes within Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) are included.

STEM education provides pathways into rapidly developing fields and can prepare women for careers in science, engineering, technology, research, innovation and related industries.

Climate

Eligible programmes related to climate are also supported.

With climate change creating increasingly significant environmental, social and economic challenges, developing expertise in climate-related disciplines can help prepare future professionals and researchers to contribute to climate resilience and sustainable development.

Who Can Apply for the Scotland Pakistan Scholarships 2026?

The Scotland Pakistan Scholarships for Young Women and Girls are specifically available to female applicants who satisfy the programme’s eligibility conditions.

Applicants must meet all of the following core requirements:

Be female.

Be a Pakistani national.

Be currently residing in Pakistan.

Be pursuing an eligible four-year bachelor’s degree or a two-year master’s degree.

Be studying within one of the scholarship’s approved subject areas.

Hold a confirmed admission offer from an HEC-recognised university in Pakistan.

Applicants should carefully review the relevant official scholarship FAQs before applying, particularly because separate guidance documents are available for bachelor’s and master’s applicants.

Encouragement for Women from Underrepresented Communities

One of the significant aspects of the Scotland Pakistan Scholarships for Young Women and Girls is its emphasis on widening access to higher education.

The programme specifically encourages applications from:

Young women with disabilities

Women from rural areas

Women from minority groups

Candidates from these backgrounds who otherwise meet the scholarship criteria are therefore strongly encouraged to consider applying.

Applicants should nevertheless carefully review all official eligibility requirements and supporting documentation before submitting an application.

HEC-Recognised University Requirement

Applicants must hold a confirmed admission offer from an HEC-recognised university in Pakistan.

This is an important eligibility condition.

The scholarship is intended to fund eligible studies undertaken within Pakistan rather than study at a Scottish or other overseas university.

Applicants should therefore verify the recognition status of their university and ensure that their programme and admission status satisfy the scholarship requirements before submitting an application.

Is This Scholarship for Studying in Scotland?

Despite the programme being funded by the Scottish Government, the Scotland Pakistan Scholarships for Young Women and Girls described in this call support eligible students pursuing their studies at HEC-recognised universities within Pakistan.

Applicants should not interpret the programme as a scholarship for travelling to Scotland or studying at a Scottish university.

The financial support is intended to improve access to higher education for Pakistani women studying in Pakistan.

Why Pakistani Women Should Consider This Opportunity

TITLE: Unilever Singapore Early Careers 2027: Applications Open for Future Leaders Programme and Leadership Internships

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Unilever has opened applications for its 2027 Early Career Opportunities in Singapore, offering students and recent graduates the chance to build professional experience at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies. The current Singapore recruitment campaign includes the Unilever Future Leaders Programme (UFLP) for graduates and the Unilever Leadership Internship Programme (ULIP) for university students.

These programmes provide two different entry routes into Unilever. The Future Leaders Programme is designed for graduates who want to develop toward future business leadership positions through structured development, rotations and challenging assignments. The Leadership Internship Programme, meanwhile, provides Bachelor’s and Master’s students with six months of practical experience across several business functions.

Applications opened in September 2026 for opportunities beginning in 2027.

Application period: Applications opened on 1 September 2026. Unilever’s campaign materials indicate applications through 30 September 2026, while the current Workday posting for the Future Leaders Programme technically displays an end date of 1 October 2026. Applicants are therefore strongly advised to submit by 30 September 2026 rather than relying on the system’s later closing timestamp.

Location: Singapore

UFLP intake: July 2027

ULIP internship period: 11 January 2027 to 30 June 2027

About Unilever Singapore Early Career Opportunities 2027

Unilever’s Early Careers recruitment is designed to bring emerging talent into areas that directly contribute to the company’s brands, customers, operations and long-term business development.

The Singapore Early Careers listings currently include a graduate leadership opportunity and six Leadership Internship Programme functions. These cover Marketing, Finance, Human Resources, Customer Development, Consumer Market Insights and Supply Chain/Procurement.

For applicants, this means the 2027 recruitment is not limited to one academic background or professional interest. Depending on the programme selected, candidates may work on brand development, consumer research, financial analytics, people management, sales and customer strategy, supply-chain transformation or procurement.

Unilever Future Leaders Programme – Marketing, Singapore

The Unilever Future Leaders Programme – Marketing is the principal graduate opportunity included in the current Singapore Early Careers recruitment.

The programme is intended to accelerate the development of individuals who demonstrate the potential to progress toward business leadership roles. Instead of remaining in a narrowly defined entry-level position, participants gain experience through challenging assignments and multiple job rotations.

The Singapore Marketing posting identifies the programme as a three-year programme, while Unilever’s description of the broader UFLP model refers to a typical duration of approximately two to three years.

The programme intake is scheduled for July 2027.

What Is the Unilever Future Leaders Programme?

The Unilever Future Leaders Programme focuses on developing tomorrow’s leaders by exposing participants to real business responsibilities at an early stage in their careers.

Successful applicants can expect a combination of:

Structured professional development

Job rotations across relevant business areas

Hands-on exposure to real commercial challenges

Learning from experienced Unilever colleagues and leaders

Formal learning programmes designed to develop leadership and business skills

Exposure to sales and go-to-market activities

Opportunities for broader or international exposure depending on programme requirements

Responsibility for projects with measurable business relevance

Unilever states that the programme is intended to accelerate participants’ readiness for future leadership responsibilities.

UFLP Marketing: What Participants Will Work On

Marketing at Unilever goes beyond conventional advertising. The function combines consumer understanding, data, brand strategy, communication and commercial execution.

UFLP Marketing participants may gain experience in areas such as brand building and brand development, including helping create strategic visions for brands and developing plans across the full marketing mix.

Participants may also manage projects involving external creative agencies and contribute to the coordination of product launches with supply-chain and category teams.

The work is therefore suited to graduates who are interested in understanding consumers, interpreting market information and translating insights into strategies that strengthen brand equity and generate business demand.

UFLP Marketing Eligibility Requirements

For the Singapore Future Leaders Programme – Marketing, Unilever currently identifies several core requirements.

Applicants must have at least a Bachelor’s degree.

The programme is intended for graduates with no more than 24 months of formal work experience after graduation.

Candidates should also demonstrate energy, motivation and leadership potential and be willing to travel where required. Geographic mobility is specifically identified as an expectation for applicants.

This makes UFLP particularly relevant to new graduates and early-career professionals rather than applicants who already have several years of full-time post-graduation professional experience.

UFLP Marketing Selection Process

Applicants should expect a multi-stage recruitment process.

Unilever currently identifies the process as:

Online application

Blended assessments

Digital interview

Phone interview

Discovery Centre

The Discovery Centre is expected to be conducted physically in October 2026.

Applicants should therefore plan for more than simply submitting a CV. Candidates may be assessed on problem-solving, communication, decision-making, motivation and leadership potential throughout the process.

Unilever also warns candidates that submitting duplicate applications for the same position or applying to multiple UFLP functions may affect the review process or eligibility.

Unilever Leadership Internship Programme 2027

Students who are still completing their university education can apply for the Unilever Leadership Internship Programme, commonly known as ULIP.

Unlike UFLP, which is designed for graduates entering a longer leadership-development programme, ULIP is a six-month internship programme.

The internship is scheduled to run from:

11 January 2027 to 30 June 2027.

The current Singapore recruitment includes six major areas:

Marketing

Finance

Human Resources

Customer Development

Consumer Market Insights

Supply Chain/Procurement

These opportunities appear within Unilever’s Singapore Early Careers recruitment portal.

1. Unilever Leadership Internship Programme – Marketing

The Marketing internship is designed for students interested in consumer behaviour, brands, digital marketing, communication and commercial strategy.

Interns can gain exposure to how Unilever’s brand teams understand consumers, interpret data and design campaigns intended to build demand and brand equity.

Work may involve:

Brand building and brand development

Developing plans across the marketing mix

Consumer and market analysis

Supporting advertising and communications

Working with external creative agencies

Supporting product launches

Digitalisation and marketing technology projects

Examples cited by Unilever from previous ULIP Marketing projects include applying AI and augmented reality technologies to beauty-related consumer experiences, supporting engagement plans for a CLEAR product in Indonesia, and developing digital brand-health dashboards for Southeast Asian brands.

The examples demonstrate that interns may be given commercially relevant assignments rather than purely administrative duties.

2. Unilever Leadership Internship Programme – Finance

The Finance internship gives students experience in how a major multinational organisation protects and creates value while managing sustainable financial performance.

Students may work with experienced finance professionals and other business teams to analyse information and support decision-making.

Examples of previous ULIP Finance projects cited by Unilever include:

Automating inventory analytics to support inventory management and business-waste governance

Partnering with business groups to provide financial insights and analysis

Creating Power BI dashboards for price analytics, benchmarking and governance

The six-month Finance internship is based in Singapore.

This opportunity may be particularly relevant for students interested in corporate finance, management accounting, business analytics, financial planning, performance management and data-driven decision-making.

3. Unilever Leadership Internship Programme – Human Resources

The Human Resources internship allows students to work on projects related to Unilever’s people, organisational culture, talent and employee experience.

Interns may contribute to strategic HR initiatives while working alongside experienced leaders and business teams.

Unilever identifies examples of previous intern assignments including supporting talent-development forums and change-management initiatives, improving employee experiences through policy implementation and onboarding, contributing to recruitment activities, supporting long-service recognition programmes and participating in employer-branding initiatives both on and off university campuses.

The role offers exposure to the connection between HR strategy and organisational performance rather than treating HR simply as an administrative function.

4. Unilever Leadership Internship Programme – Customer Development

Customer Development is closely connected with how Unilever brings its brands and products to customers and markets.

The Singapore internship can provide experience working in what the company describes as a “white space” business environment, involving different geographies, consumers and customers.

Students can learn how products are developed commercially, how market opportunities are identified and how partnerships contribute to business expansion.

Unilever provides examples of previous Customer Development intern projects involving commercial opportunities linked to consumers living outside their home markets and expanding route-to-market or brand-partner portfolios in major markets.

This programme may appeal particularly to students interested in sales, business development, commercial strategy, customer management and entrepreneurship.

5. Unilever Leadership Internship Programme – Consumer Market Insights

Consumer Market Insights, or CMI, focuses on transforming data and research into knowledge that can improve marketing and business decisions.

Interns may work with both primary and secondary research, analyse market dynamics and help convert findings into recommendations for Unilever’s brand teams.

The programme can involve areas such as:

Consumer research

Market analysis

Research design

Data interpretation

Insight generation

Visualisation and storytelling

Identifying digital and social trends

Working with external research agencies

Unilever’s examples include working with research organisations on questionnaires and research findings, tracking digital and social trends, creating visualisations and summaries, and assisting with systems used in research execution.

This may be particularly attractive to students interested in market research, analytics, consumer psychology and data-driven marketing strategy.

6. Unilever Leadership Internship Programme – Supply Chain/Procurement

The Supply Chain/Procurement internship provides exposure to the increasingly technology-driven environment behind the production, sourcing and movement of consumer products.

Unilever specifically highlights areas including real-time data, analytics and robotic process automation.

Previous ULIP projects have included supply-chain analysis for new business opportunities, logistics digitalisation, conversion of large datasets into more usable information, sustainable and traceable sourcing initiatives and negotiations with important suppliers.

Interns can also gain exposure to contracting and sourcing strategies.

This route may be especially relevant to students interested in procurement, logistics, operations, data analytics, sustainability and supply-chain management.

Who Can Apply for the Unilever Leadership Internship Programme?

ULIP has an important eligibility distinction from UFLP.

Applicants must currently be enrolled in a Bachelor’s or Master’s degree programme.

Unilever explicitly states that fresh graduates are not eligible for ULIP internships. Therefore, students who have already completed their degree and are no longer enrolled should instead examine graduate opportunities such as UFLP where they meet the requirements.

Interns must also be able to commit to at least three days per week, although Unilever indicates that full-time participation is preferred.

Across the Singapore ULIP listings, the company also looks for applicants who can work in a fast-paced and results-oriented environment, demonstrate initiative, take on new challenges and communicate effectively in both written and verbal settings.

Part-Time and Full-Time Participation

The ULIP listings describe a six-month experience with flexibility between part-time and full-time engagement, while simultaneously requiring a commitment of at least three days per week and stating that full-time commitment is preferred.

Applicants should therefore ensure their university schedule allows them to meet the minimum attendance requirement throughout the internship period from January to June 2027.

ULIP Selection Process

The six Singapore internship functions follow a broadly consistent selection process:

Online application

SOVA blended assessment

Phone interview

Virtual interview with the hiring manager

Final offer stage

Unilever indicates that successful offers are expected to be extended by approximately the first week of December 2026.

Because the internship begins on 11 January 2027, successful candidates have approximately one month between the anticipated offer stage and programme commencement.

Why Consider Unilever Early Careers?

One of the distinguishing characteristics of both UFLP and ULIP is the emphasis on actual business exposure.

ULIP descriptions repeatedly state that interns work with experienced teams and leaders on tangible projects. Examples across functions demonstrate exposure to business analytics, brand strategy, AI, consumer research, procurement, sustainability, employee experience and commercial development.

UFLP goes further by placing graduates into a structured development pathway with rotations and leadership-oriented assignments. Its purpose is not merely to provide an entry-level marketing position but to accelerate participants’ readiness for larger business responsibilities.

For students and early-career graduates seeking experience in a large multinational consumer-goods organisation, the programmes therefore provide two clearly differentiated entry routes.

Important Difference Between UFLP and ULIP

Candidates should select the programme that matches their current academic status.

UFLP is aimed at graduates. Applicants need at least a Bachelor’s degree and generally should not have more than 24 months of formal work experience after graduation. The Singapore Marketing intake begins in July 2027.

ULIP, by contrast, is specifically for students who remain enrolled in Bachelor’s or Master’s programmes. Fresh graduates are explicitly excluded from the internship route. ULIP begins on 11 January 2027 and finishes on 30 June 2027.

Candidates should therefore verify their student or graduate status carefully before submitting an application.

Application Deadline

Applications opened on 1 September 2026.

The recruitment campaign indicates an application period through 30 September 2026. The Workday system for the UFLP Marketing position currently displays an End Date of 1 October 2026. To avoid any timezone or system-closing issue, candidates should regard 30 September 2026 as the practical deadline and submit earlier whenever possible.

Applicants should also remember that recruitment processes can close or change, so the official application portal should always be checked immediately before submission.

How to Apply

Applications must be submitted through Unilever’s official Early Careers recruitment portal.

Candidates should review the individual position that matches their academic status and career interests, prepare the requested application information and submit through the online system.

Official reference and application page:
Unilever Singapore Early Careers 2027 Application Portal

Candidates should apply only through official Unilever channels. Unilever also warns applicants that it does not request money or credit-card information as part of its recruitment process.

Conclusion

The Unilever Singapore Early Careers 2027 recruitment provides a significant opportunity for both university students and recent graduates seeking exposure to a major multinational consumer-goods organisation.

Graduates can pursue the Unilever Future Leaders Programme – Marketing, a multi-year development pathway beginning in July 2027 that combines leadership development, business assignments and rotations.

Students currently completing Bachelor’s or Master’s degrees can apply for the six-month Unilever Leadership Internship Programme, with opportunities available across Marketing, Finance, Human Resources, Customer Development, Consumer Market Insights and Supply Chain/Procurement.

The internship runs from 11 January to 30 June 2027, while the UFLP Marketing intake begins in July 2027. Candidates are advised to submit applications by 30 September 2026.

Applicants should carefully select the correct programme because the eligibility conditions are substantially different: UFLP is intended for graduates, while ULIP requires applicants to remain enrolled as university students.

TITLE: University of Cape Town RAENS Masters Bursary 2027–2028: R200,000 Annual Funding for Agroecology Research in South Africa

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Research for Agroecology Network Southern Africa (RAENS) Masters Bursary 2027–2028 is inviting applications for one full-time Master’s bursary focused on understanding the social, ecological, and environmental impacts of agroecological transitions in South Africa.

The opportunity is hosted by the Department of Environmental and Geographical Science at the University of Cape Town (UCT) under the DSTI/NRF Research Chair: Environmental and Social Dimensions of the Bio-economy. The selected Master’s student will conduct research as part of the RAENS project and work with a dynamic team investigating agroecological transitions at multiple sites across South Africa.

The bursary provides R200,000 per year tax-free for two years, with additional funding available for fieldwork costs. The project will also cover UCT fees, subject to the conditions outlined in the announcement.

Applications for the RAENS Masters Bursary close on 21 September 2026 at 9:00 S.A.S.T.

RAENS Masters Bursary 2027–2028

The Research for Agroecology Network Southern Africa (RAENS) is offering a Master’s research opportunity for a suitably qualified scholar interested in agroecology and the social, environmental, ecological, and economic dimensions of agricultural transitions.

The successful candidate will join the Bioeconomy Research Chair in the Department of Environmental and Geographical Science at the University of Cape Town and contribute to research being conducted through the RAENS project.

The position is designed for a researcher who is interested not only in academic research but also in participatory and farmer-led research in rural communities across South Africa.

The full-time Master’s research will involve fieldwork at multiple pilot sites in different provinces, meaning applicants should be prepared to travel and spend several weeks at a time conducting research in different locations.

About the Research for Agroecology Network Southern Africa

The Research for Agroecology Network Southern Africa (RAENS) is the broader research project under which this Master’s bursary will be funded and completed.

RAENS aims to establish a transdisciplinary agroecology research and knowledge network in Southern Africa.

The project seeks to strengthen existing agroecological initiatives while demonstrating the potential and scalability of agroecology across the region.

Its broader objectives include:

Strengthening existing agroecology initiatives.

Showcasing the potential of agroecological approaches.

Exploring the scalability of agroecology.

Supporting changes in agricultural training.

Supporting changes in agricultural research.

Promoting agroecological and regenerative approaches to food production.

Supporting sustainable approaches to producing food, fibre, and fodder.

Informing policy.

Contributing to an enabling environment for agroecology uptake.

Strengthening agroecology research and training.

The RAENS project takes a transdisciplinary approach, bringing together different forms of knowledge and expertise to understand agroecological transitions.

About the Master’s Research Opportunity

The successful candidate will investigate agroecological transitions at various sites in South Africa.

The research is intended to understand the experiences and implications of agroecological transitions for farmers.

This makes the opportunity particularly relevant to candidates interested in the relationship between agriculture, environmental sustainability, rural communities, livelihoods, ecological systems, governance, and food systems.

The Master’s student may develop research around either ecological and biophysical dimensions or social and economic dimensions of agroecological transition.

Research Area 1: Ecological and Biophysical Dimensions

One possible research direction focuses on the ecological and biophysical aspects of agroecological transitions.

Potential areas include:

Soil Health

The student may investigate how agroecological transitions affect or interact with soil health and sustainable soil management.

Biodiversity

Research may examine biodiversity and its relationship to agroecological farming systems.

Water Conservation

Water conservation is another potential area of investigation, particularly in relation to agricultural sustainability and resource management.

Recycling

Research could explore recycling approaches within agroecological systems and their contribution to sustainable production.

Integrated Pest Management

The student may also investigate integrated pest management as part of agroecological transition.

These topics provide opportunities to explore how farming practices can interact with ecological processes and environmental sustainability.

Research Area 2: Social and Economic Dimensions

The second broad research direction focuses on the social and economic aspects of agroecological transitions.

Potential areas include:

Social Cohesion

The research may investigate how agroecological transitions influence relationships, collaboration, and social cohesion within farming and rural communities.

Livelihoods

Another potential focus is the effect of agroecological transitions on livelihoods and the economic circumstances of farmers and communities.

Territorial Markets

The Master’s research may examine territorial markets and their role within agroecological food systems.

Governance

Governance is another potential area of research, including the ways institutions, communities, and other stakeholders influence agroecological transitions.

Indigenous Food and Farming Systems

The research can also explore indigenous food and farming systems and their relationship with agroecological approaches.

Diets

Another potential theme is the relationship between agroecological transitions and diets.

Community Resilience

Students may investigate how agroecological approaches contribute to or interact with community resilience.

Cross-Cutting Research Themes

In addition to the main research areas, the Master’s research will incorporate several cross-cutting themes.

These include:

Youth

Gender

Climate change

Indigenous knowledge

These themes can be integrated into research examining either the ecological and biophysical or social and economic dimensions of agroecological transition.

This provides scope for research that examines agroecology from multiple perspectives rather than treating agricultural transition solely as a technical or environmental issue.

Fieldwork and Farmer-Led Research

A major component of the Master’s position is fieldwork.

The selected student will travel to multiple pilot sites located in different provinces of South Africa.

Fieldwork may involve spending several weeks at a time at different research locations.

The fieldwork will support participatory, farmer-led research on agroecology.

Applicants should therefore be prepared for a research programme that involves substantial engagement outside the university environment.

The opportunity may be particularly relevant to candidates who already have experience working with rural communities in South Africa.

Participation in RAENS Activities

The selected Master’s student will not only conduct their individual research.

They will also be expected to participate in:

RAENS meetings.

RAENS events.

Project-related research activities.

Engagement with the broader RAENS research team.

This means the position combines independent Master’s research with participation in a wider research network.

Duration of the Bursary

The bursary supports two years of full-time Master’s study, covering the period from January 2027 to December 2028.

The second year of funding is subject to satisfactory progress.

Applicants should therefore understand that continued funding into the second year depends on satisfactory academic and research progress.

Financial Support

The RAENS Master’s bursary provides significant financial support for the selected candidate.

Annual Bursary

The total bursary value is:

R200,000 per year

The bursary is described as tax-free.

Over two years, this represents a total bursary value of:

R400,000, assuming the second year is funded following satisfactory progress.

Fieldwork Funding

In addition to the annual bursary, additional funding is available for fieldwork costs.

This is particularly relevant because the research involves travel to multiple pilot sites in different South African provinces.

UCT Fees

The project will also cover UCT fees.

The bursary therefore combines annual financial support with project funding for fieldwork and coverage of UCT fees.

Costs Not Covered

The announcement specifically states that the bursary does not include benefits or travel/relocation costs.

Applicants should therefore take potential personal travel and relocation expenses into account when considering the opportunity.

Eligibility Requirements

Applicants must meet specific academic and research-related requirements.

Honours Degree

Applicants must hold an Honours degree with a minimum of 65% in a relevant field.

The announcement provides examples of relevant fields, including:

Environmental science

Conservation

Anthropology

Sociology

Development studies

Geography

Botany

Agriculture

Other closely related fields may potentially be relevant, but applicants should assess their academic background against the requirements stated in the official announcement.

Recent Qualification

The Honours degree must have been awarded within the last five years.

Applicants should therefore ensure that their qualification falls within this specified period.

No Existing Research Master’s Degree

Applicants should not already have a research Master’s degree.

The opportunity is intended for candidates who are seeking to undertake the relevant Master’s research programme.

Desired Competencies

Beyond the formal eligibility requirements, the project identifies several competencies that would be desirable in the successful candidate.

Strong Research Skills

Applicants should demonstrate strong research capabilities and the ability to engage with academic and field-based research.

Analytical and Conceptual Skills

Strong analytical and conceptual skills are desired because the research involves examining complex ecological, environmental, social, and economic dimensions of agroecological transition.

TITLE: “Place Students and Faculty at the Center of Digital Infrastructure Implementation” – a Senior Digital Education Expert Advises

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Mr. Moussa Traore an International Digital Education Expert from the World Bank has advised African Universities to always prioritize the needs of students and faculty when designing and implementing digital infrastructure. This is important because technological infrastructure must be used by students and faculty to achieve the intended learning outcomes and produce skilled graduates that would be able to address Africa’s developmental challenges. African Universities tend to prioritize internet access for their administrative purposes and not for teaching, learning and research needs, stated Mr. Traore. Mr. Traore said this while making a presentation during the digital transformation session at the 7th ACE Impact Regional Workshop hosted in Benin from 14-17 June 2022.

The overall “ICT for digital and remote learning” recommendations shared by Mr. Traore focused on infrastructure and equipment; technical support and training; quality digital content and resources and digital education policies and data governance.

Infrastructure and equipment

Mr. Traore advised universities to gradually migrate their applications, platforms, and related infrastructure to the cloud because this would reduce the need to invest in internal skills for maintaining the infrastructure. Cloud hosting also ensures that the digital platforms are continuously accessible and not affected by power outages.

Universities were encouraged to develop long-term plans for their infrastructure, which must include the replacement of wired and wireless cabling, devices and identifying funding sources. It was also said that university digital transformation plans must indicate how the security and protection of student data are assured.

Mr. Traore cautioned that universities needed to ensure that their servers had the capacity to meet current and future storage needs, and that they had the performance to run newer applications. “It is important to be able to easily expand the storage capacities of servers as needed”, indicated Mr. Traore. Computer servers must be replaced every 3-5 years and their software regularly updated to newer versions. ​There must be additional servers for specific tasks and services – for example, a web server for online and remote training, accounting server, database server, mail server, and others.

Connectivity

Since robust connectivity is a key enabler for online learning, African universities must therefore ensure that students and faculty have broadband access to the Internet and adequate wireless connectivity. Special focus must be on the equity of access both inside and outside of the campus.

Network Engineers were advised to plan to offer a minimum of 10 mbps total bandwidth to each student and WIFI solutions must cover the whole campus including the students’ dormitories to enable them to learn from anywhere. Campus networks must implement at least the 802.11N wireless technology standard in the 5GHZ band to facilitate maximum coverage and connection for students and faculty.

Device access

Universities were called to allow students to use their own personal wireless devices in a safe and secure manner. Mr. Traore also said that content filtering and restricted guest user access must be implemented to protect the universities’ internal network resources.

It is the duty of university leaders to ensure that every student and faculty member have at least one internet access device – a smartphone, laptop, tablet, and or desktop – including appropriate software and resources for research, collaboration, communication, multimedia content creation, and collaboration in and outside campus.

Universities ought to design and implement plans for accommodating students who either do not have access to devices or lack devices that are compatible with the official campus learning management system.

Learning Management System (LMS) Use

African Universities were advised to ensure that they offered a digital and distance learning management system (LMS) such as Moodle, Sakai, Blackboard or other preferred LMS.

There ought to be clear instructions given to students concerning how to use the LMS and tips for navigating the specifics of a course.

Technical Support and Training

Universities were advised to prepare their Information Technology (IT) support staff to provide just-in-time support to students and faculty members.

There must be a plan for continuous Professional Learning Opportunities for university IT staff. Mr. Traore mentioned observing over the period, that many of the universities were not creating such learning opportunities for their staff, therefore universities ought to refine their goals and set a focus on this area since changes happen frequently in the IT sector. Adding, that the modes and frequency of professional learning activities need to be clarified as an institutional policy.

Provide Access to Technology and Support

Universities need to identify and put in place support mechanisms to help students and faculty when they experience technical difficulties. Such a support plan, when adopted should be communicated to all faculty and students.

An annual training program on the use of the university LMS must be developed and shared with faculty and students. Offering educational technology support to faculty and students increases their digital literacy declared Mr Moussa Traore.

Quality Digital Content and Resources

The technologies that are deployed must be fit for purpose and should facilitate the management and provision of learning materials. Again, African Universities were advised to support the development and use of openly licensed educational materials to promote innovative and creative opportunities for all learners and to accelerate the development and adoption of new open technology–based learning tools and courses.​

Mr. Traore also advised universities to take inventory of all their learning technology resources and align them to intended educational outcomes.

Policies and Governance

Prioritization of the implementation of data initiatives and the collection of data to drive decision-making in African Universities was recommended by Mr. Troare. “To collect data, universities must implement robust Education Management Information System (EMIS) so that they can collect all existing data on students, faculty, and the universities”, he added.

Collected Data must be regularly analyzed to determine whether additional data need to be collected to address priorities. Mr. Traore recommended the creation of a comprehensive map and database of connectivity, device access, openly licensed educational resources, and their usage across the institution.​

Mr. Traore underscored the importance of establishing governance for learning and educational technologies to avoid problems with the efficient delivery of systems, confusion over policy, and variation in the types and quality of services and tools provided.

He stressed the importance of implementing an IT security policy, saying that cybersecurity and cyber safety training for students, faculty and staff in general needed to be prioritized. He also stated that digital and distance learning policies needed to be developed and implemented by African Universities.

Technology Planning and Purchasing

University Leaders were informed that they needed to define their Technology Budgets as a matter of priority. Existing budgets must be reviewed, and an inventory of available technology done. Vice Chancellors must work with their Directors of ICT to determine the costs for upgrading infrastructure and purchasing new devices as well as identify funds to meet short- and long-term goals.

Universities must develop a multi-year plan to support and sustain the costs of technology. Similarly, budgets must be regularly reviewed and refined to accommodate the costs of technology.

Technology Evaluation

In conclusion Mr. Moussa Traore said that the periodic evaluation of all technological solutions was important because this provides opportunities to obtain feedback and improve technological services to benefit both students and faculty. During technology evaluations, universities were advised to reflect on questions such as – Is technology being used effectively? Is technology getting in the way of pedagogy? Are the students engaged in the lessons? ​ Do the faculty staff display or have confidence in the use of the technology? Are the hardware and software installed and configured correctly?​ Are there things that the IT Support team can do to facilitate learning?​

Eligible Host Institutions

Research stays can be undertaken at eligible universities and research institutions located on Bildungscampus Heilbronn.

These include:

DHBW Center for Advanced Studies

The DHBW Center for Advanced Studies offers postgraduate study and research opportunities within the Baden-Württemberg Cooperative State University network.

DHBW Heilbronn

DHBW Heilbronn is part of the Baden-Württemberg Cooperative State University and is one of the institutions participating in the Heilbronn research ecosystem.

Ferdinand-Steinbeis-Institute

The Ferdinand-Steinbeis-Institute is an interdisciplinary research institution involved in applied research and innovation.

Fraunhofer HNFIZ

Fraunhofer HNFIZ is among the research institutions eligible to host research projects under the fellowship.

Heilbronn University of Applied Sciences

Heilbronn University of Applied Sciences is another eligible institution located on Bildungscampus Heilbronn.

TUM Campus Heilbronn

The Technical University of Munich (TUM) Campus Heilbronn is also an eligible host institution for fellowship research projects.

Applicants should establish contact with an eligible host institution and develop their research project in cooperation with the proposed host.

Duration of the Fellowship

Funding is available for research stays lasting between 1 and 12 months.

The fellowship cannot normally be extended. Special circumstances may be considered individually.

The funding is available during the programme’s funding period.

Fellowship Benefits

The Heilbronn AI Fellowship provides financial support to successful fellows.

The main benefits include:

€2,800 monthly fellowship instalment

Payments towards health, accident and personal liability insurance

A lump sum towards international travel costs

Additional support may also be available in certain circumstances.

These may include:

Support for additional costs arising from a disability or chronic illness, subject to individual assessment.

Family benefits for fellows whose funding period exceeds six months, subject to eligibility.

Other support related to special circumstances, assessed on a case-by-case basis.

Selection Process

Selection is conducted through a single-stage evaluation based on the submitted application documents.

Applications are jointly prepared by the applicant and the proposed host institution and are evaluated by independent experts in the relevant research fields.

Experts are appointed by the DAAD, while partner institutions may propose candidates. Individuals with conflicts of interest or a supervisory relationship with an applicant are excluded from the evaluation process.

Funding is awarded only after a positive evaluation by the appointed experts.

Selection Criteria

Applications are assessed according to several key criteria.

Academic Qualification

The selection process considers:

Academic performance

General grade point average

Development of academic performance

Dissertation grade

Course of study and doctorate

Academic achievements after graduation

Publications

Lectures and conference papers

Quality of the Research Project

The proposed research project is assessed based on:

Originality of the research proposal

Topicality and relevance of the project

Quality of preparation

Suitability of the selected host institution

Initial contact with the host institution

Relevance for application and technology transfer

Feasibility of the research plan

Consistency of the proposed schedule

Suitability of the applicant’s profile for the project

Potential for personal and professional development

Potential for longer-term research cooperation

The selection process also considers equal-opportunity aspects that applicants can provide information about in the application form.

Application Process

Applications for the Heilbronn AI Fellowship are submitted online through the DAAD portal.

Applicants should work with their proposed host institution when preparing the application and research project.

Step 1: Identify an Eligible Host Institution

Applicants should identify an eligible institution on Bildungscampus Heilbronn that is suitable for their proposed AI research project.

Step 2: Develop Your Research Project

Prepare a strong research proposal that clearly explains the project’s objectives, relevance, methodology, feasibility, and potential contribution.

Step 3: Prepare the Required Documents

Applicants should ensure that all required application documents are prepared according to the DAAD requirements.

Step 4: Submit the Application Online

Applications must be submitted through the DAAD online application portal.

An application is considered valid only when the required documents have been submitted through the portal by the relevant application time.

If a required document is unavailable at the time of submission, applicants should explain the reason and indicate when the document will be provided.

Application Deadline

The Heilbronn AI Fellowship operates on a rolling application basis.

There is no fixed application deadline.

Applicants should therefore review the official fellowship information and application requirements and submit their applications according to the applicable programme and funding conditions.

Important Application Information

Only one application per applicant can be considered at any given time.

Simultaneous applications cannot be processed.

Applicants should carefully review all requirements before submitting their application and ensure that the research project is appropriately connected to an eligible host institution.

Why Apply for the Heilbronn AI Fellowship?

The fellowship offers international AI researchers an opportunity to undertake research in one of Germany’s growing AI and innovation ecosystems.

By connecting researchers with universities, research institutions, industry partners, and innovation networks, the programme provides a setting for academic research as well as collaboration and technology transfer.

Researchers can use the fellowship period to advance their projects while developing connections that may contribute to longer-term research and professional opportunities.

Conclusion

The Heilbronn AI Fellowship offers outstanding international PhD candidates and postdoctoral researchers the opportunity to conduct AI research in Heilbronn, Germany, while becoming part of a growing ecosystem of academic, industry, and innovation partners.

Successful fellows can receive €2,800 per month, insurance-related support, and a travel allowance for research stays lasting 1 to 12 months.

The fellowship is open to international PhD candidates in the final year before their dissertation defense and postdoctoral researchers who obtained their doctorate no more than five years ago.

Applications are accepted on a rolling basis, with no fixed deadline.

Interested researchers should review the official DAAD requirements, identify an eligible host institution, develop their research proposal, and submit their application through the DAAD portal.
