TITLE: The Open Notebook Early-Career Fellowship Program 2027 ($6,600 stipend)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 31, 2026

Applications are open for the Open Notebook Early-Career Fellowship Program 2027. The Open Notebook offers a paid, part-time fellowship program for early-career science journalists. During the course of this fellowship, fellows work with a mentor to plan, report, and write articles for publication at The Open Notebook and become part of the TON editorial team.

This one-year program offers fellows the opportunity to explore their career interests and passions and to sharpen their skills as part of a talented, supportive, diverse community of past and present fellows and mentors. This fellowship is made possible through the generous support of the Burroughs Wellcome Fund, which has supported this program since 2013.

Benefits

The fellowship provides a stipend of $6,600.

Eligibility

The fellowship is open to early-career science journalists.

If you live outside the U.S., you are welcome to apply.

Some training and/or experience in writing for the general public is a requirement for this fellowship.

You do not need to have extensive experience or training, but you do need to have some.

Science journalists (or aspiring science journalists) must have fewer than three years of regular professional science writing experience.

Internships and student work do not count toward the fewer-than-three-years requirement.

Exceptions to this requirement may also be made for cases in which an applicant has more than three years of professional science writing experience but some or all of that experience is not in English.

Applications, including writing samples and letters of recommendation, must be in English.

Materials translated into English from another language are acceptable.

Selection Criteria

Priority will be given to applicants who demonstrate:

A strong intention to work primarily as a professional science journalist. (Note: This fellowship is intended for people whose main goal is to do journalism, as opposed to other forms of science communication.)

Some training and/or experience writing about science for the general public (it does not have to be extensive)

Some understanding of the science journalism profession, the challenges science journalists commonly face, and the ways in which you would like to grow as a science journalist

Familiarity with The Open Notebook and the types of topics we tend to cover

An ability to generate good story ideas suitable for The Open Notebook

A commitment to delivering your best work and being conscientious about deadlines

Strong writing ability (If English is not your first language, they do take this into consideration and do not expect flawless writing. However, for a successful experience in this fellowship you must have a fairly high level of proficiency in English.)

Application

The application form for this fellowship includes the following:

Responses to questions about:

Why you are interested in this fellowship and what you hope to learn

Your prior training and/or experience in writing stories about science for the general public

Any particular skills, interests, or perspectives that you would bring to this fellowship

Your overall plans for during the fellowship period (for example, will you simultaneously be finishing a dissertation? Freelancing? Seeking full-time employment somewhere? Doing something else?)

Short proposals for two TON features or multimedia stories that you think would be suitable for publication at The Open Notebook. These can take the form of behind-the-story writer interviews; reported features on some element of the craft of science writing; roundtable discussions; or some other creative, feature-length project centered on the craft of science writing. Familiarize yourself with the types of stories that The Open Notebook publishes. (Note: These are brief, 100-word proposals, not full-scale pitches.)

A resume or CV

One letter of reference. This can be from a professor, editor, mentor, supervisor, or other colleague—whoever you think can best speak to your skills and qualities as they relate to science journalism and to this fellowship experience.

Up to two writing or multimedia samples of work aimed at the general public (not scientific/academic writing). If you are sharing audio or multimedia clips, you can simply put the URLs for the work into a PDF to upload in this section. (Samples must be in English. Translated materials are acceptable.)

Optional: Additional information about you. They strongly encourage writers from all types of backgrounds to apply. If you are a member of any group or community that has historically been marginalized or underrepresented in U.S. journalism, they invite you to let them know. This is entirely optional, and any information you disclose will be kept confidential.

Click here to apply

For more information, visit The Open Notebook Early-Career Fellowship.

TITLE: Resist Urgent Action Fund Grant 2026: Apply for Up to $5,000 in Rapid-Response Funding for Grassroots Organizations

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Grassroots organizations working on urgent social justice campaigns, direct actions, accessibility initiatives, mutual aid, and community-led resistance can apply for the Resist Urgent Action Fund Grant 2026. The grant provides up to US$5,000 to eligible organizations that need timely financial support for urgent projects, campaigns, events, or programmatic activities.

The fund is designed to help frontline groups respond to immediate needs and emerging opportunities without being restricted by lengthy traditional funding processes. Resist prioritizes projects that reflect escalated resistance, organizing, campaigns, direct action, community events, accessibility, mutual aid, or other forms of grassroots movement-building.

The next application cycle is scheduled to run from September 14 to September 18, 2026. Since applications are accepted until the available funding cap is reached, interested organizations should confirm their eligibility and submit their applications as early as possible.

Overview of the Resist Urgent Action Fund Grant 2026

Resist is a foundation that supports grassroots movements working toward justice, liberation, and social change. Its grantmaking approach focuses on redistributing resources to frontline communities and organizations that are often excluded from conventional philanthropic funding.

For 2026, Resist has introduced changes to its grantmaking process to deepen its impact and provide more adaptive support to grantees. The Urgent Action Fund is intended for organizations facing urgent needs or pursuing timely opportunities that require immediate financial resources.

The fund can support a range of activities, including but not limited to:

Urgent community events.

Direct actions and demonstrations.

Accessibility-related costs.

Mutual aid initiatives.

Campaign activities.

Escalated resistance efforts.

Organizing projects.

Community-based programmatic work.

Other urgent projects connected to grassroots social justice movements.

The grant is not intended to function as a conventional long-term institutional grant. Instead, it is designed to provide flexible support when organizations need resources to act quickly.

What Is the Resist Urgent Action Fund?

The Resist Urgent Action Fund is a funding stream for organizations that require financial support for urgent projects or requests. Unlike funding programmes that may focus primarily on long-term strategic planning or annual operating budgets, the Urgent Action Fund is structured to help groups respond to immediate circumstances and timely organizing needs.

According to Resist, applications will open on the last Monday and close on the following Friday of each month until the available funding cap has been reached. The organization also indicates that projects demonstrating escalated resistance, campaigns, events, projects, or programmatic work will receive priority.

The next listed application cycle is:

September 14–18, 2026

Applicants should not wait until the final day if they are ready to apply because the fund may stop accepting applications once its funding limit has been reached.

Grant Amount

Successful applicants may receive up to:

US$5,000

The grant can help eligible organizations cover urgent costs associated with their organizing and movement-building activities. The source information does not specify that every successful applicant will automatically receive the full US$5,000. The amount awarded may depend on the application, the organization’s needs, the available funds, and the grantmaking process.

Potential uses may include costs connected to:

Community organizing.

Direct-action activities.

Campaign implementation.

Urgent events.

Accessibility arrangements.

Mutual aid efforts.

Community mobilization.

Organizing materials.

Timely programme activities.

Other urgent work aligned with Resist’s grantmaking priorities.

Applicants should explain clearly why the funding is needed urgently and how the proposed activities contribute to their broader organizing or movement-building work.

Who Can Apply for the Resist Urgent Action Fund?

The 2026 Urgent Action Fund is open to eligible organizations that meet Resist’s grantmaking requirements.

1. 501(c)(3) Organizations

Organizations with recognized 501(c)(3) nonprofit status may apply if they meet the remaining eligibility requirements.

The organization must be based in the United States, have an annual budget below US$150,000, and demonstrate that its work fits within Resist’s broader social justice and grassroots organizing framework.

2. Fiscally Sponsored Organizations

Organizations that do not have their own 501(c)(3) status may still apply if they operate under a qualifying fiscal sponsor.

A fiscal sponsor is an eligible nonprofit organization that provides administrative, legal, and financial oversight to a project or group that does not have independent tax-exempt status.

Resist confirms that organizations with fiscal sponsors may apply. Applicants should be prepared to provide accurate information about their fiscal sponsor and follow any requirements outlined in the application portal.

3. New and Returning Applicants

The fund is open to both:

New organizations applying to Resist for the first time.

Returning organizations that have previously received Resist funding.

Previous funding from Resist is not required for an organization to be considered for the Urgent Action Fund, provided that it meets the stated eligibility requirements.

4. Organizations with Budgets Below US$150,000

Eligible organizations must have annual budgets below US$150,000.

This requirement is intended to prioritize smaller grassroots groups and frontline organizations that may have limited access to traditional sources of funding.

Organizations with annual budgets of US$150,000 or more are not eligible under the stated criteria.

Geographic Eligibility

The Resist Urgent Action Fund is geographically focused on the United States.

To qualify, applicants must generally:

Be based in the United States.

Conduct their primary work within the United States.

Demonstrate that the proposed activity serves communities or movements within the United States.

Organizations whose primary work is outside the United States are not eligible under Resist’s grantmaking criteria. This means that international organizations, groups based in other countries, or applicants seeking funding for projects primarily implemented outside the United States should not assume that they qualify.

The opportunity is therefore not a worldwide grant programme, even though its themes may be relevant to social justice organizations in other regions.

Types of Work Resist Supports

Resist’s grantmaking is focused on grassroots organizing, community power, structural change, and movements for justice and liberation.

Organizations applying for the Urgent Action Fund should be able to explain how their work fits into a broader movement or organizing ecosystem.

Relevant work may include:

Grassroots Organizing

This includes community-led efforts that bring people together to address structural social, political, or economic problems. Grassroots organizing may involve coalition-building, community education, leadership development, mobilization, and collective action.

Direct Action

The fund may support urgent direct-action activities connected to progressive organizing campaigns. Examples could include organizing demonstrations, public actions, mobilization efforts, or other forms of nonviolent collective action.

Campaigns

Organizations conducting timely campaigns may be considered, particularly where the campaign responds to an urgent issue or reflects an escalated phase of organizing.

Applicants should explain:

What issue the campaign addresses.

Who is affected.

What action is being taken.

Why the activity is urgent.

How the campaign connects to the organization’s wider goals.

Accessibility

The fund may support accessibility-related needs that enable people to participate in organizing, events, campaigns, and movement activities.

Accessibility expenses may include arrangements that remove barriers for people with disabilities or others who require specific forms of support to participate meaningfully.

Mutual Aid

Urgent mutual aid activities may be eligible when they are connected to the organization’s movement work and meet Resist’s grant criteria.

Applicants should distinguish between mutual aid that is part of broader grassroots organizing and activities that function solely as general material assistance. Resist’s eligibility information indicates that it does not generally fund material aid campaigns as a standalone category.

Community and Cultural Organizing

Resist also supports work involving cultural organizing, community-led education, consciousness-raising, radical pedagogy, and other forms of movement-building.

Projects should demonstrate how the proposed work contributes to collective power, social transformation, or community-led resistance.

Resist’s General Grantmaking Criteria

In addition to the specific Urgent Action Fund requirements, applicants should consider Resist’s broader eligibility criteria.

Resist indicates that organizations aligned with its grantmaking approach generally demonstrate several of the following characteristics:

Connection to a broader social justice ecosystemThe organization understands how its work relates to other groups, campaigns, communities, and movements working toward social change.

Clear purpose within movements for social changeThe organization can explain its role, goals, strategies, and contribution to broader efforts for justice and liberation.

Intersectional or cross-issue analysisThe organization recognizes that social problems are interconnected and addresses issues through an intersectional or cross-issue perspective.

Work against structural oppressionResist’s stated criteria refer to work against white and Christian supremacy, capitalism, gender and sexual oppression, and forms of patriarchy.

Leadership by affected communitiesOrganizations should be led by, or accountable to, people most affected by the structural issues they seek to address.

These criteria are important because the fund is not simply designed for any nonprofit seeking general financial assistance. Applicants should show how their organization’s work fits within Resist’s grassroots movement-building approach.

Organizations and Activities Resist Does Not Fund

The grant page lists several categories that are generally excluded from funding. These include:

Individuals applying in their personal capacity.

Social service projects.

Research projects.

Legal defense costs or lawsuits that are not directly connected to a progressive organizing campaign.

Material aid campaigns.

Projects whose primary work is outside the United States.

Organizations with access to traditional sources of funding.

Capital campaigns.

Capital projects.

Endowments.

Other foundations or grantmaking organizations.

Organizations with annual budgets of US$150,000 or more.

Applicants should carefully review these exclusions before beginning an application.

For example, an organization that provides social services may not qualify simply because its work benefits a vulnerable population. The application should demonstrate a clear connection to grassroots organizing, community power, structural change, or movement-building.

Similarly, a project that is primarily a research study may not qualify unless it is part of a broader organizing strategy that fits Resist’s priorities.

Important Note About Movement Bank Awards

The grant page states that organizations receiving Movement Bank 2026 awards are not eligible for the Urgent Action Fund or Rapid Response funding.

Applicants should therefore confirm whether their organization has received a Movement Bank award in 2026 before applying.

The Movement’s Bank Grant Cycle is a separate grantmaking stream. For 2026, the Movement Bank is described as invite-only, with decisions made by a grant panel composed of former grantees. It provides awards of approximately US$10,000, but it is not currently accepting general applications.

Application Deadline

The next Urgent Action Fund application cycle is scheduled for:

September 14–18, 2026

The stated deadline is:

September 18, 2026

The application window is part of Resist’s monthly cycle structure, under which applications open on the last Monday and close on the following Friday until the available funding cap has been reached.

Because the funding cap may be reached before the end of the stated period, applicants should submit their applications as soon as possible rather than waiting until the deadline day.

Applicants should also verify the current status on the official Resist grants page before submitting, especially if the application window has recently opened or if the fund may have reached capacity.

How to Apply for the Resist Urgent Action Fund

All applications for Resist grants must be submitted online.

The application process generally involves the following steps.

Step 1: Confirm Eligibility

Applicants should first take Resist’s online eligibility quiz. The quiz is designed to help organizations determine whether their work, organizational structure, budget, and geographic focus fit the grant requirements.

Before beginning, confirm that the organization:

Is based in the United States.

Has 501(c)(3) status or a qualifying fiscal sponsor.

Has an annual budget below US$150,000.

Is not an individual applicant.

Does not primarily conduct work outside the United States.

Is not a 2026 Movement Bank award recipient.

Is engaged in grassroots organizing, social justice, direct action, mutual aid, accessibility, campaigning, or related movement work.

Step 2: Access the Online Application Portal

Applicants can begin the application process through Resist’s online grant application system.

The official application portal is hosted through Grant Interface:

Resist Grant Application Portal

The official grant information page is available here:

Resist Grants Open Page

Step 3: Create a User Account

Applicants must create an account before they can browse the grant programmes, read application instructions, or submit an application.

According to Resist, creating an account should take less than five minutes. Creating an account does not require applicants to submit an application immediately.

Step 4: Review the Programme Instructions

Once logged in, applicants will see information about Resist’s grant programmes and instructions for applying.

Applicants should read the instructions carefully because the specific questions, required information, and submission procedures may vary according to the grant programme.

Step 5: Prepare and Submit the Application

The application should clearly explain:

The organization’s mission and work.

The community or communities served.

The urgent need or opportunity.

The proposed activity.

Why the activity requires timely funding.

How the activity connects to grassroots organizing or movement-building.

The amount requested.

How the funds will be used.

How the work is led by or accountable to affected communities.

Applicants should ensure that the information provided is accurate, specific, and consistent with the organization’s actual work.

Application Preparation Tips

1. Explain the Urgency Clearly

Because this is an Urgent Action Fund, the application should explain why the project or request requires timely support.

Avoid presenting the proposal as a general organizational wish list. Instead, describe the immediate situation, emerging opportunity, campaign development, event, direct action, accessibility need, or urgent organizing requirement.

2. Connect the Request to Broader Organizing

Resist does not fund projects solely because they are useful or beneficial. Applicants should demonstrate how the proposed activity contributes to broader social justice organizing and collective change.

Explain:

The movement or community context.

The issue being addressed.

The organization’s role.

The people involved.

The expected contribution to the broader campaign or organizing effort.

3. Demonstrate Community Leadership

Resist prioritizes organizations led by people most affected by structural oppression. Applicants should explain how affected communities participate in:

Decision-making.

Leadership.

Strategy development.

Campaign planning.

Implementation.

Evaluation or reflection.

4. Be Specific About the Use of Funds

Provide a clear explanation of how the grant would be used. A simple budget or cost breakdown can help reviewers understand the request.

For example, an organization might describe costs related to:

Accessibility services.

Event logistics.

Organizing materials.

Transportation connected to a campaign.

Venue-related costs.

Community mobilization.

Urgent communications.

Other eligible activities.

The proposed expenses should be directly connected to the urgent project.

5. Confirm the Organization’s Budget

Since the budget must be below US$150,000, applicants should ensure that the organization’s financial information is accurate and current.

If the organization operates under a fiscal sponsor, applicants should clarify which budget figures and organizational details the application requires.

6. Review the Exclusions

Before submitting, check that the request is not primarily for:

Individual support.

A social service project.

A standalone research project.

A capital campaign.

A capital project.

An endowment.

A material aid campaign.

Work conducted primarily outside the United States.

An activity that falls outside Resist’s movement-building focus.

7. Apply Early

The September 2026 application window closes on September 18, but Resist states that applications open monthly until the funding cap is reached.

Submitting early is therefore advisable. Applicants should not assume that the fund will remain open until the final day if the available resources have already been allocated.

Technical and Application Support

Resist instructs applicants to follow the online application system’s instructions for technical support.

For application-related support, applicants may contact Nicki at:

Applicants should use the support contact for questions about eligibility, application procedures, or technical difficulties that cannot be resolved through the online portal.

What Happens After Applying?

Resist indicates that it generally aims to announce Urgent Action Fund decisions approximately one month after the submission window closes. However, the timing may vary depending on the number of applications received, and there may be small delays.

Applicants should therefore monitor their email and application account after submitting.

The grant page also states that Resist distributes grants through bank transfer. Successful grantees should watch for an email from Ramp to provide payment information.

Reporting Requirements

One notable feature of Resist’s grantmaking approach is that it does not require a formal report from grantees.

Resist states that it trusts grantees to use the funds to advance their work and does not require a report. However, the organization welcomes updates from grantees who wish to share information about their organizing and community impact.

This approach is intended to reduce administrative burdens and allow organizations to focus more of their capacity on their work.

About Resist’s Grantmaking Approach

Resist describes its funding model as a form of resource redistribution rather than conventional philanthropy. The organization seeks to support grassroots movements and frontline communities that are working toward justice, liberation, and structural change.

Its grantmaking model emphasizes:

Grassroots leadership.

Community accountability.

Flexible funding.

Reduced administrative burdens.

Participatory decision-making.

Support for organizations with limited access to traditional funding.

Movement-building rather than isolated project delivery.

Resist’s general grant decisions are made by panels of former grantees who are paid and trained to review applications. This participatory approach is intended to place decision-making power closer to the communities and movements that receive the resources.

Important Distinction: Urgent Action Fund and Movement’s Bank

Applicants should distinguish between the two grant programmes listed on the Resist page.

Urgent Action Fund

Status: Open during the stated application cycle.

Grant amount: Up to US$5,000.

Purpose: Urgent projects, direct actions, accessibility, mutual aid, campaigns, events, and related activities.

Eligibility: New and returning eligible 501(c)(3) or fiscally sponsored organizations.

Budget requirement: Below US$150,000.

Application cycle: September 14–18, 2026.

Movement’s Bank Grant Cycle

Status: Closed or not accepting applications.

Grant amount: US$10,000.

Purpose: Organizations with consistent, active, and emerging programming.

Application process: Invite-only.

Decision-making: Grant panel composed of former grantees.

Organizations should apply to the programme that matches their eligibility and current status. The Movement’s Bank is not a general open-call opportunity for new applicants in the 2026 information provided.

Conclusion

The Resist Urgent Action Fund Grant 2026 provides an opportunity for small, United States-based grassroots organizations to obtain up to US$5,000 for urgent organizing needs, direct actions, campaigns, accessibility initiatives, mutual aid, events, and other movement-building activities.

The fund is particularly relevant to organizations with annual budgets below US$150,000 that have 501(c)(3) status or operate under a fiscal sponsor. Applicants should demonstrate a clear connection to social justice movements, community-led organizing, structural change, and the needs of people most affected by oppression.

TITLE: Princeton in Asia Fellowship 2027-28: Paid Fellowship Opportunities in Asia for Bachelor’s Degree Holders

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the Princeton in Asia (PiA) 2027-28 Fellowship Program, offering immersive, paid work opportunities with host organizations and communities across Asia. The program is designed for graduates who want to develop professionally while participating in meaningful cross-cultural exchange between the United States and Asia.

For the 2027-28 cycle, Princeton in Asia expects to offer approximately 60 fellowship positions, although the number and locations of available positions may change according to host-organization needs and local or regional circumstances. The fellowships cover a broad range of professional areas, including education, public health, environmental sustainability, economic development, arts and culture, sports, STEM, and peace, justice, and access to information.

Unlike programs that are limited to a particular academic discipline, Princeton in Asia encourages applicants from a wide range of educational and professional backgrounds. The fellowship is particularly relevant for college seniors, recent graduates, and other early-career professionals seeking international work experience and a structured opportunity to live and work in an Asian community.

What Is Princeton in Asia?

Princeton in Asia (PiA) is an organization affiliated with Princeton University that facilitates immersive work fellowships in Asia. Its mission is to foster mutual appreciation and cross-cultural understanding between the United States and Asia through professional placements in host organizations and communities.

PiA describes its work as a form of person-to-person diplomacy, with Fellows expected not only to contribute professionally to their host organizations but also to develop meaningful relationships within the communities where they live and work.

The program has a long history of international engagement. According to PiA, more than 3,400 Fellows and Interns have participated in its programs across more than 30 countries and regions in Asia since its establishment.

The 2027-28 fellowship cycle therefore offers applicants an opportunity to combine professional development, international experience, community engagement, and cross-cultural learning.

Princeton in Asia Fellowship 2027-28 at a Glance

Program: Princeton in Asia Fellowship

Fellowship cycle: 2027-28

Expected positions: Approximately 60

Duration: One or two years, depending on the fellowship

Expected start period: Generally July to September 2027

Application opening date: September 1, 2026

Application deadline: November 1, 2026 at 11:59 PM EST

Location: Various host organizations and communities across Asia

Academic requirement: Bachelor’s degree by the start of the fellowship

Nationality: Applicants of any nationality may apply, subject to PiA eligibility and host-country visa requirements

English requirement: Professional proficiency in English

Age limit: None

Application fee: None

PiA’s official application timeline confirms that applications opened on September 1, 2026, and that all application materials must be submitted online by November 1, 2026 at 11:59 PM Eastern Time.

Where Can Princeton in Asia Fellows Be Placed?

The 2027-28 fellowship cycle is expected to include placements across multiple Asian countries and regions. The opportunities described for the cycle include:

Cambodia

China

Hong Kong SAR

Indonesia

Japan

Kazakhstan

Kyrgyzstan

Laos

Macao SAR

Mongolia

Singapore

Sri Lanka

Taiwan

Thailand

Uzbekistan

Vietnam

Applicants should understand that the precise list of positions and locations can change. PiA works with host organizations to determine their staffing needs, and host-country circumstances, visa requirements, and organizational needs can affect the final availability of posts.

The organization also explains that applicants will be able to indicate placement preferences during the 2027-28 application process. These preferences help PiA understand an applicant’s interests but do not function as an absolute restriction on placement. Applicants are encouraged to remain open to opportunities outside their initial preferences.

What Areas Do Princeton in Asia Fellowships Cover?

One of the defining features of the PiA program is the diversity of professional fields represented by its fellowships.

The program includes opportunities in:

1. Arts and Culture

Applicants interested in cultural institutions, creative industries, heritage, arts programming, and related fields may find positions connected to this area.

2. Economic Development

Some fellowships involve economic development, business-related activities, entrepreneurship, or work supporting economic growth and development initiatives.

3. Education

Education is an important component of PiA’s fellowship portfolio. Positions may involve teaching, educational administration, curriculum-related activities, university work, or other education-focused responsibilities.

Teaching positions have an additional English-language requirement, and candidates placed in teaching roles complete PiA’s teacher-training program.

4. Environmental Sustainability

Applicants interested in environmental issues, sustainability, conservation, climate-related work, or sustainable development may find relevant opportunities among the available placements.

5. Peace, Justice, and Access to Information

PiA also supports placements involving areas such as peacebuilding, justice, information access, and related social-impact work.

6. Public Health

Public health is another fellowship focus area, creating opportunities for applicants interested in health systems, community health, health education, and related fields.

7. Sports

The fellowship portfolio can also include positions connected to sports and community engagement through sporting activities.

8. Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics

STEM-related fellowships can involve scientific, technological, engineering, mathematical, educational, research, or related professional activities.

PiA confirms that it is not exclusively an English-teaching program. Its fellowship portfolio spans arts and culture, economic development, education, environmental sustainability, public health, sports, STEM, and peace, justice, and access to information.

What Does the Princeton in Asia Fellowship Offer?

The fellowship provides Fellows with a combination of professional placement, financial support, preparation, health and safety resources, and access to a broader international alumni community.

Paid Work Experience in Asia

PiA Fellows undertake immersive work placements with host organizations in Asia. These are professional roles rather than simply cultural exchange visits.

The work allows Fellows to contribute their skills to a host organization while developing practical experience in an international environment.

Living Stipend

Fellows receive a local living stipend from the host organization.

PiA explains that the stipend is intended to support basic living costs associated with the fellowship, including:

Housing, where housing is not directly provided by the host organization

Food and groceries

Local transportation

Telecommunications

PiA also clarifies that the stipend is designed for basic living expenses and is not intended to function as a source of substantial personal income or to finance extensive leisure travel.

Health and Safety Support

Fellows receive health, safety, and welfare support. PiA’s current program information states that Fellows receive travel medical and emergency evacuation insurance, International SOS membership, mental-health support, and pre-departure preparation and resources.

This support is particularly relevant for applicants who may be living and working abroad for the first time.

Pre-Departure Orientation

Selected Fellows participate in preparation before departing for their host country.

The 2027-28 timeline indicates that all Fellows will attend a mandatory multi-day orientation in Princeton, New Jersey in early June 2027.

This preparation is intended to help Fellows understand the practical, professional, and cultural dimensions of their upcoming placements.

TEFL Training for Teaching Fellows

Applicants do not need previous TEFL certification or teaching experience to apply to PiA.

However, candidates who receive a teaching placement will be required to complete PiA’s teacher-training course. For the 2027-28 cycle, Teaching Fellows are expected to complete a 120-hour Teaching English as a Foreign Language (TEFL) online certification course before beginning their fellowship.

Visa and Work Permit Support

Fellows work with host organizations during the visa and work-permit process.

PiA’s current information indicates that visa and work-permit costs before departure are supported, including reimbursement for applicable U.S.-side visa expenses. Fellows must still obtain the appropriate authorization and meet the immigration requirements applicable to their placement.

Travel Support

Applicants should distinguish the fellowship’s living support from international travel costs.

PiA states that Fellows are generally responsible for round-trip airfare to their host community. However, the organization provides travel grants intended to reduce this financial burden, and some host organizations cover airfare.

Country Advisors

PiA provides Fellows with access to Country Advisors who have significant experience and local knowledge of the countries where PiA operates.

These advisors can help Fellows better understand local culture, norms, behavior, and other aspects of adapting to life and work in the host community.

Alumni Network

Fellows also become part of the Princeton in Asia alumni community.

PiA provides access to its Alumni Network and mentor directory, giving participants an opportunity to remain connected to former Fellows and the wider PiA community after completing their placements.

Language Grants

PiA also identifies language grants as an available form of support, subject to application. Asian language skills themselves are not generally required for most positions, although individual fellowship descriptions may specify particular language requirements.

Who Is Eligible to Apply?

The primary academic requirement is a bachelor’s degree.

Applicants must have completed their bachelor’s degree before the beginning of their fellowship. Candidates with master’s degrees may also apply.

However, PiA does not accept candidates whose highest degree is a professional or terminal degree such as:

Ph.D.

M.D.

J.D.

Graduates of any college or university can apply. Applicants do not need to be Princeton University graduates or students.

PiA also does not impose an age limit. Although many Fellows are college seniors or recent graduates, individuals who graduated several years ago can still apply.

Can International Applicants Apply?

Yes.

Princeton in Asia states that applicants of any nationality may apply. However, citizenship alone does not determine eligibility for placement.

Applicants who are not U.S. citizens generally need to demonstrate a meaningful connection to the United States that enables them to contribute to PiA’s mission of U.S.-Asia exchange. PiA states that this generally means having either:

Attended a U.S.-accredited institution; or

Lived in the United States for one year or more.

Applicants should also understand that host-country immigration and visa regulations can affect whether a person of a particular nationality can be placed in a particular fellowship.

Therefore, being from an Asian, African, European, American, or other country does not by itself create a blanket exclusion from applying. The applicant must satisfy PiA’s broader eligibility requirements and be legally placeable in the relevant host country.

English-Language Requirements

Professional proficiency in English is required for all PiA positions.

For English-teaching positions, the requirement is higher: applicants must have native or near-native English-speaking ability.

Knowledge of an Asian language can be useful and may be specifically requested for certain placements, but Asian language skills are not required for most PiA fellowships. Applicants should therefore carefully examine the requirements of individual fellowship positions when deciding where their skills may fit.

Does an Applicant Need Previous Experience in Asia?

Not necessarily.

PiA explains that previous experience in Asia is not generally required for most positions. Some specific fellowships may require knowledge of or professional experience in Asia, including Asian-language skills, but many placements are designed for applicants who are interested in learning about Asia through an immersive experience.

PiA’s selection process places emphasis on qualities such as adaptability, resilience, resourcefulness, professionalism, self-management, commitment, and the ability to build relationships across cultures.

What Kind of Applicants Is PiA Looking For?

Academic qualifications are only one part of the application.

PiA states that it seeks candidates who can contribute to its mission of fostering mutual appreciation and cross-cultural understanding between the United States and Asia.

The organization identifies several qualities associated with its Fellows, including:

Openness to personal transformation

Willingness to become immersed in the host community

Ability to build meaningful relationships

Humility and respect for different perspectives

Commitment to mutual learning

Desire to contribute to the host organization and community

Strong work ethic

Resourcefulness

Self-management

Adaptability

Resilience

Professional readiness

Applicants should therefore be prepared to explain not only what they can do professionally but also why they are interested in an immersive cross-cultural experience and how they can contribute to the community in which they will live and work.

How Long Does the Fellowship Last?

PiA fellowships typically last one or two years.

Most positions are structured as one-year fellowships, although some positions are specifically designed as two-year placements. PiA also encourages first-year Fellows to consider staying for a second year where the particular fellowship permits it.

According to the official 2027-28 timeline, most fellowships are expected to begin in August 2027, although some may begin in July or September depending on host-organization needs. All placements are contingent upon obtaining the required visa and completing PiA’s pre-departure requirements.

Princeton in Asia 2027-28 Application Timeline

Applicants should pay close attention to the following dates:

September 1, 2026

The 2027-28 fellowship application opens.

November 1, 2026

All application materials must be submitted online by 11:59 PM EST.

December 21, 2026

Applicants are expected to be notified about whether they have been selected for interviews with PiA staff.

January 2027

Virtual interviews with PiA staff are scheduled.

Applicants are expected to receive notification of nominee status or an invitation to join the waitlist.

Late February to March 2027

Nominees submit additional materials for review by potential host organizations.

March to April 2027

Host organizations evaluate nominees and communicate their selections to PiA.

Late March onward

PiA begins extending fellowship offers on a rolling basis until positions are filled.

April to August 2027

Selected Fellows begin the visa and work-permit process with their host organizations.

April to May 2027

Teaching Fellows complete the required 120-hour TEFL online certification course.

Early June 2027

All Fellows attend a mandatory multi-day orientation in Princeton, New Jersey.

July to September 2027

Most fellowships begin, with the majority expected to start in August.

Application Deadline

The Princeton in Asia 2027-28 Fellowship application deadline is November 1, 2026 at 11:59 PM Eastern Time.

Applicants should not wait until the final hours to submit their materials because the application requires several components and late submissions may not be accepted.

APPLY HERE

What Is Required for the Application?

The PiA application includes several components designed to help the organization understand an applicant’s academic background, professional preparation, communication abilities, motivations, and suitability for the fellowship.

The application includes:

Online application form

Two written responses

One 60-second video

Resume

Unofficial college or university transcript

Demographic survey

One recommendation form completed by a selected recommender

Applicants should therefore begin preparing their materials well before the November deadline.

A strong application should provide a coherent explanation of the applicant’s academic and professional background, relevant skills, interest in the fellowship, and ability to contribute to PiA’s cross-cultural mission.

Important Application Guidance

Applicants should pay close attention to PiA’s application and placement process.

PiA advises applicants not to contact host organizations directly during the application process. Host organizations are introduced to applicants through PiA at the appropriate stage. According to PiA, applicants who circumvent the official selection process by contacting host organizations directly can be automatically disqualified from consideration.

Applicants should also understand that indicating a preferred country, issue area, or fellowship does not guarantee placement in that particular position. PiA uses applicants’ preferences as guidance while considering the needs and requirements of host organizations.

Maintaining flexibility about location and type of work can therefore be important during the placement process.

Is There an Application Fee?

No.

Princeton in Asia states that there is no fee to apply for its fellowship program.

Is the Princeton in Asia Fellowship Fully Funded?

The PiA fellowship provides substantial support, but applicants should understand what the program does and does not cover.

The fellowship includes a host-provided living stipend intended to cover basic local living costs, as well as health and safety support and assistance with visa and work-permit expenses. PiA also provides travel grants to help reduce international travel costs, while some host organizations may cover airfare.

TITLE: USNR Commander (Ret.) Mary Sears, Ph.D.

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
USNR Commander (Ret.) Mary Sears, Ph.D.

July 18, 1905 – September 2, 1997

“The Conscience of Oceanography”

Mary Sears, Scientist Emeritus, Biology. (Photo by Tom Kleindinst, © Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution)

Mary Sears was the Oceanographer of the United States Navy-the first in modern times. She played a central role in the founding and formation of the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution. Over the course of her career, Sears was an architect of the world community of oceanographers and the founding editor of Progress in Oceanography and the co-founding editor of Deep-Sea Research. She also edited the book Oceanography, which was published by the American Association for the Advancement of Science in 1961. The journals and books she edited are what oceanographic research continues to be evaluated against today.

Born in Wayland, Mass., Sears grew up exploring the natural world around her, collecting animals-particularly frogs-and setting up terrariums. This passion would forge her life’s path. She graduated from Radcliffe College in 1927, then receiving both her Master’s degree and Doctorate from Radcliffe in quick succession. Her dissertation adviser, Henry Bigelow, was the founder and first director of the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institute (WHOI) and played an important role in mentoring Sears. In particular, he introduced her to leaders in marine sciences of the day and hired her as one of the first ten research assistants at WHOI-the first and only woman of the ten-where she played a leading role by assisting in its founding and later in its purchase of two oceanographic ships.

By 1939, Sears was a junior biologist and by 1940, once WHOI was a year-round organization, a planktonologist. She served as the staff planktonologist until 1963 when she became a Senior Scientist in the Biology Department until her retirement in 1970. Sears additionally served as a research assistant to Bigelow at Harvard, tutored at Radcliffe, and served as an instructor at Wellesley College throughout the 1930s and 40s. It was her time in Peru, via Wellesley College, that finally allowed her to work onboard research ships with men-something that was considered male-only territory and forbidden to women at the time. She left WHOI briefly for a position that brought her numerous accolades and likely helped change the path of the Second World War in the Pacific Theater.

Mary Sears christened the R/V Atlantis II on September 8, 1962. Built at the Maryland Shipbuilding and Drydock Company in Baltimore, MD, the Atlantis was the first ship in the modern fleet of oceanographic research vessels built to serve the United States academic research community. Its design and planning process served as the model for a generation of research vessels to follow. (Photo courtesy of WHOI Archives © Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution)

Mary Sears at the R/V Atlantis II launching. (Photo courtesy of WHOI Archives © Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution)
A Lifetime of Service

In 1943, Sears joined the Women Accepted for Volunteer Emergency Service (WAVES) as a Lieutenant, Junior Grade. Such military service on the home front and overseas, as well as in support of work for the war effort, opened the doors of opportunity for many women around the world. Since ships were off-limits to women, Sears headed to Washington, D.C., to serve in the U.S. Navy’s Ocean Unit of the Hydrographic Office, which was understaffed, under supplied, and given menial research tasks at the time.

“We were working so hard for a common cause, I was hardly aware of any barriers.”

-Mary Sears

Within one year, Sears grew the unit into a division that would eventually become the Naval Oceanographic Office of the Navy Hydrographic Office, where she oversaw more than 400 people – more than on many Naval ships. Under Sears, the unit was charged with aiding the Navy in strategic maneuvers by providing analysis of surf heights, tides, and other pertinent information to provide mission planners and commanders with strategic advantages over the enemy. Her intelligence reports, “Submarine Supplements to the Sailing Directions,” predicted the presence of thermoclines – areas of rapid water temperature change – that allowed submarines to hide and escape surface sonar used by the enemy. Her reports provided intelligence for all possible targets for good amphibious landing operations and likely changed the course of the war in the Pacific Theater by helping to diminish the enemy’s prior ability to detect U.S. submarines. In 1946, Sears was awarded the Johannes Schmidt Medal for her contributions to marine science research and Navy oceanography during WWII. The following year, Sears returned full-time to WHOI, while maintaining her position with the U.S. Navy as a reservist. When she retired from the USN Reserves in 1963, she did so with the rank of Commander.

Mary Sears posing for a photo. (Photo courtesy of WHOI Archives © Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution)
A Powerful Force of Nature

In this 1960 photo, Mary Sears is surrounded by papers and biological samples in her Bigelow Laboratory office. (Photo by Redwood Wright, © Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution)
Throughout her life, Sears would receive numerous accolades and awards for her work. Other military awards, in addition to the Schmidt Medal, included the American Campaign Medal, Naval Reserve Medal, Armed Forces Reserves Medal, and the World War II Victory Medal. She was involved in her local community and believed in mentoring and helping those coming up the ranks. Education was incredibly important to Sears and every mailbox in her neighborhood that belonged to the house of a child would be periodically filled with books for each young person in the home-a gift from “Aunt Mary.”

Sears was a member of numerous professional organizations and societies, including the American Association for the Advancement of Science, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, the Society of Women Geographers, Sigma Xi, the American Association of Limnology and Oceanography, and the American Geophysical Union. She helped establish and chaired the First International Congress on Oceanography at the United Nations in 1959 and served on the Joint Committee on Oceanography of the International Council of Scientific Unions from 1958-1960.

At WHOI, she was a long time member of the Corporation, serving as Clerk of the Corporation from 1947-1973 and Deputy Clerk from 1973-1975, and was named Honorary Trustee and Honorary Member of WHOI in 1976. She retired from WHOI in 1970 and became Scientist Emeritus in 1978. In 1994, Sears was the first recipient of the Women Pioneers in Oceanography Award by WHOI. By 1999, two years after her death, it was renamed to include her name-The Mary Sears Women Pioneers in Oceanography Award. In 2000, the U.S. Navy named a 330-foot oceanographic survey ship after her and it is still in use.

USNS Mary Sears (TAGS-65)

USNS Mary Sears visits WHOI in July 2002. (Photo by Tom Kleindinst, © Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution)
Commissioned in 2000, the USNS Mary Sears is seen here making a port-of-call at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institute from July 24-26, 2002. The 300-foot ship was the first naval oceanographic ship named for a woman by the US Navy. Commander (Ret.) Mary Sears, Ph.D. was one of the ten founding scientists at WHOI-and the only woman. She served in the Navy WAVES during World War II creating the Naval Oceanographic Office and developing the intelligence reports for the Navy that allowed naval submarines to escape sonar detection by the enemy. She retired from the Navy Reserves in 1963 with the rank of Commander. Sears worked as a Scientist and Senior Scientist at WHOI from 1932 until her retirement in 1970. In 1978, WHOI named her Scientist Emeritus.

A 300-foot vessel, the USNS Mary Sears is officially launched on October 19, 2000 in Pascagoula, Mississippi by VT Halter Marine where it was built. It is a Pathfinder-class oceanographic survey ship that carries twenty-four civilian and twenty-seven military crew members and continues to be in service.

USNS Mary Sears Launch in Pascagoula, Mississippi. (Photo by Shelley Dawicki, © Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution)
Jascin N. L. Finger is the Nantucket Maria Mitchell Association’s Deputy Director and the Curator of the Mitchell House, Archives, and Special Collections. Maria Mitchell was America’s first woman astronomer.

Applicants using an overseas nominating authority may face separate deadlines set by that nominating organization, but those deadlines vary by country and should not be presented as the universal JSPS deadline.

The official FY2027 Standard Program should therefore be understood as a host-based, highly competitive international postdoctoral fellowship, not a direct individual online application in which a researcher simply submits independently to JSPS.

Official programme information: JSPS Postdoctoral Fellowships for Research in Japan; JSPS International Fellowships for Research in Japan 2026

About the JSPS Postdoctoral Fellowships for Research in Japan

The Japan Society for the Promotion of Science operates several international fellowship programmes designed for researchers at different stages of their careers.

These include programmes for:

Pre-doctoral researchers

Postdoctoral researchers

Early-career researchers

Experienced international researchers

Short-term research visitors

The Standard Program, however, is specifically designed to give young overseas postdoctoral researchers an opportunity to conduct collaborative research with leading research groups at Japanese universities and other eligible research institutions.

The programme emphasizes genuine research collaboration rather than simply providing a researcher with funding to work independently.

Before an application is submitted, the overseas candidate and Japanese host researcher are expected to:

Establish contact

Develop a concrete research plan

Agree on the proposed collaboration

Identify an appropriate host institution

Demonstrate how the collaboration will advance the proposed research

These factors are explicitly considered during the JSPS selection process.

Fellowship Duration

The Standard Program runs for:

12 to 24 months.

This gives successful Fellows enough time to become meaningfully integrated into the host research environment rather than undertaking only a short academic visit.

Depending on the project, a Fellow may therefore spend:

One year

18 months

Two years

conducting research in Japan.

The precise tenure is proposed through the application and should match the needs of the research collaboration.

FY2027 Number of Fellowships

The official FY2027 open-call schedule lists approximately:

120 Fellowship awards in the first recruitment round

and another:

120 Fellowship awards in the second recruitment round.

Therefore, the frequently advertised figure of “120 awards” is broadly correct for each FY2027 open-call recruitment round, rather than necessarily representing the total number of all Standard Program awards through every application route.

JSPS also receives Standard Program applications through overseas nominating authorities in selected countries and organisations.

FY2027 First Recruitment Round

The first FY2027 Standard Program open-call round had the following schedule:

Application deadline from host institution to JSPS:
28 August 2026 at 5:00 PM JST

Expected results:
Late December 2026

Permitted fellowship commencement period:
1 April 2027 to 30 September 2027

Approximate number of Fellowships:
120

As of September 2026, this first recruitment deadline has already passed.

FY2027 Second Recruitment Round

Researchers who missed the first round have another opportunity under the FY2027 Standard Program.

The second recruitment schedule is:

Application deadline from host institution to JSPS:
23 April 2027 at 5:00 PM JST

Expected results:
Early August 2027

Permitted fellowship commencement period:
1 September 2027 to 30 November 2027

Approximate number of Fellowships:
120

Prospective applicants should note that this is the deadline by which the Japanese host institution must submit the application to JSPS.

Universities may impose their own internal deadlines significantly earlier.

Candidates should therefore begin identifying a host researcher well in advance.

Important Clarification About the 15 November 2026 Deadline

A social-media version of this opportunity states:

15 November 2026

as the application deadline.

That date does not match the official FY2027 Standard Program open-call schedule published by JSPS.

The official deadlines are:

First round: 28 August 2026

Second round: 23 April 2027

However, JSPS also accepts some applications through overseas nominating authorities, and those organisations establish their own procedures and deadlines.

For this reason, a November deadline could potentially refer to a particular nomination route, but it should not be advertised as the general JSPS Standard Program deadline unless the relevant nominating authority specifically confirms it.

Difference Between the Standard Fellowship and Other JSPS Programmes

This distinction is particularly important because JSPS operates several programmes with different deadlines.

For example, the FY2027 Short-term Program (PE) currently has an official first-round deadline of:

25 September 2026 at 5:00 PM JST

and approximately 20 Fellowships are planned for that round.

That is a different programme.

The Short-term PE programme should not be confused with the:

Standard Program

which lasts 12–24 months and has approximately 120 places per FY2027 open-call round.

Fields of Research

One of the strongest features of the JSPS Standard Fellowship is its disciplinary breadth.

JSPS states that applications can be submitted in:

All fields of the humanities, social sciences and natural sciences.

This makes the fellowship relevant to researchers working across areas such as:

Anthropology

Archaeology

History

Languages

Literature

Philosophy

Political science

International relations

Economics

Sociology

Law

Education

Psychology

Mathematics

Physics

Chemistry

Engineering

Computer science

Informatics

Biology

Agriculture

Environmental sciences

Medicine

Dentistry

Pharmacy

The FY2027 review structure similarly covers disciplines including humanities, social sciences, mathematical and physical sciences, chemistry, engineering, informatics, biology, agriculture/environmental sciences, medicine, dentistry and pharmacy.

Who Is the Fellowship Designed For?

The Standard Program is intended for:

Young overseas postdoctoral researchers

who want to conduct collaborative research in Japan.

Applicants should normally be at an early stage after completing their doctorate.

The fellowship is not intended primarily for:

Undergraduate students

Master’s students

Researchers without an expected PhD by the fellowship start

Senior professors looking for short visiting appointments

Other JSPS programmes may serve some of those categories.

Doctoral Degree Requirement

For the Standard Program, an overseas candidate must normally have:

Obtained a doctoral degree within six years of the date the Fellowship begins

or:

Be expected to receive the PhD before the Fellowship begins.

The candidate’s employment status is not decisive.

JSPS explicitly states that whether the applicant currently holds a full-time position is not considered for this eligibility requirement.

This means applicants may potentially include:

Postdoctoral researchers

Research associates

Lecturers

Researchers between appointments

PhD candidates close to graduation

provided all other requirements are satisfied.

Applicants Who Have Not Yet Completed Their PhD

A candidate does not necessarily need to hold the doctorate when the application is submitted.

Researchers expected to obtain the doctoral degree before the Fellowship begins may apply.

If selected, they must submit documentation confirming the doctoral degree before their fellowship starts.

This can make the programme particularly valuable to final-stage PhD candidates planning the transition directly into postdoctoral research.

Maternity and Parental Leave Adjustment

JSPS also recognizes career interruptions connected with:

Maternity leave

Parental leave

The six-year post-PhD eligibility period can be adjusted by subtracting qualifying periods of maternity or parental leave when calculating the time elapsed since the doctorate was awarded.

This provision helps prevent researchers from being disadvantaged simply because they temporarily interrupted their academic careers for family responsibilities.

Nationality Requirement

Standard Program candidates must generally be citizens of a country that:

Has diplomatic relations with Japan.

JSPS also treats researchers from:

Taiwan

Palestine

as satisfying this requirement.

This makes the Standard Program broadly international.

It is therefore open to researchers from a very large number of countries across:

Africa

Asia

Europe

North America

Latin America and the Caribbean

Middle East

Oceania

provided the nationality requirement and all other eligibility conditions are satisfied.

Japanese Citizens and Permanent Residents

Persons who are:

Japanese citizens, or

Foreign nationals permitted permanent residence in Japan

are not eligible for the Standard Program under the published candidate rules.

The programme is specifically designed to bring overseas researchers into Japanese research institutions.

Previous JSPS Fellows

Applicants should also note an important restriction.

Researchers who previously received and started a Fellowship under the:

JSPS Postdoctoral Fellowship for Research in Japan – Standard

Pathway to University Positions in Japan

are not eligible again under the Standard Program.

Applicants who were previously selected but did not actually begin the Fellowship should consult the detailed eligibility rules applicable to their circumstances.

Financial Support

The JSPS Standard Fellowship provides an extensive support package intended to allow researchers to concentrate on their collaborative research in Japan.

The main components include:

Monthly maintenance allowance

International airfare

Settling-in allowance

Overseas travel insurance

Potential research funding through KAKENHI

Monthly Maintenance Allowance

Standard Fellows receive:

JPY 362,000 per month.

For a 12-month Fellowship, that corresponds to approximately:

JPY 4,344,000 in maintenance allowances

before considering other benefits.

For a 24-month Fellowship, it would correspond to approximately:

JPY 8,688,000

at the currently published monthly rate.

The actual total received depends on the approved fellowship duration and programme rules.

Settling-In Allowance

Successful Fellows may receive a:

JPY 200,000 settling-in allowance.

This is intended to help with costs associated with beginning a temporary research stay in Japan.

Possible relocation-related costs can include:

Initial housing expenses

Essential household setup

Local transportation

Administrative arrangements

Applicants should follow the formal JSPS rules concerning eligible circumstances and payment.

Round-Trip International Airfare

JSPS provides:

A round-trip air ticket

in accordance with its programme regulations.

This considerably reduces the cost of relocating internationally for a long research fellowship.

However, candidates who are already living in Japan with a mailing address before the Fellowship starts are not entitled to the outbound airfare or settling-in allowance under the conditions described by JSPS.

Overseas Travel Insurance

The programme also includes:

Overseas travel insurance.

The specific coverage is governed by JSPS programme regulations.

Research Funding Through KAKENHI

In addition to the personal Fellowship support, a:

Grant-in-Aid for Scientific Research

may be available for cooperative research-related expenses.

The host researcher submits the research grant application through the Japanese host institution.

This research funding is separate from the Fellow’s:

Monthly maintenance allowance

Airfare

Settling-in allowance

and is intended to support the research project itself.

Is This a Fully Funded Fellowship?

The programme can reasonably be described as a fully funded postdoctoral research fellowship because it provides:

Monthly living support

International airfare

Relocation support

Insurance

Potential research funding

However, applicants should avoid interpreting “fully funded” as meaning that JSPS separately reimburses every possible personal expense.

The official terms of support should always govern financial expectations.

Is There an Application Fee?

JSPS’s official FY2027 Standard Program materials do not list an application fee as part of the normal open-call submission process.

The more important challenge is that applicants cannot simply apply independently.

They must build a relationship with an eligible host researcher and have the formal application submitted through the Japanese host institution.

How the Application Process Works

The Standard Program uses two principal application routes:

Open Call through a Japanese host institution

Nomination through an approved overseas nominating authority

These routes should not be confused because their procedures and deadlines can differ.

Route 1: Open Call Through a Japanese Host Researcher

For the open call, the overseas researcher first needs to identify:

An eligible researcher in Japan willing to serve as host.

That host researcher then becomes the formal applicant in the JSPS system.

JSPS states that the application is made through the:

Japanese host institution

using the JSPS Electronic Application System.

The overseas candidate therefore cannot simply submit the complete application independently to JSPS.

Why Finding a Host Researcher Is Crucial

The relationship between candidate and host is central to the selection process.

JSPS expects the two researchers to have:

Established contact before applying

Created a concrete research plan

Identified the value of the collaboration

A weak application based only on the prestige of the overseas candidate is therefore unlikely to be enough.

The proposal needs to explain why conducting the research with this particular Japanese researcher and institution adds value.

Who Can Serve as a Host Researcher?

The host researcher generally needs to be affiliated with an institution eligible under Japan’s KAKENHI framework.

Eligible institutions include categories such as:

Universities

Inter-university research institutes

MEXT-affiliated research institutions

Colleges of technology

Other institutions designated by the Minister of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology

The host researcher normally needs to be eligible to apply for KAKENHI funding and capable of providing an appropriate research environment for the overseas Fellow.

Host Researchers Can Submit Several Applications

Each eligible Japanese host researcher can submit up to:

Three applications

under the programme.

Where the host submits applications for more than one candidate at the same time, priorities must be indicated.

Prospective Fellows should therefore discuss the host’s application situation clearly before beginning substantial proposal preparation.

Route 2: Overseas Nominating Authorities

JSPS also accepts Standard Program candidates through approved:

Overseas nominating authorities.

The list includes organisations in countries such as:

Australia

Austria

Belgium

Bulgaria

Canada

Czech Republic

Estonia

France

Germany

Hungary

Italy

New Zealand

Poland

Slovakia

Slovenia

Sweden

Switzerland

United Kingdom

Ukraine

United States

as well as the United Nations University.

Candidates using this route need to contact the relevant authority directly because:

Application procedures and deadlines are determined by the nominating authority.

This is another reason not to publish one third-party deadline as though it applies universally.

Required Application Materials

The FY2027 application page provides separate forms completed by the:

Japanese host researcher

Foreign candidate

Recommender

The candidate completes Form 2, while the host researcher completes the information submitted through the JSPS Electronic Application System.

A recommendation letter is also required and may be written in:

English

Japanese

Applicants should download the current FY2027 materials rather than reusing forms from an earlier year.

Selection Process

Applications under the Standard open-call route undergo a:

Two-stage competitive review process.

The stages are:

Document review

Panel review

The evaluation is undertaken by the JSPS International Program Committee, consisting of researchers in Japan.

Six Examiners Review Each Application

During the initial document-review stage:

Six examiners review each application.

Experts are assigned according to the research field.

Applications are scored on a five-point scale:

5 – Superlative

4 – Excellent

3 – Good

2 – Fair

1 – Poor

The averaged document-review score becomes an important basis for determining which applications progress through panel review.

What Reviewers Evaluate

Reviewers consider factors such as:

Research achievements

Quality of the research plan

Estimated research capacity

Future potential

Ability to establish new research networks

This means candidates should not treat the application as simply another academic CV competition.

The proposal itself matters substantially.

Importance of the Proposed Collaboration

JSPS explicitly wants the collaboration to contribute to:

Advancement of science in Japan

Advancement of science internationally

Development of the proposed field

The candidate’s research

The host researcher’s research

The proposal should therefore explain:

Why does this research need to be conducted collaboratively in Japan?

A strong answer to that question is essential.

Diversity in Selection

JSPS also states that it seeks, as far as possible, to avoid excessive concentration of selected Fellows by:

Nationality

Host institution

Area of specialization

and seeks to enable researchers from a diverse range of countries to come to Japan.

There is nevertheless no country quota guaranteeing selection.

How Competitive Is the Fellowship?

The Standard Program is highly competitive.

For the FY2026 first recruitment round, JSPS reported:

1,868 applications

145 selected Fellows

7.8% selection rate

For the second FY2026 recruitment:

2,231 applications

125 selected Fellows

5.6% selection rate

These historical figures demonstrate that meeting the eligibility criteria alone is far from sufficient.

Applicants need a strong research record, convincing host relationship and carefully designed research proposal.

Preparing a Competitive Application

1. Start by Finding the Right Japanese Host

Do not approach the host search as an administrative formality.

Look for researchers whose work genuinely intersects with yours.

Review:

Recent publications

Current projects

Research group expertise

Available facilities

Institutional strengths

Then explain specifically why collaboration would create research value.

2. Contact Hosts Early

The official JSPS deadline is not necessarily your practical deadline.

The sequence usually involves:

candidate → host researcher → host institution → JSPS.

Japanese universities may establish internal application deadlines weeks or even more than a month before the JSPS deadline.

Beginning host outreach only shortly before April 23, 2027 would therefore be risky.

3. Build a Concrete Research Plan

JSPS explicitly evaluates whether the candidate and host have developed a concrete collaborative plan.

A strong proposal should explain:

Research question

Academic significance

Methodology

Research schedule

Host institution resources

Division of collaboration

Expected outcomes

International significance

4. Explain Why Japan Is Necessary

Avoid a proposal that could be conducted anywhere.

Identify what Japan offers that is specifically relevant, such as:

Unique archives

Laboratories

Datasets

Research facilities

Field sites

Intellectual traditions

Technical expertise

Host research network

This strengthens the logic behind the Fellowship.

5. Show Future Research Potential

The fellowship is intended for early-career researchers.

Reviewers therefore consider not only what candidates have already accomplished but also their:

Future potential.

Your proposal should demonstrate how the fellowship will help build:

A coherent academic trajectory

New international collaboration

Future publications

Sustainable research networks

New methodological expertise

6. Highlight Research Achievements Strategically

Your publication list matters, but quantity alone is not enough.

Prioritize evidence demonstrating:

Research independence

Scholarly quality

Relevance to the proposed project

Ability to complete ambitious research

Applicants from fields where journal publication is less dominant should present the strongest appropriate research outputs in their discipline.

FY2027 Timeline at a Glance

Recruitment
JSPS deadline
Results
Fellowship start window
Planned awards

First FY2027 Standard round
28 August 2026, 5 PM JST
Late December 2026
1 April–30 September 2027
120

Second FY2027 Standard round
23 April 2027, 5 PM JST
Early August 2027
1 September–30 November 2027
120

Remember that these are host institution-to-JSPS deadlines.

Internal university deadlines may occur earlier.

Key Fellowship Benefits at a Glance

Programme: JSPS Postdoctoral Fellowships for Research in Japan – Standard

Country: Japan

Research level: Postdoctoral

Fields: Humanities, social sciences and natural sciences

Duration: 12–24 months

Monthly maintenance allowance: JPY 362,000

Settling-in allowance: JPY 200,000

International airfare: Round-trip ticket under JSPS rules

Insurance: Overseas travel insurance

Research expenses: Separate Grant-in-Aid may be available

FY2027 awards: Approximately 120 in each open-call recruitment round

Next official FY2027 Standard open-call deadline: 23 April 2027 at 5:00 PM JST

Official Application Links

Main JSPS international fellowship portal:

JSPS International Fellowships for Research in Japan

Standard Program:

JSPS Postdoctoral Fellowship Standard Program

FY2027 application forms and guidance:

FY2027 JSPS Application Guidelines

FY2027 Standard Program schedule:

FY2027 Standard Fellowship Application Schedule

Conclusion

The JSPS Postdoctoral Fellowship for Research in Japan 2027 – Standard Program is one of the most substantial opportunities available to early-career international researchers seeking to build a sustained research collaboration in Japan.

The programme is open across the humanities, social sciences and natural sciences and offers 12 to 24 months of support, including a JPY 362,000 monthly maintenance allowance, JPY 200,000 settling-in allowance, round-trip international airfare and overseas travel insurance, with separate research funding potentially available through KAKENHI.

Candidates must generally be nationals of countries with diplomatic relations with Japan, with Taiwan and Palestine treated as eligible for this purpose, and must have obtained their doctorate within the relevant six-year period or be expected to receive their PhD before the Fellowship begins. Japanese citizens and permanent residents of Japan are not eligible under the Standard overseas-researcher programme.

The application process is built around collaboration. Candidates need an eligible Japanese host researcher and a concrete research plan, and open-call applications are submitted through the host institution rather than directly by the overseas candidate.

For FY2027, JSPS plans approximately 120 Standard Fellowships in each of two open-call rounds. The first deadline was 28 August 2026, while the second-round host-institution deadline is 23 April 2027 at 5:00 PM JST.

Applicants should therefore disregard claims that 15 November 2026 is the universal Standard Fellowship deadline unless that date comes from a specific overseas nominating authority relevant to them.

For researchers who can develop a strong partnership with a Japanese host and articulate a compelling collaborative project, the JSPS Standard Fellowship offers substantial financial support, international research exposure and the opportunity to build long-term academic networks in Japan.
