TITLE: Fostering Business Leadership: Njala University Introduces Online MBA

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Press Release – Njala, Sierra Leone (April 29, 2024) – Njala University is pleased to announce its new online Master of Business Administration (MBA) program. Launched today, April 29, 2024, this new online program results from a collaborative partnership among Njala University, the Association of African Universities (AAU), and eLearnAfrica.

The MBA program is designed to create visionary leaders equipped with the know-how to tackle the challenges of the ever-dynamic global business landscape. The program’s curriculum integrates core business principles with emerging trends and technologies, providing students with a comprehensive understanding of the complexities of modern business environments.

Through a blend of applied readings, assignments, and discussions, participants will acquire the knowledge and skills necessary to prepare them for success in their future careers. The MBA program features core courses in strategic management, marketing management, economic analysis, human resource management, financial management and accounting, and research methodology. Students will have access to a wide portfolio of case studies and real-world examples to apply theoretical knowledge to practical business challenges. The program concludes with an applied research project or dissertation.

This new online MBA program highlights Njala University’s focus on excellence in education and provides an exciting opportunity for students to participate in a flexible online degree program. We invite you to join us in this innovative program and become part of a community of visionary leaders poised to make a significant contribution to global business.

Applications for the inaugural cohort of Njala University’s online MBA program are now open.

Click to create an account and register via this link: https://app.njala.edu.sl/2023-2024/online-mba-programme/apply. Learn more about the program: https://app.njala.edu.sl/online-mba-programme-admissions

About Njala University

Njala University (or simply Njala) has had a rich history since its establishment in 1964 as a university college based on the model of the American Land Grant University. Since then, it has metamorphosed into one of the leading universities in the country, preparing undergraduate and postgraduate students for careers in a variety of specializations, including Education, Agricultural Sciences, Environmental and Community Health Sciences, Social Sciences, Law, Natural Resources Management, and Information Technology. Njala University is a multi-disciplinary university with three campuses: the main Njala campus in the Moyamba District, the Bo campus in the Bo District, and the newly established Bonthe campus in the Bonthe District. Njala University also operate a location in Freetown.

About eLearnAfrica

eLearnAfrica is a social enterprise committed to increasing and expanding access to educational and professional development opportunities throughout Africa. ElearnAfrica’s instructor toolkit simplifies course design and presentation for professors and other facilitators, while its virtual classroom promotes thoughtful participation, learning review for mastery, and collaborative assignments and grading.

In 2016, eLearnAfrica entered a partnership agreement with the Association of African Universities (AAU), to expand online learning opportunities for students enrolled in AAU’s over 400 member institutions and counting. Its target has been to make educational opportunities available to 10 million African students. In pursuing this agenda, the AAU-eLearnAfricaLMS was launched at the 15th Quadrennial AAU General Conference of African University Leaders on July 7, 2021.

For further details, please contact: tsongu@njala.edu.sl / jfsandy@njala.edu.sl / fbakarr@njala.edu.sl /admin@elearnafrica.com or aaulms@aau.org.

TITLE: NSF Institute for Artificial Intelligence and Fundamental Interactions (IAIFI) Fellowship 2027-2030

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 7, 2026

Applications are open for the NSF Institute for Artificial Intelligence and Fundamental Interactions (IAIFI) Fellowship 2027-2030. The NSF Institute for Artificial Intelligence and Fundamental Interactions is one of the inaugural NSF AI research institutes. The IAIFI is enabling physics discoveries and advancing foundational AI through the development of novel AI approaches that incorporate first principles, best practices, and domain knowledge from fundamental physics. AI is transforming many aspects of society, including the ways that scientists are pursuing groundbreaking discoveries.

To facilitate these advances, the IAIFI seeks a talented and interdisciplinary group of researchers at an early stage of their careers to join the IAIFI Fellowship program. The role of an IAIFI Fellow is to spark vital interdisciplinary, multi-investigator, multi-subfield collaborations across some of the primary IAIFI domains of theoretical physics, experimental physics, astrophysics, and foundational AI. Such collaborations have immense power to generate new ideas and approaches in both physics and AI, to facilitate abstracting physics challenges beyond their native domains to inform the development of cutting-edge AI tools, and to instill a common language across disciplines.

Benefits

The salary range is between $71,000 to $90,000.

Eligibility

Applicants should have, or be expected to receive by the 1st of September 2027, a PhD in Physics, Astrophysics, Statistics, Computer Science, or a related field.

English language proficiency is required to obtain a J-1 Visa and therefore be employed by MIT if you are coming from outside the United States.

MIT is an equal opportunity employer. They strongly encourage applications from individuals from all identities and backgrounds. All qualified applicants will receive equitable consideration for employment based on their experience and qualifications and will not be discriminated against on the basis of race, color, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, pregnancy, religion, disability, age, genetic information, veteran status, or national or ethnic origin.

Application

Complete applications must include:

Cover letter (no more than 1 page);

CV (1-2 pages recommended, but longer accepted);

Statement of research interests (no more than 2 pages);

List of publications;

Exactly three reference letters.

Click here to apply

For more information, visit IAIFI Fellowship.

TITLE: STEM Pathways Fund 2026: Up to £150,000 in Grants to Help Young People Transition from Further Education into STEM Careers

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The STEM Pathways Fund 2026 is a major funding opportunity designed to support organisations helping disadvantaged young people in Further Education (FE) across England successfully transition into science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) careers, apprenticeships, higher education and technical training.

The fund is particularly focused on young people aged 16–19 who face financial, social, educational, structural or other barriers that can make it difficult to progress from Further Education into meaningful STEM opportunities.

Through this pilot fund, Mission 44 and Santander UK Foundation aim to support a small portfolio of organisations developing practical, sustained and collaborative approaches to improving STEM transitions.

Successful organisations could receive grants ranging from £75,000 to £150,000 for projects lasting up to 24 months.

The fund is intended not only to improve individual outcomes for young people but also to generate learning that can contribute to stronger, more equitable Further Education and employment systems.

Opportunity Category

Category: Grant

What Is the STEM Pathways Fund?

The transition from education into employment, further study or training represents a critical stage in a young person’s development. For young people experiencing disadvantage, however, this transition can be particularly difficult.

The STEM Pathways Fund has been created in response to the barriers faced by young people in Further Education who may struggle to access clear career pathways, professional networks, careers guidance, work experience, role models and other opportunities that can help them make informed decisions about their futures.

The fund recognises that Further Education plays an important role in developing the UK’s future STEM workforce. Around 1.7 million young people aged 16–19 study in Further Education settings in England, with a substantial proportion coming from disadvantaged backgrounds.

However, pressures on the FE sector can limit the capacity of colleges and other organisations to provide the sustained careers guidance, employer engagement and transition support that young people need.

The STEM Pathways Fund therefore seeks to invest in organisations that can strengthen these pathways and help young people move successfully into:

STEM employment

STEM apprenticeships

Degree apprenticeships

Higher education

Higher technical qualifications

Vocational STEM qualifications

Specialist STEM training

Other recognised education, training or employment opportunities leading towards STEM careers

The Problem the Fund Seeks to Address

Many young people in Further Education encounter multiple barriers during their journey from education into employment or further study.

These barriers can occur at several critical transition points.

1. Entry into Further Education

At around age 16, young people are often required to make important decisions about their education and future careers.

Without access to high-quality careers guidance, trusted advice and clear information, choosing the right post-16 pathway can be confusing.

Young people may not fully understand:

The range of STEM careers available

The qualifications required for different STEM careers

Apprenticeship opportunities

Technical and vocational routes

Higher education options

The skills employers are looking for

How their current studies connect to future careers

2. During Further Education

Once young people are studying in FE, additional barriers can affect their ability to remain engaged and prepare for their next step.

These may include:

Financial hardship

Transport costs

Caring responsibilities

Competing responsibilities outside education

Low confidence

Limited professional networks

Limited access to role models

Unmet special educational needs and disabilities

Unmet mental health support needs

Limited exposure to employers

Lack of meaningful work experience

These challenges can prevent young people from accessing opportunities that could improve their chances of entering STEM careers.

3. Exit from Further Education

The transition out of FE can also be fragmented.

Young people may leave college without having the employer connections, industry knowledge, work experience, careers support or confidence necessary to secure sustainable opportunities.

This can increase the risk of young people becoming NEET — not in education, employment or training.

The STEM Pathways Fund seeks to address these challenges by supporting organisations that can provide sustained transition support rather than relying on one-off interventions immediately before a young person leaves FE.

What Does the Fund Aim to Achieve?

The fund has two broad ambitions.

First, it seeks to improve outcomes for young people.

Second, it aims to contribute to a stronger and more equitable Further Education and employment system.

The fund will primarily assess projects according to the outcomes they achieve for young people while also considering how projects can contribute to wider system change.

Individual projects are not expected to transform the entire system on their own. However, applicants are expected to consider how their work can influence inclusive practices, sector priorities, policies, partnerships and approaches to supporting young people.

Direct Outcomes for Young People

Funded projects should contribute to meaningful improvements in young people’s progression.

Expected outcomes include:

Better Understanding of STEM Pathways

Young people should gain a stronger understanding of the different STEM routes available to them.

This should help them make informed decisions about education, training and employment.

Increased Confidence

Projects should help young people develop greater confidence, skills and belief that STEM careers are accessible and relevant to people from their backgrounds.

Greater Access to Opportunities

Young people should have more equitable access to high-quality STEM opportunities, including:

Employers

Professional networks

Mentors

Role models

Workplace experiences

Work placements

Internships

Industry exposure

Successful Progression

Ultimately, projects should help young people successfully transition from Further Education into:

STEM employment

Apprenticeships

Higher education

Technical education

Further STEM training

Wider System Outcomes

The fund also seeks to generate wider benefits for the FE and employment system.

Funded projects can contribute to:

Better understanding of the practical, financial and structural barriers affecting young people’s STEM progression

More equitable policy and practice

Greater recognition of Further Education as a valuable pathway into STEM

Better understanding of the support young people need to succeed

Sharing evidence and learning about effective transition approaches

Stronger collaboration between FE providers, STEM employers and community organisations

Improved quality and accessibility of STEM transition opportunities

How Much Funding Is Available?

The STEM Pathways Fund will take a portfolio approach, meaning that it intends to support a small number of organisations working across England and fund different models of transition support.

The fund anticipates awarding:

Up to four grants

£75,000 to £150,000 per grant

Projects lasting up to 24 months

The exact amount awarded to each successful organisation will depend on factors such as:

Scope of the proposed project

Ambition of the project

Proposed activities

Expected outcomes

Project budget

Organisational capacity

Overall fit with the fund’s objectives

The funding is intended to be flexible and, where appropriate, unrestricted. This approach allows funded organisations to develop solutions that respond to their local circumstances while contributing to shared outcomes.

Who Is the Fund Designed to Support?

The fund focuses on organisations supporting young people aged 16–19 in Further Education settings across England who face barriers to progressing into STEM pathways.

Particular groups include young people experiencing:

Financial hardship

Caring responsibilities

Unmet Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND)

Unmet mental health support needs

Limited access to professional networks

Limited access to STEM role models

Limited access to workplace experiences

Underrepresentation in STEM pathways

Other systemic barriers affecting education and employment outcomes

The fund specifically recognises that young people may experience multiple and intersecting barriers.

Rather than simply categorising young people according to labels, the fund wants applicants to demonstrate an understanding of their communities’ actual experiences, challenges, strengths and aspirations.

What STEM Careers and Pathways Are Covered?

The fund takes a broad approach to STEM.

STEM pathways are understood as routes that enable young people to progress into careers across science, technology, engineering and mathematics.

The fund recognises that there is no single route into a STEM career.

Young people may enter STEM through academic, technical, vocational or employment-based routes.

Eligible pathways may include:

STEM-related employment

STEM apprenticeships

Degree apprenticeships

University degrees

Higher technical qualifications

Vocational STEM qualifications

Further education

Specialist STEM training programmes

Recognised education, training or employment opportunities supporting progression towards STEM careers

The fund is therefore not limited to traditional university-based STEM education.

Projects that help young people understand the breadth of STEM opportunities and identify pathways appropriate to their interests, circumstances and aspirations are encouraged.

What Does Transition Support Mean?

The fund does not view transition support as a single intervention delivered immediately before a young person leaves FE.

Instead, it believes effective transition support should be:

Planned

Sustained

Personalised

Collaborative

Delivered over an appropriate period

Where possible, support should begin at least one year before a young person is expected to progress into STEM employment, an apprenticeship, higher education or technical training.

This means successful applicants are expected to demonstrate how their approach supports young people before, during and around critical transition points.

Who Is Eligible to Apply?

The fund is open to eligible not-for-profit organisations operating in England that work with young people aged 16–19 in Further Education.

Eligible organisations include:

Registered charities

Charitable Incorporated Organisations (CIOs)

Community Interest Companies (CICs) limited by guarantee

Community Benefit Societies with an asset lock

Cooperative Societies with an asset lock

Other not-for-profit organisations with an asset lock

Further Education Colleges

Designated Sixth Form Colleges

The fund does not accept applications from University Technical Colleges (UTCs).

School sixth forms are also not eligible. The fund specifically refers to designated Sixth Form Colleges operating as independent Further Education institutions.

Where applicable, organisations must have an asset lock ensuring that their assets and profits are used for community benefit.

What Kind of Organisations Will Be Competitive?

Eligible organisations should ideally be able to demonstrate practical experience in supporting young people aged 16–19 to progress into STEM pathways.

Applicants should demonstrate:

Experience working with young people

Experience supporting progression into employment, apprenticeships, higher education or technical training

Strong understanding of the Further Education environment

Knowledge of the challenges faced by FE learners

Understanding of the specific barriers experienced by the target groups

Evidence that the proposed intervention responds to an identified need

Capacity to deliver the proposed activities

Meaningful relationships with relevant partners

Organisations without extensive direct FE experience may still be able to apply where they can demonstrate a credible partnership with one or more FE colleges.

Partnerships Are Strongly Encouraged

The fund places significant emphasis on collaboration.

Applications may be strengthened where organisations work alongside:

Further Education colleges

STEM employers

Community organisations

Young people

Local partners

Other organisations with relevant expertise

The purpose is not to duplicate existing FE provision but to strengthen it.

A strong partnership could combine the expertise of an FE college, the industry access of STEM employers and the specialist experience of a community organisation working directly with disadvantaged young people.

Organisations Outside London Are Particularly Encouraged

The fund specifically indicates that it would especially like to hear from organisations working outside London.

It is also interested in:

Smaller not-for-profit organisations

Organisations with strong community relationships

Organisations that collaborate with young people in designing their services

Ethnic minority-led organisations

Collaborative partnerships bringing together different forms of expertise

The fund recognises the value of lived experience and local knowledge in designing effective interventions.

What Is an Ethnic Minority-Led Organisation?

For this particular fund, an ethnic minority-led organisation is defined as one where:

The Chief Executive Officer or equivalent, or Chair of the Board, self-identifies as being from an ethnic minority background; and

At least 50% of the Board of Trustees/Management Committee and/or senior leadership team also self-identify as being from an ethnic minority background.

Collaborations involving ethnic minority-led organisations are particularly welcomed where they bring important lived expertise to the work.

What Will the STEM Pathways Fund Support?

The fund is open to a range of activities that can strengthen successful transitions into STEM pathways.

Potential activities include:

Mentoring and Coaching

Projects may provide young people with sustained mentoring, coaching and guidance from people who can help them understand and navigate STEM career pathways.

STEM Role Models

Young people may benefit from exposure to STEM professionals who can demonstrate the range of careers available and help challenge perceptions about who can succeed in STEM.

Employer Engagement

Projects can create meaningful relationships between young people and STEM employers.

This could include:

Employer talks

Industry visits

Career events

Networking opportunities

Employer-led workshops

Industry mentoring

Work Experience and Placements

Applicants can propose practical experiences that allow young people to understand STEM workplaces and develop relevant skills.

These could include:

Work experience

Placements

Internships

Workplace visits

Employer projects

Careers Education

Projects may provide careers education that helps young people understand:

Available STEM careers

Entry requirements

Qualifications

Apprenticeships

Technical routes

University pathways

Employer expectations

Progression opportunities

Confidence and Skills Development

Funded activities can help young people develop confidence, employability skills and leadership capabilities required to progress.

Collaborative Transition Models

Organisations can develop collaborative approaches involving FE providers, employers, community organisations and young people.

The fund also welcomes innovative approaches that can improve transitions into STEM pathways.

What Will Not Be Funded?

Applicants should carefully consider the fund’s exclusions before submitting an Expression of Interest.

The fund will not support:

Capital costs, including building work and renovations

Spending that has already taken place

Activities taking place outside England

Party political lobbying activities

The practice or promotion of religion or particular belief systems

Loan repayments

Investment

Projects should therefore focus on eligible programme activity and future delivery rather than retrospective expenditure or capital development.

Does the Project Have to Be New?

No.

The fund welcomes both new and existing work.

An existing programme can be considered where the organisation can demonstrate how the funding would:

Strengthen the programme

Expand its reach

Enhance existing provision

Improve outcomes

Develop new partnerships

Improve STEM transition pathways

Applicants should clearly explain what the funding will enable them to achieve that they could not achieve through their existing resources.

Application Process

The application process has two stages.

Stage 1: Expression of Interest

The first stage is an Expression of Interest (EOI).

Applicants will provide information about:

Their organisation

The communities they serve

The needs they have identified

The barriers young people face

Their proposed approach

How the approach aligns with the fund’s priorities

The online EOI is expected to take approximately 45–60 minutes to complete.

Only organisations that meet the eligibility requirements and demonstrate a strong fit with the fund’s objectives will progress.

Stage 2: Full Application

A small number of organisations shortlisted through the EOI stage will be invited to submit a full application.

The full application will provide an opportunity to give more detail about:

The proposed project

Delivery approach

Project activities

Expected impact

Project budget

Organisational capacity

Due diligence information

The project proposal will have a maximum length of five A4 pages.

The full application builds on information submitted during the EOI stage, meaning shortlisted applicants will generally only be asked to provide additional information needed to support the funding decision.

Assessment and Decision-Making

Eligible applications will be reviewed by:

Mission 44

Santander UK Foundation

Mission 44 Youth Advisors

The inclusion of Youth Advisors reflects the fund’s participatory approach to decision-making.

Shortlisted applicants may be contacted if additional information is required before a final funding decision is made.

Important Application Dates and Deadline

Applicants should pay close attention to the following timeline:

Stage
Date

Expression of Interest opens
Tuesday, 28 July 2026

Expression of Interest deadline
Wednesday, 9 September 2026 at 5:00 PM

Invitation to submit full application
Monday, 28 September 2026

Full application deadline
Monday, 19 October 2026 at midday

Funding decision
Late November 2026

Grants awarded and activity begins
December 2026 – January 2027

Expected programme delivery commencement
January 2027

Main Deadline

The Expression of Interest deadline is Wednesday, 9 September 2026 at 5:00 PM.

Organisations should not wait until the final day to prepare their EOI, particularly because they need to demonstrate eligibility, local need, organisational experience and alignment with the fund’s objectives.

Accessibility Support

The EOI is submitted through a Google Form designed to make the process straightforward and proportionate.

Applicants who experience accessibility barriers when completing the application can contact the fund team at:

youth@mission44.org

Visit the Mission 44 website HERE

Who Should Consider Applying?

This opportunity could be particularly relevant to organisations that already work with disadvantaged young people in Further Education and want to strengthen their STEM progression programmes.

Potential applicants include organisations that:

Operate on a not-for-profit basis

Work with 16–19-year-olds

Operate in England

Work directly with Further Education learners

Have established relationships with FE colleges

Work with STEM employers

Provide careers or employability support

Deliver mentoring or coaching programmes

Provide work experience or placements

Support underrepresented groups in STEM

Have evidence of barriers affecting local young people

Can demonstrate measurable progression outcomes

Organisations considering applying should carefully assess their legal status and operational location before investing significant time in the application.

What Makes a Strong Application?

Although funding decisions will depend on the overall assessment process, applicants should pay particular attention to several areas.

Demonstrate a Clear Need

Do not simply state that young people face barriers.

Use evidence to demonstrate what those barriers look like in the communities you serve.

Useful evidence may include:

Local data

FE learner insights

Employer feedback

Surveys

Interviews

Focus groups

Existing programme data

Lived experience

Evidence from partner organisations

Explain Why Your Approach Is Appropriate

Applicants should clearly connect the identified problem with their proposed activities.

For example, if young people lack access to STEM employers, explain how employer engagement, workplace visits or mentoring will address that gap.

Show Strong FE Knowledge

The fund places considerable importance on understanding the Further Education environment.

Applicants should demonstrate that they understand:

How FE learners experience transitions

The pressures affecting FE institutions

The needs of disadvantaged learners

Existing support available

Gaps in current provision

How their project will complement rather than duplicate existing services

Demonstrate Collaboration

Strong partnerships can increase the reach and effectiveness of a project.

Applicants should consider how FE colleges, STEM employers, community organisations and young people themselves can contribute to the design and delivery of the project.

Involve Young People

The fund values organisations that work collaboratively with young people to inform or influence their activities, programmes or services.

Applicants should therefore demonstrate how young people have contributed to programme design or how they will have a meaningful voice during implementation.

Focus on Sustainable Progression

The ultimate objective is not simply participation in activities.

Applicants should demonstrate how their project will help young people progress towards meaningful destinations such as:

STEM employment

Apprenticeships

Degree apprenticeships

Higher education

Technical qualifications

STEM training

Why This Funding Opportunity Matters

The STEM Pathways Fund is significant because it addresses a challenge that goes beyond simply encouraging young people to study STEM subjects.

For many disadvantaged young people, the problem is not necessarily a lack of ambition.

It can be a lack of access.

Without professional networks, employers, mentors, role models, work experience and reliable careers guidance, young people may struggle to translate their interests and qualifications into real opportunities.

The fund therefore takes a broader approach to STEM progression by recognising the importance of sustained transition support.

It also recognises that different young people require different forms of support.

A student experiencing financial hardship may need help accessing workplace opportunities. Another young person may require mentoring and confidence-building. Someone with caring responsibilities may require a more flexible progression model.

The strongest approaches are likely to be those that understand these individual and intersecting barriers and respond to them appropriately.

Key Facts at a Glance

Fund: STEM Pathways Fund

Category: Grant

Lead organisations: Mission 44 and Santander UK Foundation

Geographic scope: England only

Primary beneficiaries: Young people aged 16–19 in Further Education

Funding: £75,000–£150,000 per grant

Number of anticipated grants: Up to four

Maximum project duration: 24 months

EOI opens: 28 July 2026

EOI deadline: 9 September 2026 at 5:00 PM

Full application deadline: 19 October 2026 at midday

Expected programme start: January 2027

Application process: Two stages

Eligible applicants: Eligible not-for-profit organisations and qualifying FE institutions operating in England

UTCs: Not eligible

School sixth forms: Not eligible

Activities outside England: Not eligible

Eligibility Summary: Who Qualifies?

Eligible applicant category: Not-for-profit organisations and eligible Further Education institutions operating in England.

Examples of eligible organisations: Registered charities, CIOs, CICs limited by guarantee, qualifying community benefit societies, qualifying cooperative societies, other not-for-profits with an asset lock, Further Education Colleges and designated Sixth Form Colleges.

Target beneficiaries: Young people aged 16–19 studying in Further Education in England who experience barriers to progressing into STEM education, training or employment.

Countries/regions eligible to apply: England only. This is not an international grant open to organisations from Ghana, other African countries, or other countries outside England.

Race/ethnicity: The fund is open to eligible organisations serving the target groups in England. It particularly welcomes collaborations involving ethnic minority-led organisations and recognises the value of lived experience. It is not presented as a grant restricted exclusively to applicants of a particular race or ethnicity.

Academic qualifications: The fund is not structured as an individual scholarship or academic award, so there is no stated minimum degree, diploma or academic qualification for individual applicants. Eligibility is primarily based on the applicant organisation’s legal status, location, experience, target beneficiaries and alignment with the fund’s objectives.

Conclusion

The STEM Pathways Fund 2026 offers a substantial opportunity for eligible organisations in England to strengthen the transition from Further Education into STEM careers, apprenticeships, higher education and technical training.

With grants of £75,000 to £150,000 available for projects lasting up to 24 months, the fund provides significant scope for organisations to develop or expand programmes focused on mentoring, employer engagement, work experience, careers education, confidence building, skills development and collaborative progression support.

The opportunity is particularly relevant to organisations working with young people who face financial, social, educational, structural or other barriers to STEM progression.

Applicants should focus on demonstrating a clear understanding of the local challenges, strong relationships with Further Education providers and STEM employers, meaningful involvement of young people, and a credible pathway from project activities to measurable progression outcomes.

The first and most important deadline is Wednesday, 9 September 2026 at 5:00 PM, when Expressions of Interest close. Organisations that successfully pass the EOI stage will be invited to submit a more detailed full application.

For eligible organisations in England, this fund represents an opportunity not only to secure significant financial support but also to contribute to a more inclusive STEM pipeline and help young people access opportunities that may otherwise remain out of reach.

TITLE: Call for Research Projects 2026 “Women and Science”

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Women and Science Chair at Paris Dauphine-PSL University, aims to mobilize and develop multidisciplinary approaches to analyze the determinants and the impact of the low presence of women in scientific studies and careers (mathematics, computer science, natural sciences and technology). The Women and Science Chair is member of the UNESCO chairs network, created with the support of the L'Oréal Foundation, Generali, La Poste, Amundi and Descours Family, in partnership with the Institute of Public Policies and Institut Louis Bachelier.
To this end, the Chair associates research centers and researchers both in Dauphine University and outside Dauphine. It mobilizes methods and tools from several disciplines, in particular economics (risk economics, microeconomics, applied economics, experimental economics), decision theory and mathematical modeling, sociology, management and social psychology.
Since 2019, the chair has received 446 proposals and has funded 42 research projects from Europe, North America, South America, Africa, Australia and Asia.

TITLE: EU-LAC Birregional School of Local Political Leadership for Women 2026 (Scholarship available)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: July 24, 2026

Applications are open for the EU-LAC Birregional School of Local Political Leadership for Women 2026. The EU-LAC Foundation is launching the EU-LAC Birregional School of Local Political Leadership for Women 2026, conceived as a strategic space for training, exchange and networking among women leaders from Latin America, the Caribbean and the European Union.

Their objective is to bring together women with experience in the political, community and social spheres in order to strengthen their leadership and advocacy capacities at the local level through a feminist, intersectional and human rights-based approach. The School promotes the exchange of experiences, the development of intergenerational mentoring networks and access to practical tools in areas such as political leadership, communication, negotiation and public management.

The programme will combine preparatory virtual sessions with an intensive in-person meeting, fostering both accessibility and meaningful dialogue and learning among participants from both regions. Through this initiative, the EU-LAC Foundation seeks to contribute to strengthening women’s political participation and to the development of leadership capable of driving democratic and inclusive transformations within their communities. The second edition of the Birregional School of Local Political Leadership for Women will take place in October 2026 in Panama.

Scholarships

For selected participants who indicate in their application form that they are unable to cover their travel, accommodation, subsistence and local transport costs through third-party funding, the EU-LAC Foundation will cover these expenses through the direct purchase of travel tickets, hotel reservations and a stipend to cover meals and local transport during the days in which the in-person component of the Leadership School in Panama takes place.

Eligibility

Young women

Proof of membership in a network, programme, organisation or institution, together with a letter of support endorsing their application.

A commitment is expected to participate in the preparatory modules, the in-person meeting in Panama and the follow-up activities.

Demonstrated interest in territorial political leadership will be valued, whether in formal spaces such as local councils or local governments, or in informal spaces such as feminist collectives, community organisations or neighbourhood networks. Initial training or interest in birregional relations with a focus on gender, local development or civic participation will also be taken into account.

Applicants should also show willingness to share situated experiences, learn from other territorial contexts, strengthen their emerging leadership alongside other women leaders, and have an interest in actively joining the EU-LAC WIN Network from a perspective of municipal or community political leadership, or already be part of this network.

Senior women leaders

A consolidated track record in political or community processes, with proven capacity to make an impact in their communities, municipalities or local areas.

Proof of membership in a network, programme, organisation or institution is required, together with a letter of support endorsing their experience.

These participants must have experience in territorial political leadership, whether from municipal governments, councils or community boards, or through high-impact social and community initiatives.

They are expected to actively engage in the preparatory modules, the in-person meeting in Panama and the follow-up activities, as well as to share the knowledge gained from their experience in order to enrich collective processes with women leaders from Latin America, the Caribbean and Europe.

Their participation will be marked by an active link to the EU-LAC WIN Network or an interest in joining it, and by a commitment to continue promoting gender equality and transforming their contexts from a feminist, intersectional and human rights-based perspective.

Application

The application documentation required to be considered for this call must be written in Spanish or English and consist of the following:

Signed application form

Proof of membership in a network, programme, organisation or institution

Letter of support/endorsement for this application from a person or from a network/organisation/institution
The documentation must be submitted in PDF or MS Word format.
Applications submitted after the deadline, incomplete applications, and, in general, those that do not comply with the conditions set out in these Terms of Reference will not be accepted. Applications received after the established deadline will not receive acknowledgement of receipt or any other type of communication.

Applications should be sent to the attention of Dr Anna Barrera (EU-LAC Foundation).
Email: eulacwin@eulacfoundation.org
Subject line: EU-LAC Women’s Political Leadership School 2026 + Applicant’s Name

For more information, visit EU-LAC Birregional School of Local Political Leadership for Women.

TITLE: Science history

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
1958Appointment of Jean Dieudonné, who stays at the Institute until 1964, working in many fields, including group theory and functional analysis.

Jean Dieudonné

Alexander Grothendieck
1958Alexander Grothendieck also joins the Institute. Awarded the Fields medal in 1966, he remains at IHES until 1970. He completely reshapes the foundation of algebraic geometry and its methods.

Louis Michel
1962

Louis Michel joins IHES, where he spends 30 years. He is the first theoretical physics permanent professor and promotes the use of group theory in physics and in the study of symmetry.

René Thom
1963

René Thom (1958 Fields medallist) is recruited by Léon Motchane and stays at IHES until the end of his career. He makes significant contributions to differential geometry and topology, then focuses his research on the role of singularities in morphogenesis and later on theoretical biology, linguistics and philosophy.

David Ruelle
1964

David Ruelle becomes a permanent professor of theoretical physics. He makes many lasting and important contributions to quantum field theory, statistical mechanics and the theory of the dynamical systems.

Pierre Deligne
1970

Pierre Deligne becomes a permanent professor and continues the work started by Alexander Grothendieck, of transforming arithmetic geometry. He is awarded the Fields medal in 1978 and leaves IHES in 1984.

Dennis Sullivan
1974

Dennis Sullivan arrives at the Institute and remains until 1997. He creates algebraic models for topological spaces and contributes to the study of dynamical systems and of a topological approach to hydrodynamics. He is awarded the Abel prize in 2022.

Jürg Fröhlich
1978

Jürg Fröhlich becomes a permanent professor for four years. His research is mostly on quantum field theory.

Alain Connes
1979

Alain Connes, Léon Motchane chair holder, after pioneering contributions on operator algebras, founds a «noncommutative geometry». He is awarded the Fields medal in 1982 and the CNRS Gold medal in 2004.

Oscar Lanford III
1982

Oscar Lanford III joins IHES and stays seven years to work on the theory of dynamical systems, applying to these systems concepts arising from renormalisation group theory. He also turns his attention to computer-assisted demonstrations and is responsible for IHES acquiring computer equipment for the first time.

Mikhael Gromov
1982

Mikhail Gromov is recruited by IHES. In post at the Institute for over 30 years, he completely reshapes geometry. He is awarded the Kyoto Prize in 2002 and the Abel Prize in 2009, to name just two.

Jean Bourgain
1985

Jean Bourgain joins the Institute and works on Banach spaces, harmonic analysis and ergodic theory. He is awarded the Fields medal in 1994 before joining IAS the same year.

Thibault Damour
1989

Thibault Damour becomes a permanent professor. His research is on relativistic gravitation, cosmology and new concepts of gravitation. An Einstein specialist, he has received many awards, including the Einstein medal in 1996 and the Amaldi Prize in 2010. In 2017 he was awarded the CNRS Gold Medal, the most prestigious scientific award in France, for his work on gravitational waves.

Maxim Kontsevich
1995

Maxim Kontsevich* arrives at the Institute. He belongs to a new generation of mathematicians who have been able to incorporate aspects of quantum theory into their work, opening up radically new perspectives. He is awarded the Fields medal in 1998 and many subsequent prizes: the Crafoord Prize (2008), the Shaw Prize (2012) and two Breakthrough Prizes in fundamental physics (2012) and in mathematics (2014).

Laurent Lafforgue
2000

TITLE: Doria Feminist Fund Grantmaking Cycle 7 2026: Funding for Feminist Groups and Organisations in the MENA Region

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Doria Feminist Fund (DFF) has opened its Grantmaking Cycle 7, providing an important funding opportunity for feminist groups, collectives and organisations working across the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region.

The fund is designed to provide flexible and long-term financial support to feminist movements, particularly groups working at the frontlines of social change. Rather than imposing rigid funding priorities, DFF aims to place resources, decision-making and trust in the hands of the feminist movements and communities closest to the issues they are addressing.

For feminist organisations and collectives looking for funding to strengthen their movements, launch new initiatives, produce knowledge, respond to emergencies or build their organisational capacity, the Doria Feminist Fund represents an opportunity to access funding and longer-term accompaniment.

DFF Grantmaking Cycle 7 opened on 7 September 2026, and applications are due by 19 October 2026.

Opportunity Overview

Opportunity: Doria Feminist Fund Grantmaking Cycle 7

Category: Grant

Opening date: 7 September 2026

Deadline: 19 October 2026

Target region: Middle East and North Africa (MENA)

Eligible applicants: Feminist groups, collectives and organisations

Application languages: Arabic, English and French

Registration requirement: Registered and unregistered groups can apply

Age requirement: There is no age limit

Previous funding: Applicants do not need to have received funding previously

Application type: Open call

Official organisation: Doria Feminist Fund

About the Doria Feminist Fund

The Doria Feminist Fund supports feminist groups and organisations working at the frontlines of change throughout the Middle East and North Africa.

Its approach is based on the belief that feminist movements and local communities are best positioned to understand their own circumstances, determine their priorities and decide how resources should be used.

DFF therefore focuses on providing flexible funding and long-term support, allowing communities to strengthen their work, share knowledge and develop solutions that respond to their own realities.

The fund supports both new and established feminist groups, with particular attention given to groups that may have difficulty accessing traditional philanthropic funding.

DFF’s approach also recognises that feminist movements require more than short-term project financing. Sustainable movements need resources, organisational support, knowledge-sharing opportunities, networks, safety and collective care.

What Makes the Doria Feminist Fund Different?

One of the central features of DFF is its emphasis on trust, flexibility, solidarity and community-driven decision-making.

Instead of requiring every feminist organisation to fit into a predetermined funding model, DFF’s open calls allow applicants to explain their work and priorities in their own words.

The fund’s grantmaking process is designed to understand the realities of feminist movements across the region and identify opportunities, gaps, emerging issues and areas where additional support can make a meaningful difference.

This makes the opportunity particularly relevant for groups whose work may not fit neatly into conventional funding categories.

Who Can Apply?

Doria Feminist Fund welcomes applications from feminist activists and feminist movement builders across the MENA region.

The fund particularly prioritises:

New and emerging feminist groups

Groups that have never received funding before

Established groups launching a new project

Women-led groups and collectives

Trans* groups and collectives

Feminist organisations working at the frontlines of change

Registered feminist organisations

Unregistered feminist groups and collectives

Importantly, individual applicants cannot apply independently. DFF funds collective feminist work, meaning eligible applicants must apply as a collective, group or organisation.

There is also no age limit for applicants.

Groups can have members who are men, but DFF gives priority to applications led by women and trans* groups and collectives. Groups led by cis-men are not eligible under the stated priority criteria.

Do You Need to Be a Registered Organisation?

No.

One of the notable aspects of the Doria Feminist Fund is that both registered and unregistered feminist groups can apply.

This is particularly important for grassroots movements and newly formed collectives that may not yet have completed formal registration.

DFF also states that a group does not necessarily need to have its own bank account. For groups without access to a bank account, the fund works on a case-by-case basis to identify a safe way to transfer funding while maintaining transparency and alignment with feminist values.

Countries Eligible for the Doria Feminist Fund

DFF supports feminist groups that are based in, or working across, countries in the Middle East and North Africa.

The currently listed eligible countries are:

Algeria

Bahrain

Egypt

Iraq

Jordan

Kuwait

Lebanon

Libya

Mauritania

Morocco

Oman

Palestine

Qatar

Saudi Arabia

Somalia

Sudan

Syria

Tunisia

United Arab Emirates

Yemen

Applications from groups working across the region may also be considered where their work falls within DFF’s MENA focus.

What Types of Work Does DFF Support?

Doria Feminist Fund supports feminist groups working across a broad range of issues and strategies.

The fund does not restrict open calls to a narrow list of predetermined issues. Instead, it uses a movement-informed approach to understand the needs and priorities emerging across the region.

Supported work can include areas such as:

Feminist advocacy

Campaigning

Feminist movement building

Gender equality

Women’s rights

Girls’ rights

Gender-based violence prevention and response

Sexual and reproductive health and rights

Economic empowerment

Legal reform

Service delivery

Knowledge production

Community organising

Alternative forms of activism

Organisational development

Emergency response

Safety and security initiatives

DFF’s existing programmes demonstrate the broad nature of the work it supports.

Doria Feminist Fund Grant Programmes

DFF currently operates four grant programmes alongside a broader accompaniment programme.

1. Core Funding for Emerging Groups

The Core Funding programme provides flexible funding intended primarily for new and emerging feminist groups.

The objective is to help groups establish themselves, strengthen their work and navigate their early years.

The programme supports groups advancing the rights and wellbeing of women and LBTQ+ communities, particularly those developing new concepts and ideas that challenge and transform existing feminist movement discourse.

An important principle behind this funding is that feminist groups are trusted to identify their own priorities and determine how funding should be spent.

Eligible groups include:

Registered feminist groups

Unregistered feminist groups

Groups that have not previously received DFF support

Groups based in a MENA country

Groups with no specific age requirement

2. Project Funds

Project Funds are intended for established feminist groups or collectives that want to develop a new programme or introduce a new activity within their existing organisation.

The funding can help established groups respond to changing political circumstances, community needs and emerging challenges.

Groups may also use the opportunity to broaden their existing work and adopt new practices or mechanisms that strengthen their impact.

Projects should address gender and feminist issues and be connected to work in the MENA region.

3. Knowledge Production Funds

The Knowledge Production Fund supports feminist activists and engaged scholars working on gender and feminist issues in the region.

The funding can support the creation and dissemination of knowledge through different formats.

Examples include:

Research papers

Books

Translation of publications into Arabic

Feminist meetings and convenings

Educational materials

Magazines

Comics

Podcasts

Photo essays

Other creative media

Knowledge-sharing initiatives

The programme recognises that knowledge production is an important part of feminist movement building.

Works produced through the programme are intended to be shared publicly under a Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY) licence, while ownership remains with their creators.

4. Emergency Response Grants

DFF also provides rapid and flexible support for feminist groups experiencing urgent or unforeseen circumstances.

This may be particularly important for groups facing sudden threats to their safety, political crises or other situations that place their work or members at risk.

Emergency funding can cover urgent needs such as:

Relocation

Digital security

Physical security

Legal support

Other immediate emergency expenses

The emergency response programme is designed to provide support quickly and through a simplified process when feminist groups need resources urgently.

Beyond Funding: DFF’s Accompaniment Approach

The Doria Feminist Fund’s support does not end with providing financial resources.

Current grantee partners can also receive opportunities for growth, learning and networking through peer-to-peer support and engagement with experts.

This accompaniment approach can include:

Managerial Skills

Grantee partners can receive support in areas such as:

Proposal writing

Financial management

Strategic planning

Organisational development

Skill Strengthening

Support may also help organisations develop expertise in areas including:

Feminist digital security

Knowledge production

Advocacy

Other skills relevant to their work

Networking and Knowledge Sharing

DFF facilitates opportunities such as:

Trainings

Conferences

Webinars

Workshops

Convenings

Peer-learning opportunities

Additional Financial Support

Where accompaniment or mentorship requires travel, training or other expenses, additional funding may be provided on top of the original grant to cover those costs.

DFF’s Approach to Collective Care

Collective care is another important element of DFF’s philosophy.

The fund’s Collective Care Collaborative has explored how care practices can strengthen feminist organisations and movements.

Its advocacy toolkit draws on the experiences and practices of five women’s funds and examines the role of accompaniment and organisational practices in supporting the “glue” and resilience of feminist movements.

The approach encourages funders to think beyond conventional financial support and invest in community-driven care models that prioritise:

Interdependence

Well-being

Sustainability

Organisational resilience

Movement resilience

Long-term care

This reflects a broader understanding that feminist movements require sustainable systems of support to continue their work in challenging environments.

DFF’s Grantmaking Process

DFF uses an open and movement-informed grantmaking process.

Stage 1: Call for Proposals

Applicants submit proposals for relevant funding opportunities, including core grants, project grants and knowledge production grants.

The application process is designed to allow applicants to describe their work and plans openly rather than forcing them into highly restrictive templates.

Applications can be submitted in:

Arabic

English

French

During the open-call period, DFF provides opportunities for applicants to connect with the fund, ask questions and troubleshoot their applications.

Informational sessions and webinars may also be organised for prospective applicants.

Stage 2: Review and Selection

Applications are reviewed by the DFF grants team and an activist review committee.

The activist committee plays an important role in reviewing applications and providing feedback.

The selection process considers the applicant pool, the priorities and needs of the feminist movement ecosystem and DFF’s strategic direction.

Shortlisted applicants may be contacted for additional information and due diligence.

This process is intended to be rooted in principles of:

Care

Solidarity

Trust

Transparency

Accountability

Stage 3: Onboarding and Welcome

Successful applicants receive award letters and grant agreements outlining the grant period and terms.

Grantee partners then participate in welcome calls with DFF staff and committee members.

These conversations can cover:

The grantee journey

Reporting timelines

Safety measures

Accompaniment opportunities

Available support

Doria Feminist Fund’s Impact

DFF’s recent figures demonstrate the scale of its grantmaking.

In 2025, the fund reported:

596 applications received from 19 countries

78 grants awarded

$1.46 million disbursed in grants

57 open-call grants disbursed

13 countries reached

21 grants and emergency grants renewed

For Cycle 5, DFF reported $1.117 million allocated across 78 grants, including core support, project support, knowledge production, recognition and emergency response grants.

These figures illustrate the fund’s growing role in supporting feminist movements across the region.

Why This Grant Opportunity Matters

For many grassroots feminist movements, access to flexible funding can be difficult.

Traditional grants can sometimes require organisations to have formal registration, extensive financial histories, previous grant experience or established institutional structures.

DFF takes a different approach by allowing registered and unregistered groups to apply, welcoming new and emerging movements and not requiring previous DFF funding.

This can create opportunities for grassroots groups that may otherwise struggle to access international funding.

The fund’s emphasis on flexibility also allows feminist groups to identify their own priorities rather than simply responding to priorities established by external funders.

Key Benefits for Successful Applicants

Successful grantee partners may benefit from:

Flexible financial support

Long-term engagement

Support for organisational development

Funding for new feminist projects

Support for knowledge production

Emergency financial assistance

Networking opportunities

Peer-to-peer learning

Training and workshops

Expert accompaniment

Strategic planning support

Financial management support

Digital security capacity building

Advocacy and movement-building support

Additional funding for certain accompaniment-related expenses

The combination of funding and accompaniment makes the opportunity relevant not only to organisations seeking financial resources but also to groups looking to strengthen their long-term sustainability.

Application Deadline

Deadline: 19 October 2026

Doria Feminist Fund announced that Grantmaking Cycle 7 opened on 7 September 2026, and eligible feminist groups are encouraged to submit their applications before the 19 October 2026 deadline.

Applicants should avoid waiting until the final day to begin the application process, particularly if they need to gather organisational information, develop a project proposal or consult members of their collective.

Who Should Consider Applying?

This opportunity may be particularly relevant to:

Emerging feminist groups

Grassroots feminist movements

Women’s rights organisations

Feminist collectives

Women-led organisations

Trans* groups and collectives

Established feminist organisations developing new projects

Feminist activists working collectively

Groups producing feminist knowledge

Feminist groups responding to emergencies

Organisations working on gender-based violence

Groups working on girls’ rights

Feminist movement-building organisations

Organisations working on economic empowerment

Groups working on sexual and reproductive health and rights

Organisations using advocacy, campaigning, legal reform or alternative activism strategies

However, applicants should ensure that their work and location meet DFF’s eligibility requirements before submitting an application.

Important Eligibility Reminder

DFF does not accept applications from individuals applying on their own.

Applications must come from an eligible:

Collective

Group

Organisation

Both registered and unregistered groups can be considered.

There is no age limit, and previous funding is not required.

DFF particularly encourages applications from new and emerging groups, groups that have never previously received funding and established groups launching new projects.

Eligible Countries and Region

This grant opportunity is specifically focused on the Middle East and North Africa (MENA).

Eligible countries currently listed by DFF are:

Algeria, Bahrain, Egypt, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Libya, Mauritania, Morocco, Oman, Palestine, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, Tunisia, United Arab Emirates and Yemen.

Therefore, applicants from outside this listed MENA geographic scope should not assume that they are eligible simply because they work on feminist or women’s rights issues.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Applicants should carefully explain the work their group is already doing, the community they serve and what they hope to accomplish with DFF support.

A strong application should clearly communicate:

Who your group is — Explain your collective, organisation or movement and its background.

The problem you are addressing — Clearly describe the gender, feminist or community issue your work seeks to address.

Your approach — Explain how your group is responding to the issue and why your approach is appropriate for your community.

Community connection — Demonstrate how your work is rooted in the realities, priorities and knowledge of the communities you serve.

Your proposed activities — Clearly explain what you want to do with the funding.

Expected impact — Describe what you hope will change as a result of your work.

Why funding is important now — Explain the specific financial or organisational gap that the grant would help address.

Sustainability — Where appropriate, explain how the support can strengthen the long-term resilience of your group or movement.

Applicants should also make sure that their application reflects the principles and realities of feminist movement building rather than simply presenting a conventional project proposal.

Conclusion

The Doria Feminist Fund Grantmaking Cycle 7 offers a significant funding opportunity for feminist groups and organisations working across the Middle East and North Africa.

Its emphasis on flexible funding, trust, solidarity, collective care, long-term support and locally driven priorities makes it particularly relevant to grassroots and emerging feminist movements.

The opportunity is open to both registered and unregistered groups, and applicants do not need previous DFF funding experience. The fund also provides several forms of support, ranging from core organisational funding and project support to knowledge production and emergency response.

With Cycle 7 opening on 7 September 2026 and the application deadline set for 19 October 2026, eligible feminist groups should review the requirements carefully and begin preparing their applications early.

For feminist movements seeking to strengthen their organisations, develop new initiatives, produce knowledge, respond to urgent challenges or build sustainable movements across the MENA region, the Doria Feminist Fund provides an opportunity to access both financial resources and longer-term movement support.

TITLE: CTP-LI Norms and Expectations

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The mission of the MIT Center for Theoretical Physics — a Leinweber Institute (CTP-LI) is to drive forward our understanding of the fundamental properties of the universe and to help develop the next generation of researchers, educators, and leaders in nuclear physics, high energy physics, and quantum information. We endeavor to create a lively, collegial working environment that fosters collaboration, sparks novel ideas, and generates exciting discoveries. We also strive to uphold the Department’s Physics Values Statement, and anticipate that new members of the group will read this statement and do likewise.

The primary mission of our PhD program is for students to learn how to advance the frontiers of human knowledge, and to contribute their own piece to the puzzle for the first time.

CTP-LI expectations directly flow from this sense of purpose. Generally, advisors individually set workplace norms and expectations based on the specific environment they wish to create for their own group. Below, we offer some general guidelines.

Work hours
While theoretical physics can be done from anywhere, one of the key benefits of institutions like the CTP-LI and MIT is that they bring people together in person. Being in the same space creates spontaneous interactions that can lead to new ideas and collaborations, and create a dynamic working environment. These broader connections are often an important part of a successful PhD and academic career. Thus, while working hours are flexible, many advisors feel that it is important that students/postdocs be present in the CTP-LI for a non-negligible fraction of standard business hours to facilitate such impromptu discussions, as well as attending seminars and meetings. We certainly understand that your presence in the CTP-LI is not possible 100% of the time (e.g. for childcare, daytime medical appointments, religious holidays, etc.). Also note that some faculty are okay with significant amounts of remote work. In general with all of these things you should talk about expectations with your advisor. In addition, if you have some ongoing extenuating circumstances that change your work patterns, your advisor will generally be happy to accommodate you — please do not hesitate to ask. And please do not come in when you are sick!

Graduate students should understand that a PhD program is a full-time commitment. Students are expected to devote 40 hours/week to their academic, teaching, and research program. Some people may find that certain commitments (e.g. homework, exams, giving a talk) lead these hours to fluctuate. In addition, many physicists feel passionate about their research topics and/or have specific career goals, and may choose to devote substantially more hours than this. An academic career, starting with a PhD, requires making personal choices about work-life balance, and we strive to support students in finding ways to be productive and fulfilled. You should plan on regularly talking with your research advisor about progress and expectations.

What counts as academics and work?
Postdocs and students engage in a wide variety of different physics-related activities, including but not limited to: research activities, required classes and exam preparation, physics seminars and socials (like the joint CTP-LI/CMT tea, IAIFI coffee hours, Department colloquium cookies, etc), attending conferences and schools, serving on committees, auditing extra classes relevant to a research project, professional development, teaching assistantships, and mentoring junior physicists.

Seminars
Seminars are highly valuable: you can hear about a wide range of new physics, learn by example how to give talks, and meet people whom you may consider working with one day. CTP-LI faculty have a wide range of expectations for which seminars and group meetings their trainees should attend: this is important to ask of your research advisor when you join a group. First-year students are encouraged to attend seminars such as the Monday nuclear/particle seminar, the Wednesday string seminar, the Friday QI seminar, and the Thursday department colloquium, if they do not overlap with classes. Anyone in the CTP-LI may sign up for any seminar mailing list; first-years especially may find this useful in searching for a good research fit and advisor fit.

CTP-LI seminar code of conduct: CTP-LI members and visitors are expected to uphold the fundamental MIT Physics Community values of well-being, respect, inclusion, collaboration, and mentorship, and to treat one another with respect and decency at all times. While questions, discussions, and scholarly debate are encouraged, we ask that seminar participants be mindful that their words and actions do not stifle the contributions of others, especially participants who may be affected by systemic biases. Harassment, intimidation, or inappropriate remarks about individual characteristics such as gender, race, sexual orientation, physical ability, age, national origin, religion, or citizenship status will not be tolerated.

Vacation
It is important for your mental health to take breaks from physics; you will be more productive in the long run! That being said, MIT has stringent policies on the number of vacation days allotted to Postdocs and Grad students. Students and postdocs with fellowships may have different rules from their funding agency. Note that graduate school is different from undergraduate studies, in that students do not have the summer off. Summer is typically core research time.

Please ask your advisor for approval before booking travel for personal vacation. Note that many advisors prefer that their trainees do not take personal vacation during term time (though some do not mind). We also remark that it is common for physicists to add a vacation onto the end of a conference trip, but you must personally pay any difference in travel costs out of pocket. You should ask your advisor to tell you what conferences and/or summer schools it would be beneficial for you to attend.

Research advising
A typical CTP-LI faculty member holds a one hour meeting per week for each research project (though again this is advisor-specific). Our meeting schedules may differ from what you were used to at your previous institution. Just as you are engaged in a wide variety of physics activities, so too are faculty. We often have tight schedules, but we truly care about you. Please do not hesitate to reach out if you need something. Be sure to ask your advisor about their preferred method of communication (email, Slack, carrier pigeon), and please remind us a few days later if we miss a message! Other places to catch up informally include seminars, group meetings, informal CTP-LI lunches, or simply saying hi at the coffee machine.

It is important to cultivate a wide network of many mentors to help guide you, including other students and postdocs. At this point in your career, it begins to fall on you, the mentee, to proactively seek out and conscientiously cultivate mentoring relationships, and build a large support network that can provide you advice and help propel you towards your personal goals. In turn, you can pay it forward by providing your own advice to the next crop of students and postdocs.
