TITLE: How to Prepare for a Professional Presentation

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Whether you are presenting at a conference, pitching an idea to investors, delivering a lecture, speaking at a board meeting, or leading a team briefing, a successful presentation begins long before you step onto the stage. Effective presenters are not simply confident speakers—they are well prepared, intentional, and audience-focused. A strong presentation combines clear messaging, thoughtful preparation, and confident delivery to ensure that your ideas are understood and remembered.

Start with a Clear Objective
Before opening PowerPoint or designing slides, define the purpose of your presentation. Ask yourself what you want your audience to know, feel, or do after listening to you. Every presentation should have a single central message that guides its structure and content. When your objective is clear, it becomes easier to decide what information to include and what to leave out. Understanding your audience is equally important. Consider their level of knowledge, interests, expectations, and what they hope to gain from your presentation. Tailoring your content to your audience makes your message more relevant and engaging.

Research Your Content Thoroughly
Credibility is built on preparation. Ensure that your facts, statistics, and examples are accurate and up to date. If you are discussing research findings, policy issues, business performance, or technical subjects, rely on credible sources and verify your information before presenting it. Supporting your key messages with real-life examples, case studies, or practical experiences helps your audience connect with your presentation. Rather than overwhelming listeners with large amounts of information, focus on the most important points that reinforce your central message.

Organise Your Presentation Logically
A well-structured presentation allows your audience to follow your ideas with ease. Begin with a strong introduction that captures attention, introduces the topic, and outlines what will be covered. The body of your presentation should develop your key points in a logical sequence, with each section flowing naturally into the next. Conclude by summarising the main messages and ending with a clear recommendation, call to action, or memorable closing statement. Keeping your presentation organised also helps you stay focused during delivery and reduces the likelihood of losing your train of thought.

Design Slides That Support Your Message
Slides should enhance your presentation rather than compete with it. Avoid filling slides with long paragraphs or excessive text. Instead, use concise bullet points, diagrams, charts, photographs, and simple graphics to reinforce what you are saying. Maintain a consistent design throughout your presentation by using readable fonts, appropriate colour contrast, and clean layouts. Every slide should communicate one main idea. If a slide appears crowded, simplify it. Remember that your audience came to hear you speak, not to read your slides.

Practise Before Presentation Day
Preparation builds confidence. Rehearse your presentation several times until you become familiar with the flow of your content. Time yourself to ensure that you remain within the allocated speaking time, and identify sections that may need to be shortened or clarified. Practising in front of colleagues, mentors, or friends can provide valuable feedback on your delivery, clarity, pacing, and body language. Recording yourself is another effective way to identify areas for improvement, including filler words, speaking speed, and eye contact. The goal is not to memorise every sentence but to become comfortable enough with your material that your delivery feels natural.

Prepare for Questions
Many presentations include a question-and-answer session. Anticipate the questions your audience is likely to ask and prepare thoughtful responses in advance. Consider areas where clarification may be needed or where your recommendations could be challenged. If you do not know the answer to a question, it is perfectly acceptable to acknowledge this honestly and offer to follow up afterwards. Professionalism is demonstrated not by knowing everything, but by responding thoughtfully and respectfully. Pay Attention to Delivery Your voice, posture, eye contact, and body language all influence how your audience receives your message. Speak clearly and at a comfortable pace, varying your tone to maintain interest. Avoid reading directly from your slides or notes throughout the presentation. Make eye contact with different sections of the audience, use natural gestures to emphasise important points, and pause occasionally to allow listeners time to absorb key information. Confidence often comes from preparation rather than natural ability.

Prepare Your Equipment in Advance
Technical issues can disrupt even the best presentations. Arrive early to test your laptop, presentation slides, projector, microphone, internet connection, and any videos or demonstrations you plan to use. Carry backup copies of your presentation on a USB drive, cloud storage, or email in case of unexpected technical problems. Being technically prepared allows you to focus entirely on your presentation rather than worrying about equipment failures.

Dress Professionally and Arrive Early
Your appearance contributes to first impressions. Choose clothing that is appropriate for the event, comfortable, and professional. Arriving early gives you time to familiarise yourself with the venue, meet organisers, adjust your equipment, and settle any last-minute nerves before your audience arrives.

Continue Learning After Every Presentation
Every presentation is an opportunity to improve. Reflect on what went well, what challenged you, and what you would do differently next time. Seek constructive feedback from organisers, colleagues, or audience members. Over time, these reflections will strengthen both your communication skills and your confidence.

Final Thoughts
Professional presentations are rarely the result of natural talent alone. They are the product of careful preparation, thoughtful organisation, and consistent practice. By understanding your audience, structuring your message clearly, designing effective visual aids, rehearsing thoroughly, and delivering with confidence, you increase your ability to inform, persuade, and inspire. Whether you are presenting in a classroom, conference hall, boardroom, or international forum, investing time in preparation is one of the most effective ways to ensure your presentation leaves a lasting and positive impression.

TITLE: WHO Research Officer Position 2026 | Apply in Burkina Faso

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The World Health Organization (WHO) is recruiting a Research Officer (P2) to support work on neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) through the Expanded Special Project for Elimination of Neglected Tropical Diseases (ESPEN).

Location: Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso

Position: Research Officer

Grade: P2

Contract: 12 months

Deadline: 11 September 2026 at 2:59 PM

Starting annual base salary: USD 56,046, plus applicable post adjustment and other benefits

About the Position

The Research Officer will work under the direction of the ESPEN Team Leader and direct supervision of the ESPEN Laboratory Head.

The role contributes to WHO’s work to reduce the morbidity, mortality and disability associated with neglected tropical diseases, with particular attention to diseases amenable to preventive chemotherapy. These include lymphatic filariasis, onchocerciasis, soil-transmitted helminthiasis, schistosomiasis and trachoma.

Key Responsibilities

The successful candidate will contribute to laboratory research, surveillance, GIS and capacity-building activities.

Key duties include:

Contributing to the development of laboratory protocols, standard operating procedures and diagnostic tools for NTDs.

Providing technical support for operational research related to NTD elimination.

Conducting O-150 PCR entomological testing of S. damnosum s.l. adults using molecular biology techniques.

Conducting entomological analyses.

Documenting and disseminating laboratory best practices and protocols.

Supporting collaborative operational research activities and scientific publications.

Maintaining laboratory databases.

Developing mapping of laboratory data and entomological surveillance results.

Working with the ESPEN data team in Brazzaville.

Supporting inter-country and national training activities to build laboratory and field research capacity.

Required Qualifications

Education

Applicants must have a first university degree in one of the following fields:

Computer Sciences

Information System Engineering

Geographical Information System (GIS)

Public Health

Parasitology

Medical Entomology

Advanced certification or additional qualifications in areas such as computer sciences, molecular biology, parasitology, entomology, laboratory sciences or related fields are desirable.

Professional Experience

Applicants must have a minimum of two years of national and international experience in areas including:

Applied molecular biology

Research and development of surveillance tools for onchocerciasis or other priority NTDs in Africa

GIS data transformation

Mapping and spatial modelling of onchocerciasis foci

Previous experience with WHO and a strong publication record on onchocerciasis or other NTDs are considered desirable.

Required Skills

The position requires strong technical knowledge and research capabilities.

Applicants should have:

Excellent knowledge of the epidemiology of onchocerciasis.

Knowledge of onchocerciasis transmission, distribution and socioeconomic impact.

Knowledge of disease control and elimination strategies in the African Region.

Knowledge of lymphatic filariasis epidemiology and control strategies.

Strong GIS and remote-sensing skills.

Ability to analyse biological specimens involving vectors and parasites.

Ability to conduct laboratory needs assessments.

Ability to coordinate training activities in NTD field research, GIS and mapping.

Language Requirements

Essential: Expert knowledge of French.

Desirable: Intermediate knowledge of English.

The language requirements are interchangeable according to the vacancy information.

Salary and Benefits

The position is classified at P2 level.

The annual base salary starts at USD 56,046, subject to applicable mandatory deductions for pension contributions and health insurance.

The position also includes a variable post adjustment, currently stated as USD 1,789 per month for the Ouagadougou duty station.

Other benefits include:

30 days of annual leave

Allowances for dependent family members

Home leave

Education grant for dependent children

WHO Competencies

The vacancy identifies the following core competencies:

Teamwork

Respecting and promoting individual and cultural differences

Communication

Producing results

Contract Duration

The Research Officer position is offered as a temporary appointment for 12 months.

The position is based in Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso, and is a full-time role.

Additional Information

WHO notes that a written test and/or asynchronous video assessment may be used during the screening process.

Candidates who are retained for an interview will be required to provide scanned copies of the degrees, diplomas or certificates required for the position.

WHO also notes that educational qualifications must come from institutions accredited or recognised in the World Higher Education Database (WHED), subject to the stated exceptions and review procedures.

WHO encourages applications from women, persons with disabilities, and nationals of unrepresented and underrepresented Member States.

Application Deadline

The application deadline is:

11 September 2026 at 2:59 PM

Applicants are encouraged to submit their applications before the deadline rather than waiting until the final hours.

Who Should Apply?

This opportunity is particularly suitable for professionals with backgrounds in public health, parasitology, medical entomology, molecular biology, GIS, remote sensing, epidemiology and NTD research.

The strongest candidates will combine relevant academic training with at least two years of professional experience in NTD research, surveillance, molecular biology or GIS-based disease mapping.

Conclusion

The WHO Research Officer position in Ouagadougou provides an opportunity for qualified professionals to contribute to regional efforts to control and eliminate neglected tropical diseases in Africa.

The role combines molecular biology, entomological surveillance, GIS, operational research, laboratory systems and capacity building, making it particularly relevant to professionals working at the intersection of public health, disease surveillance and scientific research.

Eligible candidates with the required academic background, professional experience and French-language proficiency should consider applying before 11 September 2026.

TITLE: Niongoze Fellowship 2026: Leadership, Mentorship and Training Opportunity for Young Tanzanian Women

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are officially open for the Niongoze Fellowship Class of 2026, Doyenne Tanzania’s flagship leadership development programme for young Tanzanian women who want to strengthen their confidence, develop practical leadership skills and become part of a community of purpose-driven changemakers.

The 2026 application window runs from:

1 September 2026 to 25 September 2026

The official Doyenne Tanzania website specifies that applications close on:

25 September 2026 at 23:59 East Africa Time (EAT).

The Niongoze Fellowship is designed around Doyenne Tanzania’s broader mission of building a generation of qualified female leaders through leadership training, mentorship, coaching and empowerment. Doyenne describes the Fellowship as its flagship programme for equipping university students with transformative leadership skills.

The programme is particularly relevant for young women who want to become more confident leaders, develop the skills needed to influence their communities, learn directly from experienced leaders and connect with other ambitious young women across Tanzania.

Official website and application access:
Doyenne Tanzania – Niongoze Fellowship 2026

About the Niongoze Fellowship

The Niongoze Fellowship is a leadership development initiative created by Doyenne Tanzania, a Tanzanian nonprofit organization dedicated to expanding leadership opportunities for girls and young women.

Doyenne describes itself as an organization committed to developing qualified female leaders through:

Leadership training

Mentorship

Coaching

Empowerment

Professional and personal development

Its wider vision is a community in which girls and women have equal opportunities to lead.

The Niongoze Fellowship sits at the centre of that mission.

Rather than focusing only on academic performance, the programme seeks to help young women understand leadership at a more personal and practical level: how they see themselves, how they work with other people, how they participate in organizations and how they create positive change in their communities.

What Does “Niongoze” Mean for the Programme?

The Fellowship is structured as a leadership journey rather than a one-off workshop.

Historically, Doyenne has described Niongoze as an annual programme combining:

Leadership training

Mentoring

Coaching

Peer learning

In-person activities

Virtual activities

Independent descriptions of the programme have characterized it as a year-long leadership development initiative in Tanzania, while Doyenne’s current website describes Niongoze as its flagship programme for university students.

The overall objective is to help young women develop the knowledge, confidence and relationships needed to take increasingly meaningful leadership roles.

Who Is the Niongoze Fellowship Designed For?

For the 2026 application cycle, Doyenne’s official website asks:

“Are you a young Tanzanian woman ready to grow in confidence, strengthen your leadership skills, and join a community of purpose-driven changemakers?”

The current website also describes the Niongoze Fellowship as:

A flagship leadership programme that equips university students with transformative skills.

This makes the opportunity especially relevant to young Tanzanian women currently building their leadership experience while pursuing higher education.

Potential applicants may include women involved in:

Student government

University associations

Community organizations

Volunteer initiatives

Youth programmes

Social-impact projects

Advocacy

STEM initiatives

Entrepreneurship

Health programmes

Environmental initiatives

Civil society activities

Professional associations

However, holding a formal leadership title should not automatically be assumed to be a requirement unless the application form explicitly says so.

What Does the Fellowship Aim to Develop?

Doyenne’s broader programme model emphasizes several interconnected dimensions of leadership.

Historical descriptions of Niongoze highlight themes such as:

Leadership

Confidence

Resilience

Wellbeing

and developing leadership understanding at:

Individual level

Group level

Community level

These areas are important because effective leadership involves more than holding a title.

The Fellowship seeks to develop young women who can understand themselves, collaborate effectively and contribute meaningfully to the people and institutions around them.

Personal Leadership

The Fellowship has historically begun by focusing on:

Leadership of self.

This may involve areas such as:

Self-awareness

Confidence

Personal values

Decision-making

Goal-setting

Resilience

Communication

Understanding strengths

Reflecting on personal growth

Doyenne’s 2024 Fellowship page, for example, describes the first colloquium as focusing on personal leadership training.

The idea is that leadership begins with understanding one’s own values, abilities and responsibilities.

Group Leadership

Another dimension concerns leadership within teams and organizations.

Previous Niongoze programme structures have included training at the:

Group level.

Relevant skills can include:

Communication

Teamwork

Collaboration

Conflict management

Listening

Delegation

Relationship-building

Working across differences

Collective decision-making

These skills are particularly useful for university students who are already involved in clubs, associations, community initiatives or student leadership.

Community Leadership

The Fellowship also extends leadership beyond the individual and group level toward:

Community leadership.

Past programme descriptions include a dedicated community leadership component.

This helps participants think about questions such as:

What problems affect my community?

How can young women contribute to solutions?

How can leaders mobilize other people?

How do we create sustainable impact?

How can leadership strengthen inclusion and participation?

This community orientation helps distinguish leadership development from purely personal career coaching.

Confidence Development

Confidence is a major theme of Doyenne’s work.

Its current website presents the 2026 opportunity as a chance for young Tanzanian women to:

Grow in confidence

while building leadership capacity.

For many emerging leaders, confidence can affect their willingness to:

Speak publicly

Express ideas

Apply for opportunities

Lead teams

Challenge established practices

Participate in decision-making

Advocate for communities

The Fellowship therefore seeks to create an environment where young women can develop both competence and the confidence to use it.

Mentorship

Mentorship forms another important part of Doyenne’s overall leadership model.

Doyenne explains that its programmes connect girls with:

Leaders

Mentors

Changemakers

so participants can learn from people who have already travelled similar leadership paths.

Mentorship can help emerging leaders understand:

Career decisions

Leadership challenges

Professional development

Personal growth

Networking

Navigating institutional environments

For university students, having access to experienced female leaders may be particularly valuable when making decisions about postgraduate study, employment, entrepreneurship, public service or community leadership.

Coaching and Leadership Development

Doyenne also identifies coaching as part of its broader organizational approach.

Coaching differs slightly from mentorship.

Where mentorship often involves learning from someone’s experience, coaching can focus more directly on helping a participant:

Clarify goals

Recognize strengths

Identify barriers

Develop action plans

Reflect on progress

Improve leadership behaviors

Taken together, leadership training, mentoring and coaching can provide participants with a broader development experience than a single short workshop.

A Community of Young Female Leaders

One of the strongest features of the Niongoze Fellowship is the opportunity to join a community of other young women interested in leadership.

The current call specifically emphasizes joining a:

“community of purpose-driven changemakers.”

Peer networks can be valuable because participants may continue to support each other long after formal programme activities conclude.

Fellows may come from different:

Universities

Academic disciplines

Regions

Leadership backgrounds

Professional interests

but share an interest in creating positive change.

Previous Niongoze Fellows Have Come From Diverse Academic Fields

The Niongoze Fellowship is not limited to a single academic discipline.

The 2024 cohort profiled by Doyenne included young women studying areas such as:

Political Science and Public Administration

Electronics and Telecommunication Engineering

Cybersecurity and Digital Forensics

Electrical Engineering

Medicine

International Relations and Diplomacy

Law

Accounting and Finance

Tourism Management

Social Work

This indicates that leadership development is intended to cut across academic and professional fields.

A woman studying medicine may want to become a health leader.

A law student may want to advance justice.

An engineering student may want to lead in technology.

A tourism student may want to champion sustainable development.

The Fellowship provides a shared leadership platform across these different aspirations.

Previous Fellows Have Represented Universities Across Tanzania

Past Niongoze participants have come from institutions including:

University of Dar es Salaam

University of Dodoma

Mzumbe University

Hubert Kairuki Memorial University

St. Augustine University of Tanzania

College of African Wildlife Management

Kilimanjaro Christian Medical University College

Dar es Salaam Institute of Technology

Dr. Salim Ahmed Salim Centre for Foreign Relations

among others.

The Fellowship therefore creates opportunities for networking beyond a participant’s own campus.

Leadership Beyond Academic Achievement

The profiles of previous Fellows also demonstrate that Doyenne looks broadly at leadership potential.

Past participants have been involved in:

Student government

Health outreach

Women’s empowerment

STEM advocacy

Child-rights advocacy

Technology initiatives

Conservation

Environmental projects

Community organizations

Entrepreneurship

Public speaking

Student clubs

Volunteer work

This suggests that applicants should think about leadership as something broader than academic grades.

Leadership can be demonstrated by:

Starting an initiative

Volunteering

Representing students

Solving a community problem

Organizing a project

Supporting peers

Advocating for change

Taking responsibility

Leadership Training Through Colloquia

Previous editions of the Fellowship have used a series of:

Colloquia

to structure leadership learning.

Doyenne’s 2024 programme description identifies:

A first colloquium on personal leadership

A second colloquium focusing on leadership at the group level

A third colloquium focusing on community leadership

Graduation as the concluding stage

Another description of Doyenne’s programme similarly notes an annual series of four colloquia delivered through physical and virtual formats.

Applicants should note, however, that Doyenne’s current public 2026 homepage does not publish the complete 2026 schedule. Participants should therefore rely on the application materials or Doyenne directly for the final Class of 2026 timetable.

In-Person and Virtual Learning

Past Niongoze Fellowship programmes have combined:

Physical activities

Virtual activities

rather than operating entirely online.

This allows Fellows to benefit from face-to-face networking while also participating in learning and mentoring across geographic distances.

The exact delivery format for the Class of 2026 should be confirmed through the application process because Doyenne’s current homepage does not publicly list every session format.

Is There a Fellowship Fee or Stipend?

The current 2026 Doyenne website does not publicly specify a stipend, cash award, travel allowance or financial benefit for selected Fellows.

Older Doyenne communications have described participation in earlier cohorts as free, but applicants should not assume that every cost or financial arrangement is identical for the 2026 class unless this is confirmed in the current application materials.

For publication accuracy, the Niongoze Fellowship 2026 should therefore not be advertised as a funded or fully funded fellowship unless Doyenne issues current 2026 financial details confirming this.

Application Period

Applications opened on:

1 September 2026

and close on:

25 September 2026.

Doyenne’s official website provides the more precise closing time:

25 September 2026 at 23:59 EAT.

Applicants should aim to submit before the final evening rather than waiting until the deadline.

How to Apply

Applications are available through the official Doyenne Tanzania website.

Apply through Doyenne Tanzania

The homepage currently displays the “Apply for the Class of 2026” option for the Niongoze Fellowship.

Applicants should follow the official application link provided there.

Contact Doyenne Tanzania

The organization lists the following contact information:

Email: info@doyenne.or.tz

Phone: +255 757 019 087

Candidates with questions about:

Eligibility

Programme schedule

Required documents

Participation costs

University status

Application form issues

should contact Doyenne directly if the information is not covered in the current application form.

Application Information Session

Doyenne also announced a Niongoze Fellowship information session and live Q&A for 10 September 2026, reflecting its effort to help applicants understand the programme and application process.

Applicants who missed that session should use the official website and Doyenne contact channels for any remaining questions.

How to Prepare a Strong Niongoze Fellowship Application

1. Explain Why Leadership Matters to You

Avoid simply writing that you “want to become a leader.”

Explain:

What type of leader you want to become

Who you want to serve

What problem you care about

What change you hope to create

A clear leadership purpose is more persuasive than a generic interest in professional development.

2. Show Leadership Through Action

You do not necessarily need a prestigious title.

Think about examples where you have:

Organized people

Solved a problem

Supported classmates

Volunteered

Started a project

Advocated for others

Taken responsibility

Helped your community

Leadership potential often appears through action rather than formal titles.

3. Be Honest About What You Still Need to Learn

A fellowship exists because applicants are still developing.

You can explain that you want to improve areas such as:

Public speaking

Confidence

Decision-making

Team leadership

Networking

Resilience

Strategic thinking

Showing self-awareness can strengthen a leadership application.

4. Connect Your Leadership Goals to Tanzania

The Fellowship is explicitly focused on developing young Tanzanian women.

Explain how stronger leadership skills could help you contribute to:

Your university

Your professional field

Your local community

Tanzania more broadly

5. Demonstrate Community Orientation

Doyenne’s Fellowship has historically moved from personal leadership to group and community leadership.

A strong applicant should therefore think beyond individual career advancement.

Consider:

Who benefits if I become a stronger leader?

That question can help shape a meaningful application.

6. Explain Why Niongoze Specifically

Rather than applying because “it is a good opportunity,” explain why you value elements such as:

Mentorship

Leadership training

Coaching

Female leadership networks

Learning from accomplished women

Peer community

This demonstrates that you understand the programme.

Important Details at a Glance

Programme: Niongoze Fellowship Class of 2026

Organization: Doyenne Tanzania

Country: Tanzania

Target group: Young Tanzanian women

Current programme description: Flagship leadership programme for university students

Focus: Leadership development

Core approaches: Training, mentorship, coaching and empowerment

Application opening: 1 September 2026

Application deadline: 25 September 2026

Closing time: 23:59 EAT

Official website:
www.doyenne.or.tz

Email: info@doyenne.or.tz

Phone: +255 757 019 087

Important Note on Age and Detailed Eligibility

Previous external descriptions of Niongoze have characterized the broader programme as serving young women around 17–25 years old.

However, Doyenne’s current 2026 public website does not publish a specific age range on the application announcement. It instead describes applicants as young Tanzanian women and describes Niongoze as a flagship programme for university students.

For accuracy, applicants should therefore check the current 2026 application form before relying on a historical age threshold.

Conclusion

The Niongoze Fellowship 2026 is an important leadership development opportunity for young Tanzanian women who want to strengthen their confidence, develop practical leadership skills and connect with an ambitious community of female changemakers.

Organized by Doyenne Tanzania, the Fellowship forms part of the organization’s mission to build a generation of qualified female leaders through training, mentorship, coaching and empowerment. The current Doyenne website identifies Niongoze as its flagship programme for university students.

Previous cohorts demonstrate the interdisciplinary nature of the programme, bringing together women studying fields ranging from medicine and law to engineering, international relations, cybersecurity, accounting and tourism.

Historically, the Fellowship has explored leadership at the personal, group and community levels and has combined physical and virtual learning experiences.

For a young Tanzanian woman who wants to become more confident, develop her leadership identity, learn from mentors and build relationships with other emerging leaders, Niongoze offers a structured pathway for personal and community-oriented growth.

TITLE: New Initiative Targets the Development of a Guiding Framework for Transforming Research Collaborations with Africa

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Association of African Universities (AAU), together with some of Africa’s major research and higher education (HE) constituencies, including , the Council for the Development of Social Science Research in Africa (CODESRIA), the African Academy of Sciences (AAS), the African Research Universities Alliance (ARUA), the Inter-University Council for Eastern Africa (IUCEA), and the Association of West African Universities (AWAU), are embarking on an initiative to co-create a framework for advancing a transformative mode of academic research collaborations between African Universities and partners from the rest of the world. The framework will serve to advance the repositioning of Africa in global knowledge production.

A first consultative meeting held on January 26, 2023, in Accra, Ghana, which was attended by the partners, and other institutions including the International Network for Higher Education in Africa (INHEA, University of Kwazulu-Natal) and the African Union Commission (AUC), designated a steering group to take forward the initiative.

Drawing on African intellectual thought, analyses of extant global scientific and equitable partnerships efforts, and dialogue with key Higher Education (HE) and research actors in Europe, North America and others across the globe, the charter will 1) articulate basic Principles on how research collaborations need to be configured to redress the multi-layered power imbalances in global-Africa knowledge dynamics; and 2) set out Goals and Guiding frameworks for institutional and HE-sector policy change to embed such a transformative collaboration mode. An initial framework and declaration will be launched on 22 June 2023 in Accra, Ghana.

This initiative recognizes that fostering transformative collaborations requires a collective effort and adequately recognises the complex nature of the power asymmetries underlying international collaborations, as well as the need for change at multiple levels: in individual mindsets and capabilities, in shared social norms and, crucially, in institutional and wider HE policies, and funding regimes above all in the ‘global North’.

Centering the concerns of Africa-based knowledge constituencies, the guiding framework, once developed, will provide a rallying point and a tool for advancing such change. The initiative is facilitated by the Perivoli Africa Research Centre (PARC) at the University of Bristol, in partnership with the University of South Africa Chief Albert Luthuli Research Chair and the University of Cape Town Institute for Humanities in Africa (HUMA).

TITLE: 2026-2027 Fulbright-Nehru International Education Administrators Award

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Fulbright-Nehru International Education Administrators Award (IEA) aims to provide Indian college and university administrators with the opportunity to familiarize themselves with the U.S. higher education system.

The two-week U.S. visit in April 2027 will enable participants to learn about various facets of U.S. higher education, including the types of institutions, accreditation, curriculum development, fundraising, student services and international education on U.S. campuses, as well as share knowledge on Indian higher education. Topics addressed during visits and meetings at select campuses and organizations will also include research collaborations, faculty and student exchanges, and study abroad.

This award is designed for Indian college and university administrators with at least two years of experience in international program development and management at their institutions in India. Applicants must be middle to senior-level college or university administrators (vice-chancellors, deans, directors of international centers or offices, foreign student advisors, registrars, etc.) who have substantial responsibility for enhancing the international dimension of their institutions and who wish to strengthen the capacity of their faculty and students through international collaborations, exchange programs, and innovative curricular design.

Grant Benefits

Selected participants will receive J-1 visa support, Accident and Sickness Program for Exchanges per U.S. Government guidelines, round-trip economy class air travel from India to the U.S., travel within the U.S., lodging and a per diem. Dependents are not permitted to accompany participants during the award period.

Eligibility Requirements

In addition to the General Prerequisites

should be mid to senior-level college or university administrators (vice-chancellors, deans, directors of international centers/offices, foreign student advisors, or registrars, etc.) working at Indian institutions;

must have at least two years’ experience in the relevant field;

should have the responsibility of enhancing the international dimension of their institutions and should wish to build capacity of their faculty and students through international collaborations and exchange and innovative curricular design;

should have demonstrated leadership in one or more of the following areas: implementing multidisciplinary education, research and innovation initiatives, technology integration and digital learning strategies, institutional governance and autonomy frameworks, and programs promoting student well-being; and

should have a high level of academic/professional achievement.

This includes civil servants in central services (such as IAS, IPS, IRS, IFS, and allied services), state government services (including state civil services), and bureaucratic staff employed in central and state ministries or departments. TITLE: The Globe and Mail Foundation Mentorship Program 2026–2027: Six-Month Investigative and Political Journalism Mentorship with Robert Fife

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Globe and Mail Foundation has opened applications for the inaugural 2026–2027 Globe and Mail Foundation Mentorship Program with Robert Fife, a six-month, project-based mentorship opportunity designed for emerging investigative and political journalists in Canada.

The program offers selected journalists an opportunity to receive intensive, one-on-one mentorship from veteran Canadian investigative and political journalist Robert Fife while developing a substantial public-interest reporting project from the initial idea or pitch through to publication.

Running from November 2026 through April 2027, the mentorship is intended to help emerging journalists strengthen their investigative reporting, writing, interviewing, editorial judgment, professional development and understanding of the media industry.

Only two emerging journalists will be selected for the inaugural cohort, making this a highly focused mentorship opportunity for journalists who are ready to pursue ambitious reporting projects and deepen their professional practice.

The application deadline is Sunday, October 11, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time (ET).

About the Globe and Mail Foundation Mentorship Program

The Globe and Mail Foundation Mentorship Program with Robert Fife has been established to provide emerging journalists with sustained access to an experienced investigative and political journalist.

Rather than being a short-term workshop or general journalism training course, the program is structured around a six-month, project-based mentorship. Participants will work closely with Robert Fife through the development of a focused public-interest reporting project.

The mentorship is intended to provide a practical environment where journalists can discuss reporting ideas, receive editorial feedback, refine their stories and develop the skills necessary to produce high-quality journalism.

Throughout the program, mentees will have opportunities to work through different stages of the reporting process, including identifying and refining a story idea, developing a reporting strategy, conducting interviews and research, writing and revising drafts, and preparing a final piece for publication.

The program therefore combines professional mentorship with practical project development.

Key Details of the 2026–2027 Robert Fife Mentorship Program

Program: The Globe and Mail Foundation Mentorship Program with Robert Fife

Opportunity type: Mentorship / Journalism Training

Cohort: 2026–2027 inaugural cohort

Number of mentees: Two emerging journalists

Mentor: Robert Fife

Duration: Six months

Program period: November 2026 to April 2027

Location requirement: Applicants must reside in Canada

Focus areas: Investigative journalism and political journalism

Experience requirement: No more than five years of reporting experience

Application deadline: Sunday, October 11, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. ET

Application method: Email

Application email: education@globeandmailfoundation.com

Subject line: “The Robert Fife Mentorship”

What Does the Mentorship Program Offer?

The program provides participants with a combination of individual mentorship, editorial guidance, project development and professional career advice.

1. One-on-One Mentorship with Robert Fife

One of the central features of the program is direct access to Robert Fife.

Each selected journalist will participate in private virtual mentorship sessions every two weeks throughout the six-month program.

These sessions are designed to create an ongoing space for discussion, reflection and editorial guidance. Instead of receiving advice only once or during a short workshop, mentees will have sustained access to an experienced journalist as they develop their reporting projects.

The regular sessions can provide an opportunity to discuss reporting challenges, story development, research approaches, interviews, writing and broader professional questions.

2. Development of a Public-Interest Reporting Project

The mentorship is centered around a substantial reporting project.

Mentees will bring or develop a focused idea addressing an issue of public interest and work on it throughout the program.

The project will be developed from the initial pitch through to final publication. This means participants can gain practical experience in the different stages involved in producing deeply reported journalism.

Depending on the nature of the project, the reporting process may involve:

Identifying a significant public-interest issue.

Refining the central reporting question.

Developing a strong story angle.

Conducting background research.

Identifying relevant sources.

Planning interviews.

Gathering information and evidence.

Conducting interviews.

Assessing information and sources.

Structuring the story.

Writing and revising drafts.

Receiving editorial feedback.

Preparing the final story for publication.

This project-based structure makes the mentorship particularly relevant to journalists who already have an area of interest they would like to investigate more deeply.

3. Editorial Feedback

Participants will receive constructive feedback on important aspects of journalism, including:

Story framing.

Writing style.

Interview techniques.

Draft development.

Reporting approaches.

Overall story structure.

For emerging journalists, editorial feedback can be an important part of developing stronger reporting habits. The mentorship provides an opportunity to discuss the reasoning behind editorial decisions and refine a story through multiple stages.

4. Industry and Career Guidance

The program also goes beyond the individual reporting project.

Mentees will receive strategic advice relating to professional development and navigating the journalism industry.

This may include guidance on working with major media organizations, developing professional relationships and building a stronger journalism network.

For emerging journalists who are still establishing their careers, this component can provide an opportunity to better understand how professional journalism operates and how ambitious reporting projects can be developed and presented.

5. Opportunities for Real-World Public Impact

The mentorship is designed around public-interest reporting.

Participants will work toward turning complex issues into deeply researched and publishable journalism. The objective is not simply to produce an academic exercise or training assignment but to develop reporting capable of contributing to public understanding of important issues.

This can be particularly relevant for journalists interested in political accountability, public policy, government, institutions, public affairs and other subjects where investigative reporting can help bring information into the public domain.

6. Possible Funding for Travel and Research

The program may provide funding to support travel and research on a case-by-case basis, where such support is considered necessary for the reporting project.

Applicants should therefore clearly explain their proposed reporting project and identify any research or travel requirements where relevant.

Funding is not described as automatic for every participant or project. It will be considered according to the needs of the proposed reporting work.

Who Should Apply for the Robert Fife Mentorship?

The program is intended for emerging journalists who want to strengthen their investigative or political reporting practice.

Applicants should be prepared to commit to a six-month, project-based mentorship and should have a clear interest in developing substantial public-interest journalism.

The program may be particularly relevant to journalists who:

Have an emerging career in journalism.

Have no more than five years of reporting experience.

Have a strong interest in investigative journalism.

Are interested in political journalism.

Want to develop a major reporting project.

Have an idea for a public-interest story or reporting area.

Want detailed editorial feedback.

Want to strengthen their interviewing and reporting skills.

Are interested in developing their professional journalism networks.

Are prepared to work consistently on a project over six months.

Eligibility Requirements

Applicants should carefully review the eligibility conditions before applying.

Applicants Must Reside in Canada

The program is specifically designed for emerging journalists residing in Canada.

Therefore, applicants from outside Canada who do not reside in Canada would not meet the stated residency requirement.

Applicants Must Have No More Than Five Years of Reporting Experience

The opportunity is aimed at journalists who are still in the emerging stage of their careers.

Applicants must have no more than five years of reporting experience.

This requirement distinguishes the program from opportunities aimed at senior or highly experienced journalists.

Applicants Should Have an Interest in Investigative or Political Journalism

Candidates should demonstrate a strong interest in either:

Investigative journalism; or

Political journalism.

Applicants should use their application materials to demonstrate how their previous work, professional interests or proposed reporting project connects to these areas.

Employed Journalists Need an Editor’s Letter of Support

Applicants who are currently employed by a media organization must include a letter of support from their editor.

This requirement is particularly important for journalists working within established news organizations and should be addressed before submitting the application.

What Materials Are Required?

Applicants are expected to submit several documents and pieces of information as part of their application.

1. Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must provide their CV, which should clearly present their journalism experience, professional background and relevant accomplishments.

Given the program’s focus on investigative and political journalism, applicants should ensure that their CV makes relevant reporting experience easy to identify.

2. Letter of Interest

Applicants must submit a letter of interest of no more than 350 words.

The letter should provide a concise explanation of the applicant’s interest in the mentorship and their journalism background.

Because the word limit is relatively short, applicants should prioritize the information most relevant to the program.

3. Two Published Work Samples

Applicants must provide two examples of published work.

These samples give applicants an opportunity to demonstrate their reporting ability and experience.

Where possible, the selected examples should help demonstrate the applicant’s strengths in areas relevant to investigative or political journalism.

4. Statement on Mentorship Goals and Reporting Project

Applicants must provide a brief statement explaining:

Their goals for the mentorship.

The reporting project they hope to develop; or

The reporting area they would like to explore.

This component is particularly important because the mentorship is project-based.

Applicants should therefore clearly communicate what they hope to accomplish during the six-month program.

5. Editor’s Letter of Support, Where Applicable

Applicants employed by a media organization must provide a letter of support from their editor.

Applicants who are not employed by a media organization do not have this stated requirement.

How to Apply for the Globe and Mail Foundation Mentorship Program

Applications must be submitted by email.

Applicants should prepare all required materials before sending their application to the Foundation.

Application Email

Applications should be sent to:

education@globeandmailfoundation.com

Applicants should use the following subject line:

The Robert Fife Mentorship

The application must be received by Sunday, October 11, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. ET.

Applicants should allow sufficient time for submission and ensure that all required materials are included.

APPLY HERE

Application Assessment and Selection Process

The Globe and Mail Foundation will assess applications based on several factors.

These include:

Commitment to investigative or political journalism

Applicants should demonstrate a genuine interest in developing their work in investigative or political reporting.

Clarity of goals

Applicants should clearly explain what they hope to achieve through the mentorship.

Feasibility of the proposed project

The proposed reporting project or area should be sufficiently focused and realistic for development during the six-month program.

Potential public value

The Foundation will consider the potential public value of the proposed reporting.

Readiness to benefit from sustained mentorship

Applicants should demonstrate that they are prepared to engage meaningfully with a six-month mentorship and use the guidance provided.

Following the initial assessment, shortlisted applicants will be contacted for an interview.

Program Timeline

The inaugural mentorship cohort will run for six months.

Application Period

Applications are currently open for the 2026–2027 cohort.

Application Deadline

Sunday, October 11, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time.

Mentorship Period

The program will run from:

November 2026 to April 2027

During this period, selected journalists will participate in regular mentorship sessions and work on their reporting projects.

Why the Project-Based Structure Matters

One of the distinctive features of the program is its emphasis on developing a specific reporting project.

Rather than treating journalism mentorship as a purely theoretical exercise, the program connects professional guidance with actual reporting.

A participant can therefore use the six-month period to move a story from an early idea toward a publishable piece.

The process can involve repeatedly refining the story as new information emerges, receiving feedback and reconsidering the framing or reporting approach.

This type of sustained development can be particularly useful for emerging journalists who have ideas for important stories but need additional editorial guidance, professional experience or resources to develop them fully.

About Robert Fife

The mentorship is led by veteran Canadian journalist Robert Fife, whose career has included prominent investigative and political reporting.

Fife served as The Globe and Mail’s Ottawa Bureau Chief and previously held the position of Ottawa Bureau Chief at the National Post. He was also associated with CTV National News and hosted CTV’s Question Period.

His career includes extensive work covering Canadian politics, government and public affairs.

Fife has received numerous awards for his investigative journalism.

Among the investigations associated with his career was his reporting on the SNC-Lavalin affair, which led to the resignations of two senior cabinet ministers, a senior adviser to the prime minister and the Clerk of the Privy Council.

He also played a major role in reporting on the Senate expense scandal, which emerged as a significant political issue in Canada in the early 2010s and resulted in the resignation of then-Prime Minister Stephen Harper’s chief of staff, Nigel Wright, as well as significant reforms relating to Senate expenses.

In 2021, Maclean’s Magazine named Fife among Canada’s 50 most powerful people.

He is also the author of several books, including:

A Capital Scandal: Politics, Patronage and Payoff

Why Parliament Must Be Reformed

Kim Campbell: The Making of a Politician

His experience in investigative and political journalism forms the professional foundation of the mentorship program.

Important Considerations Before Applying

Prospective applicants should carefully consider whether the program matches their professional experience and goals.

The opportunity is specifically targeted toward emerging journalists in Canada, rather than journalists at any career stage.

Applicants should therefore confirm that they:

Reside in Canada.

Have no more than five years of reporting experience.

Have an interest in investigative or political journalism.

Can commit to a six-month mentorship.

Have two suitable examples of published work.

Can articulate clear mentorship goals.

Can obtain an editor’s letter of support if currently employed by a media organization.

Tips for Preparing a Strong Application

Although the final selection is made by the Globe and Mail Foundation, applicants can take several practical steps to present their experience and proposed project clearly.

Demonstrate Your Reporting Experience

Your CV and published work samples should make your journalism experience easy to understand.

Focus on reporting experience that demonstrates your ability to investigate issues, gather information, conduct interviews, explain complex subjects or produce public-interest journalism.

Choose Relevant Published Work

The two work samples should provide a meaningful picture of your journalism abilities.

Applicants should consider selecting work that demonstrates strong reporting, research, interviewing, writing, investigative thinking or political coverage.

Develop a Focused Project Idea

Because the mentorship is project-based, applicants should avoid presenting an overly broad reporting concept.

Instead, explain the issue you want to explore and identify what makes the proposed reporting relevant to the public.

Clearly Explain Your Goals

The Foundation wants to understand how the mentorship would contribute to your development.

Applicants should therefore explain the specific skills, knowledge or professional capabilities they hope to strengthen.

Keep the Letter of Interest Within the Word Limit

The letter of interest must be no more than 350 words.

Applicants should edit carefully to ensure that the letter remains within the stated limit while still communicating their strongest points.

Prepare Early

Because the application requires multiple components, applicants should avoid waiting until the deadline to begin preparing.

This is especially important for applicants employed by media organizations because they may need time to request an editor’s letter of support.

TITLE: PO graduate students help organize the 17th Graduate Climate Conference in Woods Hole

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Photo provided by Elena Perez

The 17th annual Graduate Climate Conference (GCC) was held on November 2 – 4, 2023, hosted by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, the first GCC to be held at Woods Hole since the pandemic. Around 100 graduate students participated, including seven from WHOI’s PO department. This year the conference accommodated a record number of students from different fields and universities, a total of 21 different fields and 58 institutions in the U.S. and abroad!

The Conference featured two outstanding keynote speakers, six oral sessions, four poster sessions, and four student-run workshops. Social activities during the weekend included a Jeopardy Game, a Movie night, a Halloween costume party, and a guided tour of Boston after the conference. The Marine Biological Laboratory provided meals, refreshments, and lodging.

First held in 2006, the GCC has grown greatly while remaining true to its core mission of highlighting student-led work in diverse climate-related fields at a conference run by graduate students for graduate students. This year, four WHOI PO graduate students helped organize the conference. Hosting responsibilities have alternated yearly between students at UW and students from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)’s Program on Atmospheres, Oceans, and Climate. The 18th annual Graduate Climate Conference will be held at the University of Washington’s Pack Forest center in fall 2024.

TITLE: Mitacs Globalink Research Award (GRA) Program 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: Unspecified

Applications are open for the Mitacs Globalink Research Award (GRA) Program 2026. Grow your potential, expand your innovation horizons, build new or strengthen international research collaborations with another university, through the Globalink Research Award (GRA) program.

The Mitacs Globalink Research Award (GRA) program supports research collaborations between Canada and eligible countries and regions through intern(s) international mobility. Under the joint supervision of a home and host professor, successful senior undergraduate students, graduate students, and postdoctoral fellows can do one or two 12-24 weeks internship(s).

The program is offered through two streams:

Allocation stream: Participating Canadian universities receive a set number of internship units per year. Each university will manage their allocation. Rules and conditions may vary. Contact your local Mitacs advisor for details, before starting to develop a project.

Quantum stream: Open to all Canadian universities. The project must be in the quantum sector (includes but not limited to: Quantum computation (hardware), algorithms, and software – Quantum communication, networks, and cryptography – Quantum metrology, sensing, imaging, and materials.). No limit of projects per Canadian university and does not count in the university’s allocation.

Funding

Each intern will receive $6,000 per internship unit (IU):

$6,000 research award to conduct one 12- to 24-week research project in the other country. This is one internship unit (IU).

$12,000 research award to conduct one 24- to 48-week research project or two 12- to 24-week research projects in the other country. This is two internship units (IUs).

Eligibility

Intern

Must be registered as full-time senior undergraduates, graduate students, or postdoctoral fellows at an eligible Canadian institution or eligible international institution and remain as such throughout their Globalink Research Award.

Postdoctoral fellows may apply if their date of graduation from a PhD program is no more than five years prior to the proposed start date of the research project and they have postdoctoral status at an eligible institution.

Cannot undertake a research project at an institution where they have previously completed a degree.

Cannot undertake a research project in a country where they hold citizenship.

Permanent residents or citizens of Canada who are enrolled in an eligible country other than Canada and who wish to do a project in Canada are eligible to apply.

Permanent residents or citizens of Canada who are enrolled in a Canadian institution and who hold citizenship in an eligible country may apply to do a project there.

Must be the legal age of majority in Canada (18 years of age or older).

Must meet travel requirements for their intended destination, including visa and/or immigration requirements and associated documentation.

Cannot hold more than two Globalink Research Award or Mitacs-JSPS Summer Program Award per academic lifetime.

Interns may not participate in more than one MITACS internship at the same time.

Supervisor

Must hold a faculty position at an eligible university.

Must be eligible to supervise graduate students.

Supervisors at Canadian institutions: Must be eligible to hold Tri-Agency funding.

Application

Note the application process may vary depending on the Canadian university and its internship unit allocation. Check with your local Mitacs Advisor to determine if your project fits the funding requirements for your institution and to request the link to the GRA Application Portal.

Awards are offered in partnership with Mitacs’s academic partners and are subject to available funding. It is recommended applicants apply at least 16 weeks prior to the planned start date.

For more information, visit Mitacs Globalink Research Award (GRA) Program.

The fellowship seeks women who have the potential to contribute to:

Political negotiations

Decision-making

Democratic transitions

Conflict resolution

The programme therefore provides an opportunity for young women whose experiences of displacement have shaped their leadership and who are positioned to contribute to positive change in their countries of origin or host countries.

TITLE: Workshop on Research Leadership, Communication, Partnerships and Collaboration

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
March 11-14, 2019 | Nairobi, Kenya

The Association of African Universities is inviting stakeholders to its 3rd Workshop on Research Leadership, Communication, Partnerships and Collaboration.

Research is fundamental for Africa because it is an important source of new knowledge and provides solutions to pressing challenges. There is a need to strengthen Research Leadership so that more resources can be channelled to strengthen research and support African researchers to conduct relevant research.

Universities in Africa continue to be challenged to focus on relevant and demand driven research. If universities are going to do this effectively they must have the capacities to engage communities, work with industry and manage multi-stakeholder relationships. This has an impact on how universities work and how they position themselves to respond to pressing societal problems.

Significant financial and human resources are
spent conducting research. However, because of ineffective communication of
research findings by researchers – the intended beneficiaries of the research
don’t always get to know about it. It is crucial that researchers develop
skills to effectively communicate research findings for impact and uptake by
its most needed stakeholders. There is a
plethora of emerging research communication tools that researchers could
employ.

Strategic Partnerships and Collaboration are
key for universities in the 21st century and beyond. The African
Universities need to learn how to nurture, identify and strengthen mutually
beneficial partnerships. They need to understand how they can position
themselves / brand themselves to attract beneficial collaborations. No university
can exist as an island and be able succeed in its objectives. Therefore,
building capacities for key staff in universities to advance strong
partnerships and collaborations is fundamental to the success of African universities.

WORKSHOP OBJECTIVES

The Association of African Universities (AAU)
Secretariat hosted the inaugural workshop on Research Communication &
Commercialisation in May 2018 at the AAU Secretariat in Accra, Ghana, and the
second edition in Livingstone, Zambia in collaboration with the Africa Centre
of Excellence for Infectious Diseases of Humans and Animals (ACEIDHA), of the
University of Zambia.

The workshop focuses on:

Developing
the Research Leadership Skills of Researchers
Building
capacities for Demand Driven Research Approaches
Discussing
strategies for disseminating Research findings and Enhancing Researchers’
Online Visibility
Developing
capacities for strategic Partnerships and Collaboration

TARGET PARTICIPANTS

This workshop
targets the following participants from universities in Africa and from the
Africa Centers of Excellence:

Research Directors from higher education
institutions
All researchers in higher education
institutions (both public and private)
Academic Staff – Deans, professors, lecturers
Research consultants
Researchers from national Research Councils
and Science Granting Councils
Directors of Departments from the Ministries
of Higher Education, Science, technology, etc

STYLE OF WORKSHOP DELIVERY

The objectives of the workshop will be
achieved through lead lectures, skills practice activities, guided feedback,
and intensive participant interaction over carefully selected cases and other
materials in a process facilitated by experienced Resource Persons.

WORKSHOP FEES

This is a fee-based workshop – we will charge US$300 for AAU member institutions and US$400 for Non-AAU member institutions. The registration fees cover the facilitators costs, workshop materials and conference package including certificates, tea/coffee and lunch for the five days of the workshop.

Participants are responsible for other costs such as flight, accommodation and upkeep.

CERTIFICATION

All participants who undergo the training
course will be awarded certificates of participation by the AAU at the end of
the workshop.

Area of Physics

Astrophysics Observation, Instrumentation, and Experiment (Instrumentation/Exoplanets/Low Mass Stars)

Research Interests

Juliana García-Mejía is broadly interested in developing novel astronomical instrumentation to enable the study of exoplanets, their atmospheres, and their low mass stellar hosts.

She is the PI of The Tierras Observatory, a new 1.3-m ultra-precise fully-automated photometer located atop Mt. Hopkins, Arizona. Having spent her entire Ph.D. building Tierras, she is currently focused on using the facility to uncover temperate terrestrial planets, search for Moons around exoplanets, and study their low mass stellar hosts.

Juliana is also pursuing the design of a high throughput, extremely-high resolution pathfinder spectrograph to enable narrow-wavelength atmospheric structure and velocity dynamic studies of exoplanets, and to expand cosmochronological and magnetic field studies of stars of varied spectral types. In the future, this instrument could enable the detection of molecular oxygen in a terrestrial exoplanet atmosphere.

In the News

MIT welcomes 2023 Heising-Simons Foundation 51 Pegasi b Fellow Juliana García-Mejía
MIT News Office, April, 4, 2023

Biographical Sketch

Although born in the US, Juliana grew up in the city of Medellín (Colombia) surrounded by a numerous and eclectic family of proud coffee growers and fitness entrepreneurs enamored with the night skies.

At age 15, Juliana decided to move back to the US on her own to finish high school and pursue a career in aerospace engineering. During her sophomore year at Harvard she discovered that building astronomical instruments, not rockets, was her true calling. She pursued numerous instrument-based projects at sub-mm wavelengths with Dr. Qizhou Zhang, and in the optical regime with Prof. John Johnson, Dr. Andrew Szentgyorgyi, and Dr. Jason Eastman at the CfA.

For her Ph.D. thesis supervised by Prof. David Charbonneau at Harvard, Juliana led the design, construction, commissioning and initial science operations of the Tierras Observatory. Tierras is an ultra-precise photometer to study low mass stars and their terrestrial planets.

Outside astronomy, Juliana’s interests reflect her whimsical upbringing. She has a growing coffee business where she sells her family’s goods, and can be found indoors reading sci-fi, or outdoors triathloning, hiking, and snowboarding depending on the season.

TITLE: (New Dates) Strengthening the delivery of post-graduate Education in African Universities

Workshop on Innovations in Teaching and Learning

Strengthening the delivery of post-graduate Education in African Universities

Hosted by AquaFish ACE LUANAR & AAU

19-23 November 2018, Lilongwe, Malawi

NEW DATES: 4-8 FEBRUARY 2019

Registration Link: https://www.research.net/r/AquaFish

Background

Teaching if done properly results in “quality” academic outputs, that is, the graduates and research. The indicators of quality graduates include ability to conduct research, possessing critical thinking skills, ability to facilitate multi-stakeholder engagements, having entrepreneurial skills, ability to make presentations, exhibiting good written and verbal communication skills, having confidence, displaying life-long learning skills and having the ability to synthesize key information, among several other indicators. African Higher Education institutions continue to be challenged to produce graduates that can solve problems and contribute to the development of their countries. This therefore implies that universities must review how they teach and reflect on how their students learn effectively.

Examples of Innovative teaching and learning methods

Confucius, a Chinese teacher, editor, politician, and philosopher is quoted as having said “I hear and I forget. I see and I believe. I do and I understand”. This statement links very well with the concept of being innovative in teaching. Clearly innovative methods of teaching and learning require a total mindset change in terms of the roles of the professors and the learners. The innovative methods also allow the learning to be two-way. These new ways facilitate practical exposure for students, experiential learning and role-based learning. The new learning solutions and methods thus become student centered with the objective of producing that “quality graduate”. Some examples of innovative teaching and learning methods include:

Flipped Classroom

Role-based learning

Internships in relevant industries and corporate organizations

Problem Solving linked to real Community Engagements

Twinning programs to promote cross-learning

Regional seminars to facilitate sharing of expertise

Case based learning for fields such as medicine and health

Problem based learning

Group work assignments

Field Visits

Technology-assisted learning (mobile, learning management systems, multimedia technologies, etc)

Excellence in Education and Research Capacity and Development Impact

The Disbursement Linked Indicator 2 (DLI 2) under the Africa Centers of Excellence project places emphasis on “excellence in education and research capacity and development impact”. The sub-indicators further expound on “improved teaching and learning environment as per approved proposal”. The DLI document states that the “implementation plan for each ACE will clearly describe 4 annual main milestones for improving of teaching and learning environment based upon the specific activities to be undertaken by the ACE”. Besides `the creation of conducive physical learning environments through constructing classrooms and equipping of laboratories it is important for the ACEs to articulate how else they are strengthening their teaching delivery methods so that they produce quality graduates.

About the proposed workshop

The Association of African Universities and AquaFish ACE hosted by Lilongwe University of Agriculture and Natural Resources will deliver a five-day workshop on ‘Innovations in Teaching and Learning’ to spark discussions and understanding how AquaFish ACE is implementing innovative teaching methods and what else they could be doing to improve in this area. The key objectives of the workshop will be to:

Discuss key concepts and case studies on innovative teaching and learning methods

Deliberate on the challenges and opportunities associated with supervising graduate students

Exploring the use of technology to improve teaching delivery methods in African Universities

Participate in learning visits to institutions in Lilongwe that have begun implementing innovative methods of teaching and learning

Draft Program

DAY
PROPOSED ACTIVITIES

DAY 1

A broad presentation that lays the ground on key concepts around innovative teaching and learning methods and practices

Hold a brainstorming session in small groups:

to discuss why teaching methods need to be reviewed and what to change? This is meant to help in identifying major deficiencies in current higher education delivery by African Universities. This will also discuss the question of “are students graduating from the African Universities adequately trained to respond to the needs of the society?”

to discuss the ‘How’ question and share ideas – and suggest proposals to correct the identified deficiencies.

Role play the practical implementation of Experiential Learning

Importance of the student-supervisor relationship and the various factors that influence it.

Strategies to overcome the challenges of a range of supervisory contexts

Developing resources for effective research supervision practices

Foundational Theories: Review of Relevant Concepts

Principles of E-learning Course Design & Development

Experiential Learning Visit to an institution in Lilongwe that has done well in implementing e-learning

TITLE: A webinar on a continental platform for sharing African Scholarship

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The growth of the African continental publishing platform

The open access (OA) movement has been growing across the world albeit not at the anticipated pace. As much as this philanthropic movement advances the open sharing of scholarship, the movement has evolved with a strong bias towards the global north. A typical example is the lauded transformative agreements. This transformative agreement strategy is developed through a global north lens which unfortunately entrenches the Global North-Global South knowledge divide: the publishing strategy unintendedly entrenches the marginalization of research voices from Africa and most of the global south.

Poynder (2019) asserts that since the 2002 Budapest Open Access Initiative, the OA movement has had unintended consequences that would include the marginalization of research voices from the Global South. He goes on to say that the Global South needs to develop its own alternative strategy. To open channels for the distribution of African scholarship, the University of Cape Town (UCT) has launched a new continental platform for publication of open access journals, monographs and textbooks. UCT draws from the view that the OA movement in Africa must have a transformative world view of OA which is driven by social justice imperatives and equity principles for inclusion resulting in growth and development of society: hence this publishing platform.

This alternative publishing stream is viewed as transformational in that it challenges the traditional Global North dominated publishing landscape. In so doing, the continental platform addresses the issue of the marginalization of African research voices and research and provides one of many solutions to the existing inequality in the publishing landscape. In the African context, library publishing addresses more than the financial barriers, it is a social justice driven service that supports the de-northernization of the publishing landscape, that is, making provision for the sharing of African scholarship; it addresses the issue of inclusivity and brings balance to knowledge dissemination.

The ultimate goal of the continental platform is to transform access and distribution of scholarship for the growth and development of Africa’s research agenda; and, to nurture and grow a culture of civil society accessing and manipulating scholarly content for economic and social emancipation. Further, the African research landscape needs to be transformed to address local research imperatives while contributing to bridging the ‘research-exchange divide’.

It is anticipated that the platform will bridge the prevailing skills shortage and poor information technology infrastructure in Africa resulting in the advancement in publication of journals and books. The University of Cape Town (UCT) Libraries, in collaboration with its central Information and Communication Technology Services, developed the platform using a tenant model. In conceptualising this model, each participating institution will retain its unique identity, that is, the look and feel will be prescribed by the institution.

Key Note Speakers: Ms Heather Joseph, Prof Mamokgethi Phakeng and Prof Etienne E. Ehile

The Association of African Universities, in collaboration with the UCT, will be hosting a webinar on 9 September 2021 from 1030am to 1230pm GMT.

TITLE: The Association of African Universities presents 10 new policy briefs
