TITLE: Carnegie African Diaspora Fellowship Program Announces Partnership with the Association of African Universities and Selects New Fellows

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
NEW YORK, and ACCRA, GHANA June 27, 2022 – The Carnegie African Diaspora Fellowship Program (CADFP) announces the award of 56 fellowships to individuals and institutions to take part in joint academic projects with resident institutions in Africa. To date, the CADFP has funded 584 fellowships for African-born scholars from the United States and Canada to collaborate with over 203 institutions of higher learning in Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, Rwanda, Senegal, South Africa, Tanzania, and Uganda in the areas of collaborative research, curriculum co-development and graduate student teaching and mentoring.

Nearly a decade since the launch of CADFP, the Carnegie Corporation of New York and the Institute of International Education (IIE) continue working with partners, Fellows and Hosts to deepen and strengthen the highly successful CADFP model. In addition to an Advisory Council of prominent African academics, the program has established a new partnership with the Association of African Universities (AAU), a Pan-African higher education institution with a membership of over 400 universities, and focused on higher education development and policy. With the diaspora as a strategic priority, AAU engages governments across Africa on various issues, including advocacy for incremental investments in the higher education sector. The Association also collaborates with key stakeholders to support human capacity development, academic scholarship and innovative research, ultimately aimed at propelling the higher education sector to contribute more effectively to the continent’s transformation and development agenda.

In April of this year, AAU, IIE, and CCNY convened the Advisory Council to select the 56 awardees and hosted a highly successful CADFP Stakeholder Forum in Accra, Ghana. The forum brought together country-level participants including Ghana’s former Minister of Education, Hon. Prof. Jane Naana Opoku Agyemang; the Director of Tertiary Education, Ministry of Education, Dr. Eric Nkansah; the Director of Diaspora Affairs, Office of the President, Ghana, Mr. Akwasi Ababio; as well as international development partners, host institutions, fellows and alumni of the CADFP. CADFP fellows traveling to Africa will collaborate with academics at their host institutions on a variety of projects, ultimately aimed at working synergistically to improve the quality of African higher education. A full list of the most current projects can be found here. Through these initiatives, CADFP aims to find solutions to some of the most pressing challenges facing Africa and the world.

How the Projects and Fellowships Work:

Fellowships match host universities with African-born scholars from Canada or the United States, individually or in groups, and cover the expenses for project visits of up to three months. All scholar and project proposals are evaluated by an independent review committee and must be approved by the Advisory Council. Public and private higher education institutions in Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa, Tanzania, and Uganda, along with member universities or affiliates of the African Research Universities Alliance including Addis Ababa University, Cheikh Anta Diop University, University of Mauritius, and University of Rwanda are invited to submit a project request to host a scholar for 21 to 90 days. Prospective hosts are eligible but not required to name a proposed scholar in their request. Many African institutions and prospective Fellows collaborate on ideas for a project that is then submitted by the institution. IIE maintains a scholar roster to facilitate matches, according to the discipline specializations, expertise, activities and objectives described in a project request. Candidates are required to have a terminal degree in their field and can hold any academic rank. When a scholar is successfully matched with a selected project, he or she is awarded a Fellowship to conduct a project visit to the host institution.

See a full list of projects, hosts, and scholars and their universities.

The Carnegie Corporation of New York funds the program, with IIE providing comprehensive fellowship design, management and evaluation expertise. An Advisory Council of prominent African academics and AAU provides strategic direction.

Please direct all questions related to AfricanDiaspora@iie.org.

About The Institute of International Education (IIE):

Established in 1919, IIE is a global not-for-profit that creates and implements international education programs, conducts research, and provides life-changing opportunities for students and scholars worldwide. IIE collaborates with a range of corporate, government and foundation partners across the globe to design and manage scholarship, study abroad, workforce training and leadership development programs. IIE has a network of 16 offices and affiliates worldwide and over 1,600 member institutions. Visit iie.org.

About Association of African Universities (AAU):

The AAU is an international non-profit, non-governmental organization created by African Universities to promote cooperation among them on the one hand, and between them and the international academic community on the other. Created in 1967, the AAU is the voice of higher education in Africa and aims to improve the quality of African higher education, and to strengthen its contribution to Africa’s development by supporting the core functions of higher education institutions and facilitating critical reflection and consensus building on issues affecting higher education. The AAU is headquartered in Accra, Ghana, has a membership of more than 400 Higher Education Institutions and is the technical implementing arm of the African Union Commission (AUC) in higher education. The Association is also the coordinating agency of the Higher Education Cluster of the Continental Education Strategy for Africa (CESA 16-25). Through our guidance, our member universities are responsible for implementing the Science, Technology and Innovation Strategy for Africa (STISA 2024) of the AUC. Given the importance of the African Academic Diaspora to the advancement of the continent’s higher education sector, the AAU prioritises engagement with this group and has a strategy and program in place focusing on the academic diaspora. TITLE: AfricaLics PhD Visiting Fellowship Programme 2027: Fully Supported 3-Month Research Fellowship in South Africa for African PhD Students

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The AfricaLics PhD Visiting Fellowship Programme (VFP) 2027 Cohort is now inviting applications from eligible PhD students enrolled at universities in African countries for an opportunity to strengthen their research, academic skills, dissertation quality and professional networks in the field of Innovation and Development (I&D).

The 2027 programme combines online academic activities, research training, mentorship and a three-month study visit at the University of Johannesburg (UJ) in South Africa. The study visit is scheduled for 6 September to 3 December 2027, with additional online activities before and after the physical residency.

The fellowship is particularly relevant to doctoral researchers examining how innovation, technology, learning, institutions and competence-building interact with economic, social or environmentally sustainable development in Africa.

Successful fellows will receive access to an international research environment, academic and research training, specialist mentoring, accommodation, return international airfare, a living-cost stipend of approximately US$600 per month, and support for programme-related activities.

About the AfricaLics PhD Visiting Fellowship Programme

The AfricaLics Visiting Fellowship Programme was established to strengthen the research capabilities of African PhD students working in Innovation and Development studies.

The programme was established in 2015 with financial support from the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (Sida). Since its establishment, African PhD students from low- and lower-middle-income countries have participated in the programme and received research training and mentorship.

The 2027 cohort continues this objective by bringing selected doctoral researchers into an intensive academic environment involving:

Online preparatory activities

Academic writing training

Research training

Paper presentation opportunities

Individual and joint mentoring

Interaction with researchers at the University of Johannesburg

A three-month research stay in Johannesburg

Face-to-face meetings

Dissertation development

Academic networking

Post-fellowship alumni engagement

The programme is intended to complement, rather than replace, the doctoral student’s existing PhD programme at their home university.

AfricaLics also confirms that the programme aims to strengthen students’ academic and research qualifications, improve the quality of their dissertations and prepare them for future careers in academia, the private sector, government and policymaking.

What Is Innovation and Development Research?

The AfricaLics programme focuses on the intersection between innovation and development.

Innovation is understood broadly. It can involve new inventions, but it can also involve the adoption, diffusion and use of technologies that are new to a particular user or context.

Innovation can also involve:

New products

New production processes

New ways of organising activities

New approaches to doing things

Technology adoption

Learning and competence-building

Social innovation

Technological innovation

Institutional and organisational change

Innovation and Development studies therefore examine how technological and social innovation interact with economic, social and environmental development.

This makes the fellowship multidisciplinary.

Applicants may come from backgrounds such as:

Economics

Sociology

Political Science

Science and Technology Policy

Geography

History

Development Studies

Science

Technology

Engineering

Mathematics

Manufacturing

However, STEM and manufacturing-related research should have a relevant social-science perspective and connect to the broader relationship between innovation and development.

Research Areas Covered by the Programme

AfricaLics recognises a broad range of research areas at the intersection of innovation and development.

Potential areas include:

Energy

Sustainable development

Sustainable transformation

Health

Gender

Agriculture

Manufacturing

Work organisation

Big data

The Fourth Industrial Revolution

Technology and innovation policy

Economic development

Social development

Environmental sustainability

The programme is therefore not restricted to researchers whose PhD is formally titled “Innovation and Development.”

The key consideration is whether the doctoral research addresses an important relationship between innovation and economic, social or environmentally sustainable development.

AfricaLics Research Coordination Areas for 2027

For the 2027 cohort, particular encouragement is given to PhD students whose research relates to one or more of the four AfricaLics Research Coordination Areas (RCAs).

1. STI Measurement in Africa

This area focuses on science, technology and innovation measurement in African contexts.

Research may examine how innovation and technological capabilities are measured, understood and used to inform development policy and decision-making.

2. Global Value Chains, Innovation and Industrialization

This research area examines innovation, industrial development and the role of African economies within global value chains.

Researchers may investigate issues surrounding:

Industrialisation

Production networks

Technology upgrading

Firm-level innovation

Competitiveness

Global production systems

3. Innovating Resilience

This area focuses on inclusive agricultural innovation and climate resilience in Sub-Saharan Africa.

It is particularly relevant to researchers examining how innovation can contribute to:

Agricultural resilience

Climate adaptation

Inclusive development

Food systems

Rural development

Sustainable agriculture

4. Innovation and Sustainable Energy Transition in Africa

Known as i-SET Africa, this area focuses on innovation and the transition toward sustainable energy systems across Africa.

Researchers examining energy innovation, clean energy technologies, energy policy, sustainability and related development questions may find a strong connection with this research area.

The four RCAs are explicitly highlighted in the 2027 call as areas in which applicants are particularly encouraged to conduct research.

Fellowship Structure

The AfricaLics VFP is not simply a three-month study-abroad opportunity.

It is a longer programme involving activities before, during and after the physical study visit.

The 2027 cohort is expected to begin with online activities during the first half of February 2027.

The programme will then include the three-month study visit at the University of Johannesburg from:

6 September – 3 December 2027

After the Johannesburg study period, fellows will participate in additional online activities in December 2027 and early 2028.

This structure is designed to make the fellowship an integrated component of the student’s PhD rather than an isolated research trip.

Online Academic Activities

Before and around the study visit, fellows participate in online activities designed to strengthen their academic and research capabilities.

The programme includes training in academic writing and research.

Three short online courses are highlighted in the 2027 programme:

How to Write an Academic Journal Article

How to Do Systematic Literature Reviews

Additional writing and research skills activities

Fellows will also have opportunities to participate in paper presentation seminars.

Each visiting fellow can present and participate in up to five paper presentation seminars, including a presentation during the AfricaLics PhD Academy 2027, which is expected to take place in April 2027.

These activities can help doctoral students improve their ability to communicate their research to academic audiences and receive constructive feedback before completing their dissertations or publishing their work.

Three-Month Study Visit at the University of Johannesburg

One of the central components of the programme is the three-month research stay at the University of Johannesburg in South Africa.

The study visit is scheduled for:

6 September – 3 December 2027

During this period, fellows will be exposed to an international research environment focused on Innovation and Development, including transformative innovation processes and the Fourth Industrial Revolution.

The study visit is designed to give students dedicated time away from their normal duties to focus on their doctoral research.

During the residency, students can work on areas such as:

Consolidating their research

Analysing fieldwork data

Improving theoretical arguments

Developing dissertation chapters

Writing academic articles

Refining research questions

Presenting their research

Receiving feedback

Connecting with other doctoral researchers

Engaging with experienced scholars

The University of Johannesburg’s research environment therefore forms an important part of the fellowship experience.

Mentorship from AfricaLics and Globelics Scholars

A major feature of the programme is its mentorship component.

Each fellow will be matched with one or two scholars whose expertise corresponds to the student’s research area.

The final mentor selection will depend on:

The student’s research topic

The student’s academic background

The available expertise within the AfricaLics and Globelics networks

The compatibility between the student’s research and potential mentors

The mentors are intended to help strengthen the fellow’s research capabilities and provide intellectual guidance throughout the programme.

However, applicants should understand an important distinction:

AfricaLics mentors are not formal PhD supervisors.

The student remains responsible for their PhD, and their official supervision continues to be provided by their home university supervisors.

Integration with the Student’s Existing PhD

The AfricaLics VFP is designed to complement the doctoral programme at the student’s home institution.

Applicants are encouraged to discuss the fellowship with their PhD supervisors and university before applying.

The programme may be integrated into different stages of a student’s PhD work, including:

Theoretical studies

Coursework

Fieldwork

Data analysis

Exchange activities

Academic writing

Dissertation preparation

Journal article development

At the beginning of the fellowship, each fellow must develop a specific one-year work plan in consultation with their home supervisor, mentors and the academic coordinator of the VFP.

Once the work plan has been finalised, it must be signed by:

The student

The home supervisor

The mentors

The approved work plan functions as an agreement specifying the main research outputs the student intends to work toward during the fellowship.

Joint Supervision and Academic Collaboration

The programme places considerable emphasis on communication between the student, their home supervisors and AfricaLics mentors.

Trilateral meetings will be organised to help align expectations and ensure that the visiting fellowship contributes meaningfully to the student’s PhD.

Students are expected to remain in communication with their mentors and home supervisors through:

Other online communication platforms

Formal meetings

Research discussions

Shared notes and documentation

This structure is intended to create continuity between the student’s home university and their fellowship activities in South Africa.

Face-to-Face Meetings

For the 2027 cohort, two face-to-face meetings are scheduled.

First Face-to-Face Meeting

The first meeting is expected to take place alongside the AfricaLics PhD Academy, tentatively scheduled for April 2027 in Kenya.

Second Face-to-Face Meeting

The second meeting is expected to take place in November 2027, during the student’s study visit at the University of Johannesburg.

The meetings will focus on areas such as:

Joint PhD supervision

Research planning

Alignment between supervisors and mentors

Expectations

Dissertation development

Paper and chapter presentations

Feedback on research

Students will have opportunities to present their work in larger seminars as well as smaller meetings involving their supervisors and mentors.

Fellowship Funding and Financial Support

The AfricaLics VFP provides substantial support for the three-month Johannesburg study visit.

The programme states that the following costs are covered or supported.

Return International Airfare

AfricaLics will cover the return economy-class flight from the fellow’s nearest international airport to Johannesburg.

This is an important component for students traveling from other African countries to South Africa.

Accommodation

Accommodation in Johannesburg is covered by the fellowship programme.

AfricaLics and University of Johannesburg staff will assist with arranging accommodation near the UJ-TRCTI offices where students will have their working space.

The programme aims to provide a private bedroom where possible, but this is not guaranteed.

Depending on availability, selected fellows may have:

Shared bedrooms

Communal kitchens

Shared living spaces

Shared bathrooms

Applicants should therefore understand that accommodation is provided, but private accommodation cannot necessarily be guaranteed.

Monthly Living Stipend

Fellows receive approximately US$600 per month during the Johannesburg study visit.

The stipend is intended to cover living expenses and local travel associated with the fellowship, including transportation to and from the University of Johannesburg.

Training and Mentorship Costs

AfricaLics covers costs associated with:

Joint courses

Mentorship

Fellowship-related academic activities

A small amount of funding may also be available for students to participate in a short course that is considered important to their PhD research but is not normally available in their home country.

Face-to-Face Meeting Costs

The AfricaLics Research Capacity Strengthening project also covers costs related to the two planned face-to-face meetings between students, home supervisors and mentors.

What the Fellowship Does Not Cover

Applicants should also understand the limitations of the financial support.

The programme does not cover costs for accompanying family members, including:

Spouses

Children

Other accompanying individuals

The fellowship also does not normally fund additional personal travel within South Africa unless that travel forms part of an approved VFP activity.

Students should therefore plan carefully before making personal travel arrangements around the fellowship.

Travel Insurance and Health Coverage

Travel insurance is issued together with the fellowship ticket and serves as health insurance during the fellowship period.

However, the programme notes that this travel insurance generally provides coverage for minor ailments occurring during the stay.

Successful candidates with existing health conditions are advised to check whether their own health insurance remains valid in South Africa and, where necessary, upgrade their coverage before travelling.

Who Can Apply?

The AfricaLics VFP 2027 is specifically targeted at PhD students enrolled at universities in African countries.

Applicants must meet several academic and geographic requirements.

1. Must Be a PhD Student

Applicants must be actively enrolled as PhD students in a relevant programme at a university in Africa.

The programme is therefore not intended for:

Undergraduate students

General master’s students

Individuals who have already completed their PhD

Researchers who are not enrolled in a PhD programme

The core applicant category is current African-university PhD students.

2. Preferably Have Completed the First Year of the PhD

Applicants should preferably have completed their first year of PhD studies by December 2026.

This helps ensure that candidates have developed sufficiently advanced research projects to benefit from the fellowship’s research training, mentoring and study visit.

However, selection is ultimately based on the quality and relevance of applications, available funding and the possibility of identifying suitable mentors.

3. Research Must Relate to Innovation and Development

The doctoral research must focus on the relationship between:

Innovation and economic development

Innovation and social development

Innovation and environmentally sustainable development

The programme accepts applicants from different academic disciplines as long as their research fits within this broad Innovation and Development framework.

4. Adequate English Literacy

Applicants must have adequate literacy in English.

The programme states that documentation may be requested to demonstrate this ability.

Academic Backgrounds That May Qualify

The call specifically mentions applicants with backgrounds such as:

Economics

Sociology

Political Science

Science and Technology Policy

Geography

History

Development Studies

Applicants working in STEM fields may also be eligible, including those in:

Science

Technology

Engineering

Mathematics

Manufacturing

However, the research should have a relevant social-science perspective and connect to Innovation and Development.

This makes the fellowship suitable for multidisciplinary PhD research rather than restricting applications to one department or academic discipline.

Selection Criteria

AfricaLics uses a rigorous assessment process to evaluate applications.

1. Research Focus and Relevance

The proposed research should demonstrate clear relevance to:

Innovation and Development studies

African development

The AfricaLics research agenda

Applicants should clearly explain their research problem and research questions.

2. Theoretical and Conceptual Framework

Applicants should demonstrate an appropriate theoretical and conceptual framework rooted in Innovation and Development studies.

The framework should be clearly connected to the research questions.

3. Methodological Clarity and Rigor

Applicants must demonstrate that their methodology is appropriate for answering the research questions.

The application should provide clarity concerning:

Research methods

Data sources

Data collection

How the research questions will be addressed

These three areas form the core assessment criteria.

Additional Selection Considerations

Beyond the quality of the research proposal, the selection process also considers whether the applicant is at an appropriate stage of their PhD to benefit from the fellowship.

The availability of appropriate mentors is also considered.

In addition, female applicants and applicants from low-income African countries receive special consideration as part of AfricaLics’ objective of improving diversity within the Innovation and Development research community.

Application Requirements

Applicants must submit a complete application through the AfricaLics online application system.

The application requires several documents.

1. Motivation and Expected Outcomes Statement

Applicants must submit a brief application of approximately one page or 500 words.

This should explain:

Their academic background

Their motivation for applying

What they expect to gain from participating in the fellowship

The statement should demonstrate that the applicant understands the purpose of the VFP and can explain how the programme fits into their PhD journey.

2. PhD Project Outline

Applicants must submit a brief outline of their current PhD project.

The document should include their PhD training plans and must be no more than five pages.

This is a particularly important component because reviewers need to understand:

What the PhD research is about

The research problem

Research questions

Theoretical approach

Methodology

Current stage of the project

How the fellowship could contribute to the research

3. Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must submit a current CV, including PhD courses attended so far.

The CV should provide a clear picture of the applicant’s academic background and research experience.

4. Letter from the Main PhD Supervisor

Applicants must provide a letter of support from their main PhD supervisor.

The call states that the letter should confirm that the student will have completed their upgrade/probation by the specified date, or explain why the student is considered suitable for participation if this requirement has not been met.

Applicants should therefore contact their supervisor well before the application deadline.

5. Letter from University Administration

A separate letter of support from the university administration at the institution where the applicant is enrolled is also required.

This makes it important for applicants to start the application process early because obtaining institutional documentation can take time.

6. Academic Certificates

Applicants must provide copies of academic certificates.

At minimum, the application requires:

Bachelor’s degree certificate

Master’s degree certificate

These documents should be prepared before beginning the application.

7. Writing Sample

Applicants must provide one writing sample, such as:

An academic article; or

A chapter from their current PhD programme.

The writing sample gives the selection committee an opportunity to assess the applicant’s academic writing and research ability.

Application Deadline

The deadline for applications to the AfricaLics PhD Visiting Fellowship Programme 2027 is:

2 October 2026

Applications must be submitted by:

23:00 East Africa Time (EAT)

on 2 October 2026.

Applicants should submit all required documents through the online application form before the deadline.

What Happens After the Johannesburg Study Visit?

The fellowship does not end when the three-month study visit ends.

After returning home, fellows are expected to continue their PhD work and complete their dissertations according to the requirements of their home universities.

However, AfricaLics encourages fellows to remain connected with the network through:

Alumni activities

Webinars

Research events

AfricaLics conferences

National AfricaLics chapters

Research Coordination Areas

Future academic collaborations

This creates an opportunity for participants to remain connected to an international African research network beyond the formal fellowship period.

Opportunities for Conference Participation and Networking

AfricaLics fellows are also encouraged to develop and submit papers to relevant academic conferences.

The programme specifically mentions opportunities such as:

Globelics Conference 2027

AfricaLics Conference 2028

Conference participation can provide:

Academic exposure

Networking

Feedback on research

Opportunities to identify collaborators

Potential research partnerships

Exposure to the wider AfricaLics and Globelics community

AfricaLics may provide travel support where funding is available, although fellows must apply for conference participation under the same conditions as other participants.

Why the AfricaLics Fellowship Is Valuable

For an African PhD researcher, the VFP can provide a combination of academic development opportunities that are difficult to obtain through a conventional doctoral programme alone.

The fellowship can provide exposure to:

International research networks

African and international scholars

Innovation and Development research

Academic writing

Systematic literature review methods

Research presentation

Research mentoring

Peer learning

Dissertation development

International academic collaboration

University-based research in South Africa

AfricaLics and Globelics networks

The programme is especially valuable for researchers who want to develop their research beyond their home institution while remaining connected to their existing PhD programme.

How to Prepare a Competitive Application

Applicants should avoid treating the VFP application as a generic scholarship application.

The programme has a clearly defined research focus, and the application should demonstrate a strong connection between the applicant’s PhD research and Innovation and Development studies.

Step 1: Clearly Define Your Research Problem

Your application should make it immediately clear what problem your PhD research addresses.

Avoid describing your topic only in broad terms.

Explain:

What problem exists?

Why does it matter?

What gap in knowledge are you addressing?

What are your research questions?

Step 2: Explain the Innovation Component

Because AfricaLics focuses on Innovation and Development, applicants should clearly identify the innovation dimension of their research.

Ask yourself:

What is being innovated?

Who is developing or adopting the innovation?

What technology or social process is involved?

How does innovation affect development?

What economic, social or environmental outcome is being investigated?

Step 3: Connect the Research to Africa

The programme is specifically concerned with Innovation and Development in Africa.

Applicants should therefore clearly demonstrate the African relevance of their research.

Step 4: Strengthen the Methodology

The selection committee assesses methodological clarity and rigour.

Your application should clearly explain:

Research design

Data sources

Data collection

Analytical approach

Relationship between methodology and research questions

Step 5: Explain Why AfricaLics Is Important to Your PhD

Do not simply state that you want international exposure.

Explain specifically how the programme can help you:

Improve your dissertation

Analyse your data

Develop academic articles

Strengthen your theoretical framework

Receive specialist feedback

Develop research collaborations

Improve your academic writing

Step 6: Identify Relevant Research Coordination Areas

If your research fits one or more of the four AfricaLics Research Coordination Areas, explain that connection clearly.

This can help reviewers understand how your work fits into the broader AfricaLics research agenda.

Application Process

Applicants should follow these steps:

1. Confirm eligibility

Ensure that you:

Are currently enrolled in a PhD programme

Are enrolled at an African university

Are researching Innovation and Development

Preferably completed your first PhD year by December 2026

Have adequate English literacy

Have existing basic funding for your PhD

2. Prepare the motivation statement

Prepare the required one-page/500-word statement explaining your background, motivation and expected outcomes.

3. Prepare the PhD project outline

Develop the maximum five-page outline of your current PhD project and training plan.

4. Update your CV

Ensure your CV includes your PhD courses and relevant academic and research experience.

5. Contact your supervisor

Request the required supervisor support letter early.

6. Obtain university administration support

Begin the process of securing the required institutional support letter.

7. Prepare academic certificates

Have your Bachelor’s and Master’s certificates ready.

8. Select your writing sample

Choose a strong article or PhD chapter that demonstrates your academic writing and research ability.

9. Submit through the online application system

Complete the AfricaLics VFP application form and upload all required attachments.

10. Submit before the deadline

Conclusion

The AfricaLics PhD Visiting Fellowship Programme 2027 is a valuable opportunity for African doctoral researchers working at the intersection of innovation and development.

Rather than offering only financial assistance, the programme provides a structured research-development experience combining online training, academic writing courses, research presentations, specialist mentorship, international networking and a three-month study visit at the University of Johannesburg.

The financial support is also substantial for a short-term research mobility programme. Successful fellows receive approximately US$600 per month for living costs, accommodation in Johannesburg, a return economy-class international flight, programme-related training and mentorship support, and assistance with the costs of the programme’s face-to-face meetings.

The fellowship is particularly suitable for PhD students whose research examines how innovation, technology, social change, learning, industrialisation, agriculture, energy, health, gender, sustainability or related processes contribute to development in Africa.

Applicants should remember that this is not intended to fund an entire PhD. Candidates must already have basic funding for their doctoral studies, while the AfricaLics VFP provides complementary research training, mobility, mentorship and study-visit support.

Interested researchers should begin preparing their documents early, particularly the supervisor and university administration letters, academic certificates, PhD project outline and writing sample.

The application deadline is 2 October 2026 at 23:00 East Africa Time. Applications must be submitted through the official AfricaLics online application form.

TITLE: EJN Story Grants to Report on Asia’s Endangered Apes 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: July 19, 2026

Applications are open for the EJN Story Grants to Report on Asia’s Endangered Apes 2026. As part of EJN’s Empowering Media for the Conservation of Apes in Africa and Asia, they will award up to 10 story grants to journalists in Asian range countries seeking to report on the threats faced by apes (in the wild and in captivity), and the conservation solutions that must be scaled to safeguard animal, human and environmental health in the years to come. This project is supported by the Arcus Foundation.

They welcome story ideas that focus on the following themes, including, but not limited to:

The threats to both wild and captive apes, with particular focus on industrial and agricultural development, fragmented forest, illegal trade and poaching;

Participatory and science-based conservation efforts and other tried-and-tested solutions to safeguard ape health and welfare;

National and international laws, policies and treaties related to ape conservation—and the challenges in implementing them;

The role of protected areas, national parks and other reserves in mitigating risks to ape health wellbeing and preserving ecosystems;

Zoonotic spillover and One Health at the human-ape interface, i.e. stories that connect the dots between human health, animal health and environmental health.

Grants

They expect to award up to 10 grants with budgets of up to US$1,500 each.

Eligibility

Applicants must be from one of the following nine gibbon- and/or orangutan-range countries in Asia: Cambodia, China, India, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, Thailand and Vietnam.

Preference will be given to those who completed the workshop.

For the purposes of this opportunity, they will only be accepting applications in English. Unfortunately, they do not have the capacity to consider applications in other languages at this time.

Groups of journalists are encouraged to apply. However, the application must be made in the name of one lead applicant. Lead applicants are responsible for communicating with EJN and receiving funds on the group’s behalf, if awarded.

Applications are open to journalists working in any medium (online, print, television, radio) and other media practitioners with experience covering conservation issues.

They welcome applications from early-career journalists and experienced reporters with a track record of covering conservation issues. TITLE: Sign-up for the course on Commercial Real Estate Investments today

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Course Name: Commercial Real Estate Investments

Duration: 14 weeks

Target group: Real Estate Investors And Aspiring Real Estate Investors, Real Estate Valuers And Analysts, Real Estate Practitioners And Advisors, Real Estate Agents And Brokers etc.

OVERVIEW OF THE COURSE

For many seasoned investors, commercial real estate is regarded as the foundation asset and is no longer deemed as an alternative asset class. Although less liquid than many traditional assets, the real estate asset class is capable of providing great long-term value and stability to an investor’s portfolio. Yet, for many retail investors, real estate investing can be both legalistic and daunting and may sometimes need a large financial commitment for a relatively longer period than the typical traditional asset. This course provides you with the concepts that you need to facilitate your understanding of the complex world of real estate investing and the tools to enable you to analyse real estate investment opportunities to make sound investment choices.

The basic principles of real estate assets and the market for space are introduced at the beginning. This is followed by fundamental principles of investments such as risk and return assessment and cash flows. Subsequently, the course delves deeper into concepts specific to commercial real estate investing such as real estate investment analysis and valuation. Finally, opportunities available in the real estate capital markets are covered at length. The course makes generous use of case studies to strengthen the transition from conceptual knowledge to real-life applications.

The course is facilitated by one of the few valuation experts on the African continent with a long experience as a Finance educator, one of whose renowned strengths is conveying in a simple and easy-to-follow way, subjects that ordinarily appear esoteric to many Prof. Kodongo is currently on the faculty at The University of the Witwatersrand, Johannesburg, and has held visiting positions in many institutions of higher learning including the African Economic Research Consortium. He is a co-founder of the African Development and Financial Economics Institute.

By the end of this course, you should be able to:

Identify and describe investment opportunities available in the real estate sector.

Estimate the investment value of a commercial real property.

Prepare accurate and reliable commercial real estate valuation reports and advice on real estate investment decisions.

Develop real estate investment models in Excel.

Assess the benefits and challenges of real estate capital markets in the global and the African contexts.

Evaluate and advise on opportunities available in real estate capital markets.

NB: At the end of the course, participants who would like a certificate will be required to write a three-hour examination.

TITLE: Call for Papers – 3rd International Conference for Women in Leadership Positions in Higher Education (WoLPHE)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Theme: Women’s Participation in Science Programmes in Africa

November 26 -29, 2019

Abuja, Nigeria

Host: African University of Science and Technology (AUST)

The Association of African Universities (AAU) is calling for papers for its Third International Conference for Women in Leadership Positions in Higher Education (WoLPHE) taking place in Abuja, Nigeria from 26th – 29th November 2019.

As the apex organization and forum for consultation, exchange of information and co-operation among institutions of Higher Education in Africa, AAU has been leading the campaign on gender inclusiveness in its various initiatives and projects. The promotion of gender equality is firmly rooted in the AAU’s Strategic Plan (2016 – 2020) where reference is made to expanding gender programmes to facilitate the attainment of objectives spelt out in the African Women’s Decade (2010 -2020) Plan of Action.

The International Conference for Women in Leadership Positions in Higher Education (WoLPHE) is one of such key platforms provided by AAU for the discussion of innovative and creative ways of empowering women, especially young women in higher education to reach their full potential and aspire to the topmost leadership positions in their chosen fields.

The maiden edition, which was held in Accra, Ghana was highly successful and brought women across national and international boundaries together to share knowledge, ideas and strategic management skills required for success in various leadership positions.

The WoLPHE second edition, held in Nairobi, Kenya attracted mostly women in academia, politics and business as well as few men who share the grand vision of women advancement in science-based careers. In attendance were various dignitaries including the Kenyan government representation through the Cabinet Secretary, Professor Margaret Kobia, the Head of Education Division at the Human Resources, Science and Technology (HRST) Department of the African Union Commission, Dr. Beatrice Njenga, and former Vice Chancellor of Kenyatta University and Director of the Centre for Innovative Leadership and Governance, Prof Olive Mugenda. The conference drew participants from higher education institutions in Kenya, Ghana, Tanzania, Burkina Faso, Uganda, South Africa, Mauritius, Sudan, Egypt among others. Key organisations such as the Forum for African Women Educationalists (FAWE) and the Organisation for Women in science in the Developing World (OWSD) were also present.

FOCUS ON WOMEN IN STEM

As reflected by the theme, the focus of this upcoming WoLPHE conference to be held in Abuja is on the theme Women’s Participation in Science Based Programmes in Africa.

Africa’s progress is challenged by a myriad of problems ranging from lack of employment for its youth, the existence of tropical diseases, weak entrepreneurial drive and low levels of university-industry linkages, among others. It is widely accepted, that Science and Technology do have a key role to play in overcoming the continent’s developmental challenges.

However, studies have revealed that though the number of women in science and engineering is growing, men continue to outnumber women, especially at the upper levels of these professions (AAUW, 2010). With only 24% of Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) occupations being filled by women, various barriers, ranging from culture, implicit bias and subtle stereotyping to willful ignorance and blatant discrimination have been identified as contributing factors (Pierce, Margo, 2013).

Africa needs to ensure that its human resource – both men and women, are fully engaged in the STEM fields in solving its developmental challenges, and thus should make significant investment into women in STEM to increase their contribution to solving the continent’s challenges. The promotion of Women in Science to contribute massively and equally to a developed Africa must therefore form an integral part of various plans and strategies aimed at achieving the African Union’s vision of ‘The Africa We Want’ by the year 2063.

CONFERENCE THEME AND SUBTHEMES

The Conference Theme is: Women’s Participation in Science Programs in Africa.

Based on the Conference theme, the AAU is calling for papers under the following subthemes:

a) Current Developments on Women Participation in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics in Africa.

b) Key Challenges Faced by Women in Science.

c) Gender Mainstreaming in STEM programmes in Africa.

c) Resource Mobilization Strategies to support STEM research

d) Policies, Strategies and Mechanisms to support Women in STEM.

Further information and the concept paper for this conference is accessible here – https://blog.aau.org/call-for-participants-3rd-international-conference-for-women-in-leadership-positions-in-higher-education-wolphe/

The Conference Registration Link is also available here : https://event-mgt.aau.org/e/3WoLPHE

SPONSORSHIP

With support from the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (Sida), authors whose papers are accepted for presentation will be provided with a roundtrip economy ticket and accommodation to make their presentation at the conference

SUBMISSION PROCESS AND TIMELINES

Paper abstracts not exceeding two pages, must reach the AAU Secretariat not later than October 25, 2019

The abstract should indicate the scope of the research, research objectives and methods of inquiry. The paper abstracts must also include research results and conclusions, as well as a discussion of how these findings differ from previous work on the same subject.

Please submit abstracts online at: https://event-mgt.aau.org/e/3WoLPHE

Presenters of successful Abstracts will be notified by November 4, 2019 and full papers will be expected to be submitted by Friday, November 22, 2019.

Additional information about the Conference will be shared with authors whose papers will be selected. Abstracts should include name(s), institutional affiliation(s), contact details of author(s) and the paper title.

Authors of papers not selected will have the option to do a poster exhibition during the conference on condition that they fund their participation.

TITLE: 2027 Tools Competition: Multi-Million-Dollar Funding Opportunity for Innovative Education Technology, AI Tools and Learning Datasets

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The 2027 Tools Competition is now open, inviting innovators, education technology developers, researchers, entrepreneurs, organisations and other solution-builders to propose tools and public infrastructure that can improve learning, teaching and access to opportunity.

The competition supports education technology innovation that uses digital technology, data, artificial intelligence and learning science to address urgent challenges facing learners and educators. Its seventh cycle comes at a time when artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly common in education, work and everyday life, creating new opportunities while also raising important questions about trust, safety, privacy, effectiveness and responsible implementation.

Rather than rewarding technology simply because it is new, the 2027 Tools Competition seeks proposals that demonstrate how tools can produce meaningful results in real-world learning environments. Strong proposals should explain how their solutions can be responsibly used, trusted, sustained and adapted to the needs of learners, educators and institutions.

The Tools Competition is a programme of Renaissance Philanthropy and is organised by The Learning Agency.

About the 2027 Tools Competition

The Tools Competition is a multi-million-dollar funding opportunity focused on education technology innovation. It supports tools and public infrastructure that use digital technology, big data and learning science to respond to pressing needs across education and workforce development.

The 2027 competition recognises that technology access alone does not automatically improve learning outcomes. A tool must be relevant to the learning context, easy to use, inclusive, evidence-informed and designed with the realities of learners and educators in mind.

The competition therefore encourages proposals that address questions such as:

Does the tool help learners understand what they know and what they still need to learn?

Does it provide timely and useful support?

Does it strengthen teaching practice rather than create unnecessary burdens?

Does it make learning more engaging, practical and learner-driven?

Does it help individuals navigate education-to-work transitions?

Does it improve the availability of high-quality education data?

Does it protect privacy, promote safety and support responsible technology use?

Can the solution be sustained and used effectively in real learning environments?

The strongest proposals will be those that demonstrate not only what technology or artificial intelligence can do, but also how the proposed solution can be implemented responsibly and generate meaningful benefits.

Why the Competition Matters

Artificial intelligence and digital tools are rapidly changing how people learn, work and access information. Many learners are already using generative AI to complete assignments, improve efficiency, understand difficult concepts and support their learning.

However, the increasing use of AI in education also creates challenges. Learners may not always know whether information generated by AI is accurate. Educators may lack guidance on how to integrate AI into instruction. Institutions may face concerns about privacy, unequal access, bias, academic integrity and the long-term effects of technology on learning.

The 2027 Tools Competition responds to this changing environment by encouraging the development of tools that are grounded in evidence and designed around actual learning needs.

The competition places particular emphasis on solutions that:

Improve the quality and usefulness of learning experiences.

Support educators in delivering effective instruction.

Provide inclusive and actionable information about student progress.

Help learners become more independent and confident.

Connect education with real-world opportunities.

Strengthen the infrastructure needed for future education research and development.

Integrate safety, privacy and responsibility into design and implementation.

This approach moves beyond technology for its own sake. It focuses on whether a tool can make education more effective, equitable, engaging and responsive.

2027 Tools Competition Tracks

The 2027 Tools Competition features four main tracks. These tracks cover K–12 education, postsecondary learning, the transition from education to work, and the development of high-quality datasets.

Applicants should review the tracks carefully and select the one that most closely matches the purpose, users and intended impact of their tool or idea.

1. Strengthening Teaching

The Strengthening Teaching track focuses on tools that improve instructional effectiveness while also making the teaching profession more sustainable.

Teachers often face multiple demands, including lesson planning, assessment, classroom management, administrative responsibilities, reporting and adapting instruction to different learner needs. Technology can help reduce unnecessary workload and provide educators with better information for making instructional decisions.

This track seeks tools that can support teachers in meaningful and practical ways. Proposed solutions should demonstrate how they can improve teaching quality, support professional practice and contribute to a more sustainable teaching environment.

Potential areas of focus may include:

Tools that support lesson planning and instructional preparation.

Systems that help educators identify student learning needs.

Platforms that provide timely instructional feedback.

Resources that improve classroom engagement.

Tools that reduce repetitive administrative work.

Solutions that support differentiated instruction.

Technologies that help teachers access and use evidence.

Tools that strengthen collaboration and professional learning.

A strong proposal for this track should explain how the tool supports educators without replacing professional judgement or adding unnecessary complexity.

Applicants can learn more through the official Strengthening Teaching track page:

Explore the Strengthening Teaching track

2. Reimagining Assessment

The Reimagining Assessment track focuses on tools that strengthen K–12 assessment by providing more continuous, actionable and inclusive information about student learning.

Traditional assessments may provide only a limited picture of what students know at a particular point in time. The competition encourages solutions that help educators and learners understand progress more continuously and use assessment information to improve learning.

Tools under this track may support the collection, interpretation and use of learning evidence in ways that are timely and useful.

Potential areas of focus may include:

Formative assessment tools.

Systems that identify learning gaps.

Platforms that provide immediate feedback.

Inclusive assessment approaches for diverse learners.

Tools that help teachers adjust instruction.

Solutions that make assessment more meaningful and less burdensome.

Technologies that provide clearer information about student progress.

Assessment tools that support personalised learning pathways.

Successful proposals should explain how the tool can produce reliable information and how that information can be used to improve learning outcomes.

Applicants can learn more through the official Reimagining Assessment track page:

Explore the Reimagining Assessment track

3. Navigating Postsecondary Learning and Work

The Navigating Postsecondary Learning and Work track focuses on tools that help learners build the skills, relationships, information and support needed to navigate education and employment in an increasingly AI-driven world.

The transition from secondary education to higher education, vocational training or employment can be difficult. Learners may need help identifying suitable programmes, developing relevant skills, finding mentors, understanding career pathways, building professional networks and making informed decisions.

This track seeks solutions that support learners during these transition points and help them connect education with real-world opportunities.

Potential areas of focus may include:

Career exploration and guidance tools.

Platforms connecting learners with mentors or professionals.

Tools that help students identify skills gaps.

Systems supporting postsecondary planning.

Resources that connect learners to internships, apprenticeships or jobs.

Tools that help learners build professional networks.

Technologies that support career readiness.

Platforms that improve access to information about education and work opportunities.

Solutions that help learners make informed decisions in changing labour markets.

Proposals should demonstrate how the tool can help learners navigate uncertainty with greater clarity, confidence and connection.

Applicants can learn more through the official Navigating Postsecondary Learning and Work track page:

Explore the Navigating Postsecondary Learning and Work track

4. Building Better Datasets

The Building Better Datasets track focuses on high-quality education datasets that can support future research, product development and innovation.

Data is essential for understanding learning, evaluating educational tools and developing systems that respond to the needs of diverse learners. However, education datasets may be incomplete, difficult to access, poorly documented or insufficiently representative of different populations and learning environments.

This track encourages the development of datasets that capture the diversity of learners, educational contexts and learning settings.

High-quality datasets may help researchers and developers:

Study learning patterns and outcomes.

Improve education technology tools.

Develop and evaluate artificial intelligence systems.

Understand differences across learning environments.

Support evidence-based education policy.

Improve the inclusiveness and reliability of educational research.

Identify gaps in existing education data.

Develop tools that are more responsive to real-world needs.

Applicants should explain the value of the proposed dataset, the population or learning context it represents, how the data will be collected or developed, and how privacy, consent, security and responsible use will be addressed.

Applicants can learn more through the official Building Better Datasets track page:

Explore the Building Better Datasets track

What Types of Proposals Are Encouraged?

The competition is intended for proposals that address important challenges in learning, teaching and opportunity. While the specific requirements may differ by track, strong proposals are likely to demonstrate several important qualities.

Evidence-informed design

Proposals should be grounded in relevant research, learning science, user experience evidence or practical knowledge of the problem being addressed. Applicants should explain why the proposed solution is likely to work and what evidence supports its approach.

Clear understanding of the target users

Applicants should identify who will use or benefit from the tool. Depending on the track, target users may include:

K–12 students.

Teachers and school leaders.

Postsecondary students.

Adult learners.

Career seekers.

Researchers.

Education institutions.

Workforce development organisations.

Policymakers.

Developers and education technology providers.

A strong proposal should demonstrate an understanding of the needs, constraints and experiences of the intended users.

Real-world usefulness

The competition is focused on tools that can function in real learning environments. Applicants should explain how their proposed solution will be used in practice and what problem it will solve.

Proposals should avoid focusing only on technical novelty. They should demonstrate how the tool will create practical value for learners, educators, institutions or researchers.

Responsible technology use

Safety, privacy and responsibility are central to the 2027 competition. Applicants should consider how their tool will protect users and avoid potential harm.

Relevant considerations may include:

Data privacy.

Informed consent.

Data security.

Bias and fairness.

Accessibility.

Transparency.

Responsible artificial intelligence.

Protection of children and vulnerable users.

Appropriate human oversight.

Accountability in design and implementation.

Potential for sustainability and scale

Strong proposals should consider how the tool can be maintained, adopted and sustained beyond an initial pilot. Applicants may need to explain the resources, partnerships, infrastructure or implementation strategies required for long-term use.

Who Should Consider Applying?

The competition may be relevant to a broad range of individuals and organisations working on education technology, learning science, digital infrastructure and workforce development.

Potential applicants may include:

Education technology startups.

Non-profit organisations.

Researchers and research teams.

Universities and academic institutions.

Education-focused companies.

Developers and technology innovators.

Social enterprises.

Data scientists.

Learning designers.

Educators developing innovative tools.

Organisations working in K–12 education.

Organisations supporting postsecondary learners.

Workforce development organisations.

Teams developing education datasets.

Collaborations involving researchers, educators, technologists and community organisations.

Applicants should consult the official competition rules and the specific requirements for their preferred track before preparing a submission. The overview page alone does not provide a complete list of all eligibility conditions, submission requirements, funding amounts per award or selection criteria.

Geographic Eligibility

The 2027 Tools Competition overview describes its goal as supporting learning, teaching and opportunity needs in real-world settings and refers to learners worldwide. However, the provided overview does not explicitly state a complete country-by-country eligibility list or a definitive nationality restriction.

Therefore, individuals and organisations from outside the United States should review the official eligibility requirements, rules and submission information to confirm whether they can apply. Applicants from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, the Caribbean, Oceania and other regions should not assume eligibility solely based on the global focus of the competition.

The official eligibility quiz and rules should be consulted for clarification:

Check eligibility through the official eligibility quiz

Read the official competition rules

Application and Submission Information

The competition’s official website provides a Submit Here link for applicants who are ready to submit their proposals.

Applicants should review the relevant track page and official rules before submitting. They should ensure that their proposal addresses the specific problem, target users, expected impact and implementation context associated with the selected track.

A strong submission may benefit from including the following information, subject to the official application requirements:

Problem statement

Clearly explain the educational or workforce challenge the proposed tool intends to address.

Target users

Identify the learners, educators, institutions, researchers or other groups that will use or benefit from the solution.

Proposed solution

Describe how the tool, platform, dataset or infrastructure will work.

Evidence and rationale

Explain the research, learning science, user feedback or practical evidence supporting the approach.

Expected outcomes

Describe how the proposed solution could improve learning, teaching, assessment, career navigation or education research.

Implementation plan

Explain how the solution will be developed, tested, introduced or used in real-world settings.

Safety and privacy measures

Describe how the proposal will address data protection, responsible AI, accessibility, fairness and user safety.

Sustainability plan

Explain how the tool or dataset can be maintained, improved and used over time.

Applicants should rely on the official submission form and rules for the precise format, documentation and information required.

Submit a proposal through the official competition website:

Submit to the 2027 Tools Competition

Competition Information Session

The organisers have announced an information session for prospective applicants.

Interested participants can register for the information session scheduled for:

Date: September 15, 2026

The session may provide additional guidance about the competition, its tracks, eligibility, application process and expectations for proposals.

Register for the 2027 Tools Competition information session

Applicants should confirm the session time, format and registration requirements through the official registration page.

Application Deadline

The provided competition overview announces that the 2027 Tools Competition is live, but it does not state a final application deadline.

Application Deadline: Not specified in the provided competition overview.

Applicants should visit the official submission page, official rules and relevant track pages for the latest deadline information. Since competition timelines may be updated, prospective applicants should avoid relying on unofficial deadlines or outdated announcements.

Organisers and Programme Partners

The 2027 Tools Competition is supported and organised by two organisations:

Renaissance Philanthropy

Renaissance Philanthropy is identified as the programme behind the Tools Competition. The organisation supports initiatives intended to advance innovation and address important challenges through philanthropic investment and strategic programmes.

Visit Renaissance Philanthropy

The Learning Agency

The Learning Agency is responsible for organising the Tools Competition. The organisation works on initiatives related to learning, education, research, innovation and the development of tools that can improve learning outcomes.

Visit The Learning Agency

How to Prepare a Strong Proposal

Applicants can improve their readiness by taking the following steps:

1. Select the most appropriate track

Review all four tracks and identify which one best matches the purpose of the proposed tool or dataset. Avoid submitting a general idea that does not clearly align with a competition priority.

2. Define the problem precisely

Explain the problem in clear language. Identify who experiences the problem, why it matters and what limitations exist in current approaches.

3. Demonstrate user need

Use research, interviews, surveys, pilot findings, classroom experience or other evidence to show that the problem is real and significant.

4. Explain what makes the solution different

Describe how the proposed tool improves on existing approaches. The difference may involve better accessibility, stronger evidence, improved usability, greater inclusiveness, better data quality or more effective implementation.

5. Include evidence of feasibility

Explain whether the team has already developed a prototype, conducted a pilot, tested the concept or gathered feedback from potential users. If the solution is still at an early stage, clearly describe the next steps.

6. Address responsible innovation

Explain how the proposal will handle privacy, safety, fairness, accessibility, transparency and responsible use of artificial intelligence or data.

7. Plan for real-world adoption

Consider how the tool will be used by schools, educators, learners, institutions, researchers or other stakeholders. A proposal should demonstrate awareness of practical constraints such as cost, training, infrastructure and user support.

8. Review the official rules

Before submission, applicants should read the official rules, confirm eligibility and ensure that their proposal meets the required format and criteria.

Conclusion

The 2027 Tools Competition presents a major opportunity for innovators, researchers, education technology developers, organisations and data specialists working to improve learning, teaching and access to opportunity.

Through its four tracks—Strengthening Teaching, Reimagining Assessment, Navigating Postsecondary Learning and Work, and Building Better Datasets—the competition seeks solutions that address real challenges across K–12 education, postsecondary learning, career transitions and education research.

The competition’s focus extends beyond technological novelty. It encourages tools that are evidence-informed, practical, inclusive, safe, privacy-conscious and capable of producing meaningful outcomes in real learning environments.

Potential applicants should carefully review the relevant track, complete the official eligibility check, read the competition rules and confirm the final submission deadline. The information provided in the competition overview does not specify a final deadline, so applicants should consult the official website for the latest updates.

TITLE: Earth Observation Groundbreaking Science Discoveries

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
PUBLICATIONS

Earth Observation Groundbreaking Science Discoveries

A publication by the European Space Sciences Committee (ESSC) and the result of a collaborative effort led by the ESSC Earth Sciences Panel, working with the European Science Foundation (ESF), the European Space Agency (ESA) and professional graphic designers, explores how Earth observation satellites have transformed our understanding of the planet whilst addressing some of the greatest challenges of our time.

The document draws on examples from the atmosphere, polar regions, oceans, and land to explain – in straightforward terms – the groundbreaking scientific discoveries enabled by EO satellites. Central to this effort was the “translation” of complex scientific publications into accessible language, complemented by impactful visuals created through close collaboration between scientists and professional graphic designers. The twelve examples presented offer merely a glimpse of the impact that EO satellites deliver. They were crafted to showcase the range of scientific discovery, the significance of the issues addressed, the originality of the findings, and their enduring contribution to knowledge.

The process developed for this document offers a template for future promotion of space-based scientific excellence. The resulting document serves multiple audiences: not only high-level decision-makers, but also the general public and students, who can grasp complex Earth science issues through clear, straightforward storytelling. Adopting this approach more broadly is not merely a matter of public relations; it is a strategic imperative. Clear, compelling communication fosters the informed public discourse necessary to sustain investment in the long-term missions that benefit all humanity. It inspires the next generation of scientists and ensures that knowledge derived from these satellites continues to inform policy and strengthen our collective capacity to address global challenges.

Ultimately, this work illustrates that the true impact of large-scale scientific endeavours lies not only in the data they generate, but in how effectively their stories are shared; transforming knowledge into understanding and understanding into meaningful societal progress. The model presented here also demonstrates a fundamental truth: the value of big science is most powerfully revealed not in the complexity of its data, but in the clarity of its story.

TITLE: Guidelines for addressing intellectual property

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
PUBLICATIONS

Image: Designed by pikisuperstar / Freepik

ESF Guidelines for addressing intellectual property

Recurring intellectual property rights (IPR) issues observed across multiple EU-funded projects have highlighted the need for clear, practical guidance. Horizon Europe places strong emphasis on Open Science and responsible exploitation of results, requiring beneficiaries

to balance transparency with protection of intellectual assets. This dual obligation often creates challenges in collaborative environments, where partners must reconcile diverse institutional policies and approaches, national and EU regulations, and varying processes regarding ownership, access rights, and dissemination.
These guidelines respond to those challenges by providing a structured reference for project

partners and all stakeholders involved in research management. They build on the provisions of

the Horizon Europe Programme, the Annotated Grant Agreement, and European Commission factsheets on IPR, complemented by insights

from practice. The aim is not to offer exhaustive legal advice, but to present actionable best practices for managing IP throughout the research lifecycle, covering issues such as background identification, joint ownership, access rights, licensing, and open access obligations.
By fostering a common understanding of key concepts and obligations, these guidelines help prevent misunderstandings, reduce risks, and ensure compliance with Horizon Europe principles of fairness, transparency, and impact maximization. Ultimately, they support the creation of an environment where innovation can thrive, results can be disseminated responsibly, and legitimate interests of all partners are safeguarded.

TITLE: An evaluation of eight global ocean reanalyses for the Northeast U.S. continental shelf

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Carolina Castillo-Trujillo, A., Kwon, Y.-O., Fratantoni, P., Chen, K., Seo, H., Alexander, M. A., & Saba, V. S., 2023. An evaluation of eight global ocean reanalyses for the Northeast U.S. continental shelf. Progress in Oceanography, 103126. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pocean.2023.103126

The Northeast U.S. continental Shelf (NES) extending from the Gulf of Maine to Cape Hatteras, is a dynamic region supporting some of the most commercially valuable fisheries in the world. This study aims to provide a systematic assessment of eight widely used, intermediate-to-high spatial resolution global ocean reanalysis products (CFSR, ECCO, ORAS, SODA, BRAN, GLORYS, GOFS3.0, and GOFS3.1) against available in situ and satellite ocean observations. In situ observations include water level from tide gauges, and temperature and salinity from various sources including shipboard hydrographic data, and moorings on the NES. The figure shows the difference between reanalysis and observed Bottom Temperature (BT). Observations are provided by the NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) Northwest Atlantic Regional climatology. Reanalysis are mostly biased towards warmer temperatures with GLORYS reproducing best the observations. (Image provided by Alma Carolina Castillo-Trujillo)

This prestigious fellowship, offered by the UK Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), provides an exceptional opportunity for external researchers from academia and industry to work at the intersection of science, evidence, and policymaking.

Now in its fourth year, the Defra R&D Fellowship Programme has become one of the UK’s leading policy-focused fellowship opportunities, giving researchers the chance to spend up to 12 months working directly within government while helping shape policies on environmental protection, climate change, agriculture, biodiversity, food security, and many other national priorities.
